t.pilgrimage routes kumano sankeimichi k@3:
Mount Kōya is one of Japan's great sacred places, a high basin in the mountains of northern Wakayama where the monk Kūkai founded a monastic centre for Shingon Buddhism in the early ninth century. Today it is a town of over a hundred temples, many of which take in overnight guests, set among towering cedars. South of the summit plateau, deep in the forested ridges, run the old pilgrim trails that link Kōya with the Kumano shrines, part of the network inscribed by UNESCO as the Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range.

The Kohechi, the route that crosses from Kōya south to Kumano Hongū, is the toughest of the Kumano paths, going over several passes above a thousand metres. The trails themselves are for walking, of course, but the roads around them are some of the most rewarding motorcycle country in central Japan. The Kōya Ryūjin Skyline, a scenic mountain road running south from Kōya along the ridges toward the hot spring village of Ryūjin, is famous among Japanese riders for its views and endless curves. It closes or becomes hazardous in winter when snow and ice arrive, and fog can roll in fast.

Remember that Japan drives on the left and that speed limits are low and enforced. Roads are generally beautifully surfaced but narrow in the mountains, with blind corners, and you will meet tour buses on the main routes to Kōya, especially at weekends and in autumn when the maples turn. The forest is dense cedar and cypress, with mossy stone lanterns and statues along the old paths, and the air is cool and damp even in summer.

Kōya town, around fifteen kilometres away, has fuel stations, convenience stores and plenty of places to eat. Staying overnight in a temple lodging, a shukubō, is the classic experience, with vegetarian monastic cuisine called shōjin ryōri and the option of joining early morning prayers. Do not miss Okunoin, the vast cemetery where Kūkai is believed to remain in eternal meditation; walking it at dusk with lanterns lit is unforgettable. Hashimoto, further north, is the nearest larger town on the lowland side.
t.nara palace site@34.7,135.8:
For most of the eighth century, Nara was the capital of Japan. The city, then called Heijō-kyō, was laid out on a grid modelled on the Chinese capital Chang'an, and at its northern end stood the imperial palace, Heijō-kyū, a vast compound of halls, offices and gardens. When the court moved away at the end of the century, the palace was abandoned and the land eventually returned to rice fields. Today the Nara Palace Site is a huge open space on the western side of the modern city, part of the UNESCO-listed Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara.

What you see now is a mixture of open ground, excavated foundations and full-size reconstructions. The great Suzakumon gate at the southern entrance and the Former Imperial Audience Hall, the Daigokuden, have been rebuilt using traditional techniques, their vermilion pillars and sweeping tiled roofs giving a sense of the scale of the original. Excavated areas and museums on the site display the wooden tablets, roof tiles and everyday objects found in the ground. The sheer emptiness of the space is part of its effect: it is easy to stand in the middle and imagine the vanished city around you.

Nara as a whole is compact, and the famous sights cluster in the park to the east: Tōdai-ji with its giant bronze Buddha, Kōfuku-ji and its pagoda, Kasuga Taisha with its thousands of lanterns, and the deer that wander everywhere and bow for crackers. Riding in the city is slow and busy, with narrow streets and heavy tourist traffic, so the bike is best parked while you explore on foot. Japan drives on the left; motorcycle parking in cities is regulated, so look for designated bike spaces rather than leaving it on the pavement.

For riding out of Nara, the Nara Okuyama Driveway climbs into the hills behind the city, and further afield, the roads south into the mountains of Yoshino and the Kii peninsula are excellent. Fuel, food and everything else is plentiful in Nara. Try kakinoha-zushi, sushi wrapped in persimmon leaves, a local speciality. Spring cherry blossom and autumn colour bring the biggest crowds and the best light.
t.yoshino and omine ominesan ji@34.3,135.9:
Ōminesan-ji is a temple on the summit of Mount Sanjō, one of the peaks of the Ōmine range in the heart of the Kii peninsula, and it holds a special place in Japanese religion. It is a centre of Shugendō, the mountain ascetic tradition that blends Buddhism, Shinto and older mountain worship, and its practitioners, the yamabushi, undergo arduous training on the ridges. The temple is famous for another reason too: the mountain is still closed to women by tradition, one of the last such places in Japan, which has become a subject of ongoing debate.

The summit is reached on foot, typically from the hot spring village of Dorogawa, a climb of a few hours through forest, with sections involving chains and rock. The temple is open only during the summer season, roughly from May to September. Along the route, practitioners undertake ordeals such as being dangled over a cliff edge. For a rider, the mountain is a backdrop and a story rather than a destination, unless you are prepared to hike.

Dorogawa itself is a charming little onsen village with wooden inns and a single main street lined with lanterns, and it makes a good base. The roads into this area are classic Kii peninsula riding: narrow, twisting mountain routes through steep forested valleys, with the occasional tunnel and bridge. Route 309, which passes nearby, is a scenic mountain road with many bends. Expect landslide repairs, single-lane stretches and gravel on the surface, and be very careful in wet weather. Japan drives on the left.

Yoshino, about seventeen kilometres away, is famous for its cherry trees, which cover the slopes in tens of thousands and draw enormous crowds in early April. Fuel stations are scarce in the mountains, so fill up in Yoshino, Gojō or another town before heading in. Convenience stores are a lifesaver here for food and coffee. The local water from the springs of Dorogawa is renowned for its quality. In autumn, the maples on the mountainsides turn deep red, and the air is crisp and clear.
t.buddhist monuments in the horyu ji area@:
If you want to stand in front of the oldest wooden buildings in the world, this is the place. Hōryū-ji, a Buddhist temple in the town of Ikaruga south-west of Nara, was founded by Prince Shōtoku in the early seventh century, and although it burned and was rebuilt not long after, its central buildings, including the main hall and the five-storey pagoda, date from around the end of the seventh century. They were among the first sites in Japan inscribed by UNESCO, in 1993.

The temple complex is large, with the western precinct holding the main hall and pagoda, and the eastern precinct centred on the octagonal Hall of Dreams. The Great Treasure House displays Buddhist statues and objects of extraordinary age and delicacy, including the Kudara Kannon, a tall slender figure of the bodhisattva. Nearby temples, such as Hōrin-ji and Hokki-ji, also have ancient pagodas, and together they make up the World Heritage site. Plan on at least two hours.

Prince Shōtoku is one of the great figures of Japanese history, credited with promoting Buddhism and with drafting a seventeen-article constitution. He was so revered that his portrait appeared on banknotes for decades.

Ikaruga is a quiet town, and the area around the temples is pleasant, with rice fields and small roads. For riders, the temples are best treated as a cultural stop: the surrounding roads are urban and suburban, with traffic lights and congestion. For better riding, head west into the hills of the Ikoma range on the Shigisan Nobosan road, or south toward the mountains of Yoshino and beyond. The Shinto shrine on Mount Shigi, to the west, is associated with the tiger and has fine views over the Nara basin.

Ikaruga has fuel, convenience stores and restaurants, and Nara is only a short ride away. Local food in the Nara area includes the persimmon-leaf sushi and a rich rice porridge made with tea, called chagayu. Spring and autumn bring the best weather and the biggest crowds; summer is hot and humid; winter is cool but clear, and quieter at the temples.
t.yoshino and omine kimpu jinja@34.3,135.9:
Mount Yoshino, in the mountains of Nara Prefecture, is famous throughout Japan for one thing above all: cherry blossom. Some thirty thousand trees cover its slopes, planted over the centuries as offerings, and each spring they bloom in waves from the lower slopes to the summit. Kimpu Shrine, Kimpu-jinja, stands near the top of the mountain, in the area known as Oku Senbon, the inner thousand trees, and it is part of the UNESCO-listed Sacred Sites of the Kii Mountain Range.

The shrine is dedicated to the god of the mountain and is said to protect the gold of the mountain, which is what its name means. It is a simple, quiet place compared with the busier temples further down, surrounded by tall cedars. Nearby is a small hut where the warrior Minamoto no Yoshitsune, one of Japan's most romantic historical heroes, is said to have hidden while fleeing his brother's forces in the twelfth century. Yoshino has many such stories: it was also the seat of the Southern Court during a period of rival emperors in the fourteenth century.

The main street of Yoshino runs along the ridge, lined with temples, inns and shops selling kuzu, a starch made from the arrowroot plant that grows in the mountains and is used to make sweets and noodles. Kinpusen-ji, with its huge wooden hall, is the head temple of Shugendō, the mountain ascetic tradition.

The roads up Yoshino are narrow and steep, and during cherry blossom season traffic is restricted and parking is extremely limited. Outside that season, the mountain is quiet and the roads into the surrounding mountains are wonderful: narrow, winding routes through forested valleys toward Dorogawa, Kawakami and the deep south of the Kii peninsula. Japan drives on the left, and mountain roads often have single-lane sections and blind corners.

Yoshino town, about six kilometres away, has fuel and convenience stores. Inns on the mountain serve local cuisine, including persimmon-leaf sushi and dishes with mountain vegetables. Autumn, when the maples turn red and gold, is a beautiful and much less crowded alternative to spring.
t.byodo in@34.9,135.8:
Take a ten-yen coin out of your pocket in Japan and you are holding a picture of this place. The Phoenix Hall of the Byōdō-in in Uji, with its wings stretching out on either side of a central hall and bronze phoenixes on the roof, is one of the most famous buildings in the country. It was built in 1053 by Fujiwara no Yorimichi, a member of the most powerful aristocratic family of the Heian period, who converted his father's villa into a Buddhist temple. Its reflection in the pond in front was meant to evoke the Pure Land paradise of the Amida Buddha.

The Phoenix Hall survived centuries of wars and fires that destroyed much of Kyoto, which makes it one of the very few original buildings from the Heian period. Inside sits a gilded statue of Amida, surrounded by small wooden figures of celestial beings playing instruments and dancing, which are displayed in the modern museum on the site. The temple is part of the UNESCO-listed Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.

Uji is a small city on the river of the same name, between Kyoto and Nara, and it is famous throughout Japan for its green tea. The streets leading to the temple are lined with tea shops selling matcha, sencha and every imaginable tea-flavoured sweet, from ice cream to noodles. Uji is also the setting for the final chapters of The Tale of Genji, the great Heian-era novel, and there is a museum dedicated to it.

For riders, Uji is a city stop: traffic is heavy and parking is limited, so leave the bike in a designated space and walk. But the area around Uji has good riding: the roads that follow the Uji river upstream toward Lake Biwa through a forested gorge, and the hills to the east toward Shiga, offer bends and views. Japan drives on the left, and city traffic requires patience.

Uji has fuel, convenience stores and plenty of places to eat. Try matcha soba, green tea noodles, or a traditional tea ceremony at one of the tea houses. Spring, with wisteria blooming at the temple in late April, and autumn are the most beautiful times to visit.
t.chapel of the former hacienda of buenavi:
North of the city of Querétaro, the land rises into dry hills dotted with cactus, mesquite and the remains of old haciendas. These estates were the economic engines of colonial Mexico, producing grain, livestock and pulque for the cities and mines of the north. The chapel of the former Hacienda of Buenavista stands in this landscape near the village of the same name, close to Santa Rosa Jáuregui, and it is part of the UNESCO-listed Camino Real de Tierra Adentro.

The Camino Real, the royal road of the interior, ran for more than two and a half thousand kilometres from Mexico City to what is now New Mexico, carrying silver south and settlers, missionaries and goods north for nearly three centuries. Haciendas and their chapels were waypoints on this route, and many have survived in various states of repair. The chapel at Buenavista is a modest building with a simple façade, typical of rural churches of the colonial era, where the hacienda's workers and families would have attended mass.

Querétaro itself is one of Mexico's most attractive colonial cities, its centre a World Heritage site in its own right, with a famous aqueduct and baroque churches. It played a central role in Mexican history: the conspiracy that led to the independence movement in 1810 was plotted here, the treaty ending the war with the United States was signed here in 1848, and the Emperor Maximilian was executed on the Cerro de las Campanas in 1867.

The riding north of Querétaro is a mix of highways and quieter rural roads. The route toward San Miguel de Allende and Dolores Hidalgo, the cradle of Mexican independence, passes through rolling hills and farmland. Traffic around Querétaro can be heavy, and Mexican roads have their own hazards: topes, the speed bumps found at the entrance to every village, potholes and livestock. Toll roads are generally better maintained and safer.

Santa Rosa Jáuregui, about nine kilometres away, has fuel and food, and Querétaro has everything. Local cuisine includes enchiladas queretanas and gorditas. The dry season, from November to May, is the best time to ride; the summer rains bring afternoon storms.
t.motoyakushiji temple site@34.5,135.8:
In the late seventh century, before Nara became the capital, the Japanese court was based in the Asuka region, south of the Nara basin, and the Emperor Tenmu ordered the construction of a great temple, Yakushi-ji, dedicated to the Buddha of healing, to pray for the recovery of his sick empress. The temple was built in the new capital of Fujiwara-kyō, and when the court moved to Nara in 710, a new Yakushi-ji was built there. The original temple, known as Motoyakushiji, the original Yakushi-ji, was gradually abandoned.

Today, the Motoyakushiji site is a quiet place in the fields of Kashihara, with the foundation stones of the main hall and the two pagodas still in place, surrounded by rice paddies. It is part of the area associated with the ancient capital and has been proposed for World Heritage status as part of the Asuka-Fujiwara sites. In late summer, the fields around the site are planted with water hyacinths, which bloom in a sea of pale purple, and the site becomes a popular spot for photographers.

The Asuka region is full of such places: ancient tombs, the kofun, stone monuments of mysterious purpose, and the remains of palaces and temples. Asuka village has kept its rural character, with rice fields and small roads, and it is a pleasant place to explore. The Ishibutai Kofun, a huge stone burial chamber, is the most famous of the tombs, and the Takamatsuzuka and Kitora tombs have famous wall paintings.

The riding in this area is gentle, through rice fields, villages and low hills. The roads are narrow and often busy with local traffic, and the towns of Kashihara and Sakurai are suburban. For more interesting riding, head south into the mountains of Yoshino and the Kii peninsula, or east toward the hills of Uda. Japan drives on the left, and roads in rural areas are narrow with many blind corners.

Kashihara, about two kilometres away, has fuel and all services. Local food includes miwa sōmen, thin wheat noodles from nearby Sakurai, and kakinoha-zushi. Late summer, for the water hyacinths, and autumn are the best times to visit.
t.blashausgraben wachtturm@48.3,15.4:
The Wachau is the most beautiful stretch of the Danube in Austria, a narrow valley between Melk and Krems where the river winds between steep hills covered in vineyards and forest, with castles, abbeys and villages on its banks. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site in its own right. Near the village of Aggsbach, on the southern bank, a small Roman watchtower stood in the Blashausgraben, a side valley, as part of the Danube frontier of the Roman Empire.

The Danube was the northern frontier of the Roman province of Noricum, and the Romans built forts and watchtowers along its banks to control traffic and watch for raids. The Danube Limes in Austria was added to the UNESCO list in 2021 as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire. The remains of the watchtower in the Blashausgraben are modest, but there are better-preserved Roman remains elsewhere in the Wachau, such as the fortified tower in Bacharnsdorf and the fort in Mautern.

Above Aggsbach, on a rock high above the river, stand the ruins of the castle of Aggstein, once the lair of robber barons who preyed on Danube shipping. Upstream, the Baroque abbey of Melk, a vast yellow building on a rock above the river, is one of the most famous monasteries in Europe, with a magnificent library and church. Downstream, Dürnstein, with its blue church tower and ruined castle, where Richard the Lionheart was held prisoner on his way home from the Crusades, is the most visited village in the valley.

The riding along the Wachau is very pleasant, though it can be busy. The roads on both banks follow the river, with gentle bends and wonderful views of vineyards, castles and the water. The southern bank is quieter. The roads climbing out of the valley into the Dunkelsteiner Wald and the Waldviertel offer more challenging riding, with tight bends and forest. In spring and autumn, traffic is lighter.

Aggsbach has a few inns, and Melk, about seven kilometres away, has fuel. The Wachau is known for its apricots and its white wines, Grüner Veltliner and Riesling. Spring, when the apricot trees blossom, and autumn are the best times to visit.
t.ybbs kleinkastell@48.2,15.1:
Ybbs an der Donau and Persenbeug face each other across the Danube in Lower Austria, connected by a hydroelectric dam that was one of the first built on the Austrian Danube after the war. Persenbeug is dominated by its castle, perched on a rock above the river, which belonged to the Habsburgs and was the birthplace of Emperor Charles I, the last emperor of Austria-Hungary. On the Ybbs side, the remains of a small Roman fort have been found, part of the Danube frontier of the Roman Empire.

The Romans fortified the Danube with a chain of forts and watchtowers, and the small fort at Ybbs guarded the river and the mouth of the Ybbs valley. The Danube Limes in Austria is part of the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire site. Little remains above ground at Ybbs, but the location is significant, and the river views help to explain why the Romans chose it. Ybbs itself is a small town with a pleasant old centre, with houses from the Renaissance and Baroque periods and a long riverside promenade.

The area between Ybbs and Melk is known as the Nibelungengau, after the Nibelungenlied, the medieval epic poem, part of which is set along this stretch of the Danube. Pöchlarn, downstream, is identified with Bechelaren, the home of a character in the poem. On the hills above the river, the pilgrimage church of Maria Taferl offers wide views over the valley and on clear days to the Alps.

The riding along this stretch of the Danube is gentle and scenic, with the road following the river on both banks. The roads that climb from the river into the hills, toward Maria Taferl or into the Strudengau, offer good bends and views. South of the river, the roads into the Mostviertel, a region of orchards and pear cider, are pleasant and quiet, with rolling hills. Traffic is moderate, and surfaces are good.

Ybbs has fuel and food, and Amstetten, about seventeen kilometres away, is the nearest larger town. The Mostviertel is famous for its Most, a cider made from pears and apples. Spring, when the pear trees blossom, and autumn are the best times to ride here.
t.kalwaria zebrzydowska the mannerist arch:
In 1600, Mikołaj Zebrzydowski, a Polish nobleman, began to build a chapel on a hill south-west of Kraków, modelled on the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. Over the following decades, he and his descendants added dozens of chapels and churches spread over the hills, laid out to recreate the Passion of Christ and the life of the Virgin, with the landscape itself standing in for Jerusalem. The result, Kalwaria Zebrzydowska, is one of the most important pilgrimage sites in Poland and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1999.

The Bernardine monastery at the heart of the complex is a Baroque building with a basilica, and around it, over several kilometres of paths through woods and fields, stand some forty chapels in a variety of architectural styles, from Mannerist to Baroque. During Holy Week, the site hosts one of Europe's oldest Passion plays, with thousands of pilgrims following the actors from chapel to chapel. The pilgrimages in August, for the Assumption, also draw huge crowds.

Karol Wojtyła, who became Pope John Paul II, grew up in Wadowice, about fourteen kilometres away, and visited Kalwaria often as a boy. Wadowice has a museum in his family home, and the town is famous for the kremówka, a cream cake that the Pope fondly recalled from his youth.

The riding in this part of Lesser Poland is pleasant. The hills of the Beskid Mały and Beskid Makowski rise to the south, with roads that wind through forests and villages, and further south, the Tatra mountains and Zakopane are within reach for a longer ride. The roads around Kalwaria are generally good, but traffic can be heavy on the main routes to Kraków, and village roads may be rough. Polish drivers can be impatient, so ride defensively.

Kalwaria Zebrzydowska has fuel and food, and Kraków, about thirty kilometres away, has everything. Local food includes pierogi, dumplings, żurek, a sour rye soup, and oscypek, a smoked cheese from the mountains. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons.
t.fujiwara palace site@34.5,135.8:
Before Nara, before Kyoto, there was Fujiwara-kyō. In 694, the Empress Jitō moved the Japanese court to a new capital in the southern part of the Nara basin, the first in Japan to be laid out on a Chinese-style grid of streets, with the imperial palace at its centre. It lasted only sixteen years, until the court moved north to Nara in 710, but it marked a turning point in the history of the Japanese state.

The palace site, Fujiwara-kyū, lies in the fields of Kashihara, surrounded by three low hills, the Yamato Sanzan, which feature in ancient Japanese poetry. Today, the site is a wide open space, with the foundations of the great audience hall and other buildings marked by red posts and mounds. The site has been put forward for UNESCO listing as part of the Asuka-Fujiwara sites, together with Asuka's tombs and palaces. In different seasons, the fields around the site are planted with flowers: rapeseed in spring, lotus in summer, and cosmos in autumn, which turn the site into a sea of pink and white.

The Yamato Sanzan, the three mountains of Yamato, Unebi, Miminashi and Kagu, are small but culturally important, and Mount Kagu in particular is sacred in Japanese tradition. At the foot of Mount Unebi stands the Kashihara Shrine, dedicated to the legendary first emperor, Jimmu. The Nara Prefectural Kashihara Archaeological Institute museum displays finds from the area.

The riding around Kashihara is suburban and rural, through rice fields, villages and small towns. The roads are narrow and often busy, with lots of traffic lights. For more interesting riding, head south into the mountains of Yoshino and the Kii peninsula, or east toward the plateau of Uda and the Murō area, with its temple in the forest. Japan drives on the left.

Kashihara, about two kilometres away, has fuel and all services. Local food includes the Miwa sōmen noodles and the persimmons of the Nara area, which ripen in autumn. Autumn, with the cosmos in bloom, is the best time to visit.
t.cacai mutije@22.7,-102.8:
Out here on the high plateau west of Zacatecas the land is all wide sky, nopal, mesquite and red-brown earth, and it takes a while to understand that you are standing on a pilgrimage path. Cacai Mutijé is one of the sacred places of the Wixárika, the people outsiders long called Huichol, on the route their pilgrims follow from their home communities in the Sierra Madre Occidental across Zacatecas to Wirikuta, the desert of San Luis Potosí where they gather hikuri, the peyote cactus, and where in their cosmology the sun was born. The path has been walked for centuries and was recognised by UNESCO only recently, which tells you something about how long the rest of the world took to notice.

That matters for how you behave here. These are not ruins or monuments in the European sense; a spring, a rock, a hill or a pool can be the sacred thing, and offerings of candles, arrows, beadwork and small yarn pieces are left by people for whom this is living religion. Look, do not touch, never pocket anything, and keep the bike well away from anything that looks like an offering. A photograph of the landscape is fine; a photograph of people at prayer without asking is not.

The riding around here is a high-altitude affair. Zacatecas city sits well above two thousand metres and the plateau around it is not much lower, so engines breathe a little harder and the sun bites through a jacket at midday. Roads out toward Malpaso and Cieneguillas are mostly straight, two-lane and quiet, with long views across farmland and dry hills, the odd tope speed bump at village entrances, and livestock that does not care about your schedule. Wind can push hard across the open ground in the afternoon, and the summer rainy season brings sudden thunderstorms that turn dirt tracks to grease in minutes. Mornings in the dry months, roughly October to May, are the sweet spot: cool air, low sun, sharp light on the hills.

Malpaso is a small town with basic shops, but for dependable fuel, a proper meal and somewhere to sleep you want Zacatecas, about twenty kilometres away. It is a pink-stone colonial mining city with a cathedral of wildly carved cantera, a cable car over the old town and a deep tradition of silver, and after a day on the plateau it is a good place to eat a plate of birria or asado de boda and let the bike tick as it cools. Carry water when you head out again; shade is rare and shops are far apart.
t.tachibana dera temple site@34.5,135.8:
Asuka is where Japan as a state began to take shape, and Tachibana-dera sits right in the middle of it, among rice paddies and low hills in a small valley south of Nara. Tradition holds that Prince Shōtoku, the regent who promoted Buddhism and wrote Japan's first constitution in the early seventh century, was born here, and the temple claims to have been founded by him. The present buildings are much later, but the site is ancient, and the atmosphere of the quiet temple grounds, with their wooden halls, gravel courtyards and a curious stone carved with two faces, one good and one evil, is very special.

The Asuka area is dotted with remains of the period when the imperial court resided here, roughly the sixth and seventh centuries: burial mounds, palace sites and enigmatic stone monuments. The Ishibutai kofun, a huge tomb of massive stones whose earth mound has eroded away, is a short distance away, as are the Kameishi turtle stone and the Asuka-dera temple, home to what is often called the oldest Buddha statue in Japan. Many people rent bicycles to tour the area, and the paths between rice fields and villages are gentle and scenic.

On a motorcycle, Asuka is easy to explore, but take it slowly. The local roads are narrow, often without sidewalks, and shared with cyclists, walkers and farm vehicles, so a calm pace is essential. The surrounding hills offer some winding roads, especially toward Yoshino to the south, famous for its cherry blossoms, and the mountain roads of the Kii peninsula, which are a riders' paradise of endless curves through cedar forests. Spring and autumn are the most beautiful seasons, with cherry blossoms in early April and red maples in November, but they are also the most crowded.

Kashihara, about five kilometres away, is a larger city with fuel, convenience stores and restaurants. Asuka itself has small cafés and shops selling local specialities, such as kudzu sweets and Asuka strawberries. Sakurai, a few kilometres east, is home to the Ōmiwa shrine, one of the oldest Shinto shrines in Japan, where the mountain itself is considered the deity. Japanese traffic rules are strictly enforced, and riding on the left takes some getting used to for those from continental Europe.
t.cupuri mutiu@22.6,-103.0:
Jerez de García Salinas is the reason most riders end up here, and it is a happy accident if they do. This colonial town in the west of Zacatecas state, a couple of kilometres from the point, is a Pueblo Mágico with a leafy plaza, an ornate little theatre, the Teatro Hinojosa, said to be modelled on Ford's Theatre in Washington, and the childhood home of Ramón López Velarde, the poet whose verses about provincial Mexico every schoolchild there knows. Jerez is a ranchero town at heart, with saddle makers, boot shops and men in hats, and the Easter fair with its horses and music draws people from across the region.

Cupuri Mutiu is a sacred place on the Wixárika route, the pilgrimage path that runs from the Wixárika homeland in the mountains of Jalisco and Nayarit across Zacatecas to the desert of Wirikuta in San Luis Potosí. For the pilgrims, the journey retraces the steps of their ancestors, and each spring, waterhole or hill along the way has a name and a meaning. It is not a tourist attraction; there may be nothing visible to an outsider, and if you do encounter offerings or pilgrims, give them space and respect.

The country around Jerez is ranching land at roughly two thousand metres, with dry hills, oak and mesquite, and green valleys where water allows. The road from Zacatecas to Jerez is a good two-lane highway with gentle curves; heading west or south from Jerez, toward Susticacán or Tlaltenango, the roads get narrower and climb into the Sierra de Morones and the canyons beyond, with views and corners that reward the effort. Watch for topes at every village and livestock on the open range. The rainy season, from June to September, brings green hills but also afternoon storms; the dry months are clear and cool in the mornings.

Jerez has fuel, banks, hotels and plenty of places to eat. Try birria, slow-cooked goat or beef in a rich chili broth, or the local sweets sold around the plaza. If you are riding on toward the sacred sites of the route, fill up in Jerez and carry water, as services become scarce in the hills. Zacatecas city is about an hour east, and the two towns make a natural pair.
Santiago de Querétaro's skyline is defined by its aqueduct, seventy-four tall stone arches striding across a valley into the city, built in the early eighteenth century at the expense of the Marqués de la Villa del Villar del Águila to bring fresh water from the hills. Legend says he did it for love of a nun; the more prosaic version says he wanted to improve public health. Either way, it is one of the great engineering works of colonial Mexico, and the view of the arches at dusk, lit up against the sky, is unforgettable.

The historic centre is a UNESCO site, and it is a joy to explore on foot: plazas shaded by Indian laurel trees, churches and convents of pink and ochre stone, elegant mansions with courtyards and balconies. The layout is unusual, combining the regular grid of the Spanish town with the winding streets of the indigenous Otomí quarter. Querétaro played a central role in Mexican history: the conspiracy that led to independence in 1810 was hatched here, Emperor Maximilian was executed on the Cerro de las Campanas in 1867, and the current Mexican constitution was drafted in the city's theatre in 1917.

Querétaro is one of the fastest-growing cities in Mexico, a centre of industry, especially aerospace and automotive, and traffic on its ring roads and highways can be intense. Riding into the centre is manageable, but parking is limited, so find a secure garage and explore on foot. The surroundings offer great riding: the Sierra Gorda to the northeast, a biosphere reserve with spectacular mountain roads and Franciscan missions, the wine and cheese region around Tequisquiapan and Bernal, with its giant monolith, and the colonial towns of San Miguel de Allende and Guanajuato to the northwest.

The city has every service you need, from fuel to motorcycle shops. The food scene is excellent, with traditional dishes like enchiladas queretanas, gorditas and nopal salads, as well as modern restaurants and wine bars serving local wines. The climate is temperate and dry most of the year, with a rainy season in summer; mornings can be cool and afternoons warm. Plan for at least a full day to enjoy the city before heading out on the road.
t.koyasan jison in@34.3,135.5:
Before you ride up to Mount Koya, the great mountain monastery of Shingon Buddhism, stop at its doorstep. Jison-in sits in the Kii river valley at Kudoyama, below the mountain, and it was founded by Kukai, the monk also known as Kobo Daishi, in the early ninth century as the administrative office and supply base for the new monastery above. Its most loved story concerns his mother. Women were barred from Koyasan for over a thousand years, so she lived here, and tradition says Kukai walked down nine times a month to visit her. That, the locals will tell you, is where the name Kudoyama, nine-times mountain, comes from.

Jison-in became known as the Koya of women, and it still feels gentle and domestic. Look for the small wooden plaques shaped like breasts hanging in the hall, offered by women praying for safe childbirth, good milk and, these days, recovery from illness. Just up the slope begins the Choishi-michi, the old pilgrim path to the summit, marked by stone posts set roughly every hundred metres all the way up. Walking pilgrims still use it, and it is a beautiful forest trail if you have the time and the boots.

Kudoyama is also persimmon country. In autumn the terraced orchards around the valley turn orange with fruit, and the local dried persimmons are worth buying for the road.

On the bike, the climb to Koyasan is the main event: a narrow mountain road with switchbacks through cedar and cypress, tight hairpins, damp shaded corners and the occasional tour bus coming down in the middle of the lane. Ride it in the morning before the coaches, or in the late afternoon when the light slants through the trees and the mountain town above is settling into evening prayers. Remember that Japan drives on the left, that speed limits are low and enforced, and that mountain roads can close after heavy rain or in winter snow.

Hashimoto, a city of over fifty thousand a few kilometres west, is the place for fuel, convenience stores and a proper meal; the small towns nearer the temple have less. Fill the tank before you climb, take a cold drink from a vending machine and give the old temple its due before the mountain.
t.zwentendorf kastell@48.3,15.9:
The Danube flows broad and brown past Zwentendorf, a quiet village on the Tullnerfeld plain west of Vienna, and for once the most famous building in the area is not the oldest one. Zwentendorf is where Austria built a nuclear power station in the 1970s and then, after a national referendum in 1978, decided never to switch it on. The plant still stands by the river, complete and unused, now a training site and a curiosity.

The older story lies quietly in the fields. Under the turf near the village are the remains of a Roman fort on the Danube Limes, the frontier line that ran along the river protecting the province of Noricum from the peoples to the north. A chain of forts, watchtowers and small towns lined this bank, and the whole system is now part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire World Heritage site. There is not much above ground to see here, so bring imagination: picture a rectangle of walls, barracks and gates, with soldiers watching the far bank for raiders crossing on the ice in winter.

The land around is flat river country, maize and sugar beet fields, poplars along drainage channels and floodplain woods by the Danube. The riding on the plain itself is straight and simple, with the occasional crosswind, but the hills on both sides are where the fun begins. North of the river, the Wagram escarpment rises in a long bank of terraced vineyards growing Grüner Veltliner, with villages of wine cellars and some fine twisty lanes. To the south, the Dunkelsteinerwald forest offers quiet wooded roads, and a short ride west brings you into the Wachau, one of the most beautiful river valleys in Europe, which is worth a day on its own.

Tulln, about thirteen kilometres east, is the town for fuel, food and supplies. It is also the birthplace of the painter Egon Schiele, and has a museum to him in the old jail building by the river, as well as a riverside promenade and a famous garden show. Zwentendorf itself has a few local services, a church and the riverbank, which makes a pleasant place to sit and watch barges pushing upstream against the current.
t.kumano sanzan kumano hongu taisha@33.8,1:
Deep in the mountains of the Kii Peninsula, where forested ridges fold one behind another like the scenery in a woodblock print, stands the head shrine of the Kumano faith. Kumano Hongū Taisha is one of the three grand shrines of Kumano, and for over a thousand years emperors, aristocrats and ordinary pilgrims have walked here along the network of mountain trails known as the Kumano Kodō, now part of the Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range listed by UNESCO.

The shrine you see today stands on a hill above the river, dark wood and cypress bark roofs set among tall cedars. It once stood on a sandbank called Oyunohara, where the rivers meet, until a great flood in 1889 washed much of it away. The main halls were rebuilt on higher ground, and the old site is now marked by an enormous torii gate, one of the largest in Japan, rising above the rice fields. Look out for the three-legged crow, Yatagarasu, a messenger of the gods in Kumano legend, which appears everywhere here and is also the emblem of the Japanese football association.

The area is also blessed with hot springs. Yunomine, one of the oldest onsen in Japan, has a tiny riverside bath called Tsuboyu that is itself part of the World Heritage site, and nearby Kawayu has a river where hot water bubbles up through the gravel, so you can dig your own bath on the bank.

The riding to get here is superb. Route 168 runs up from Shingū on the coast along the gorge of the Kumano river, with deep green water, wooded cliffs and long sweeping bends, while Route 311 crosses from the west through quieter mountain country. Both are well surfaced but narrow in places, with tunnels, tight turns and log trucks. Rain is heavy in this region, especially in the early summer rainy season and during typhoons in late summer, and landslides occasionally close roads. Ride on the left, keep to the speed limits and allow more time than the map suggests.

Shingū, about twenty-three kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size for fuel and supplies. Hongū itself has a few shops and places to eat; a bowl of noodles and a long hot bath in the onsen after the ride is the classic end to a day here.
t.horyu ji area@34.6,135.7:
The buildings at Hōryū-ji are around thirteen hundred years old, and some of them are among the oldest wooden structures anywhere in the world. Founded in the early seventh century by Prince Shōtoku, a regent remembered as a champion of Buddhism and a founding figure of the Japanese state, the temple was rebuilt after a fire later in the same century, and parts of that rebuilding still stand. In 1993 it became one of the first sites in Japan to be listed by UNESCO, as the Buddhist Monuments in the Hōryū-ji Area.

The western precinct holds the main hall and the five-storey pagoda, both with deep, sweeping eaves and the subtle swelling columns that show influences from the Asian mainland. Inside, statues and treasures from the Asuka period, some of them unique, are kept in dim halls and a modern treasure house. The eastern precinct has the octagonal Hall of Dreams, built on the site of Shōtoku's palace. It is a quiet place compared with central Nara, especially on weekday mornings, and the gravel paths between the walls are lovely to walk.

The town around is called Ikaruga, a pleasant, low-rise place in the western part of the Nara basin, with fields, persimmon orchards and small temples. A famous haiku by Masaoka Shiki links the sound of the temple bell to eating a persimmon at Hōryū-ji, and in autumn the fruit hangs heavy on the trees.

The riding around Hōryū-ji itself is suburban, with traffic lights, narrow streets and lots of cyclists. The fun lies in the hills to the west, where the Ikoma range separates Nara from Osaka. The Shigi-Ikoma Skyline, a toll road along the ridge, offers flowing bends and views over the Osaka plain on one side and the Nara basin on the other, especially beautiful at night. Mountain roads in the area are narrow, and weekend traffic can be heavy. Remember to ride on the left and to respect the low speed limits, which are strictly enforced.

Fuel, convenience stores and restaurants are easy to find in the area. Try kakinoha-zushi, a local speciality of pressed sushi wrapped in persimmon leaves, which can be bought in boxes and makes a perfect picnic on the temple steps or at a viewpoint.
t.kengoshizuka mounded tomb@34.5,135.8:
In the gentle hills of Asuka, south of Nara, the first capitals of Japan rose and fell in the sixth and seventh centuries, and the land is still dotted with the tombs of the powerful. Kengoshizuka is one of them, a mound on a low ridge that excavations revealed to be octagonal in shape, a form used for imperial tombs in that period. Inside were found twin burial chambers cut from stone, and many scholars believe it to be the tomb of Empress Saimei, who reigned twice in the seventh century, with her daughter buried beside her. Restoration work in recent years has given the mound back its original shape, faced with stones, so it is far more legible than many overgrown kofun.

Asuka feels like a living museum. Rice paddies, persimmon orchards and wooded hills surround mysterious stone monuments: Ishibutai, a huge tomb whose earth mound has eroded away, leaving massive stones exposed, the strange carved Sakafuneishi, and the painted tombs of Takamatsuzuka and Kitora, decorated with images of the constellations and guardian animals. Much of the area is protected, and building is restricted, which keeps the landscape remarkably quiet.

The best way to explore Asuka is slowly. Many visitors rent bicycles, and lanes between the sites are narrow, so a motorbike needs to move gently and give way to cyclists. Kashihara, the city next door, has Kashihara Jingū, a large Shinto shrine dedicated to the legendary first emperor, Jimmu, set in a wide forest.

Riding further south takes you into the Yoshino mountains, famous for their cherry blossoms in spring, and onwards into the Kii peninsula with long, winding mountain roads through cedar forests and deep valleys. These roads are well surfaced but narrow and often damp, with tight bends and tunnels. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, while the summer rainy season and typhoons can bring heavy rain and landslides.

Kashihara, about five kilometres away, is a city of over a hundred thousand people, with fuel, shops and restaurants. Asuka itself has small cafés and restaurants, some serving dishes made with ancient rice or local vegetables. A bowl of noodles or a set lunch, followed by a slow look at the tomb in the afternoon light, is a fine way to spend a few hours.
t.pilgrimage church of st john of nepomuk:
On a low wooded rise called Zelená hora, Green Mountain, just outside Žďár nad Sázavou, stands one of the strangest and most beautiful churches in Central Europe. The architect was Jan Blažej Santini-Aichel, a Prague builder of Italian descent who loved to mix Gothic forms with Baroque drama, and here he built a pilgrimage church to St John of Nepomuk in the 1720s, shortly before the saint was even canonised. Everything in it plays on the number five: a star-shaped ground plan, five gates, five altars, five-pointed geometry repeated in the cloister around it. The reason is the legend that five stars appeared over the Vltava when John's body was thrown into the river in Prague, and the saint's tongue, said to have been found uncorrupted, is the other motif you will spot once you know to look for it. UNESCO listed it in 1994.

The church belonged to the Cistercian monastery in the valley below, and Santini also worked on the monastery itself, which is now a château with museum spaces and a lovely lake beside it. Allow time for both if you like architecture; the mix of pale walls, dark forest and water is quietly lovely.

The riding here is pure Vysočina, the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands: rolling uplands at five to eight hundred metres, spruce forests, fishponds and small villages with onion-domed churches. Roads are mostly quiet two-lane routes with long, flowing bends and short climbs; some secondary roads are patched and bumpy, so keep an eye out after winter. Nové Město na Moravě, ten kilometres north, is known for cross-country skiing and biathlon, which tells you what the weather is like from November to March. In summer the light over the ponds in the evening is the reward.

Žďár is a town of around twenty thousand, so fuel, supermarkets and restaurants are easy, and the parking near the church is usually calm outside summer weekends. Try a plate of svíčková or a simple soup and a Czech lager if you are stopping for the night; if not, a coffee near the château lake and a walk up the hill to the church will do nicely before you ride on into the highlands.
t.koyasan kongobu ji@34.2,135.6:
Getting to Kōyasan feels like a pilgrimage even on a motorcycle. The roads climb out of the Kinokawa valley through dense cedar forest, switchback after switchback, until you emerge onto a high basin at around eight hundred metres where a whole town of temples has grown up. The monk Kūkai, known after his death as Kōbō Daishi, founded the monastery here in the early ninth century as the centre of Shingon Buddhism, and Kongōbu-ji is the head temple of the sect. Its halls, painted sliding doors and the large rock garden are worth an unhurried visit, and the whole mountain is part of the UNESCO listing of the Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range.

The most unforgettable place is Okunoin, the vast cemetery that stretches for a couple of kilometres through ancient cedars to Kūkai's mausoleum, where believers hold that he remains in eternal meditation. Moss-covered stone lanterns and gravestones of samurai clans, emperors and modern companies line the path. Walking it at dusk, when the lanterns are lit, is extraordinary. Many visitors stay overnight in one of the temple lodgings, sleeping on tatami, eating shōjin ryōri, the vegetarian Buddhist cuisine, and joining the monks for morning prayers.

For riders, the roads around Kōyasan are a treat. The climb up from Hashimoto and the Kinokawa valley is steep, twisting and well surfaced, but busy with tour buses at weekends. Even better is the Kōya-Ryūjin Skyline, which runs south along the mountain ridges toward the hot spring town of Ryūjin, with long, flowing corners, panoramic views and few cars on weekdays. Be careful in the rainy season, when the road is wet and leafy, and in winter, when snow and ice can make the high roads dangerous or close them.

Kōya town, with around five thousand inhabitants, has basic services, including fuel, but do not count on long opening hours. Hashimoto, twelve kilometres away, is a larger town in the valley with more choice. The mountain is cool in summer and cold in winter, so pack an extra layer, and bring cash, as some smaller places do not accept cards. A bowl of sesame tofu, a Kōyasan speciality, is a quiet pleasure after the climb.
t.pilgrimage routes kumano sankeimichi i@3:
The Iseji is the eastern branch of the old pilgrimage roads to the three great Kumano shrines, running down the coast of the Kii Peninsula from the Grand Shrines of Ise to Kumano. For centuries, pilgrims followed it through forests and over passes, and stretches of its stone paving still survive in the hills, laid to keep the path usable in one of the rainiest parts of Japan. Owase, a little up the coast, regularly ranks among the wettest towns in the country, and the moss on the stones and the dripping cedar forests show it. The Iseji forms part of the UNESCO listing of the Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range.

The coast around here is wild and dramatic. Near Kumano city, the waves have carved the Onigajō rocks into caves and terraces, and Shishi-iwa, a rock shaped like a lion, guards the shore. South of town, Shichiri-mihama is a long pebble beach that sweeps toward Shingū, where Kumano Hayatama Taisha, one of the three grand shrines, stands near the mouth of the Kumano river. Behind the coast, the mountains rise steeply, cloaked in dark forests of cedar and cypress, cut by clear rivers.

National Route 42, the coastal road, is the main artery, linking the fishing towns along the shore. It is a mix of seaside sections with views over the Pacific, tunnels through the headlands and a few inland climbs. Traffic is moderate, with trucks and local cars, but it rarely feels crowded. For more challenging riding, head inland along the river valleys into the Kii mountains, where narrow roads twist through forests and over passes. Watch out for rain, which can be torrential, and landslides after heavy storms. Typhoon season in late summer and early autumn can close roads entirely.

Shingū, about nineteen kilometres away, and Owase, about twenty-three, both have full services, including fuel and supermarkets. Smaller villages along the coast have convenience stores, often with good coffee and snacks. Try sanma-zushi, pressed sushi with saury, or mehari-zushi, rice balls wrapped in pickled mustard leaves, both local favourites. And if you are tempted to walk a piece of the old route, wear good shoes; the stones are slippery when wet.
t.former hacienda of chichimequillas@20.8,:
On the high, dry plain northeast of Querétaro, the village of Chichimequillas grew up around an old hacienda, one of the many great estates that lined the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the Royal Inland Road that connected Mexico City with Santa Fe, in what is now New Mexico, for nearly three centuries. Silver, mercury, cloth, livestock, missionaries and soldiers travelled this route, and haciendas like this one supplied food, water and rest. The route was listed by UNESCO in 2010 as a series of sites, and the hacienda is one of them; its old buildings, chapel and walls hint at the wealth and power once concentrated here.

The name comes from the Chichimecas, the semi-nomadic peoples of the northern frontier whom the Spanish fought for decades. The Bajío, as this fertile highland region is called, became the breadbasket of New Spain and later the cradle of Mexican independence. Querétaro, the state capital, played a leading role in the conspiracy of 1810, saw Emperor Maximilian executed on the Cerro de las Campanas in 1867 and hosted the drafting of the Mexican Constitution of 1917. Its historic centre, with a long colonial aqueduct, baroque churches and lively plazas, is also on the UNESCO list.

The riding on the plateau is wide open. At around nineteen hundred metres, the air is thin and clear, and the roads cross farmland, scrub and low hills with long straights and gentle curves. Traffic can be heavy near Querétaro, which has grown into a major industrial city, but the back roads are quieter. Watch for topes, the speed bumps found in every village, and for stray dogs and livestock. The dry season, from October to May, is the best time to ride, with sunny days and cool nights; in the rainy season, expect afternoon thunderstorms.

Chichimequillas itself is a small village with basic shops. The nearest town with full services is Amazcala, about ten kilometres away, and Querétaro has everything. Try gorditas, thick corn cakes stuffed with various fillings, or enchiladas queretanas, served with potatoes and carrots. The region also produces wine and cheese, especially around Tequisquiapan and Ezequiel Montes to the east.
t.hokki ji area@34.6,135.7:
Ikaruga, a quiet town on the western edge of the Nara basin, is where Japanese Buddhist architecture begins. The temple of Hōryū-ji, founded by Prince Shōtoku in the early seventh century, has wooden buildings counted among the oldest surviving in the world, and in 1993 the Buddhist Monuments in the Hōryū-ji Area became, along with Himeji Castle, the first Japanese sites on the UNESCO list. A short distance north, among rice fields and houses, Hokki-ji is a smaller temple with a single treasure: a three-storey pagoda completed in the early eighth century, the oldest of its type in Japan. Seen across the fields with the hills behind, it is a lovely, peaceful sight.

Prince Shōtoku is a towering figure in Japanese history, a regent credited with promoting Buddhism, drafting a seventeen-article constitution and opening diplomatic relations with China. His legacy is everywhere in Ikaruga: in the temples, in the street names and on the souvenirs. The area is green and gentle, with persimmon orchards, rice paddies and wooded hills, and in autumn the colours of the maples and the orange persimmons are spectacular.

Riding in the Nara basin is mostly a matter of navigating suburban roads, with traffic lights, convenience stores and narrow streets around the temples. Traffic is moderate, but watch for cyclists and pedestrians, and be patient. For more exciting riding, head west into the Ikoma and Shigi mountains that separate Nara from Osaka, where winding roads climb through the forest to temples and viewpoints, with views over the plain. There is also a toll road along the Ikoma ridge, short but scenic, famous for its night views over the lights of Osaka.

Hōryūji town, a kilometre away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Nara city, nine kilometres away, has everything. Try kakinoha-zushi, sushi wrapped in persimmon leaves, a Nara speciality, or a bowl of soba. Many temples in the area have small cafés or tea houses, perfect for a break. Bring cash, as smaller places may not accept cards, and remove your shoes before entering temple halls.
t.todai ji@34.7,135.8:
Nothing quite prepares you for the scale of Tōdai-ji. You walk through the great Nandaimon gate, past two fierce wooden guardian kings carved in the thirteenth century by Unkei, Kaikei and their workshop, and there it is: the Daibutsuden, the Great Buddha Hall, for centuries the largest wooden building in the world, even though the current structure, rebuilt in the early eighteenth century, is smaller than the original. Inside sits the Daibutsu, a bronze Buddha some fifteen metres tall, commissioned by Emperor Shōmu and consecrated in 752 with a ceremony that drew monks from as far away as India. The temple is part of the UNESCO listing of Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara.

One of the pillars in the hall has a hole at its base said to be the same size as the Buddha's nostril, and those who squeeze through are promised enlightenment, or at least good luck. Children wriggle through easily; adults sometimes need help. Up on the hillside behind the main hall, Nigatsu-dō hosts Omizutori every March, a ceremony in which monks swing huge flaming torches from the balcony, scattering sparks over the crowd below.

The temple stands in Nara Park, where more than a thousand deer roam freely, considered messengers of the gods. They bow to visitors in exchange for special crackers, and they can be pushy, so keep your maps and snacks out of reach. The park is busy with tour groups, school trips and families, especially in spring, when the cherry trees bloom, and autumn, when the maples turn red.

Riding in Nara is easy, but the centre gets congested, and parking for motorcycles is limited near the temples. Head east into the hills for more interesting roads: there are winding routes through the forest to the village of Yagyū, once home to a famous school of swordsmanship, and toward the tea fields in the uplands. Nara has fuel, food and accommodation everywhere. Try narazuke, vegetables pickled in sake lees, or a bowl of noodles with nyūmen, warm thin somen in broth, and take a break in a traditional tea house.
t.baden bei wien@48.0,16.2:
The Romans already knew about the hot sulphur springs at Baden, just south of Vienna, but it was in the early nineteenth century that the town became the summer playground of the Habsburg court. Emperor Franz I spent his summers here, and the aristocracy and the wealthy bourgeoisie followed, building elegant villas, parks and bathhouses in the Biedermeier style. Beethoven came to take the waters too, staying many times and working on his Ninth Symphony in a house that is now a museum. In 2021, Baden was listed by UNESCO as one of the Great Spa Towns of Europe, alongside Bath, Baden-Baden, Karlovy Vary and others.

Today, the spa still draws visitors, and the warm, sulphurous water, which smells faintly of eggs, is used in a large modern thermal complex. The town centre is compact and elegant, with a plague column, a theatre, a casino and the Kurpark, a hillside park with fountains, statues and a pavilion where concerts are held in summer. The town is surrounded by vineyards, part of the Thermenregion wine area, and the local Heurigen, rustic wine taverns, serve young wine, cold cuts and spreads.

The riding is very good. West of Baden, the Helenental valley leads into the Vienna Woods, with winding roads through forests and past castles, ruins and monasteries. The road to Mayerling, where Crown Prince Rudolf and Mary Vetsera died in 1889, and on to the Cistercian abbey of Heiligenkreuz, is popular with riders, with flowing curves and good surfaces. Further south, the Semmering pass and its UNESCO-listed railway offer more mountain riding. On weekends, expect plenty of other motorcyclists, cyclists and day-trippers from Vienna, and police speed checks.

Baden, with twenty-six thousand inhabitants, has everything you need: fuel, supermarkets, cafés, restaurants and hotels. Try a Wiener Schnitzel, a Tafelspitz, boiled beef with horseradish and apple sauce, or a slice of Sachertorte in one of the coffee houses. The local wines, Zierfandler and Rotgipfler, are rare white varieties found almost only in this region, and well worth tasting once the riding is done.
t.yakushi ji@34.7,135.8:
Yakushi-ji is one of the great temples of Nara, the capital of Japan in the eighth century. It was founded by Emperor Tenmu in the late seventh century, praying for the recovery of his ill empress, and moved to its present site when the capital moved to Nara in 710. Dedicated to Yakushi Nyorai, the Buddha of healing, it is part of the UNESCO-listed Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara. The East Pagoda, which has stood since the eighth century, is one of the few surviving buildings from that era, and its layered roofs, with smaller roofs between each storey, create a rhythm described by one admirer as frozen music.

Most of the other buildings, including the bright red West Pagoda and the main hall, were rebuilt in the late twentieth century after centuries of fires and decay. Their colours may surprise visitors used to weathered wood, but they show how the temples looked when they were new. The main hall holds a bronze Yakushi triad, considered among the masterpieces of Japanese Buddhist sculpture.

Yakushi-ji is in the Nishinokyo area, south-west of central Nara, near Toshodai-ji, another important temple founded by the Chinese monk Ganjin. The two can be visited together on foot. The area is calm and residential, with rice fields and small streets.

For riders, Japan is orderly but strict. You drive on the left, speed limits are low, and the police enforce them. Fuel stations are everywhere, though many close at night in rural areas. Temples usually have parking. The ride from Nara toward Horyu-ji, a short distance south-west, takes you to the oldest wooden buildings in the world, and the hills to the east and south lead toward Asuka and the mountains of Yoshino, famous for cherry blossoms. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the weather is mild and the colours spectacular.
t.sanctuary of jesus nazareno de atotonilc:
From the outside, the Sanctuary of Jesús Nazareno de Atotonilco is plain: thick whitewashed walls, a modest bell tower, a dusty plaza in a small village on the dry plateau of Guanajuato. Step inside and every surface erupts in colour. The church was founded in the eighteenth century by the priest Luis Felipe Neri de Alfaro as a place of penitence and spiritual retreat, and its walls and ceilings were covered over decades with murals by the painter Miguel Antonio Martínez de Pocasangre, full of saints, angels, Biblical scenes and verses. People call it the Sistine Chapel of Mexico, and the comparison is less exaggerated than it sounds. It is listed by UNESCO together with the nearby town of San Miguel de Allende.

Atotonilco also has a place in Mexico's national story. In September 1810, at the very start of the War of Independence, the priest Miguel Hidalgo and his followers passed through here and took a banner of the Virgin of Guadalupe from the sanctuary, which became the first flag of the insurgent army. Pilgrims still come in large numbers, especially during Lent and Holy Week, when the retreat house fills with penitents.

The ride from San Miguel de Allende, about eleven kilometres away, follows a two-lane road across a high, arid plain of mesquite, cactus and farmland, with mountains on the horizon. The altitude is close to two thousand metres, so mornings are cool and afternoons hot and bright. Watch for topes, the speed bumps that appear without warning at village entrances, as well as dogs, livestock and slow trucks. The name Atotonilco means place of hot water, and the area has several thermal spas where you can soak after a day in the saddle.

San Miguel de Allende is the place for fuel, food and lodging: a colonial town of pink stone churches and cobbled streets, popular with artists and foreign residents, with excellent restaurants. Guanajuato, the state capital, lies about an hour to the west through the mountains, a winding and scenic ride. Come early in the day, before the tour buses, and spend a quiet moment under those painted ceilings.
t.palace and gardens of schonbrunn@48.2,16:
Schönbrunn was the summer residence of the Habsburgs, the dynasty that ruled a large part of Europe for centuries. The palace, on the western edge of Vienna, was rebuilt in the Baroque style in the eighteenth century under Empress Maria Theresa, and it has more than a thousand rooms. It began as a hunting lodge on land where, legend says, Emperor Matthias found a beautiful spring, the schöner Brunnen that gave the place its name. The gardens are vast and formal, with avenues of trees, fountains, statues, a maze, and the Gloriette, a colonnaded structure on the hill above the palace with views over Vienna. The palace and gardens were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1996.

Inside, the state rooms are richly decorated, with gilded stucco, chandeliers, porcelain and paintings. The young Mozart performed here for Maria Theresa, and Emperor Franz Joseph was born and died here. The palace also hosts the oldest zoo in the world still in operation, founded in 1752, and a palm house, a large glass and iron greenhouse.

For riders, Vienna is a city stop. Traffic is heavy, trams and cyclists are everywhere, and the city has strict parking rules, with short-term parking zones across most districts. Leave the bike in a garage or designated area and use public transport, which is excellent. Fuel is easy to find on the outskirts. Austria requires a vignette for motorways. Arrive at opening time if you want the state rooms without a crowd; the gardens are free and at their best early, when the gravel paths are freshly raked and the city is still waking up.

When you are ready to ride, head west into the Vienna Woods, the Wienerwald, where winding roads through beech forests lead to villages known for their heurigen, wine taverns serving local wine and simple food. South, the Semmering pass and its UNESCO-listed railway, built in the nineteenth century, offer scenic mountain roads. Vienna's food is legendary: Wiener schnitzel, tafelspitz, sachertorte and apfelstrudel, best enjoyed in one of the city's traditional coffee houses.
t.tugendhat villa in brno@49.2,16.6:
When the architect Ludwig Mies van der Rohe designed a house for the young couple Grete and Fritz Tugendhat in Brno at the end of the 1920s, he created one of the masterpieces of modern architecture. Completed in 1930, the villa sits on a slope above the city, with a vast open-plan living room enclosed by glass walls that could be lowered into the floor, a wall of onyx, and chrome-plated steel columns. It was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2001, and it remains one of the most influential houses of the twentieth century.

The Tugendhat family, who were Jewish, fled Czechoslovakia in 1938, before the Nazi occupation. The house was confiscated, damaged during the war, and used for various purposes over the following decades. In 1992, the leaders of the Czech and Slovak republics met here to sign the agreement that led to the peaceful division of Czechoslovakia. The villa was carefully restored and reopened in 2012.

Visits are by guided tour only and must be booked well in advance, often weeks or months ahead, especially in summer. The house is in the residential area of Černá Pole, a short ride from the city centre, and the garden below the terrace gives a lovely view across the rooftops toward Špilberk castle. Even if the tours are full, it is worth walking past to see how modestly the house presents itself to the street.

Brno, the second largest city in the Czech Republic, with a population of over three hundred and sixty thousand, has a lively centre, with a castle, cathedral and many cafés and bars. It is also home to the Masaryk circuit, where the Czech MotoGP was held for many years. For riders, the countryside around Brno is pleasant, with winding roads through the Moravian Karst to the north, with caves and gorges, and the wine region of South Moravia to the south, with the Lednice-Valtice cultural landscape, another UNESCO site, with its chateaux and parks. Czech motorways need a vignette.
t.cerro altamirano@20.0,-100.1:
Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies fly thousands of kilometres from Canada and the United States to spend the winter in the fir and pine forests of central Mexico. Cerro Altamirano, near the village of Contepec in the state of Michoacán, is one of the mountains where they gather, part of the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. When the butterflies are here, roughly from November to March, the branches of the trees are covered with them, so thickly that they sag under the weight.

The arrival of the monarchs coincides with the Day of the Dead at the start of November, and in local tradition the butterflies are linked to the souls of the dead returning. The phenomenon is one of the great spectacles of nature. On sunny days, as the air warms, the butterflies take to the air in clouds, filling the forest with the soft sound of their wings. Sanctuaries are open to visitors in the season, usually with local guides, and the walk up through the forest at altitude can be tiring, so go slowly.

The riding in this part of Michoacán and the neighbouring State of Mexico is mountainous and varied. Roads climb through forests and farmland, with sharp bends, steep grades and occasionally poor surfaces, potholes and topes, the speed bumps that appear without warning in every village. Traffic includes trucks, buses and livestock. The altitude, over 2,500 metres in places, means cool mornings and evenings even in the dry season, and afternoon storms are common in summer. The best riding weather, and the butterfly season, is the dry winter months.

Contepec is a small town with basic services, and Temascalcingo and Maravatío, larger towns nearby, have fuel and more choice. Local food is hearty: corundas, triangular tamales from Michoacán, and carnitas, slow-cooked pork. In the sanctuaries, follow the guides' rules: stay on the paths, keep quiet and do not touch the butterflies. Arriving in the late morning on a sunny day gives the best chance of seeing them in flight, and the sight of the forest coming alive with orange wings is unforgettable.
t.klosterneuburg kastell und vicus@48.3,16:
Klosterneuburg Abbey rises on a terrace above the Danube just north of Vienna, its baroque domes topped with an imperial crown and an archducal hat, and few visitors realise that beneath its walls lie the remains of a Roman fort. The Romans guarded this stretch of the Danube frontier, the Limes, with a chain of forts, and Klosterneuburg's position on a hill overlooking the river made it an obvious choice. The fort and the civil settlement around it are part of the UNESCO site of the Danube Limes, inscribed in 2021.

The abbey was founded in the twelfth century by Margrave Leopold III of the Babenberg dynasty, later canonised as Saint Leopold, patron saint of Lower Austria and Vienna. According to legend, he chose the site when he found his wife's veil, blown away by the wind, caught on a bush here. The abbey's greatest treasure is the Verdun Altar, a masterpiece of medieval enamel work by Nicholas of Verdun, completed in 1181. The abbey also owns extensive vineyards, and its winery is one of the oldest in Austria.

The riding around Klosterneuburg is a mix of city and countryside. The Vienna Woods, the Wienerwald, rise behind the town, with winding roads through beech forests and over hills, popular with Viennese riders on weekends. The Höhenstraße, a scenic road built in the 1930s, runs along the hills above Vienna with views over the city and the Danube; parts of it are cobbled and slippery when wet. Along the Danube, the road to Tulln and the Wachau is flat and easy. Traffic near Vienna is heavy, and speed limits are strictly enforced.

Klosterneuburg is a town of fifteen thousand with fuel and all services, and its centre has cafés and restaurants. The Heurigen, wine taverns serving new wine and simple food, are a Viennese tradition, and there are many in Klosterneuburg and the neighbouring villages. Remember the strict drink-driving limits. The abbey offers guided tours, and the view from its terrace over the Danube is lovely, especially in the evening when the river turns silver and the lights of Vienna come on in the distance.
t.sierra de organos@23.9,-103.8:
Pipes of a giant church organ, frozen in stone: that is what the Spanish saw when they named the Sierra de Órganos, a range of rock formations in the north-west of the state of Zacatecas, near the border with Durango. The columns and pinnacles of volcanic rock rise from the high desert, carved by wind and water into strange shapes, and the area is a national park, protected for its geology and its landscape of grassland, oak and pine.

The landscape has attracted filmmakers for decades. Durango and the surrounding region became a centre for the production of Western films in the mid-twentieth century, and many Hollywood Westerns were shot in the area, including some starring John Wayne, who loved the region. The rocks and open spaces of the Sierra de Órganos provided dramatic backgrounds. Today, the park has camping areas, cabins and trails for walking and climbing among the rocks, and it is a peaceful place far from the cities.

The riding in this part of Mexico is through high, open country, with long straight roads across the plains and some winding sections in the hills. The altitude, over two thousand metres, means cool mornings and evenings, even in summer, and the light is bright and clear. The roads are generally paved, but surfaces vary, and topes, speed bumps, appear without warning in villages. Traffic is light, but trucks are common on the main roads. The rainy season, from June to September, brings afternoon storms, and the dry season is the best time to visit.

The nearest larger towns are Sombrerete, a colonial mining town with fine churches, and Vicente Guerrero, both with fuel and services. Villages closer to the park have basic services. The local food is northern Mexican: carne asada, gorditas, thick corn pockets filled with meat or beans, and caldillo duranguense, a beef stew from Durango. Watching the sunset over the rock formations, with the columns glowing red and orange against the sky, is a spectacular experience.
t.natsitacua@23.0,-101.5:
Every year, groups of Wixárika people, known in Spanish as Huichols, leave their homes in the Sierra Madre Occidental and walk, ride or drive hundreds of kilometres east to Wirikuta, the sacred desert in San Luis Potosí where, in their tradition, the sun was born. Along the way they stop at a series of sacred places, springs, hills and water holes, where they leave offerings and perform ceremonies. Natsitacua is one of these places, out on the high plains near the border of Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí, and the names of the neighbouring stops on the route, such as Nihuetaritsié, are in the Wixárika language.

The pilgrimage route to Wirikuta has been proposed for recognition as a World Heritage Site, and it is one of the oldest living pilgrimage traditions in the Americas. The pilgrims collect peyote, a sacred cactus, in the desert, and the journey is a spiritual renewal for the communities. Mining projects in the Wirikuta region have caused conflict in recent years, as the Wixárika fight to protect their sacred lands. Visitors should treat these places with great respect, and avoid disturbing offerings or ceremonies.

The riding in this part of Mexico is across the vast high plateau, the altiplano, at over two thousand metres, with long straight roads through semi-desert, dotted with yuccas, cacti and mesquite. The distances are great and the villages few, so carry water and plan fuel stops. The roads are paved on the main routes but can be rough and unpaved on the minor ones, and topes in villages are frequent. The sun is intense, and the nights can be cold. The dry season, from October to May, is the best time to ride.

The nearest settlement listed is La Herradura, a small village about twenty kilometres away, so fuel and services are limited; fill up in larger towns such as Zacatecas, Fresnillo or Salinas before setting off. Real de Catorce, an old silver mining town in the mountains of San Luis Potosí, near Wirikuta, is a popular destination, reached through a long tunnel. Mexican food on the road is simple and good: tacos, gorditas and enchiladas. Riding across the altiplano at dawn, with the light spreading over the desert, is unforgettable.
t.traismauer kastell sudwestlicher fachert:
Traismauer is a small wine town on the south side of the Danube, just where the Traisen river comes down from the Alpine foothills to meet the big river, and it has been a fortified place for something like eighteen centuries. The Romans called their fort here Augustianis, one link in the chain of camps and watchtowers that guarded the frontier of the province of Noricum. In 2021 the Danube Limes was added to the UNESCO list, and Traismauer is one of the places where you can still see the old walls doing a job.

The south-western corner is the bit to look for. Late Roman builders strengthened their forts with projecting towers, and a fan-shaped corner tower like the one here was designed to let defenders cover the walls on both sides. Much of the town grew up inside and on top of the Roman footprint, so the medieval gate tower and later houses lean on masonry that was laid by soldiers. It is a quiet, almost domestic kind of history; you walk between gardens and garages and suddenly notice that the wall in front of you is Roman.

Riding in, you come across the flat Tullnerfeld, a broad plain of fields and orchards where the roads are straight and the main hazards are tractors, crosswinds off the river and the occasional village speed check. Head west and things get far more interesting: Krems is about twelve kilometres away, and beyond it the Wachau opens out, with terraced vineyards, apricot orchards and the river road through Dürnstein and Spitz. That stretch is lovely on a weekday morning and can be slow on summer weekends when every cyclist and coach in Lower Austria has the same idea.

Traismauer itself is big enough for basics. You will find a café or a Heuriger, the local wine taverns that open when they have new wine to sell, and the Traisental around the town is known for its Grüner Veltliner. For a proper choice of fuel stations and shops, Krems is the reliable bet. The nearby Danube cycle path means bakeries and benches are never far off.

The light here is soft and wide, with the river hidden behind its floodplain forest and the hills of the Wachau rising blue to the west. On a hot afternoon the shade of the old walls is a fine place to stop, eat something and imagine the frontier as the Romans saw it: the river, the forest and the unknown on the far bank.
t.nihuetaritsie@22.8,-101.6:
High desert stretches away in every direction here, dotted with yucca, nopal cactus and mesquite, under a sky that seems twice as big as anywhere else. For centuries the Wixárika have made pilgrimages from their homeland in the Sierra Madre Occidental across these plains to Wirikuta, the sacred desert near Real de Catorce, stopping at springs, hills and other holy places along the way. This is one of those places, a spot that matters in their ritual geography even if, to an outsider, it looks like empty desert.

That is worth keeping in mind. Sacred sites for the Wixárika are not tourist attractions, and pilgrims leave offerings, candles and arrows that should never be disturbed. Visit quietly, respect any signs or local guidance, and leave nothing behind but tyre tracks on the road.
