The riding on the altiplano is about distance and space. Roads are long, straight and mostly well paved, crossing open plains at altitudes of around two thousand metres, with mountains rising on the horizon. Traffic is light, but trucks, buses and livestock are common, and topes, the Mexican speed bumps, appear without warning at the edges of villages. Wind can be strong, and sun and dryness are relentless, so carry water and protect your skin.

Salinas de Hidalgo, about twenty-six kilometres away, is the main town, with fuel, food and basic lodging. As its name suggests, it has a long history of salt production from the nearby salt lakes, which supplied the silver mines of the colonial era with salt used in refining. Smaller villages nearby have little more than a store and perhaps a taco stand.

Local food is simple and hearty: gorditas filled with beans or meat, enchiladas potosinas with their red-tinted dough, and cold drinks from village shops. Come in the dry season, from November to April, when days are warm and nights cool, sometimes cold. The light at dawn and dusk turns the desert gold and violet, and the silence is deep. Give the place the respect it is owed, and it will give you one of the purest open-road experiences in Mexico.
t.town of pinos@22.3,-101.6:
Pinos was a silver town before most of Mexico had towns at all. Founded in the late sixteenth century, after silver was found in the hills, it grew into an important mining centre on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road that ran north from Mexico City toward Santa Fe in New Mexico, carrying silver south and supplies and settlers north. The town is part of the UNESCO listing of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, and it is also a designated Pueblo Mágico, with colonial churches, cobbled streets and old mining buildings.

The town sits high in the mountains of south-eastern Zacatecas, well above two thousand metres, and its streets climb steeply up the hillsides. The churches, including the parish church of San Matías and the chapel in the old Tlaxcalan quarter, founded by indigenous settlers brought from central Mexico, are worth a look, and the views from the hills over the town and the surrounding plains are wide. Pinos is also known for its mezcal, produced in old haciendas around the area from agave grown on the dry slopes.

Riding to Pinos means climbing from the altiplano through hills and valleys, with long views, winding roads and occasional rough patches. The roads are mostly paved but can have potholes, loose gravel and, as everywhere in rural Mexico, topes that demand your full attention. Traffic is light, but expect trucks, buses and wandering animals. The altitude makes nights cold, even in summer.

Pinos is a town of more than five thousand people, with fuel, food and basic accommodation. Small restaurants serve local dishes like asado de boda, a rich pork stew in a red chile sauce traditionally served at weddings, and gorditas filled with everything from beans to chicharrón. Try a glass of local mezcal, of course only when the riding is done for the day.

Come in the dry season, from October to April, when skies are clear and days warm. The rainy season, from June to September, brings afternoon storms that can make roads slippery and cut visibility. Late afternoon is the hour for Pinos, when the light softens, the domes glow against the hills and the plaza fills with families and ice cream.
t.zeiselmauer kastell hufeisenturm@48.3,16:
Zeiselmauer is a village that grew up inside a Roman fort, and it never quite moved out. The late Roman fort of Cannabiaca guarded this stretch of the Danube near Tulln, part of the frontier of the province of Noricum, and its walls, gate and towers were absorbed into the village over the centuries. One of the best-preserved features is a horseshoe-shaped tower, typical of late Roman fortifications, and a later fortlet within the fort, with walls standing several metres high, is one of the most impressive Roman buildings in Austria. Zeiselmauer is part of the Danube Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2021.

Walking around the village, you come across Roman walls in gardens, alongside houses and behind the church, and information boards help to piece the fort back together. The atmosphere is quiet and rural, with vineyards, fields and the floodplain forest of the Danube nearby.

The riding is a pleasant mix. The Tullnerfeld is flat, with straight roads through farmland and villages, but just to the south rise the hills of the Wienerwald, the Vienna Woods, a classic riding area for the Viennese, with twisting roads through beech forest, over passes like the Riederberg, and down to wine villages. The roads are popular with motorcyclists, and the police are attentive, with speed checks and noise controls, especially on weekends. The Danube cycle path runs nearby, so expect cyclists everywhere.

Zeiselmauer is a small village, so for fuel and full services head for Stockerau, across the river, about seven kilometres away, or Tulln, a pleasant town with a riverside promenade and a museum dedicated to the painter Egon Schiele, who was born there. Klosterneuburg, to the east, has a magnificent abbey, famous for its wine and its medieval altarpiece.

Local food includes Heuriger fare: cold cuts, cheeses, spreads and bread with a glass of new wine. Come in spring, when the vineyards and forests turn green, or in autumn, when the grape harvest brings festivals and the Wienerwald glows gold. Summer can be hot and busy. Stop in the village, walk around the walls and enjoy a quiet slice of Roman Austria before heading into the forest roads.
t.tatei matiniere@22.9,-101.7:
Every year, Wixárika pilgrims walk or drive hundreds of kilometres from their homeland in the Sierra Madre Occidental to the desert of Wirikuta in San Luis Potosí, where they collect peyote, the sacred cactus they call hikuri, and perform ceremonies to renew the world. Along the way, they stop at sacred places, and Tatei Matinieri, a group of springs in the semi-desert of the Altiplano, is one of the most important. The Wixárika route through these sacred sites was listed by UNESCO in 2025, recognising a living tradition that goes back centuries.

The springs lie in a wide, dry landscape of yuccas, cacti and creosote bushes, under a huge sky. The pilgrims leave offerings by the water, prayer arrows, small gourds decorated with beadwork and candles. It is a place of deep spiritual significance, and visitors should be respectful: do not disturb the offerings, do not take photographs of ceremonies without permission, and do not pick peyote, which is protected and whose collection is illegal for non-indigenous people. Further north, Real de Catorce, a former silver mining town reached through a long tunnel, is the gateway to Wirikuta.

The riding on the Altiplano is about space and light. The roads run for long distances across the plain, straight and empty, with mountains on the horizon and occasional villages. The tarmac is decent on the whole on the main highways but can be broken on minor roads, and there may be livestock on the road. The sun is strong, the air dry and the temperature can vary greatly between day and night. Summer brings afternoon thunderstorms; winter mornings can be cold.

Salinas de Hidalgo, about thirty kilometres away, is the nearest town of size, with fuel, shops and food; it is known for its salt flats. Villa de Ramos and La Herradura are smaller. Mexican food on the Altiplano is simple and filling: gorditas, enchiladas potosinas with red chile dough, cabrito, roast kid, and strong coffee. Carry water and fuel for long distances, and travel in daylight. Check the current security situation in the region before you go. At the springs, stand quietly, look across the desert, and feel the weight of all the journeys that have passed through here.
t.historic ensemble of the city of aguasca:
Aguascalientes means hot waters, and the city got its name from the thermal springs that the Spanish found here in the sixteenth century, when they founded a settlement on the road from Mexico City to the silver mines of Zacatecas. That road, the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, ran north for over two thousand kilometres to Santa Fe in New Mexico, and it is listed by UNESCO, with sites along its route. The historic centre of Aguascalientes is a pleasant mix of colonial churches, eighteenth-century houses and nineteenth-century buildings around the Plaza de la Patria and its cathedral.

The city is best known for the Feria Nacional de San Marcos, held every year from mid-April to May, which is the biggest fair in Mexico, with bullfights, concerts, cockfights, rides and millions of visitors. It is also the birthplace of José Guadalupe Posada, the engraver whose skeleton figures, especially La Catrina, an elegant lady skeleton, became icons of Mexican culture and the Day of the Dead. A museum dedicated to his work is in the historic centre. The railway workshops that once made the city an important industrial centre have been converted into a cultural complex.

The riding here is a mix of urban and open roads. Aguascalientes is a modern city of almost a million people, with heavy traffic and wide avenues. Outside the city, the roads across the plateau run through farmland and semi-desert, with long straights and mountains in the distance. North of the city, the former hacienda of Pabellón de Hidalgo, where Miguel Hidalgo was stripped of his command in 1811, is part of the Camino Real listing. The surface on main roads is generally good; watch for topes, speed bumps, which can be brutal.

Fuel, food and services are easy to find. Local food includes birria, a spicy meat stew, enchiladas, and guava sweets. The thermal baths, some of them historic, are a good place to relax after a long ride. Read up on local safety before travelling. Walk around the Plaza de la Patria in the evening, when families gather, the cathedral is lit up and street vendors sell snacks, and enjoy the friendly, unhurried atmosphere of a city that is proud of its traditions.
t.wixarika route through sacred sites to w:
West of Jerez, in Zacatecas, the land starts to fold into the long ridges of the Sierra Madre Occidental, and somewhere in these hills runs the path that Wixárika pilgrims follow from their homeland in the mountains of Jalisco and Nayarit toward Wirikuta, their sacred desert far to the east. The route, listed by UNESCO in 2025, is not a road in the usual sense but a chain of sacred places, springs, hills and caves where the pilgrims stop to pray, leave offerings and remember the journey of their ancestors, who according to tradition walked this way at the beginning of the world.

Jerez de García Salinas, thirty kilometres away, is one of Mexico's Pueblos Mágicos, a charming colonial town with a beautiful small theatre, the Teatro Hinojosa, said to be modelled on Ford's Theatre in Washington, and the birthplace of the poet Ramón López Velarde, whose poem Suave Patria is learned by schoolchildren across the country. Its Easter festivities are famous.

The riding here is genuinely good. The roads climbing west from Jerez into the hills are twisty and quiet, with views over valleys and ridges, and the climate is pleasant thanks to the altitude, warm in the day and cool at night. Surfaces vary from good to rough, and there are topes, the Mexican speed bumps, in every village. Livestock wander onto the road, and afternoon storms in the summer rainy season can bring sudden downpours and washed-out gravel. Travel in daylight and plan your fuel stops carefully, as stations are spread out.

Jerez has fuel, hotels, restaurants and a lively market. Zacatecan food is hearty: asado de boda, a pork stew in a rich chile sauce traditionally served at weddings, gorditas filled with everything imaginable, and mezcal from the region. Ask locally about road conditions and safety before heading into the more remote parts of the sierra. As for the sacred sites, they are not tourist attractions: if you find one, keep your distance, leave everything as it is, and let the pilgrims and their ancestors have the hills to themselves.
t.traismauer kastell romertor@48.3,15.7:
A Roman gate still stands in Traismauer, a small town on the Traisen just before the river reaches the Danube, and cars and bicycles pass through it every day. The Römertor, as it is called, is one of the best preserved Roman gates in Austria, part of the fort of Augustianis, which guarded the Danube frontier, the Limes, here. The fort was modified and reused in later centuries, and towers and walls survive in the town's fabric. Since 2021, the Danube Limes has been a piece of the World Heritage property for the frontiers of the Roman Empire.

Traismauer has another claim to fame: it appears in the Nibelungenlied, the medieval German epic, as a stop on Kriemhild's journey to the court of Etzel, king of the Huns. The town is small, with a few thousand inhabitants, a castle and a pleasant square. It lies at the eastern end of the Wachau, the Danube's famous valley of vineyards, apricot orchards and medieval towns, and the Traisental around it is a wine region in its own right, known for its crisp Grüner Veltliner.

The riding is easy and enjoyable. The roads along the Danube are flat and smooth, with views of the river and the vineyards, and the Wachau to the west offers some of the most beautiful riverside riding in Europe, between Krems and Melk, with terraced vineyards climbing steep slopes and castles on the crags. On weekends, the Wachau roads are busy with motorcyclists, cyclists and tourists, so weekdays are better. Speed limits are strictly enforced, and some roads have seasonal restrictions for motorcycles. The hills of the Dunkelsteiner Wald to the south offer quieter roads with curves.

Traismauer has fuel and shops, and Krems, twelve kilometres away, has everything, including a lovely old town. Food in the region is Austrian at its best: Wiener schnitzel, apricot dumplings in season, and heurigen, wine taverns where winemakers serve their own wine with cold cuts and spreads. The heurigen are open only at certain times of the year, marked by a bundle of pine branches over the door. Ride through the Roman gate, park the bike and have a look at the stones; legionaries marched through this same arch, though without the scooters.
t.wien legionslager zentralbereich@48.2,16:
Under the Hoher Markt, one of the oldest squares in Vienna, lie the foundations of the Roman legionary fortress of Vindobona. The Tenth Legion was stationed here for centuries, guarding the Danube frontier, and the camp covered much of what is now the inner city. Its outline can still be traced in the pattern of streets: the curve of the Graben follows the line of the fortress moat, and the old Roman road toward the west became today's Herrengasse. A small museum on the Hoher Markt displays the remains of officers' houses, with their heating systems, and finds from the camp.

Vienna has grown over Vindobona like ivy over a ruin. The Hoher Markt today is surrounded by elegant buildings, and above it hangs the Ankeruhr, an Art Nouveau clock where figures from Viennese history, from Marcus Aurelius, who may have died in the city, to Joseph Haydn, parade across a bridge between two buildings, with a full procession at noon. The cathedral of St Stephen, a few minutes' walk away, dominates the skyline with its tall spire and colourful tiled roof.

Riding in central Vienna requires patience. The inner city has narrow streets, pedestrian zones, one-way systems, trams and a lot of traffic, and parking is restricted. Motorcycles may park in some designated places, but rules are strict, and you should check the signs. The Ring, the grand boulevard around the inner city, is lined with palaces, museums and parks, and a slow ride around it is a fine introduction. Outside the city, the Vienna Woods to the west offer twisty roads through forests and vineyards, and the Höhenstraße climbs to viewpoints over the city.

Fuel stations are on the main roads outside the inner city. Viennese food is an institution: schnitzel, Tafelspitz, boiled beef with horseradish and apple sauce, goulash, and cakes in the great coffee houses, such as Sachertorte and apple strudel. The coffee houses are places to linger, with newspapers and marble tables. Park the bike outside the centre, take the underground, and walk to the Hoher Markt; then stand under the Ankeruhr and remember that the city's story began here, with a Roman camp on the Danube.
t.rusovce gerulata@48.1,17.1:
Three countries meet in the fields south of Bratislava, and the Romans had a fort here long before anybody drew those borders. Gerulata was an auxiliary fort on the Danube frontier, in what is now Rusovce, a district at the southern edge of the Slovak capital. Its remains have been excavated, and a small museum displays foundations and finds, from coins to pottery and gravestones. The site is part of the Danube Limes listed by UNESCO, a frontier that ran from Germany to the Black Sea.

Rusovce is a quiet suburb with a large manor house in a park, an English-style château that once belonged to the Habsburgs. Nearby, the Danube is wide and slow, divided by islands and dams, and the water sports centre at Čunovo has white-water channels used for international canoe races. The Danubiana art museum stands on a peninsula in the river, a striking modern building surrounded by water and sculptures. The tri-border point between Slovakia, Austria and Hungary lies a few kilometres south, near the villages of Čunovo, Deutsch Jahrndorf and Rajka, and you can stand in three countries at once.

The riding here is flat and easy. The roads cross farmland and follow the Danube, with dykes, forests and wetlands. Traffic around Bratislava can be heavy, but the minor roads are quiet. The landscape is not dramatic, but it has a certain charm, with wide skies, poplar trees and the river glinting in the sun. Wind across the plain can be strong. To the south, the Neusiedler See, a large shallow lake on the border between Austria and Hungary, is a short ride away, with vineyards and villages.

For fuel, Bratislava has everything, and Kittsee, on the Austrian side, is close by. Food here mixes Slovak, Austrian and Hungarian influences: bryndzové halušky, goulash, schnitzel and fish soup. Wines from the Little Carpathians and the Burgenland are excellent. Visit the Roman fort, then ride to the tri-border point, park the bike, and walk around the monument, taking a step into Austria and another into Hungary. The Romans would have found the idea of a border without guards very strange indeed.
t.pilgrimage routes kumano sankeimichi n@3:
The Kumano Kodō is a web of ancient pilgrimage trails across the mountains of the Kii Peninsula, south of Osaka, leading to the three grand shrines of Kumano: Hongū, Hayatama and Nachi. For over a thousand years, emperors, aristocrats and ordinary pilgrims walked these paths through cedar and cypress forest, stopping at small subsidiary shrines along the way. The Nakahechi, the most popular of the routes, leaves the coast near Tanabe and climbs inland through the hills. It is part of the Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range, listed by UNESCO in 2004, one of only two pilgrimage routes on the list along with the Camino de Santiago, with which it is twinned.

Walking even a short section is a magical experience. The stone-paved paths wind through tall trees, moss-covered steps lead up to tiny shrines, and the air is cool and damp, filled with birdsong. Villages along the way are small and quiet, with tea houses and guesthouses. The forest smells of wet earth and cedar.

For riders, the roads that follow the routes are a joy. National Route 311 runs inland from near Tanabe towards Hongū, roughly parallel to the Nakahechi, through forested valleys with fast, smooth bends and little traffic. Smaller roads branch off into the mountains, narrow and twisting, often single-track with blind corners and steep gradients. Japanese roads are generally well maintained, but watch for fallen leaves, moss and wet patches in the shade, and for slow-moving trucks. Driving is on the left, and you will need an international driving permit of the right type.

The region is also famous for its hot springs. Yunomine, near Hongū, has one of the oldest onsen in Japan, and Kawayu has a river where hot water bubbles up through the gravel, so you can dig your own bath. After a long ride, there is nothing better.

Tanabe, on the coast, is the gateway town, with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. In the mountains, fuel stations are scarce and close early, so fill up before heading inland. The best times to visit are spring, with fresh green leaves, and autumn, with red and gold foliage. Summer is hot and humid, with heavy rain, and typhoons can strike in late summer.
t.yashimazuka kofun@34.6,135.6:
In the southeastern suburbs of Osaka, among houses, rice paddies and railway lines, rise wooded mounds surrounded by moats. These are kofun, burial mounds built for the elite of ancient Japan between the third and seventh centuries, and the Furuichi group around Fujiidera and Habikino contains some of the largest in the country. Yashimazuka is one of the smaller mounds in the group, standing close to much bigger keyhole-shaped tombs attributed to emperors and empresses. Together with the Mozu group in Sakai, these mounds were listed by UNESCO in 2019 as the Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group.

The keyhole shape, round at the back and square at the front, is unique to Japan, and seen from the air the biggest mounds are astonishing. From the ground, they look like small forested hills, and access to many of them is restricted, since they are managed by the Imperial Household Agency as imperial tombs. You can walk around the moats, and there are viewpoints and small museums that explain the history. It is a strange experience, these ancient monuments sitting quietly in the middle of a modern city.

The area is densely populated, part of the sprawling Osaka metropolitan region, with houses, shops and small factories filling every gap. Kashiwara, Fujiidera and Habikino are suburban towns, busy and practical, with railway stations, supermarkets and noodle shops.

The riding here is urban, with heavy traffic, traffic lights and narrow streets. To escape, head east into the hills that separate Osaka from Nara. The Shigi-Ikoma Skyline, a toll road along the ridge of the Ikoma mountains, has views over the Osaka plain and is popular with riders, especially at night when the city lights spread out below. Further south, the Kongō mountains offer winding roads through forests. Across the hills, Nara has its own treasures: the great temples of Tōdai-ji and Hōryū-ji, the deer park, and the ancient capital's quieter streets.

Fuel, food and everything else are readily available. Driving is on the left, and Japanese traffic rules are strictly enforced, with speed cameras on major roads. The best seasons are spring, for the cherry blossoms, and autumn, for the foliage; summer is very hot and humid. Take a walk around the moat of a big kofun in the early morning, when the herons are fishing.
t.cuhixu uheni@22.8,-101.9:
Every year, groups of Wixárika pilgrims, the people known to outsiders as the Huichol, walk hundreds of kilometres from their homeland in the mountains of Jalisco and Nayarit to Wirikuta, a sacred desert in San Luis Potosí. The route crosses a chain of sacred places, springs, hills and rocks, where offerings are left and ceremonies performed, and Cuhixu Uheni, near the small town of Villa de Ramos, is one of them. The pilgrimage route as a whole has been put forward for World Heritage status as a living cultural landscape.

Wirikuta itself lies further east, in the high desert around the mountains of Real de Catorce. For the Wixárika it is the place where the sun was born, and where they gather peyote, a sacred cactus central to their religion. The area has been the focus of conflict in recent years over mining concessions, and many people, both indigenous and not, have campaigned to protect it. If you visit any of the sacred sites, behave with discretion and respect; these are places of active worship, not tourist attractions.

The landscape is the Chihuahuan desert at its most austere: a high, flat plain at around two thousand metres, with yucca trees, cacti, creosote bushes and distant blue mountains. The light is intense, the sky enormous, and the silence profound. In the evenings, the colours of the desert change from gold to red to purple.

The riding is straightforward on the main roads, long straights across the plain with little traffic, and wind that can be strong and gusty. Real de Catorce, a former silver mining town in the mountains to the east, is reached by a long cobbled road and then a single-lane tunnel over two kilometres long, with traffic controlled in alternate directions. It is a memorable ride, and the town, a mix of ruins and restored buildings, is fascinating.

Villa de Ramos is a small town with basic services, but for reliable fuel and supplies, Salinas or the city of San Luis Potosí are better bets. Carry plenty of water; the desert is hot by day and can be cold at night. Check current travel advice before riding in this part of Mexico, and avoid riding after dark, when livestock, potholes and unlit vehicles make the roads dangerous.
t.historic centre of telc@49.2,15.5:
Ride into the main square of Telč for the first time and you may laugh out loud, because it looks too perfect to be real. A long, tapering square is lined on both sides by Renaissance and Baroque houses, each with a different gable, painted in soft pastels, cream, pink, green and yellow, with arcades running along the ground floor. After a fire in the sixteenth century, the town was rebuilt under its lord, Zachariáš of Hradec, who had travelled in Italy and brought back a taste for Renaissance style. His château, at the end of the square, has richly decorated halls and a garden. The historic centre was listed by UNESCO in 1992.

The town is surrounded by ponds, created in the Middle Ages as defences and fish farms, and the reflections of the houses and towers in the water are lovely, especially in the evening. A walk around the ponds takes less than an hour.

Telč lies in the Vysočina, the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands, a region of rolling hills, forests, fields and fishponds between Prague and Brno. It is a quiet, rural area, with small towns and villages, and the riding here is a delight. The minor roads wind through the hills, with gentle bends, short climbs and descents, and very little traffic. Surfaces vary from excellent to patched, and you will meet tractors, cyclists and the occasional deer. Nearby Dačice, a small town to the south, claims to be the place where the sugar cube was invented in the nineteenth century, and has a monument to prove it. Further south, the border with Austria and the Waldviertel region offer more good riding.

The Czech Republic has strict rules for riders: dipped headlights at all times, zero tolerance for alcohol, and a vignette for motorways. Speed cameras are common in towns. Note that the main square may have restrictions on vehicles at certain times.

Telč has fuel, shops, cafés and restaurants, many of them with tables under the arcades. Try a plate of svíčková, beef in a creamy sauce with dumplings, or fried carp from the local ponds, a Christmas tradition. Czech beer is famously good and famously cheap, but save it for the evening. Spring and autumn are lovely; summer can be busy with tourists, and winters are cold and snowy.
t.former hacienda of san diego de navacoya:
East of the city of Durango, where the high plateau of northern Mexico stretches flat and wide under a vast sky, the old hacienda of San Diego de Navacoyán stands among irrigated fields and dusty farm roads. Its buildings, with thick adobe walls, a chapel and the remains of the main house, recall the centuries when great landed estates dominated this region, raising cattle, growing wheat and supplying the mining towns of the north. The hacienda is one of the sites listed as part of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the Royal Road of the Interior Land, which UNESCO inscribed in 2010. This was the long trade and colonisation route that ran from Mexico City north to Santa Fe in present-day New Mexico, more than two thousand kilometres through deserts and mountains.

Durango was founded in the sixteenth century as a frontier town, a base for silver mining and for the push north into what were then the lands of nomadic indigenous peoples. Its old centre has a fine cathedral and colonial buildings, and the surrounding landscape became famous in the twentieth century as a backdrop for Hollywood westerns, with film sets still standing in the desert outside the city. The haciendas along the Camino Real were essential for supplying travellers, mule trains and wagons.

Riding here is about space. The roads east of Durango are long and straight, crossing a high plain at around 1,900 metres, with mountains on the horizon and very little traffic away from the main highways. It can be windy, and the sun is fierce at this altitude, so cover up and drink plenty. Toward the west, the famous road from Durango to Mazatlán crosses the Sierra Madre Occidental with hundreds of curves and spectacular views, including the stretch known as the Espinazo del Diablo, now supplemented by a modern highway with tunnels and a huge bridge.

The hacienda lies in a rural area, so fuel and supplies are best taken care of in Durango, a city of over half a million people about eleven kilometres away. The city has everything, from fuel to restaurants to accommodation. Local dishes include caldillo duranguense, a beef stew with chilli, and gorditas. Ride out in the morning, when the light on the adobe walls is soft and warm, walk around the old buildings, and picture the mule trains plodding north toward the frontier.
t.former hacienda of cienega de mata@21.7,:
On the high plains where Jalisco meets Aguascalientes, the village of Ciénega de Mata gathers around the remains of what was once one of the largest haciendas in New Spain. In the colonial period, the estate covered an enormous territory, with cattle, sheep and horses grazing over a territory measured in leagues rather than fields, and its owners were among the most powerful families of the region. The surviving buildings, including a chapel and parts of the main house and its walls, are listed as part of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the great colonial road that linked Mexico City with the far north. Haciendas like this were the backbone of the colonial economy, supplying food, animals and shelter to the endless traffic of the road.

The region around it is the Altos de Jalisco, a highland area known for its ranching culture, its horsemanship and its deeply rooted Catholic traditions. It was a heartland of the Cristero War in the 1920s, when Catholic rebels rose against the anticlerical policies of the federal government, and the memory of that conflict is still strong. The highlands are dairy country too, producing cheeses and cajeta, a sweet caramel made from goat's milk.

The roads here are mostly long and straight, crossing a rolling plateau at around two thousand metres with fields of maize and beans, scrubland and occasional stands of nopal cactus. Traffic is light on the secondary roads, but watch out for livestock, slow farm vehicles and the ubiquitous topes in villages. The sky is huge, the light hard and bright, and afternoon storms are common in the rainy season, from June to September. Toward Aguascalientes and Encarnación de Díaz, the main highways carry more traffic, including heavy trucks.

The village is small, so for fuel and services, head for Encarnación de Díaz or Aguascalientes, a city with all amenities, or the town of Palo Alto, about twenty-five kilometres away. Small stores in the village sell drinks and snacks, and you may find a family kitchen offering simple food. Stop in the plaza, take a look at the chapel and the old walls, and imagine the hacienda at its height, with vaqueros driving herds across the plains. It is a quiet, windswept place, and its history is far bigger than its present.
t.temple of san pantaleon martir in the to:
San Martín is a small farming town on the high plateau of western Zacatecas, a dozen or so kilometres from the old mining city of Sombrerete, and at its heart stands a colonial church dedicated to San Pantaleón Mártir. The building, with a sturdy stone facade, a bell tower and a cool, simple interior, is one of the sites listed as part of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the colonial road that ran north from Mexico City through the silver country to New Mexico. Churches like this one marked the stopping places along the route, and they served the small communities of farmers, muleteers and miners who lived in this harsh, beautiful landscape.

Sombrerete was founded in the sixteenth century once silver was found in its hills, and it grew into one of the richest mining towns of New Spain, with grand churches and mansions paid for by the mines. It still has a well-preserved centre and is one of Mexico's designated Pueblos Mágicos. The Sierra de Órganos, a strange landscape of rock towers and pinnacles used in many western films, lies a short ride to the west and is worth a detour. The whole region feels like the edge of the frontier, which for centuries it was.

The riding is high-plateau riding at its best. The roads are long and mostly straight, crossing open country at well over two thousand metres, with mesquite, cactus and grassland stretching toward the mountains. Federal Highway 45, the main road through the region, follows the old Camino Real route in places and carries heavy truck traffic, so the secondary roads are more relaxing. The sun is strong, the air thin and dry, and the wind can be fierce across the open land. Afternoon thunderstorms in the rainy season can be spectacular, but they can also make roads slippery and visibility poor.

San Martín itself is small, with a few shops and basic services, so plan to refuel in Sombrerete, which has a population of over twenty thousand and offers fuel, restaurants and accommodation. Zacatecan food is hearty: try asado de boda, a pork stew in a rich chilli sauce, and gorditas filled with all kinds of stews. Stop by the church, pause in the plaza under the trees, and enjoy the quiet of a town that has watched travellers pass for centuries without making much fuss about it.
t.semmering railway@47.6,15.8:
Carl von Ghega's railway over the Semmering was a bold idea in the 1840s, when many engineers doubted that a conventional locomotive could haul a train over a mountain pass. Built between 1848 and 1854, the line climbs from Gloggnitz to the Semmering summit through fourteen tunnels and across sixteen viaducts, some with two tiers of stone arches, curving around the flanks of the mountains on ledges cut into the rock. It became the first mountain railway inscribed on the UNESCO list, in 1998, and it still carries trains between Vienna and the south, with the new Semmering Base Tunnel under construction beneath it to take over the heavy traffic.

The railway turned Semmering into a fashionable resort for Viennese society around 1900, with grand hotels and villas built on the slopes, and writers, artists and aristocrats came here for the mountain air. Some of the grand hotels still stand, a little faded, and the walking trail that follows the railway, the Bahnwanderweg, gives superb views of the viaducts, including from a famous viewpoint that once featured on the Austrian twenty-schilling banknote.

For riders, the Semmering pass, at 985 metres, is a classic outing from Vienna. The old pass road, the B306, climbs from Gloggnitz through Schottwien with curves and steady gradients, and descends on the Styrian side toward Mürzzuschlag. It is popular with motorcyclists on weekends, which means traffic, police controls and sometimes restrictions, so keep the throttle civilised. The surroundings offer more: the Höllental gorge toward Schwarzau, the Rax and Schneeberg mountains, and the Preiner Gscheid pass all offer superb riding with tighter, more technical corners. Weather on the Semmering can change quickly, and fog is common.

Semmering itself is a small village with a few cafés and hotels, and fuel is available in larger nearby places such as Gloggnitz, Payerbach or Mürzzuschlag, which is around thirteen kilometres to the south. Stop at one of the viewpoints near the railway, watch a train crawl across a viaduct, and admire what nineteenth-century engineers achieved without modern machinery. Then reward yourself with a slice of strudel or a Kaiserschmarrn at a café before continuing over the pass.
t.vlkolinec@49.0,19.3:
At the end of a narrow road climbing out of Ružomberok, a single street of log houses runs up a hillside meadow beneath the forests of the Veľká Fatra. Vlkolínec has been a World Heritage Site since 1993, chosen as the most complete surviving example of a traditional Central European mountain village of its kind, and it remains a lived-in place rather than an open-air museum, with residents, gardens and the occasional dog asleep in the sun.

The houses are timber on stone footings, painted in soft blues and whites, with shingled roofs and tiny windows. Many have small farm buildings behind and a long narrow plot running up the slope. Halfway along stands a wooden belfry, and a stream runs in a channel down the village, past an old well. The name comes from the Slovak word for wolf, and wolves still live in the surrounding Carpathian forests, along with brown bears, so treat the woods with proper respect if you wander off the paths.

The road up from the town is steep, narrow and twisty, with a couple of tight bends, and in practice you leave the bike at the car park below the village and walk the last stretch. Go early or late if you can, because coaches arrive in the middle of the day in summer. Ružomberok down in the valley is a working industrial town; when the wind is wrong, the smell of its big paper mill drifts across the Váh. It has everything a rider needs: fuel, supermarkets and garages, and it is the gateway to the ski hill at Malinô Brdo.

The wider riding is excellent. Route 59 heads south from Ružomberok over the Donovaly saddle towards Banská Bystrica, a fast, flowing climb through spruce forest with good surfaces and plenty of traffic on summer weekends. North, the same road runs to Dolný Kubín and into Orava. East, the Liptov basin opens up with the High and Low Tatras on either side, though the main highway along the Váh is busy with lorries and best used only to cover distance.

For food, this is the land of bryndzové halušky, small potato dumplings with sheep's cheese and bacon, and sheep farms sell fresh cheese and žinčica, the sour whey drink, in summer. A late lunch in Ružomberok after the walk up the village is the natural rhythm of the day.
t.historic centre of zacatecas@22.8,-102.6:
Silver built Zacatecas, and you can see it in every street. The city lies in a narrow ravine at around 2,400 metres on the high plateau of north-central Mexico, founded in the 1540s after Spanish prospectors found rich silver veins in the surrounding hills. For centuries the mines here poured wealth into the Spanish crown, and the miners and merchants spent their share on churches, mansions and plazas of pinkish quarried stone. The centre became a World Heritage Site in 1993, and the city is also on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the long colonial road that ran from Mexico City to New Mexico.

The cathedral is the showpiece, its façade a dense riot of carved saints, vines and angels in the local Baroque style. Above the city rises the Cerro de la Bufa, a rocky hill with a chapel and a commanding view, where Pancho Villa's forces won a decisive battle in 1914 during the Mexican Revolution. A cable car links the Bufa to another hill across the valley, and an old mine, El Edén, can be visited underground, its tunnels running beneath the city.

As a riding destination, Zacatecas offers high-altitude plateau roads with long straights, open views and big skies, interrupted by sudden mountain ranges. Federal highways 45 and 49 meet near the city and carry heavy truck traffic, while the smaller roads west towards Jerez, a pretty colonial town, and the rock formations of the Sierra de Órganos are much more enjoyable. At this height the air is thin, the sun burns quickly and evenings are cold, even in summer. Thunderstorms build on many summer afternoons during the rainy season.

The region also lies on the pilgrimage routes of the Wixárika, or Huichol, people, who travel to the sacred desert of Wirikuta further east, a living tradition that runs alongside the colonial history.

Fuel is plentiful at the Pemex stations in and around Zacatecas and Guadalupe. Safety is a real consideration: parts of the state have seen cartel violence, and travel advisories should be checked before you go. Ride in daylight, stay on main roads and ask locally about current conditions. Food is a reason to stop, from gorditas filled with stews to asado de boda, the rich red chile pork served at weddings.
t.lestiny@49.2,19.4:
Leštiny is a small village in the Orava region of northern Slovakia, a short distance from Dolný Kubín, and its pride is a wooden Lutheran church that looks, from outside, more like a large farmhouse than a place of worship. This is one of the articular churches, built under strict conditions imposed in the late seventeenth century, and it is part of the World Heritage Site of Wooden Churches of the Slovak part of the Carpathian Mountain Area, inscribed in 2008.

The story behind it is fascinating. After decades of religious conflict in the Kingdom of Hungary, the Diet of Sopron in 1681 allowed Protestants to build churches, but only in designated places, called articles, and under restrictions: they had to be made of wood, without stone foundations, without towers and outside the centre of the village. The result was a church that disguised itself, plain outside and richly painted within. Inside Leštiny, the walls and ceiling are covered with floral decoration, biblical scenes and inscriptions, and a beautiful altar and pulpit glow in the light from small windows.

Orava is a land of rivers, hills and forests, with the Orava river winding through it and the mountains of the Malá Fatra and the Western Tatras on the horizon. A few kilometres away, at Oravský Podzámok, Orava Castle rises on a sheer rock above the river, one of the most dramatic castles in Central Europe. It famously appeared in the 1922 film Nosferatu. The poet Pavol Országh Hviezdoslav, a giant of Slovak literature, came from this region, and Dolný Kubín celebrates him.

Riding in Orava is excellent. Route 70 follows the Orava river past the castle, with gentle curves and views, while minor roads climb into the hills with tight bends and quiet villages. The road to Zuberec and the Western Tatras is especially beautiful, and the Oravská priehrada reservoir to the north makes a pleasant stop. Weather is changeable, with rain and cool temperatures even in summer, and snow from November to April at higher elevations.

Dolný Kubín, five kilometres away, covers fuel, groceries, garages and a decent lunch. Local specialities include bryndza cheese, sheep's milk products and smoked cheeses, and the region's traditional wooden architecture can be seen in open-air museums as well as in villages like this one.
t.durrenstein lassingtal@47.7,15.0:
Dürrenstein-Lassingtal is a wilderness area in the Ybbstal Alps of Lower Austria, where the limestone mountains rise above deep valleys covered with forests of beech, spruce and fir. It includes the Rothwald, one of the largest remaining primeval forests in Central Europe, a forest that has never been logged, and it is part of the transnational World Heritage Site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe. Here trees grow, die and decay naturally, creating a rich habitat for insects, fungi, birds and mammals.

Access to the core of the wilderness is restricted, and visits are possible only on guided tours. But the surrounding valleys and mountains offer plenty to see and do. Lunz am See, a small village with a lake, has a long tradition of scientific research, and nearby, in a sinkhole called the Grünloch, scientists recorded one of the lowest temperatures ever measured in Central Europe, around minus 52 degrees, a striking reminder of how cold air pools in these limestone hollows.

This is serious riding country. Roads wind through narrow valleys, past rivers and lakes, and over passes with views of the mountains. The road through the Lassing valley towards Wildalpen, the climb to the Hochkar ski area and the roads around Göstling and Lunz are all worth riding. The tarmac is mostly well kept, traffic is light and the corners keep coming. Watch for wildlife, especially deer, and for logging trucks.

The region is sparsely populated, with small villages and farms. The valleys are cool and damp, and the forests smell of moss and resin. In spring, the beech trees burst into fresh green, and in autumn they turn copper and gold. Winter brings snow, and some roads, like the one to Hochkar, may be closed or require chains.

Fuel is not plentiful in these valleys. Göstling and Lunz are small villages, so fill up before you enter the area; the nearest town listed with more than five thousand people is Trofaiach, thirty-five kilometres away, though other towns lie along the main valleys. Food is traditional Austrian: schnitzel, goulash, dumplings and cakes. A stop at a mountain inn for coffee and strudel, with nothing but forest noise around you, makes the slow fuel logistics easy to forgive.
t.former hacienda of cieneguilla@21.7,-102:
The Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road of the interior, ran for more than two thousand kilometres from Mexico City north to Santa Fe in present-day New Mexico, and for close to three centuries it carried silver south and settlers, soldiers, priests and goods north. Along it grew towns, missions, bridges and haciendas, and the former hacienda of Cieneguilla, on the high plain in the state of Aguascalientes, is one of the places inscribed by UNESCO in 2010 as part of that route.

A hacienda in colonial Mexico was a world unto itself: a big house for the owner, chapel, granaries, stables, workshops and housing for the workers, surrounded by fields and pasture. Many of them supplied the mining towns of the north with grain, mules and meat. What survives at Cieneguilla is the shell of such an estate, with thick walls and arches of local stone standing on the plain, a reminder of the wealth and the hardship that the silver road brought with it.

The landscape here is the high central plateau, around nineteen hundred metres above sea level, with dry grassland, mesquite and nopal cactus, farms irrigated in the river valleys, and mountains on the horizon. The light is sharp and the sky enormous. Mornings can be cool, even cold in winter, and afternoons hot; in the summer rainy season, storms build up over the hills in the afternoon and break with sudden force, so plan to ride early.

The roads in the area are a mixture: wide, straight federal highways between the cities, with fast traffic and heavy trucks, and smaller country roads that are quieter but can have potholes, speed bumps in every village, and the odd herd of cattle. The topes, the speed bumps, are the first thing every rider in Mexico learns to fear; some are unmarked and brutal. To the west, the road toward Calvillo, known for its guavas, climbs into hills with better curves.

Fuel is easy in Villa Hidalgo, fifteen kilometres away, and in Aguascalientes city, a short ride to the east, which has everything. The city is famous for the Feria de San Marcos, one of the biggest fairs in Mexico, held in spring, and for its old hot springs, which gave the place its name. Eat birria or enchiladas in a market and remember that you are standing on a road that once ran all the way to New Mexico.
t.tuy mayau@23.1,-101.4:
Out in the high desert of San Luis Potosí, near the town of Charcas, lies a landscape that for the Wixárika people, often called the Huichol, is the most sacred place on earth. Wirikuta is the land where, in their cosmology, the sun was born, and each year pilgrims walk or travel hundreds of kilometres from their homeland in the Sierra Madre Occidental of Jalisco and Nayarit to reach it, visiting a chain of sacred springs, hills and other sites along the way.

The landscape here is open and austere: creosote bush, yucca, barrel cactus and grasses on a plain at around two thousand metres, broken by the long ridges of the Sierra de Catorce. The light is clear and hard, the days hot, the nights cold. For the Wixárika, peyote, the small cactus that grows in this desert, is a sacrament at the heart of their ceremonies, and for that reason it is illegal and deeply disrespectful for outsiders to collect it. Visitors should approach these places as one would a church or a temple, without leaving marks, taking anything away or intruding on ceremonies. Mining projects in Wirikuta have been strongly opposed by the Wixárika and their supporters, and the area remains contested.

Most riders who come here are heading for Real de Catorce, the old silver-mining town high up in the Sierra de Catorce, once among the richest in New Spain, then almost deserted, and now revived by tourism. The final approach is a long cobbled road that climbs through the mountains and enters the town through the Ogarrio tunnel, more than two kilometres long, single lane and controlled with alternating traffic. The cobbles are rough and slippery in the wet, so take them steadily. Below the town, the desert plain stretches out toward Wirikuta, and the views at sunset are unforgettable.

Fuel is available in Charcas, about twenty-five kilometres away, and in Matehuala, the larger town on the main highway to the east; carry water and sun protection, because there is little shade in the desert. In Real de Catorce, small restaurants serve gorditas, enchiladas potosinas and hot drinks against the cold evenings. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons; summer heat is intense on the plain, and winter nights in the mountains can drop below freezing.
t.tulln kastell hufeisenturm@48.3,16.1:
Egon Schiele was born in Tulln in 1890, in the station building where his father was stationmaster, and the town that produced one of the most provocative painters of Viennese modernism is today a quiet, prosperous place on the Danube, known as Austria's garden town. Long before that, it was the Roman fort of Comagena, part of the frontier along the Danube that protected the Roman province of Noricum. One of the fort's towers has survived remarkably well: the so-called Salzturm, a horseshoe-shaped tower on the riverbank, one of the best-preserved Roman structures in Austria. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire – The Danube Limes, listed by UNESCO in 2021.

The tower stands near the river promenade, and a short walk takes you to the Schiele Museum and the Egon Schiele birthplace at the railway station. The town has a large garden show area and is known for its flower festivals. In summer, the riverbank is lively with cafés and walkers.

For riders, Tulln is a good stop on the way between Vienna and the Wachau. The roads along the Danube are flat and fast, with long straights and gentle curves, and traffic can be heavy, especially near Vienna. To the north, across the river, the Wagram, a long loess terrace covered in vineyards, offers more interesting riding on small roads through wine villages, and beyond lies the Kamptal, with its winding valley road and wineries. To the west, the Wachau, a stretch of the Danube between Krems and Melk lined with vineyards, castles and monasteries, is one of the most beautiful river landscapes in Europe and a classic ride, though busy on summer weekends.

To the south, the Wienerwald, the Vienna Woods, rises in forested hills, with twisty roads popular with riders. Their popularity with riders has brought lower speed limits and frequent police checks on the favourite routes, so ride them with restraint and check for any local restrictions before you go.

Tulln, a town of over twelve thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a Wiener Schnitzel with potato salad, or in autumn, a glass of Sturm, the young fermenting wine, in a Heuriger, a wine tavern, in one of the villages of the Wagram. And stand for a moment by the Roman tower on the riverbank, watching the barges go by, and think about the soldiers who watched the same river nearly two thousand years ago.
t.litomysl castle@49.9,16.3:
Bedřich Smetana, the composer of Má vlast and The Bartered Bride, was born in 1824 in the brewery of Litomyšl Castle, where his father was the brewer, and the town has never forgotten it. Every summer, the castle courtyard hosts an opera festival named after him, Smetanova Litomyšl, and his birthplace in the brewery building is a small museum. The castle itself, an elegant Renaissance building with arcaded courtyards, was built in the sixteenth century for the Pernštejn family and is famous for its sgraffito decoration: the facades are covered with thousands of rectangular panels, each with a slightly different pattern. It was listed by UNESCO in 1999.

Litomyšl lies in eastern Bohemia, on the old trade route between Bohemia and Moravia, and its long town square, lined with arcaded houses, is one of the largest in the Czech Republic. The town has a reputation for culture and education, with schools, museums and galleries, and its modern architecture, much of it built since the 1990s, has won awards. Nearby, the Portmoneum, a house painted inside by the artist Josef Váchal, is a strange and wonderful place.

For riders, eastern Bohemia offers gentle, pleasant riding. The roads around Litomyšl pass through rolling farmland, forests and villages, with gentle curves and generally good surfaces, and traffic is light outside the main routes. To the north, the Orlické hory, the Eagle Mountains, on the border with Poland, offer more challenging roads through forests and hills. To the south, the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands, the Vysočina, are a quiet region of lakes, forests and small towns.

The motorways and some expressways in the Czech Republic require an electronic vignette, though motorcycles are exempt; check the current rules before you go. The main roads are free. Speed limits are enforced, and police checks are common.

Litomyšl, a town of over ten thousand people about a kilometre away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a plate of svíčková, beef in a creamy vegetable sauce with dumplings and cranberries, a classic Czech dish, or roast pork with dumplings and sauerkraut, and wash it down with a glass of Czech beer, preferably from a local brewery. In the evening, sit in the castle gardens or on the square and listen for the music drifting from the courtyard if the festival is on.
t.hronsek@48.6,19.2:
The wooden church at Hronsek looks at first like a large barn with a steep shingle roof, standing among old lime trees in a village in the Hron valley. It is in fact one of the rarest kinds of building in Central Europe: an articular church, built for Lutheran worshippers in 1726 under strict conditions imposed by the Catholic Habsburg authorities. After decades of religious conflict, the Hungarian diet of 1681 allowed Protestants to build churches in certain places, but they had to be made entirely of wood, without stone foundations or metal nails, outside the village centre, with no tower, and built within a single year. The Hronsek church was constructed of spruce and larch, held together by wooden joints, and it can seat more than a thousand people. A separate wooden bell tower stands beside it. Along with other wooden churches in the region, it was listed by UNESCO in 2008.

Inside, the simple timber structure is softened by galleries, a painted altar and an organ, and the scent of old wood is strong. The church is still used for services, and the guides are proud of it.

The Hron valley lies between Zvolen and Banská Bystrica, two of the main towns of central Slovakia. Zvolen has a Gothic castle in the middle of town, and on the hill above stands the ruin of the older Pustý hrad, one of the largest castle sites in Central Europe. Banská Bystrica was a rich mining town, with a beautiful square surrounded by burgher houses, and a museum dedicated to the Slovak National Uprising of 1944, which began here against the Nazi occupation and the collaborationist government. Nearby, Kováčová is a small spa village with thermal baths.

The riding is good. The main roads through the valley are busy and fast, but the side roads into the surrounding mountains, the Poľana, the Kremnica hills and the Low Tatras to the north, offer twisty climbs through forests and meadows, with little traffic. The road north from Banská Bystrica towards Donovaly and the Low Tatras is a favourite with Slovak riders.

Zvolen, eight kilometres away, has fuel, garages and plenty of places to eat. Try bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese and bacon, the national dish. Slovak motorways require an electronic vignette; the minor roads do not.
t.koyasan niukanshofu jinja@34.3,135.5:
In the foothills below Mount Kōya, in the village of Kudoyama, stands the Niukanshōfu shrine, dedicated to the deities who protect the sacred mountain. In the ninth century, the monk Kūkai, known after his death as Kōbō Daishi, founded a monastery on the plateau of Kōyasan as the centre of Shingon Buddhism, and he established an administrative office here, at the foot of the mountain, to manage the supply of the monastery. Nearby, the temple of Jison-in is associated with Kūkai's mother, who according to tradition lived here because women were not allowed on the mountain, and her son came down to visit her. The shrine and temple mark the start of the Chōishi-michi, the pilgrim path to Kōyasan, marked every 109 metres by stone posts, which climbs about twenty kilometres to the monastery. The sites are part of the UNESCO listing of the Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range.

Kudoyama is a quiet village in the valley of the Kinokawa river, surrounded by orchards. The region is famous for its persimmons, and in autumn the trees are hung with orange fruit, and dried persimmons hang from the eaves of farmhouses.

The ride up to Kōyasan is one of the great experiences of the Kii peninsula. The roads climb from the Kinokawa valley through cedar forests in a seemingly endless series of tight bends, steep and narrow in places, to the plateau at around eight hundred metres. The surface is excellent, but the road is busy with tour buses at weekends, and the bends demand concentration. Once at the top, you enter a town of more than a hundred temples, many offering lodging to pilgrims, with vegetarian Buddhist cuisine and morning prayers. The Okunoin cemetery, with hundreds of thousands of graves among giant cedars, leading to Kūkai's mausoleum, is unforgettable, especially at dusk.

Further on, the Kōya-Ryūjin Skyline runs south along the ridges towards Ryūjin hot springs, a wonderful, flowing mountain road with views over endless forested peaks.

Hashimoto, about seven kilometres away, has fuel, convenience stores and restaurants. Fuel is available in the town of Kōya on the plateau too, but stations on the mountain roads are rare. In winter, snow and ice make the roads dangerous; spring and autumn, with cherry blossoms or red maples, are the best seasons.
t.ujigami jinja@34.9,135.8:
Uji is a small city on the river of the same name, south of Kyoto, and it holds two treasures that face each other across the water. On the west bank stands the Byōdō-in, a temple whose Phoenix Hall, built in 1053, appears on the Japanese ten-yen coin. On the east bank, up a quiet lane, is Ujigami-jinja, a modest shrine whose main hall is considered the oldest surviving Shinto shrine building in Japan, dating from the late Heian period, in the eleventh century. Its simple wooden structure, with a cypress-bark roof, stands in a small courtyard surrounded by trees, and it is far less crowded than the Byōdō-in. Both are part of the UNESCO listing of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.

Uji has a literary fame too. The last ten chapters of The Tale of Genji, written by Murasaki Shikibu in the early eleventh century and often called the world's first novel, are set here, and a museum in the city is dedicated to the book. A statue of the author stands near the bridge.

Above all, Uji is famous for tea. The hills around the city have been growing green tea since the Middle Ages, and Uji matcha, the powdered green tea used in the tea ceremony, is considered among the finest in Japan. The street leading to the Byōdō-in is lined with tea shops, where you can taste matcha and buy sencha and gyokuro, and many sell green tea ice cream, green tea noodles and green tea sweets of every kind. The Uji river flows swiftly through the city, clear and green, with islands in the middle connected by bridges. In summer, cormorant fishing takes place in the evenings, a traditional technique where trained birds catch fish for the fishermen.

Riding around Uji is a mix of urban traffic and pleasant country roads. The roads south and east of the city climb into hills covered in tea plantations and forests, with tight bends and views over the valley. The roads towards Lake Biwa, following the river upstream through a gorge, are scenic and winding. Traffic is dense in the Kyoto area, and the speed limits are low.

Uji has fuel, convenience stores and restaurants. Come in spring, for the cherry blossoms along the river, or in autumn, for the maples, and arrive early to avoid the crowds.
t.kitora mounded tomb@34.5,135.8:
Kitora is a small, round burial mound on a hillside in Asuka, the cradle of the Japanese state, south of Nara. From the outside, it looks like a grassy hump, unremarkable. Inside, when researchers inserted a fibre-optic camera in 1983, they found a stone chamber painted with some of the most extraordinary images in Japanese art: the four guardian animals of the cardinal directions, the black tortoise-snake of the north, the blue dragon of the east, the white tiger of the west and the red phoenix of the south, along with figures of the twelve zodiac animals with human bodies, and on the ceiling an astronomical chart showing the constellations, one of the oldest such star charts in the world. The tomb dates from the late seventh or early eighth century, and its occupant remains unknown. To preserve them, the paintings were removed from the walls and restored, and some are displayed at the Shijin no Yakata, a museum built next to the tomb.

Asuka was the seat of the imperial court in the sixth and seventh centuries, when Buddhism arrived from Korea and China, and Japan adopted Chinese-style government, writing and culture. The area is full of traces of that time: temples, palace sites, mysterious stone sculptures like the Sakafune-ishi and the Kame-ishi, and other painted tombs, including Takamatsuzuka, opened in 1972 with paintings of court ladies.

The landscape is gentle and rural, with rice fields, persimmon orchards and low wooded hills, and in early autumn red spider lilies bloom along the edges of the paddies. Asuka has strict regulations to preserve its historic landscape, so there are no high buildings and little development.

The roads around Asuka are narrow and quiet, winding through fields and villages. The area is popular with cyclists, and you can rent bicycles in the village, which is a good way to explore the scattered sites. On a motorcycle, the roads south into the Yoshino mountains, famous for their cherry blossoms, offer more challenge, with tight bends through cedar forests.

Kashihara, Gose and Sakurai, all about seven kilometres away, have fuel, convenience stores and restaurants. The best seasons are spring and autumn. Try kakinoha-zushi, sushi wrapped in persimmon leaves, a speciality of the Nara region.
t.historic centre of the city of lagos de:
Lagos de Moreno is a colonial town in the highlands of Jalisco, the Altos, on the old Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the Royal Road of the Interior Land that linked Mexico City to Santa Fe, in what is now New Mexico. For three centuries, silver, mercury, goods and people travelled along it, and towns grew up at its stopping points. Lagos de Moreno was one of the most important, and its historic centre is part of the UNESCO listing of the Camino Real, inscribed in 2010. The town has handsome churches, including a baroque parish church with an elaborately carved façade of pink stone, mansions with wrought-iron balconies, a theatre and a hospital from the colonial era.

The town's most famous monument is a stone bridge over the river Lagos, built in the nineteenth century. According to a local story, the bridge was finished long before people were allowed to use it, and someone posted a sign saying, in effect, that this bridge was built in Lagos and is crossed from above, a dry joke that the townspeople still enjoy. Lagos also takes pride in being a cradle of the charro tradition, the Mexican horseman culture, with its elaborate costumes and competitions, and the Altos de Jalisco are known for their cattle ranches, dairy products and conservative, Catholic culture.

The landscape is high plateau, around two thousand metres, with rolling hills, mesquite, nopal cacti and farmland. The air is clear and dry, the sun intense, and the nights cool. The rainy season, from June to September, turns the hills green.

The riding is good. The roads through the Altos de Jalisco connect colonial towns like San Juan de los Lagos, a major pilgrimage centre, Teocaltiche and Encarnación de Díaz, with long, open bends and wide views. The main highway between León and Aguascalientes passes nearby, busy with trucks. The surface is generally good on the main roads, but topes, the Mexican speed bumps, appear without warning at the entrance to every village, and livestock may be on the road.

Lagos de Moreno has fuel, mechanics and plenty of restaurants. Try birria, a spicy stew of goat or beef, and the local dairy sweets. Check current travel advice for Jalisco before you go, ride in daylight, and use toll highways where possible.
t.historic ensemble of the city of sombrer:
Sombrerete is a silver town in the northwest of Zacatecas, founded in the 1550s when Spanish prospectors found rich veins of ore in the hills. The name comes from a hill nearby shaped like a small hat. In the colonial era, Sombrerete's mines produced enormous wealth, and the town grew into an important stop on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road linking Mexico City with the far north. That wealth built a remarkable collection of churches, convents and mansions, many in the pinkish local stone, and the historic ensemble is part of the UNESCO listing of the Camino Real. The Franciscan convent, the church of Santo Domingo, and the chapel of the Tercera Orden, with its unusual oval plan, are among the highlights. The town has a slightly faded, unhurried atmosphere, far from the tourist crowds of the more famous colonial cities.

The mining history is everywhere: old mine shafts on the hillsides, stone aqueducts, the haciendas where ore was processed. Mining continues in the region today, though on a smaller scale.

West of Sombrerete lies the Sierra de Órganos, a national park of strange rock formations that rise from the high plateau like the pipes of an organ, hence the name. The landscape has been used as a backdrop for many Western films, and it is easy to see why: pinnacles, boulders and mesas glowing red and gold in the evening light, with junipers and oaks among the rocks. Trails lead among the formations, and camping is possible.

The riding is high, dry and open. Sombrerete sits at over two thousand metres on the central plateau, and the roads cross wide valleys and low ranges, with long straights and sweeping bends. The main highway from Zacatecas to Durango passes through town, busy with trucks. Smaller roads lead into the mountains and to the Sierra de Órganos, with variable surfaces. Watch for livestock, topes and slow-moving vehicles. The climate is dry, with intense sun and cool nights; the rainy season, in summer, brings afternoon thunderstorms.

Sombrerete has fuel, mechanics and restaurants. Try gorditas, thick corn cakes stuffed with stews, and the local cheeses. Check the current travel advice for Zacatecas before you go, ride in daylight, and keep to main roads where possible.
t.macuipa@22.8,-102.6:
Macuipa lies on the edge of Zacatecas, the silver capital of northern Mexico, and the name points to the sacred geography of the Wixárika, the Huichol people, whose pilgrimage route passes through this region on its way from their homeland in the Sierra Madre Occidental to Wirikuta, the sacred desert in San Luis Potosí. For centuries, Wixárika pilgrims have walked this route, hundreds of kilometres long, visiting springs, hills and rocks where their deities dwell, leaving offerings and performing ceremonies. The route has recently been recognised by UNESCO. Exactly what is to be seen at Macuipa is not easy to say from a distance; treat it as a place where two very different worlds, the Spanish silver city and the indigenous sacred landscape, meet.

Zacatecas itself is a stunning city, built in a narrow ravine between hills, with a historic centre of pink stone that is a UNESCO site. The cathedral, completed in the mid-eighteenth century, has one of the most elaborate baroque façades in Mexico, covered in carvings of saints, angels and plants. Above the city rises the Cerro de la Bufa, a rocky hill crowned with a chapel and a monument to the Battle of Zacatecas of 1914, when Pancho Villa's army took the city in one of the bloodiest battles of the Mexican Revolution. A cable car crosses the city to the hill, and the Edén mine, an old silver mine in the heart of the city, can be visited by small train.

The city's silver financed much of the Spanish empire, and its mansions, churches and convents reflect that wealth. Today it is a lively university town, with festivals, music in the streets in the evenings, and a famous tradition of callejoneadas, processions with musicians and a donkey carrying mezcal through the alleys.

The riding around Zacatecas is high and dry. The city sits at about two and a half thousand metres, and the roads out cross semi-desert plateaus with cacti, mesquite and distant mountains. The highways are generally good, but the city streets are steep, narrow and cobbled, which demands care.

Zacatecas and Guadalupe have fuel, mechanics and everything else. Try asado de boda, a pork stew in a rich red chilli sauce served at weddings. Check the current travel advice for Zacatecas state before you go, and ride in daylight.
t.huiricuta maxa yaritsie@23.5,-100.9:
Wirikuta, or Huiricuta, is the sacred desert of the Wixárika people, a high, arid plain at the foot of the Sierra de Catorce in San Luis Potosí. In Wixárika belief, it is the place where the sun was born, and each year pilgrims travel here from their homeland in the Sierra Madre Occidental, hundreds of kilometres away, to collect hikuri, the peyote cactus, which plays a central role in their ceremonies, and to leave offerings at sacred sites. Maxa Yaritsié is one of those sites. The Cerro del Quemado, the burnt hill, rising above the desert near Real de Catorce, is the most sacred of all, the place where the sun first rose. Visitors should behave with respect: these are living religious sites, not tourist attractions, and collecting peyote is illegal for non-indigenous people and deeply offensive to the Wixárika.

The landscape is hauntingly beautiful. The desert plain is covered with creosote bushes, yuccas, Joshua-like palms and many kinds of cacti, and it stretches to distant mountains in every direction. The light is intense and clear, the silence total, and at night the stars are extraordinary.

Real de Catorce, above the desert in the mountains, was a rich silver mining town in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, then almost abandoned when the mines closed, and it has become a destination for travellers drawn by its ghostly atmosphere, its ruins and its cobbled streets. The only road access is through the Ogarrio tunnel, a single-lane tunnel more than two kilometres long cut through the mountain, with traffic alternating in each direction. Before that, a long cobbled road climbs from the highway into the mountains; it is bumpy and demanding on a motorcycle, especially a heavy one, but the views are worth it. In town, the streets are steep and cobbled, and a pilgrimage church draws large crowds in October for the feast of Saint Francis.

The riding on the desert roads is straight and lonely, with long distances between towns and few services. The tracks into the desert itself are sandy and rough, suitable only for experienced off-road riders. The heat is intense in summer, and the nights are cold in winter.

Matehuala, about thirty kilometres away, has fuel, mechanics and restaurants. Carry plenty of water and fill up before heading into the desert. Check the travel advice for San Luis Potosí before you go.
t.architectonic ensemble of the town of ch:
Chalchihuites is a small town in the far west of Zacatecas, on the edge of the Sierra Madre Occidental, and it lies on a stretch of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the Royal Road of the Interior Land. Its architectural ensemble, with a parish church and colonial houses around a plaza, is part of the UNESCO listing of the Camino Real. The name comes from the Nahuatl word for jade or greenstone, chalchihuitl, a reference to the turquoise-like stones found in the area, which were prized by the peoples of Mesoamerica.

The town's greatest treasure, however, is much older. A few kilometres away, the archaeological site of Alta Vista was a ceremonial centre of the Chalchihuites culture, which flourished in the first millennium AD on the northern frontier of Mesoamerica. The site sits almost exactly on the Tropic of Cancer, and its builders seem to have known it: the buildings are aligned with the sun's movements, and at the equinoxes and solstices the sun rises over the peak of a nearby mountain, the Picacho Chapín, in a precise alignment. The site includes a hall of columns, a labyrinth and platforms, and it seems to have been an astronomical observatory as well as a ceremonial centre. The area also had extensive mines, where the people of Alta Vista extracted minerals and stones, possibly traded far to the south.

The landscape is high plateau and mountains, with oak and pine forests on the slopes of the Sierra Madre and semi-desert in the valleys. The air is clear and dry, and the views are long. The town is quiet, traditional and far from the tourist trail.

The riding is excellent for those who like empty roads. The roads from Sombrerete and Súchil climb into the foothills of the Sierra Madre with gentle bends, and the scenery becomes more dramatic as you go west, towards the mountains of Durango. Traffic is minimal, but the surface is variable, with potholes and gravel in places, and livestock on the road. Topes appear at the entrance to every village.

Chalchihuites has a few shops and small restaurants, and probably fuel, but it is safer to fill up in Sombrerete, about thirty kilometres away. Check the current travel advice for Zacatecas before you go, ride in daylight, and carry water.
t.temples in the town of cuencame and cris:
Cuencamé is a small town in the semi-desert of eastern Durango, on the old Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, and it is known throughout northern Mexico for its devotion to the Cristo de Mapimí, a crucifix that is venerated in a sanctuary in the town. The image, according to tradition, was brought here in the colonial period after miracles attributed to it, and each year pilgrims arrive from across the region to pray and give thanks. The town's temples, including the parish church and the sanctuary, are part of the UNESCO listing of the Camino Real. They are simple, solid buildings, with thick walls designed to resist the heat, and their interiors are filled with offerings, candles and the quiet murmur of prayer.

The town is small, quiet and traditional, a place where life follows the rhythm of the seasons and the religious calendar. The plaza, shaded by trees, is the centre of social life in the evenings, when families gather and vendors sell snacks and ice cream.

The landscape around Cuencamé is the northern semi-desert, a vast expanse of creosote bush, mesquite, cacti and yucca, with distant ranges of bare mountains. The colours change with the light, from pale yellow at noon to deep red at sunset, and the sky is enormous. The Durango desert has been used as a backdrop for many Hollywood Westerns, and it is easy to see why.

The riding is long and straight. The main highway between Torreón and Durango passes near Cuencamé, crossing the desert with long straights and few curves, and it is used by trucks. Wind can be strong, and dust storms are possible in spring. The heat in summer is intense, and the distances between towns are long, so plan fuel and water carefully. The surface is generally good on the main highways but poorer on smaller roads. Livestock may wander onto the road, especially at night.

Cuencamé has fuel, small restaurants and shops. Try the gorditas, filled with stews, and the local cheese. Torreón, to the east, and the city of Durango, to the west, are larger towns with all services. The city of Durango has a fine colonial centre and a film museum dedicated to the many Westerns shot in the state. Check the current travel advice for Durango before you go, and ride in daylight.
t.wien canabae west und graberfeld@48.2,16:
Vienna began as a Roman legionary camp, Vindobona, on a terrace above the Danube, and its streets still follow some of the old lines. The camp itself was in what is now the inner city, around Hoher Markt, and the canabae, the civilian settlement that grew up beside it, spread out to the west and south with workshops, taverns, houses and cemeteries. The Gräberfeld, the field of graves, lay beyond, as Roman custom demanded. The remains here are mostly underground and under pavements, which suits a city that has built on every layer of its past.

Vindobona was a frontier post on the Danube limes, the long line of forts and watchtowers that marked the edge of the empire, and the legions stationed here guarded a river crossing and a trade route. Tradition says the emperor Marcus Aurelius died in the area in AD 180 while campaigning against the tribes north of the Danube, though historians argue about whether it was here or elsewhere. The Danube limes is now a World Heritage Site, and the sections in Vienna are part of that story.

Riding in Vienna is a different sport from the Alps. The city is compact and orderly, with trams, cobbles on some old streets, wet rails in rain, and sharp traffic lights that change quickly. The Ringstrasse, the grand boulevard around the old centre, is a pleasure to ride at a leisurely pace on a quiet morning, with views of the opera, parliament and town hall, but avoid the rush hour, when it is slow and tense.
