Parking for motorcycles is easier than for cars, and many streets have designated bays, so look for those rather than leaving the bike on the pavement.

Fuel is easy to find on the main roads in and out of the city, though the immediate centre has few stations, so top up at the outskirts. Food ranges from the classic coffee house, with its newspapers and slices of cake, to the wine taverns called Heurigen on the edge of town, where new wine and cold cuts are served in gardens in summer. A morning is enough to see the Roman remains at Hoher Markt and walk through the old quarter, and then you can ride up to the Kahlenberg for the view.
t.richu tenno ryo kofun@34.6,135.5:
You cannot really see a kofun. That is the first lesson of Richu-tenno-ryo, one of the great keyhole-shaped tombs of the Mozu group in Sakai, south of Osaka. These are burial mounds built in the fifth century for the early rulers of Japan, shaped like a keyhole with a round back and a wide front, and surrounded by moats. The Richu mound is about three hundred and sixty metres long, among the largest in the country, and you walk around the water on a path, catching glimpses through the trees of a green hill that looks like a wooded island. From the ground it simply looks like a park.

To grasp the shape you have to look from above, and the nearby city offices have an observation deck for that purpose. The whole Mozu-Furuichi group was added to the UNESCO list in 2019. The tombs are still managed by the Imperial Household Agency, which restricts entry, so the stop is about walking the perimeter, reading the signs and imagining the labour involved, hundreds of thousands of people moving earth with baskets.

Sakai is a big city of nearly eight hundred thousand, with a long history as a free merchant port and a centre for knife-making that still produces some of the finest kitchen blades in the world. Fuel and food are easy everywhere, and the bay roads give you straightforward riding, though honestly this is dense urban Japan, with traffic lights, expressways, factories and little scenery. The Hanshin Expressway runs along the bay and costs tolls, and local roads are flat and steady.

The second half of the ride goes inland to Hōryū-ji, in Nara prefecture, which has the oldest wooden buildings in the world, dating from the seventh century. The two sites together tell the story of how early Japan buried its rulers and then built temples for its faith. Choose a spring or autumn morning, before the heat and the haze, and bring patience for the slow pace of local roads. Takaishi, to the south, is a quieter town with a pleasant coastline and good places to eat grilled fish.
t.kumano sanzan fudarakusan ji@33.6,135.9:
Fudarakusan-ji is a small temple on the coast of the Kii Peninsula, in the town of Nachikatsuura, and its odd history is a sea journey. In the old days some monks believed Fudaraku, the paradise of the bodhisattva Kannon, lay far across the ocean to the south, and from this beach they set off in boats nailed shut, with a little food and water, to sail toward it and not come back. The practice is called Fudaraku Tokai, and the temple remembers the monks who made the voyage, which gives the sea in front of it a haunting quality.

It is one stop on the great pilgrimage network of Kumano, where the old trails, the Kumano Kodō, link the three grand shrines of Hongū, Hayatama and Nachi. Nachi is the one here, with its famous waterfall, a hundred and thirty metres high, which is itself an object of worship, falling in a single thread beside a red pagoda against dark forest. Walk the stone steps from the road, and the air turns cool and damp and smells of cedar.

The town, a fishing harbour, is famous for tuna, and the market and restaurants serve it every way you can think of. Shingū, a few tens of kilometres to the east, is a town of about thirty thousand and the sensible place for fuel and a longer meal, but the coast has pumps at intervals as well, and the road is never remote.

For a rider the Kii coast is the quiet side of the Kansai region, a long, wavy road along rocky headlands and inlets. Route 42 follows the shore, with views of the Pacific, tunnels and small fishing villages, and the surface is generally good but the traffic includes trucks and slow campers. Rain is heavy here, one of the wettest parts of Japan, and typhoons in late summer and early autumn can close roads, so check the forecast. Spring and late autumn are the sweetest seasons, with mild air and clear light on the sea, and leaving early lets you have the waterfall steps to yourself before the tour buses arrive.
Shingū sits where the Kumano River meets the Pacific, and Hayatama Taisha stands in the middle of the town, a vermilion shrine among tall trees, so close to the ordinary streets that it feels like part of daily life. It is one of the three grand shrines of Kumano, and the legend of its founding is tied to a great rock above the town, Gotobiki-iwa, where the deity is said to have descended before moving to the shrine below. The rock is reached by a steep stone stairway through the woods and the view from it is wide and quiet.

In the shrine's grounds stands an old tree, a Nagi, said to be nearly a thousand years old, and sacred to pilgrims who carry its leaf as an amulet. The three-legged crow, Yatagarasu, the divine guide who showed the first emperor the way through the Kii mountains, appears on charms and flags everywhere here, and also on the badge of the Japanese national football team, which is a useful fact for football fans. The stone paths and the cedar forest make a walk of twenty minutes feel older than it is.

Shingū is a town of around thirty thousand, so it has fuel, supermarkets and a few good restaurants, and it is the natural base for the area. The riding is excellent in and out of town. Upstream the Kumano River twists through a deep forested valley, past the gorge of Dorokyō, where jet boats run in summer, and over the passes toward Hongū and the high country. Roads in the mountains are narrow, with tight bends, shaded surfaces that stay damp and wet leaves in autumn, so be careful on corners and expect rockfall after storms. Traffic is light except at holiday times.

The Kii mountains are an old region of faith, where Buddhism, Shinto and mountain asceticism blended, and the pilgrim routes were walked by emperors and commoners alike for a thousand years. That mixture is why UNESCO treats the whole area as a sacred landscape, with the trails, shrines and temples listed together. Come in spring or autumn, bring rain gear whatever the forecast, and leave time for a slow lunch. The mountains are better after you have eaten.
t.iza kelemantia@47.7,18.2:
The Danube makes a border here, and so it did two thousand years ago. On the north bank, at Iža in what is now Slovakia, stood the Roman fort of Celemantia, and on the south bank, near Almásfüzitő, another fort called Azaum guarded the Pannonian shore. Together they were part of the Danube Limes, the river frontier of the Roman Empire, and UNESCO listed sections of it in 2021. Close by, at Szőny, lay Brigetio, a legionary base and a real town with an amphitheatre. The river was the road, the wall and the defence all in one, and the legions patrolled it in boats.

The modern border towns of Komárom and Komárno share a story that is half Roman, half Habsburg. They were one town until the treaty of 1920 drew the border down the middle of the Danube, and now Komárom lies in Hungary and Komárno in Slovakia, joined by a bridge. Komárom has a huge nineteenth-century fortress, the Monostor, one of the largest in Central Europe, and the old town has a market square with a plain, handsome look. The fort at Iža is a Slovakian site and the nearby Hungarian bank has several others.

The riding is flat and straightforward, along the broad Danube plain, with fields of sunflowers and wheat and a distant line of low hills. The roads are decent but often busy with lorries, because the main road from Budapest to Vienna and the motorway cross this country. Back lanes along the river are quiet, with a few villages and the odd fisherman's hut. A strong wind is common, and in summer the air is hot and heavy. Early autumn, when the light is long and gold, is the pleasant time.

Komárom has nearly twenty thousand people and good fuel and food, and Komárno across the bridge is bigger. Both have thermal baths, since this part of Hungary sits over hot water. Try a bowl of halászlé, the paprika fish soup of the Danube, at a riverside restaurant, and finish with a coffee. Bring your passport for the bridge, though the border is open now, and be ready for the heavy traffic in the centre.
t.gango ji@34.7,135.8:
Nara lives in the shadow of its grand temples, Todai-ji and Kofuku-ji, but Gango-ji is the one with the best sense of age. It started life in Asuka, in the late sixth century, as Asuka-dera, the first true Buddhist temple in Japan, founded by the powerful Soga clan. When the capital moved to Heijo-kyo in the early eighth century, the monks followed, and the temple was rebuilt on a new site in what is now the Naramachi district, with some of the original roof tiles carried across the plain and reused. You can still pick out the older, darker tiles on the roof of the main hall, a faint line of continuity across thirteen centuries.

The surroundings are Naramachi's old merchant streets, lined with narrow wooden townhouses with latticed windows, most of them now tiny shops, cafes and guesthouses. It is nothing like the broad avenues and deer parks of the main sights, and for that reason it is a good place to leave the bike in a car park and walk. The temple grounds are small, quiet and a little ragged in a way that is entirely appealing, with stone Buddhas under the trees and a lotus pond that catches the light in summer.

Riding in Nara city is slow and constrained. The roads are narrow, one-way in places, and the deer, which are famously sacred and famously aggressive about snacks, wander into traffic near the park. Parking a motorcycle in the old town is difficult, so use a car park on the edge. Once you are out of town, the Yamanobe-no-michi, one of the oldest roads in Japan, runs toward Tenri along the foot of the hills, and the back lanes through the persimmon and rice country of the Nara basin are a delight in autumn.

Nara-shi has plenty of fuel and any number of convenience stores and noodle shops. For a local treat, try kakinoha-zushi, the persimmon-leaf-wrapped sushi from this part of Japan, and Nara's pickles, which have been around for centuries. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; July and August are sticky and hot.
t.takamatsuzuka mounded tomb@34.5,135.8:
The mound itself is easy to miss: a small, round hump of grass in a quiet corner of the Asuka countryside, surrounded by rice fields and persimmon trees. What made it famous is what was inside. In 1972, archaeologists opened a stone chamber here and found painted walls, with women in bright, flowing robes, a procession of men, and the guardian animals of the four directions, among them the Blue Dragon and the White Tiger. The paintings date from around the end of the seventh century or the start of the eighth, and show the strong influence of Korea and China on the early Japanese court. It was the first wall painting of its kind found in Japan and caused a sensation.

The story since then is a cautionary one. The murals began to deteriorate from mould and the tomb was eventually dismantled in the 2000s, with the painted plaster removed in sections to a controlled conservation facility. The mound stands as a landscape feature now, with a small museum and a replica of the paintings nearby, which is the best that can be done. It is oddly humbling to stand here knowing the original is hidden away, and it says something about how fragile all this art is.

Asuka is where the Yamato state took shape, and the whole village is dotted with earlier and stranger relics: the huge stone chamber of Ishibutai, the mysterious carved granite figures, tumuli on nearly every hillside. The roads between them are narrow and quiet, most of them barely wide enough for two cars, with rice fields on both sides and low hills in the distance. A bicycle is the traditional way to see it, but a small motorcycle works as well provided you go slowly and give way to the farm trucks. Spring brings cherry blossom and rapeseed, autumn the red spider lilies along the paddy banks.

Kashihara and Sakurai are the nearest real towns and both have fuel, shops and plenty of places to eat. The Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes begin farther south, and this part of Nara is the northern gateway, so you may see walkers heading toward Yoshino with their staves and their scallop-shell badges. The weather is hot and muggy from June to September, and winter can be cold but is rarely snowy on the plain.
t.sanctuary of plateros@23.2,-102.8:
Plateros is a small town on the edge of the high desert plateau in Zacatecas, a few kilometres from the silver city of Fresnillo, and it exists, more or less, because of one small figure on an altar. The Santo Nino de Atocha, a child dressed as a pilgrim and carrying a basket and a staff, is revered here as a protector of travellers, prisoners and the sick. The devotion came from Spain, where the original image belongs to the shrine of Atocha in Madrid, and it was carried across the Atlantic by the Spanish miners who came for Zacatecas silver. The sanctuary at Plateros became one of the most important pilgrimage sites in Mexico.

Inside, the walls are almost covered by small tin paintings and photographs left by people who believe the child answered a prayer. These retablos and ex-votos are charmingly crude and sometimes startling, with car crashes, operations, floods and narrow escapes, each with a short, painfully sincere caption. It is hard not to be moved. Outside, the market stalls sell candles, baby shoes for the figure, and little clay toys, and the pilgrims arrive in groups on foot, by bus, and on bicycle. The sanctuary is part of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro listing, the old silver road that ran from Mexico City to the northern frontier.

For the rider, this is good open-country motorcycling, though not exactly twisty. Highway 45 runs through a plain of mesquite, nopal cactus and dry grassland at about 2,200 metres, so the air is thin and the nights are cold, even when the days are warm. Distances are long, trucks are many, and shoulders are narrow. The main interest is the wide sky and the hills in the distance, red and violet at sunset. In summer, sudden storms roll in with intense lightning.

Fresnillo, six kilometres away, is a mining city of well over a hundred thousand people, with fuel, hotels and plenty of tacos and fruit juices. Zacatecas city, with its pink-stone baroque centre and cable car, is a rewarding hour or so to the south-east.
t.historic centre of the city of durango@2:
Durango was founded in 1563 by Francisco de Ibarra as the capital of Nueva Vizcaya, a huge northern province that stretched toward the unconquered frontier, and it still has the look of a frontier capital that became rich and then politely stopped. The historic centre is a tidy grid of colonial buildings in pink and yellow stone, with the Plaza de Armas at its core and the great baroque cathedral facing it. Mining money, mostly silver, paid for the arcades, mansions and theatres, and the streets are remarkably free of the clutter you find in larger cities.

Durango also has an unlikely cinematic history. Its dry plains and sierra made it a favourite location for American Westerns from the 1950s on, and John Wayne, among others, shot films here. You can still visit an old film set outside the city. The city's other claim to fame is its scorpions: the alacran is the local emblem, there is a scorpion festival, and the sellers in the market offer them in candy form. The food is good, too. Caldillo durangueno, a beef and chile stew, and the thick gorditas are staples.

The riding that matters begins to the west. The highway from Durango to Mazatlan crosses the Sierra Madre Occidental in one of Mexico's most famous mountain drives, famous for its long climbs, switchbacks and the stretch known as the Espinazo del Diablo, the Devil's Backbone, where the road runs along a narrow ridge with drops on either side. A modern bridge, the Baluarte, which is among the highest cable-stayed bridges in the world, now carries part of the route. It is a serious road, with fog, trucks and occasional rockfalls, but it is magnificent when the weather is clear. Durango city itself sits at about 1,900 metres, so mornings are crisp.

The city has all the fuel, hotels and restaurants you need, and the old centre is easy to walk in the evening, when families fill the plazas. If you are planning the mountain road, fill up before you leave and give yourself daylight; the sierra has its share of long stretches without services.
t.budapest@47.5,19.0:
Budapest is two cities that were joined in 1873: hilly, historic Buda on the west bank of the Danube, and flat, lively Pest on the east. The river between them is wide and powerful, crossed by a string of bridges, of which the Chain Bridge, opened in 1849, is the oldest and most graceful. From the Buda side, the castle hill rises above the water with its palace and the spire of Matthias Church, and across the river the neo-Gothic Parliament building stretches along the bank, lit gold at night. It is one of the best-looking capitals in Europe, and it knows it.

The city also sits on a network of hot springs, which is why it has some of the finest thermal baths on the continent. The Gellert baths, in a grand Art Nouveau hotel, the Szechenyi baths in the City Park with their yellow baroque halls, and the older Ottoman bathhouses from the sixteenth century are all good places to recover from a day in the saddle. Old men play chess in the steaming outdoor pools, and in winter the sight of steam rising into the cold air is a marvel. The food is as warming, with goulash, lángos, which is fried dough with sour cream and cheese, and chimney cake from the street stalls.

The ride called the Danube Bend begins here, and it is one of Hungary's best. The road heads north along the river, past Szentendre, an artists' town of cobbled lanes and church towers, to Visegrad, where a ruined hilltop fortress commands a sharp turn in the Danube, and on to Esztergom, where a huge basilica dominates the skyline on the border with Slovakia. The road is gentle and scenic, with long views, vineyards and ferry crossings, though weekends bring heavy traffic.

In the city, riding takes concentration. Trams run on rails that can be slippery, the cobbled streets are rough and parking is limited. Fuel is available at stations throughout the city and on the ring road, the M0. Summer is hot and crowded, and spring and early autumn are perfect, with mild temperatures and fewer visitors. Beware of speed cameras, and leave the bike behind when you visit the baths.
t.wachau cultural landscape@48.4,15.4:
Between Melk and Krems, the Danube runs through a valley of steep terraced vineyards, apricot orchards and tiny medieval towns, and the whole stretch is a UNESCO cultural landscape. The Wachau is one of the most beautiful river valleys in Europe, and it has been shaped by human hands for two thousand years. Walls of dry stone hold the terraces in place, and above them, forests climb to the plateau. The vineyards produce some of Austria's best white wines, mostly Gruner Veltliner and Riesling, and the orchards produce the Marille, the apricot, which blossoms in April and is made into jam, schnapps and dumplings in July.

Spitz and Weissenkirchen are two of the prettiest villages. Spitz has a church with a crooked tower, narrow lanes and a famous vineyard slope, and Weissenkirchen has a fortified church and a lively wine tavern culture. Between them lies Durnstein, with the blue tower of its baroque abbey and a ruined castle above, where, according to tradition, King Richard the Lionheart was held prisoner in 1192 after returning from the Crusades. You can take a small ferry across the river at Spitz, one of the few left on the Danube, and drink a glass of wine in a courtyard, called a Heuriger when the winemaker serves his own.

The riding along the river is gentle, with the road following the valley floor. It is a delight on a weekday, with the river on one side and the vineyards on the other, but on sunny weekends, the Wachau fills with cyclists, tourists and motorbikes, and traffic can slow to a crawl. For a quieter experience, take the side roads up to the plateau, through forest and farmland, where the views over the valley are splendid. The best seasons are spring, for the blossom, and autumn, for the grape harvest and the colours.

Spitz is small, and fuel is better bought in Krems, the larger town to the east, though villages along the river have a petrol pump or two. Wine taverns serve cold plates and local wine, and many have gardens by the river. If you plan to taste wine, give yourself time, or leave the riding for the next morning.
t.st johann im mauerthale wachtturm@48.3,1:
Above the Wachau, in the forested hills on the south bank, a watchtower stood in the Roman period, and its stones are a quiet reminder that this valley was once the border of an empire. The Danube was the northern frontier of the province of Noricum, and the Romans guarded it with forts and signal towers every few kilometres, a chain that now forms part of the UNESCO listing for the Danube Limes. The tower near St Johann im Mauerthale was one of these, placed to see along the river and warn of anyone crossing from the north. Not much remains but the foundations, and they sit in a place with a long view.

St Johann im Mauerthale is a tiny hamlet with a small church in the hills above the village of Aggsbach, in a landscape of woods and clearings. Aggsbach itself has the ruins of a Carthusian monastery, and above it stands the castle of Aggstein, a ruin on a rock spur high over the Danube. Its most famous owner, a medieval robber baron of the Kuenringer family, is said to have imprisoned captives on a tiny rock ledge, called the Rosengartlein, the little rose garden, to extort ransom, and let them starve if they refused to pay. Whatever the truth, the castle is a dramatic sight and a good walk.

The riding in these hills is quieter than along the river, with narrow, winding lanes through woods, orchards and farms. The surfaces are mostly good, though a few are patched or gravelly, and the gradients can be steep. Weather in the hills is changeable, and the fog in autumn can be thick. The lane from Spitz up to the plateau and the Jauerling, the highest point of the area at 960 metres, is a pleasure, with long views and a sense of space. Traffic is light, and the farm shops sell apricot jam and schnapps.

Spitz, three kilometres away, has a few shops and cafes, and Krems is the nearest place to be sure of fuel. Look for a farm stall selling honey and cheese, and try the apricot cake in a village inn. In late summer, the plums are ripe, and in autumn, the walnut harvest begins, and the smell of wood smoke fills the air.
t.historic centre of vienna@48.2,16.4:
Vienna's historic centre has been rebuilt many times, but it never lost its sense of itself as the capital of an empire. The medieval city grew around the cathedral of St Stephen, whose patterned tile roof and soaring south tower have dominated the skyline since the fourteenth century, and later the Habsburgs added the Hofburg palace, the baroque palaces of the nobility and the grand squares. In the 1850s, the old city walls were pulled down and replaced by the Ringstrasse, a wide boulevard lined with the Opera, the Parliament, the university, the city hall and the museums, all in historic styles, which is itself a part of the listed ensemble.

What makes Vienna special is not only the grandeur but the way it is lived in. The coffee houses, with marble tables, newspapers on wooden holders and waiters in black, are a cultural institution of their own. The Sachertorte, the apple strudel and the Wiener Schnitzel are all served in the old places, and the evening wine taverns of the suburbs, the Heurigen, serve new wine and cold plates in gardens. Music is everywhere, and the city's history as home to Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert and Mahler is part of the air.

The ride called Zwentendorf refers to a Roman fort on the Danube, and a fine day trip leads west along the river from the city. In the city itself, riding is slow, with tram lines, cobbles and a lot of traffic. The Ring is wide enough to be easy, but the inner streets are narrow, and parking in the first district is expensive, so park outside and use the tram. For a taste of the countryside, the Kahlenberg and the Wienerwald hills on the northern edge of the city offer winding roads, forest and views over the city and the Danube.

Fuel is available in all districts and on the main roads out. Austria requires a vignette for the motorways, including for motorbikes, so be sure to buy one before using them. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild weather and fewer visitors than in summer. In winter, the Christmas markets fill the squares, and the cold can be sharp.
t.hakuchoryo kofun@34.6,135.6:
South-east of Osaka, on the plain where the rivers of the Yamato basin spill out toward the bay, the land is dotted with enormous green islands. They are kofun, the keyhole-shaped burial mounds that the ruling clans of Japan raised in the fourth to sixth centuries, and the cluster at Furuichi is one of the two big groups that were inscribed as World Heritage in 2019, the Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group. Hakuchoryo is among them, traditionally held to be the tomb of Prince Yamato Takeru, a hero of the ancient chronicles.

The legend explains the name. When the prince died on a campaign far from home, so the Kojiki tells us, his spirit rose from the grave as a great white bird, a hakucho, and flew toward the land of Yamato, settling here and there along the way. Mounds were raised at each place where it landed, and this is one of them. The mound is keyhole-shaped, with a round rear section and a square front, and a broad moat surrounds it, filled with water and often with ducks.

You do not walk on a kofun. The Imperial Household Agency manages most of the large tombs, and the mounds are closed to the public, so what you see is a wooded hill ringed by water, with a small worship platform at the front and a gravel path along the edge. That is more than enough, and many visitors find the stillness oddly moving. The woods are mostly old camphor and evergreen oak, and the moat is a haven for herons.

The approach through Habikino and the neighbouring towns is ordinary suburban Japan, with narrow roads, level crossings, vending machines and small shops, and the kofun appears suddenly behind a row of houses. Traffic is tidy and slow, speed limits are low, and police are strict, so keep to them. Matsubara and Kashihara, both with tens of thousands of people, have fuel and convenience stores. Spring, when cherry blossom lines the moat, and the clear days of late autumn are the best times, and the plum rains of June are best avoided.

The Katsuragi and Kongo mountains rise to the east, with twisty hill roads and quiet temples, and are far better riding than the plain. Take the kofun as a calm start to a longer day.
t.maruhoyama kofun@34.6,135.5:
Look at a satellite photograph of the city of Sakai and you will see something odd. Among the grey grid of roofs lie dark green shapes, some shaped like keyholes, ringed by water, sitting between houses and rail lines as if the city were growing around them. These are the Mozu kofun, great burial mounds raised for the rulers of the Yamato kingdom in the fifth century, and they form the western half of the Mozu-Furuichi group that was inscribed as World Heritage in 2019. The largest, the Daisen Kofun, is traditionally attributed to Emperor Nintoku and is one of the biggest tombs in the world by area, about half a kilometre long.

Maruhoyama sits in that landscape, one of the smaller companions of the giants, and it is here that the scale of the group becomes clear. Kings were not buried alone. Around the great mounds lay satellite tombs for relatives, officials and perhaps favourites, and when you walk the paths between them you realise it was a whole political landscape in earth and water. Workers placed haniwa, hollow clay figures of houses, horses and people, on the mounds, and some of these are on display in the Sakai City Museum.

Riding in is straightforward but needs patience. Sakai is a port city of nearly eight hundred thousand people on Osaka Bay, with heavy industry and busy roads, and the old moat paths and parks sit between the main thoroughfares. Use side streets for the final stretch, keep to the low limits, and park in a designated space, because bikes left on pavements in Japanese cities attract quick attention. Fuel is plentiful in the surrounding suburbs, and Matsubara, a few kilometres east, has more than a hundred thousand people. Sakai was once a rich merchant town, famous for its knives, which are still made here, and for the tea master Sen no Rikyu, who was born here in the sixteenth century.

Autumn mornings are cool and clear, with mist sometimes on the moats, and spring brings cherry blossom. Summers are brutally humid, and typhoon rain can come in September. The Kongo and Katsuragi hills, a short ride south-east, give you the twisting mountain roads this plain lacks, so consider the kofun a calm first stop, with the real riding afterwards.
t.yoshino and omine yoshino mikumari jinja:
In early April the mountain at Yoshino turns pink from the bottom up, wave after wave of wild cherry blossom climbing the ridge, and for a few days the whole of central Nara Prefecture seems to hold its breath. The trees are mostly the white mountain cherry known as shiro-yamazakura, planted over many centuries as offerings to Zao Gongen, the fierce mountain deity of the Shugendo tradition, and by tradition thousands of them line the slopes in four zones, lower, middle, upper and inner, so that the bloom moves uphill over about three weeks. Yoshino-jinja and the Mikumari shrine belong to the mountain's older story, a place for water and the pleas of farmers, since the name Mikumari is linked with the dividing of water.

The mountain mattered long before the picnickers came. Emperor Go-Daigo fled here in 1336 and set up the Southern Court after losing Kyoto, and the little ridge became, for decades, a rival capital. The warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi held a lavish flower-viewing party here in 1594, arriving with a vast retinue, and the shrine and temples were later part of the Shugendo pilgrimage route to Omine, the great yamabushi trail south along the ridge to Kumano, which now belongs to the World Heritage listing for the Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range.

Getting here by bike is a real pleasure out of season. The road follows the Yoshino river through a narrow, green valley, with cedar and cypress plantations rising steeply on both sides, tunnels and small bridges, and the sound of water below. Further south, the long Route 169 climbs through the mountains of Nara towards Kamikita and Totsukawa, quiet, twisty and often empty, and a magnet for Kansai riders on summer weekends. Autumn colour is spectacular and quieter than the cherry rush.

At blossom time, expect heavy traffic and parking restrictions on the approach, with congestion on narrow roads and limited places to leave a bike, so go on a weekday or at dawn, or skip the weekend entirely. The ropeway from the foot of the mountain and the local buses are alternatives. The village is steep, with temple lodgings, tea houses and shops selling kudzu sweets, persimmon-leaf sushi and local sake.

Yoshino has fewer than nine thousand people and Gojō, about sixteen kilometres away, is the larger town for fuel and shopping. Wrap up in cooler months, because the air in these hills is sharp, and watch for wet leaves and sudden fog.
t.historic centre of the city of queretaro:
Querétaro is the city where Mexico was twice made, once by the Spanish and once by its own lawmakers. In the old centre, the streets run from one small square to the next, each with a baroque church, a fountain and a few trees, and the pace is calmer than in the big cities. The city was founded as an Otomí settlement and became a Spanish colonial town in the sixteenth century, and the historic centre was added to the World Heritage list in 1996 for its mix of baroque architecture and its unusual layout, which blends the regular Spanish grid with the winding lanes of the indigenous quarter.

History is everywhere. In 1810 a plot against Spanish rule was hatched here, and the conspirators included the mayor's wife, Josefa Ortiz de Dominguez, whose warning to the rebels set off the war of independence. In 1867 the Emperor Maximilian was executed on the Cerro de las Campanas just outside the city, which ended the French adventure in Mexico, and in 1917 the present constitution was signed in the city's theatre. The grand aqueduct, completed in the 1730s, strides across the east of the city on seventy-four tall arches, and it was built to bring spring water to the convent and the city, financed in part by a local marquis.

For riders, Querétaro is a gateway, with good highways in every direction. The old centre is busy, with narrow cobbled streets, one-way lanes and pedestrian zones, so park outside it, in a garage, and walk. Toll roads, called cuotas, are quick and expensive, and the free roads, libres, are slower and have more traffic and speed bumps, called topes, which are often poorly marked and can be savage. Fuel is easy in a city of more than six hundred thousand people. The best months are October to April, with warm days and cool nights, and summer afternoons bring heavy rain.

From here the road to Guanajuato runs west across the Bajio, a fertile plain of maize, sorghum and vegetables, with silver mountains rising beyond. The cuisine includes enchiladas queretanas, tamales and local cheeses and wines, and a stroll through the Plaza de Armas at night is a good way to end the day.
t.tatei nihuetucame@22.8,-102.6:
Zacatecas sits high in the Mexican north, around 2,400 metres above the sea, in a bowl of red hills that were once a mountain of silver. The Spanish arrived in the 1540s after local people showed them silver outcrops, and within a few decades the city was one of the richest in the New World, its wealth carried south on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the Royal Road of the Interior Land that ran all the way to Santa Fe. The old centre, with its pink-stone cathedral, narrow stepped lanes and colonial mansions, is inscribed as World Heritage, and the road itself is listed too.

The place name Tatei Nihuetucame belongs to a different tradition. It is a name from the Wixarika, the Huichol people, who live in the mountains of the Sierra Madre Occidental to the south-west, and whose cosmology is rich with sacred places across a huge territory. Every year they make long pilgrimages to sites in the desert and mountains, leaving offerings and gathering plants for ceremonies, and the sites have their own names and stories.

The ride into Zacatecas is a good one. The highways cross high, dry plains of cactus, mesquite and scrubby grassland, with long straights and sudden hills, and the air is thin and clear. Be ready for cold nights and sudden thunderstorms in summer, as well as strong sun at altitude. Cuota roads are fast, but the old roads through the mining villages are more interesting. The cable car crossing the city to the Cerro de la Bufa gives a magnificent view of the rooftops and the surrounding hills, and the old Eden silver mine can be visited on a tour.

Zacatecas and its neighbour Guadalupe have well over a hundred thousand people each, so fuel, food and lodging are easy, and the evenings are lively with students and musicians. The cuisine includes asado de boda, a spicy pork stew, and the local mezcal, and walking the lanes at dusk is an ideal way to finish a day.
t.pochlarn kastell hufeisenturm west@48.2,:
The Danube has been a border for a long time, and Pöchlarn is one of the places where you can feel it. The Romans knew it as Arelape, one of the forts on the river frontier of the province of Noricum, and the Horseshoe Tower, the Hufeisenturm, is what is left of the western side of that fort. A horseshoe-shaped tower is just what it sounds like: a defensive bastion with a curved outline that lets the garrison cover the wall in more directions. It is a modest ruin, not a Colosseum, and its charm is that you find it between houses rather than in a field of tickets.

The town itself, Pöchlarn, sits on the south bank of the Danube in Lower Austria, just upstream of Melk, with roughly 3,500 people. The Nibelungenlied, the medieval German epic, mentions Bechelaren, which is understood to be Pöchlarn, as the home of Rüdiger, a margrave and a model of loyalty in the poem. Locals have never been shy about this. There is also a link to the painter Oskar Kokoschka, who was born here in 1886, and the town keeps a small museum to him.

The riding is the real draw. Roads follow the river on both banks, flat or gently rolling, with the odd bend where the valley squeezes. It is relaxed riding rather than technical, and it suits the long light of a summer evening, when the water goes silver and the vineyards and orchards on the slopes pick up colour. Traffic is steady on the main roads, quieter once you go onto the minor ones, and cyclists on the Danube Cycle Path share a lot of the corridor, so slow down near the crossings.

Practical matters are easy. Pöchlarn has the basics for a town of its size, and for a larger choice of fuel and supermarkets you can run to Melk, a short distance downriver, which has its famous abbey on a rock above the town. Amstetten, about 27 km away, is the nearest bigger town in the data. A coffee by the river, a slice of the local apricot cake in season, and a look at the tower make a pleasant hour. If you are riding the Roman frontier theme, this is a good place to slow down and think about how many years soldiers were posted along this very bank, watching the far side.
t.traismauer kleinkastell@48.4,15.7:
Traismauer is a small town with a very long memory. Before it was a market town on the Traisen river, it was the Roman fort of Augustianis, one of the posts on the Noricum stretch of the Danube frontier, and some of the Roman wall still stands in the town. The Kleinkastell, the small fort, is part of that chain: a compact stone enclosure, a few watchtowers and a garrison, one of the many modest strongpoints that made the limes more than a line on a map.

The town has about 2,750 people, sits where the Traisen leaves the hills, and still has the shape of a place that was fortified for a reason. Look for the Roman Tower and the Römertor, the old gate, which are among the best-preserved Roman remains in Lower Austria. The medieval town and its castle add further layers to a short walk. The real fun is spotting where Roman stone has been reused in later walls, a habit of every century that came after.

The surrounding country is easy for motorbikes. The flat Tullner Feld lies to the east, the Danube floodplain is close to the north, and roads run through orchards and fields with the odd line of poplars. Tracks lead towards the Danube floodplain and the long dykes where you can pick up cycling traffic. It is not a technical ride, more a pleasant rolling day, best in late spring when the blossom is out or in early autumn when the Heuriger wine taverns around Krems and the Wagram open their gates. Look for the green branch hung over a door, the old sign that a winegrower is serving his own wine.

Fuel and food are simple. Traismauer itself has the basics, and Krems an der Donau, with about 14,000 people some 12 km away, has bigger stations, supermarkets and the famous Wachau gateway. St. Pölten, the provincial capital, is a short run to the south. If you are on the Roman frontier circuit, take a few minutes at the tower, imagine the Danube patrol boats that once moved along the river, and then go and find a cold drink. The summer heat in this flat basin can be stronger than in the hills, so carry water.
t.lednice valtice cultural landscape@48.8,:
The princes of Liechtenstein owned this corner of southern Moravia for centuries, and they treated it as a canvas. Over more than three hundred years they shaped a landscape of about 200 square kilometres between the towns of Lednice and Valtice, with palaces, hunting lodges, ponds, avenues and follies set out as part of a single garden. UNESCO listed it in 1996 as one of the largest artificial landscapes in Europe, and the effect is that you pass from one scene to another as if you were walking through a painting.

Lednice Castle is the showpiece, a Neo-Gothic palace with pointed windows and turrets, and its park holds a Minaret, a slender tower about 60 metres high built in the late eighteenth century as a decorative fantasy. You can climb it for a view across the plain. Valtice, a few kilometres south, has a large Baroque palace and the national wine salon, a collection of Czech wines. Between them runs the Thaya river, the Dyje, with floodplain forest, oak woods and ponds full of birds, and the Pálava hills rise to the east. The whole region is also a centre of Moravian wine, and white wines such as Veltliner and Riesling are the thing to try.

For a rider, the ride is flat and gentle, along straight, shaded avenues and quiet roads through vineyards. Many people explore by bicycle, and the roads are shared with cyclists, especially at weekends in summer, so ride calmly. Spring and early autumn are beautiful, and the grape harvest in September adds colour and the sweet smell of fermenting must in the villages.

Lednice is a small village of about 2,300 people, and Podivín and Hlohovec nearby have a few shops. For fuel and larger supermarkets, Břeclav, about 7 km away with roughly 26,000 people, is the nearest, and Mikulov, with its castle on a hill, lies a short way south. The border with Austria is close, and Vienna is about an hour's drive. A glass of wine on a terrace, a plate of fried cheese and a walk along the pond makes an easy afternoon.
t.higashiumazuka kofun@34.6,135.6:
The Yamato basin, in the middle of Nara prefecture, is where Japan's early rulers raised their great earthen tombs, and Kashihara sits at the heart of it. Around the third and fourth centuries and for several hundred years afterward, the leaders of the Yamato court were buried under mounds, many in a distinctive keyhole shape, a round tomb joined to a trapezoidal front. These are the kofun, which simply means old mound. They were ringed with clay cylinders called haniwa, some formed into the shapes of houses, horses, warriors and dancers, and many were surrounded by moats.

Higashiumazuka is one of the lesser-known mounds in this country, a small tomb tucked into the countryside among villages and fields. Kashihara is dominated by the shapes of three famous hills, Unebi, Miminashi and Kagu, a trio celebrated in the oldest Japanese poetry, and Kashihara Shrine at the foot of Mount Unebi was founded in 1890 to honour Emperor Jimmu, the legendary first emperor. The archaeological museum nearby holds finds from the surrounding mounds, and it explains what was found.

The roads around Kashihara are flat and urban, with the typical Japanese mix of narrow lanes, level crossings and small shrines on corners. Rural lanes between rice fields are only wide enough for one car, and irrigation channels run beside them without barriers, so go carefully. Traffic is heavy on the main roads at rush hour, and parking at small tomb sites is limited, so check the details. Many of the tombs are also managed as imperial sites, with limited access, and you will often view them from outside the fence.

Kashihara, a city of about seventy-nine thousand people, has plenty of fuel and food, including noodle shops and set-meal restaurants. If you want a ride with some curves, the hills to the south lead toward Asuka, another early capital, and beyond it the mountain roads toward Yoshino. Spring, with its blossom, and autumn, with its red maple leaves, are the best times. Summer is hot, humid and loud with cicadas, and the rainy season in June is best avoided.
t.terayama minamiyama kofun@34.6,135.5:
Sakai is a port city on Osaka Bay, and its most extraordinary feature is that it is built around tombs. The Mozu group, named after the old name of this district, includes Daisen, the tomb attributed to Emperor Nintoku, which is among the largest burial monuments in the world by area, a keyhole-shaped mound nearly five hundred metres long, surrounded by triple moats. Standing beside it you see only a wooded hill behind a wall of water, and the true shape is visible only from the air. Smaller mounds, including those at Terayama and Minamiyama, lie scattered among streets and houses, each with a fringe of trees.

The mounds date from the fifth century, in the Kofun period, when the Yamato kings controlled a powerful state that traded with Korea and China. They were covered in stones, surrounded by rows of haniwa clay figures, and filled with weapons, armour and mirrors. The group is part of the Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group, recognised as World Heritage in 2019.

Sakai has more to offer than tombs. In the sixteenth century it was a rich merchant republic, where the tea master Sen no Rikyu was born and where Portuguese trade brought guns and tobacco. The town still makes fine kitchen knives, and it is the home of the bicycle components company Shimano, so cyclists get respect here. The Sakai Museum near Daisen tells the story well, and a nearby observation deck gives a glimpse of the tomb's shape.

Riding in Sakai is city riding. Roads are dense and fast, with elevated expressways, trams and narrow side streets, and parking near the tombs is limited. Cycle lanes run beside the moats, and the park paths are popular with joggers, so go slowly. There is no shortage of fuel stations, restaurants and convenience stores. Try the local Sakai-style udon and, in spring, look for cherry blossom reflected in the moat. For better riding, head for the Kongo and Katsuragi mountains to the east, where winding roads climb through cedar forest, or cross to the Kii Peninsula. Summer is hot and humid, so early mornings are best.
t.yoshino and omine yoshimizu jinja@34.4,1:
Yoshino is the most famous cherry-blossom mountain in Japan, and it earns the fame. Tens of thousands of trees, planted over centuries as offerings by pilgrims, climb the ridge in four zones, so the bloom moves up the mountain through April like a slow pink tide. But Yoshino is older and stranger than a flower festival. It is the gateway to the Kii mountains, a vast tangle of steep forested ranges where mountain ascetics of the Shugendo tradition have walked for more than a thousand years, and the pilgrimage path of Omine runs along the high ridges to Kumano, passing places so sacred that women were long banned from entering. The Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range were inscribed by UNESCO in 2004.

Yoshimizu Shrine sits on the slope above the town, a small building with a turbulent history. In 1185 the warrior Minamoto no Yoshitsune hid here while fleeing from his brother, and in the fourteenth century Emperor Go-Daigo took refuge in Yoshino and set up a rival court, the Southern Court. The shrine's rooms are simple, with low ceilings and old screens, and from the terrace you can look down over the valley. Hideyoshi held a lavish cherry blossom party here in 1594.

Riders come here for the mountains. The roads from Nara and Osaka climb into the Kii range through cedar forest, with long curves, tunnels and drops into deep valleys. Route 169 runs south toward Kumano along the Totsukawa and Kitayama rivers, a classic long ride with few services. In cherry season the road to Yoshino jams with cars and tour buses, so come at dawn or after the bloom, and in winter parts of the high roads are icy.

Yoshino has fewer than ten thousand people, with a handful of shops, tea houses and inns serving kuzu mochi and persimmon-leaf sushi. Fuel stations are in the valley town, so fill up before going further into the mountains. The ropeway and the upper slopes are best on a weekday.
t.zenizuka kofun@34.6,135.5:
Mozu is an old word for the shrike, a small predatory bird that impales its prey on thorns, and the name belongs to the stretch of Sakai where the biggest tombs lie. A chronicle tells how, when workers were building the tomb of Emperor Nintoku in the fifth century, a deer suddenly fell dead on the site, and a shrike flew out of its ear. The story is a legend, of course, but it gave the district its name, and it hints at how strange and mysterious these monuments seemed even to later Japanese.

Zenizuka is one of the small mounds that cluster around the great ones. These satellite tombs were probably built for relatives, officials and retainers of the king, and they are often square or round, grassed over and overshadowed by pines. They are easy to miss, wedged between houses and car parks, and have names that are earthier than royal, like Zenizuka, the Coin Mound. Whether the name has to do with coins or a nearby legend, local people have long folded these hills into daily life, drying laundry in their shadow and walking dogs around their moats.

This is flat, crowded urban Japan, so riding means threading through neighbourhoods and expressway ramps. Lanes are narrow and one-way streets are common, and cyclists and pedestrians share space everywhere. Stop signs and pedestrian crossings are strictly observed, and police are firm about speed. Parking for motorcycles is limited and often paid, so find a coin car park and walk. Typhoon season in late summer brings heavy rain and flooding, and winter days are mild and dry.

Sakai is a city of nearly eight hundred thousand people, so fuel, vending-machine coffee and noodle shops are on every street, and there is a good local tradition of grilled eel and sweet confectionery. Early morning in spring is the best moment to come, when the pines are green, the moat water is still and the light is soft. A little further out, the hills of Kongo and Izumi give you proper bends and forested slopes after the grid of the city.
t.gobyoyama kofun@34.6,135.5:
The Gobyoyama tomb is the resting place attributed to Emperor Richu, the seventeenth emperor in the traditional count, and it is a giant: a keyhole-shaped mound in Sakai more than three hundred metres long, one of the biggest in the whole country. It was built in the late fourth or early fifth century, and its builders moved an enormous amount of earth. Surfaces were covered with fitted stones, and rows of haniwa figures stood on the terraces, so that in its day the whole mound would have gleamed like a stepped pyramid.

What makes the tomb interesting is the clay figures. Haniwa began as simple cylinders and developed into models of houses, boats, horses, warriors, falconers and women with offerings, and they give us a rare glimpse of the daily life of the early Yamato court, since no written records survive from the period. The tomb is managed by the Imperial Household Agency, which restricts entry, so most of it is seen from a path on the moat's edge. You see a wooded hill and a ring of water where egrets stand like statues.

The riding around Gobyoyama is city riding. Roads are wide where the old tomb avenues were laid and tight where homes press close, and tram tracks and level crossings are not unusual. There are small parking areas for motorcycles near some of the larger tombs, and it is easy to walk around the moat, a circuit that takes the better part of an hour. Weekdays are quiet, and weekends see locals walking, cycling and fishing at the edge of the moat.

Sakai has all the services you would expect from a big city. In the evening an izakaya with grilled skewers and beer is a good place to finish. Spring and autumn bring the kinder weather, with clear skies and gentle temperatures, while summer can be oppressive and rainy. If you want to see the whole shape of the tomb, the observation deck at the city hall of Sakai gives a distant view, and from there the other tombs of the group can be spotted among the roofs.
t.nabezuka kofun@34.6,135.6:
Nabezuka is a modest mound in the Kashihara district of Nara prefecture, in the part of Japan where the country's first centralised state took shape. It is the sort of site that does not make the headlines. A rounded hill in a field, perhaps with a few trees, it belongs to the thousands of burial mounds scattered across the Yamato plain, and its main interest is that it forms part of a whole landscape of tombs rather than being a single sight. If you want the big picture, the archaeological museum in Kashihara explains how the mounds changed from large keyholes to small round or square tombs as the centuries passed.

South of Kashihara the land leads towards Asuka, the cradle of the Japanese state in the sixth and seventh centuries, where you can see stone burial chambers like the Ishibutai tomb, a huge corbelled mound of granite blocks. The change from the earth mounds to stone-lined chambers marks the end of the kofun age and the arrival of Buddhism, and by the early eighth century the court had moved to Nara. A few kilometres of country lane here take you through a thousand years of history.

The riding is quiet and gentle. Rice paddies and small orchards cover the flat parts, and the lanes between them are narrow and sometimes unmarked. In June the paddies are flooded and reflect the sky, and in autumn they turn gold. Traffic is light outside the commuting hours, though trucks use the main roads, and local drivers are patient with bikes. Be cautious at blind corners where irrigation channels run close to the road. If you want more twists, the Nara mountains to the east, with cedar forests and tight bends, are not far.

Kashihara has about eighty thousand people and offers plenty of fuel and meals. Persimmon and strawberry are local crops, and the kakinoha sushi, wrapped in persimmon leaves, is a specialty of the region. Spring has cherry blossom and autumn has fine light, while July and August are hot and heavy with cicadas.
t.toshodai ji@34.7,135.8:
Toshodai-ji exists because a blind monk would not give up. Ganjin, a Chinese master of Buddhist law, was invited to Japan in the eighth century to teach proper monastic ordination, and he tried to cross the sea five times, defeated by storms, pirates and official obstruction, until he went blind. On the sixth attempt, in 753, he arrived in Japan, and in 759 he founded this temple in Nara. His own ordination hall still stands in the grounds, and a dry-lacquer statue of him, said to be a faithful likeness, is kept at the temple and shown only occasionally.

The temple's main hall, the Kondo, is one of the finest surviving buildings of the Tenpyo period, with a row of eight great pillars, a wide tiled roof and a calm, balanced shape that influenced centuries of Japanese architecture. Inside it holds a huge gilded thousand-armed Kannon surrounded by other statues. The hall was restored in a long project that finished in 2009, and the roof has been reassembled with great care. The temple is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara, a World Heritage group, but it is quieter than the better-known temples, and the pines and moss give the grounds a feeling of calm.

You arrive from Nara by quiet streets that run through the western part of the city, where the old capital's grid still shapes the roads. It is flat and suburban, with narrow lanes, bicycles and small shops. There is parking at the temple, and the staff are friendly, though motorbike spaces are limited. Nearby Yakushi-ji, with its elegant pagoda, is a short walk. For more adventurous riding, the roads over the hills toward Ikoma and the Katsuragi range give proper bends and good views over the Nara basin.

Nara has a population of more than three hundred and sixty thousand, so petrol and food are easy to find. Try narazuke pickles and kakinoha sushi. Autumn colours in November and spring blossom are the prettiest seasons, but the grounds are pleasant at any time, especially in the early morning.
t.historic monuments of ancient nara@34.7,:
Nara was Japan's capital for only seventy-four years, from 710 to 784, but it left a mark out of all proportion to the time. The court modelled the new city on Chang'an, the Chinese capital, with a grid of streets and a palace at the north, and it was here that Buddhism took root as the state religion, that the first histories and poetry anthologies were compiled, and that the great temples were built. Eight monuments are included in the World Heritage listing: Todai-ji, Kofuku-ji, Kasuga Taisha, Gango-ji, Yakushi-ji, Toshodai-ji, the site of Heijo Palace and the Kasugayama Primeval Forest.

The best known is Todai-ji, where the Great Buddha, a bronze figure about fifteen metres tall, sits inside what is still one of the largest wooden buildings in the world. The statue was dedicated in 752, and the original hall has been rebuilt after fires, each time a little smaller than before. The temple grounds are also where Nara's famous deer wander, around a thousand of them, treated as divine messengers. They bow for crackers and have been known to nibble maps, hats and sleeves, so keep your belongings close.

For a rider, Nara is a gentle place to wander, but traffic is heavy around the park at weekends and in cherry and maple seasons. The centre is a mix of narrow streets and one-way lanes, parking is limited and paid, and deer cross the roads at will, sometimes at night, so slow down. Outside the city, the hills to the east lead to Yamato-Aoga and the Murou mountains, where the roads are quieter and the bends tighter.

Nara has all the services of a mid-sized city, with fuel stations, small restaurants and shops selling kuzu sweets and green tea. Early morning, before the tour buses arrive, is when the park is at its best, with mist hanging between the cedars. November brings the red leaves, and the Shuni-e fire festival at Todai-ji marks the beginning of spring in March.
t.nagayama kofun@34.6,135.5:
Most of the great keyhole tombs of Sakai are surrounded by houses, and the ordinary life of the neighbourhood goes on right up to the moat. Nagayama Kofun is one of the smaller ones, a mound that rises behind residential streets, with a path along the edge and a ring of trees. Locals use the moat's edge for the morning walk, children play on the grass nearby, and old men fish for carp in the water. It is a mixed picture of an ancient monument living quietly inside the modern city.

The tombs here were built in the fifth century, when the Yamato kings held the Inland Sea trade routes and the port of Sakai was a gateway to the continent. Over time, many of the mounds were forgotten, and trees and farms covered them. In the nineteenth century the new Meiji state made a point of identifying the tombs of the ancient emperors, and the Imperial Household Agency has managed them ever since. Many are thus closed to excavation, though archaeologists have worked on the smaller ones.

For a rider, the pleasure is of a slower kind, getting to know the streets of an ordinary Japanese city. Roads here are narrow, flat and busy, but the drivers are calm and the tram line is a historic, charming one. Keep to low speeds, watch for cyclists coming out of side streets and respect pedestrian crossings. Motorbike parking is sometimes easy to find near convenience stores and sometimes impossible, so be prepared to walk. There is a lot of vending-machine coffee and small bakeries, plus family restaurants.

Sakai has all the fuel stations and food you need, and the nearby commercial district around the station is lively. Sakai's old harbour area has a historic lighthouse and warehouses, and the great merchant history is kept alive by museums. In spring, cherry trees along the moat bloom pink, and autumn has clear air. The summer humidity is heavy, so start early.
t.genemonyama kofun@34.6,135.5:
A tomb moat is a pond with a purpose, and over the centuries it has become something else: a habitat. Genemonyama Kofun is another of the Sakai mounds, and what strikes you first is the water, dark green and quiet, with lotus pads in summer, ducks in winter and grey herons standing at the edge. The moats were dug to separate the tomb from the world and to supply earth for the mound, and farmers later used the water for irrigation, so that the tombs became part of the local water system. Today they shelter fish, turtles, kingfishers and a surprising amount of insect life.

The mound itself is a wooded hill that few people climb, because entry is restricted, but a path runs around the outside, and there are places where you can glimpse the slope and the old stone steps. Autumn brings red and gold leaves, winter brings migrating ducks, and spring brings a haze of blossom. The sound of the neighbourhood, with trains, school bells and the clatter of bicycles, mixes with birdsong.

Riding here is straightforward and slow. Sakai is flat, and the roads around the tombs form a grid with a few busier arterial roads, where traffic from the port moves in heavy lines. The surfaces are good and signage is clear, though the roads are often narrow. Parking for bikes is limited and sometimes expensive, so use paid lots. In June the rainy season brings long grey days, and in late summer typhoons can flood low roads, so check the forecast.

With nearly eight hundred thousand inhabitants, Sakai has services everywhere, and a bowl of noodles or a plate of takoyaki, the octopus balls of Osaka, is never far away. For something quieter, ride out to the hills on the south-east edge of the city, with their reservoirs, cedar woods and small farms. Early morning is the best time to see the moat, when the mist lifts and the herons are still, and weekdays are quietest.
t.kasuga taisha and kasugayama primeval fo:
Kasugayama is a forest that has been protected since the ninth century, which is why it feels different from any other woodland in the region. Hunting and logging were banned here in 841, because the hill is sacred to the Kasuga shrine, and the result is a primeval stand of cedar, cypress, oak and evergreens on the slopes just east of Nara. Deer roam through it, as they do through the park below, and in autumn their calls echo through the trees. In the shrine's grounds, thousands of stone lanterns line the paths, donated by worshippers over the centuries, and thousands of bronze lanterns hang from the eaves, lit twice a year during the lantern festivals.

Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768 by the Fujiwara family, the most powerful clan of the age, to protect the new capital, and its vermilion halls, with their painted pillars and sweeping eaves, are among the most beautiful in Japan. For centuries the buildings were rebuilt every twenty years, a Shinto custom of renewal, and the shrine remains alive with priests, dancers and festivals. A walk up through the forest to the shrine is gentle and beautiful, with moss, ferns and the smell of cedar.

This is a site to visit on foot, but the roads nearby are good. The Nara Okuyama Drive Way, a toll road that winds through the hills east of the city, is a popular route for riders, with steady curves and views over the basin, though check whether it is open to motorcycles on the day. Traffic builds in the cherry and maple seasons, and the park roads fill with tour buses at the weekend. Deer cross without warning, particularly at dusk.

Nara has everything a visitor needs, with petrol stations on the main roads and plenty of cafes near the park, where you can try warabi mochi and kudzu noodles. Entry to the main shrine area and the inner sanctuaries may require a fee, and hours vary. Go early on a weekday, preferably in the misty light of November or the fresh green of late April, when the forest is at its best.
San Miguel de Allende sits at about 1,900 metres in the highlands of Guanajuato, and its centre looks like a film set because it has hardly changed in two centuries. Cobbled streets climb between rose-pink and ochre walls, doors open onto courtyards full of bougainvillea, and over everything rise the pink Gothic spires of the Parroquia, the parish church, which was given its fairy-tale appearance in the late nineteenth century by a self-taught local builder, Zeferino Gutiérrez, who is said to have based the design on postcards of European cathedrals.

The town was founded in the sixteenth century on the silver road, the Camino Real, that led from Mexico City to the northern mines, and it prospered as a stop for traders and muleteers. In 1810 it became part of Mexican history when Ignacio Allende, a captain born in San Miguel, joined the priest Miguel Hidalgo in the uprising that began Mexico's war of independence. The town added his name later. In the twentieth century artists and foreigners settled in, and today a large expatriate community lives in the hills and haciendas around.

Riding in the Bajío is pleasant. The highway from Querétaro or Guanajuato is fast and well kept, and the land is a dry plateau of scrub, prickly pear and rocky hills, with bright skies. Rain falls in summer, mostly in afternoon storms, and the dry winters are cool in the mornings. The town centre is another matter: the streets are steep, cobbled, narrow and often one-way, and the stones are polished and slippery after rain. Leave the bike at a guarded car park and walk.

San Miguel has about seventy thousand people, with fuel stations on the outskirts and countless cafes and restaurants in the centre. Mexican breakfast of chilaquiles with a strong coffee suits the cool morning, and the rooftop terraces are good for sunset. The best months are October to April, and on weekends and holidays the centre is busy.
t.former royal hospital of san juan de dio:
The Order of San Juan de Dios was founded in the sixteenth century by a Portuguese-born soldier turned nurse, Juan Ciudad, who opened a hospital in Granada, and it spread across Spain's empire. In the colonial towns of New Spain, its brothers ran hospitals for the poor, the sick and the travelling, and a royal hospital in San Miguel belonged to this tradition. In a silver town on the great trade road the need was real: muleteers, miners and soldiers fell ill, and the church and crown shared the cost of caring for them.

Buildings like this tell you how colonial society worked. A hospital had a chapel, courtyards, wards around a cloister and a small pharmacy, and it was supported by donations, rents and royal grants. The architecture is modest but sturdy, with thick walls of local stone, arched arcades, and heavy wooden doors. Today old hospitals and convents in Mexico are often reused as cultural centres and schools, and San Miguel is no exception, with its old religious buildings now housing art classes, galleries and museums.

The centre of San Miguel is a World Heritage zone, together with the Sanctuary of Atotonilco outside town, so the colonial fabric is protected. Strolling here, you notice the details: carved stone portals, iron balconies, thick wooden doors with brass studs, and tiled house numbers. Streets slope steeply, and every corner opens a view of domes and bell towers.

For riders, the same advice applies as elsewhere in the centre: park outside, preferably in a guarded lot, and walk. The cobbles are rough, the gradients are sharp, and the tourists are slow, so a bike is more trouble than pleasure inside the old town. Outside, the roads towards Dolores Hidalgo and Guanajuato run through open country and are enjoyable, with good views of the dry hills and the occasional hacienda.

Fuel stations are on the edge of town and along the main roads, and food is everywhere, from market stalls to fine restaurants. Try the fresh fruit water and the sweets sold near the main square. Mornings are the best time for walking, while the afternoon sun is strong, and thunderstorms in summer clear the air by evening.
t.protective town of san miguel and the sa:
Fifteen kilometres from San Miguel, on a dusty road through scrub and fields, the village of Atotonilco holds a church that is nicknamed the Sistine Chapel of Mexico. From the outside the Sanctuary of Jesús Nazareno looks like a plain fortress of stone and whitewash with a domed roof, and then you step inside and every surface is covered, floor to ceiling, in painted scenes and swirling patterns. The paintings were made in the eighteenth century by a local artist, Miguel Antonio Martínez de Pocasangre, working for the priest Luis Felipe Neri de Alfaro, who founded the sanctuary in the 1740s as a place of penance and spiritual retreat.

The imagery is extraordinary: Christ's suffering, demons and angels, the sins and the virtues, and a folk-baroque style that mixes European devotion with the colours and energy of Mexico. Pilgrims still arrive on foot, particularly during Lent, when they walk through the night from San Miguel, carrying crosses and heavy loads, in a tradition that goes back to the eighteenth century. In 1810 Ignacio Allende and his fellow rebels took a banner of the Virgin of Guadalupe from this church and carried it into the war of independence.

The sanctuary is a World Heritage site together with the town of San Miguel. Nearby there are hot springs, and several spa resorts fed by thermal waters have grown up around the village. The road from San Miguel is easy and short, with open fields, mesquite trees and views of the hills. It is a good route in the early morning, when the light is soft, and traffic is lighter. Watch for cattle and potholes after the rains, and for topes, the speed bumps at village entrances.

Atotonilco has only basic services, with small shops and a few eateries, so for fuel and supplies, go back to San Miguel. Dress respectfully, with shoulders covered, and keep a low voice inside. The church usually opens during the day, but check for services and special events, as the pilgrimage season gets crowded. October to April is the most comfortable time, with warm days and cool nights.
t.bridge of san rafael@20.9,-100.8:
The map gives this stop a name, the Bridge of San Rafael, and a spot on the edge of the valley of the Río Laja, west of San Miguel de Allende, close to the small settlement of La Cieneguita. What I can say is how a bridge like this fits the country. San Miguel stands on the slopes above the Laja, a river that wanders across the highland plateau of the Bajío, and for centuries the traffic of mule trains, wagons and pilgrims had to cross it somewhere. A stone bridge on a colonial road is a small, sturdy thing, of arches and cutwaters, and it is often older than anything else for miles.

The land around is open, dry and gently rolling, covered in mesquite, huisache and prickly pear. In the rainy season, from June to September, the river fills and the fields turn green, and afternoon storms bring a smell of wet dust. Cattle graze among the scrub, and small ranches and chapels dot the roads. Further on lies the Presa Allende, a large reservoir that attracts herons and pelicans, handy for a quiet picnic.

Roads here are typical of rural Guanajuato: narrow, patched asphalt with no shoulders, sudden speed bumps called topes at the edge of each village, and potholes that appear after storms. Local drivers are quick, and trucks and pickups sometimes overtake in places where they should not, so keep to the right and ride defensively. Dogs and livestock wander onto the road, and after dark visibility is poor, so do your riding in daylight.

La Cieneguita is a tiny settlement with a few shops, and San Miguel, some six kilometres off, has fuel, restaurants and everything else a rider might want. Late afternoon, with the low sun on the stone and the hills turning purple, is the nicest hour. Carry water, sunscreen and a light waterproof, because the highland sun is strong at nearly two thousand metres, and the evenings turn cool.
t.cape town@-33.9,18.4:
Cape Town sits at the foot of Table Mountain, a flat-topped sandstone wall about a kilometre high, and on a day when the tablecloth of cloud spills over the edge it is one of the great sights of the world. The city lies between the mountain and the Atlantic, with a harbour that was founded in 1652 by the Dutch East India Company as a supply station for ships on the route to the East. It grew into a port of many cultures, and the mix of Dutch, Malay, African and British influences is still visible in its food, language and architecture.

Robben Island, visible from the waterfront, was where Nelson Mandela spent eighteen of his twenty-seven years in prison, and ferries run from the Victoria and Alfred Waterfront. The city centre has the Company's Garden, the Castle of Good Hope, the colourful Bo-Kaap quarter and the lively bars of Long Street. The winds can be fierce, especially the southeaster known as the Cape Doctor, which blows in summer and can make riding hard work.

For riders the city is a base and a beginning. Route 62, the long scenic alternative to the coastal N2 highway, starts inland and heads through wine country and the Karoo, with a few passes along the way. For a taste of coastal riding, Chapman's Peak Drive on the Atlantic side cuts along cliffs above the sea, and the Cape Peninsula leads to the Cape of Good Hope and Cape Point. Traffic can be heavy at rush hour, and in the city centre you should watch for minibus taxis, which stop without warning.

Fuel, repair shops and hotels are everywhere. Keep your valuables out of sight, and park in guarded areas where possible, since car and motorcycle crime exists in some neighbourhoods. The best months are from October to April, when the weather is warm and dry. Winter brings storms and cold rain from the Atlantic, but also bright clear days after the front has passed. Eat fish and chips on the harbour, and see the sunset from Signal Hill.
t.bacharnsdorf wachtturm@48.4,15.4:
The Wachau is a stretch of the Danube between Melk and Krems where the river runs through a gorge, with terraced vineyards on the slopes and small towns of white walls and baroque towers beside the water. UNESCO listed the cultural landscape in 2000, and it is one of the most beautiful stretches of the river. Bacharnsdorf is a tiny village near Spitz, the town at the heart of the valley, and Weissenkirchen is only a few minutes away.

Here, on a hillside above the river, stood a Roman watchtower. The Danube was the northern frontier of the Roman Empire for several centuries, and a chain of forts, towers and camps stretched along the south bank to watch for movement on the far side. The remains of this line, known as the Danube Limes, were listed by UNESCO in 2021. The watchtower at Bacharnsdorf is a small piece of that system, a place where soldiers kept an eye on the river and signalled to neighbours in the case of trouble.

The Wachau is famous for apricots, called Marillen, and in spring the orchards bloom white and pink. You will find apricot jam, schnapps, dumplings and cakes in nearly every cafe. The wine is excellent, especially the Gruner Veltliner and Riesling grown on the terraces, and the local winemakers serve their own wine in taverns called Heurigen, identified by a bundle of branches over the door. A modest lunch at one of them, with the river in view, is a very good way to spend an hour.

The riding is easy. The B3 follows the river through the valley, with the water on one side and vineyards on the other, and it is narrow in places, so traffic builds on sunny weekends. A small ferry crosses at Spitz, and a ride on the far bank is quieter. Fuel is thin in the valley, so fill up at Krems or Melk before you start. Autumn is the best season, when the vineyards turn gold and red and the light is soft. Spring offers apricot blossom, and midsummer is hot and busy.
Pochlarn is a quiet town on the Danube, but it has been famous for a long time. The Romans had a fort here called Arelape, built to guard the river and the mouth of the Erlauf, which flows in from the south. Later, in the medieval epic known as the Nibelungenlied, the town appears under the name Bechelaren, home of the margrave Rudiger, a loyal knight who is torn between his oath and his love. The region from Melk to Pochlarn is still called the Nibelungengau because of this.

More recently, Pochlarn was the birthplace of Oskar Kokoschka, the Expressionist painter, who was born here in 1886. A small museum in the town honours him with a collection of his work and memorabilia. Kokoschka became one of the leading painters of the twentieth century, known for intense portraits and bold landscapes, and he travelled and lived all over Europe. It is a pleasing detail that a town of three and a half thousand people produced him.

The Roman fort is mostly buried now, though traces have been found under the town. Archaeologists have mapped the layout, and parts of the wall have been found and recorded. The fort was part of the Danube Limes, the chain of Roman frontier posts that UNESCO listed in 2021. In summer, a quiet walk along the river path brings you past willows and reeds, with barges passing slowly.

Riding here means the B3, the old Danube road, with gentle curves and small villages, and the cycle path beside the river means you share the valley with bicycles. Melk, with its enormous baroque abbey, is a short distance upstream, and the Wachau begins beyond it. Pochlarn itself is big enough for fuel and simple meals, and the cafes on the main square are good for a coffee. Behind the town the hills rise towards the Alpine foothills, and the Kalkalpen National Park is within reach for those who want a bigger day. Early autumn is lovely here.
t.pochlarn kastell hufeisenturm ost@48.2,1:
The word Hufeisenturm means horseshoe tower, and it is the sort of detail that tells you about the Roman world when it was under pressure. In the fourth century, with raiders crossing the Danube more often, the Romans rebuilt many of their frontier forts with a new style of defence. Instead of square corner towers, they built tall towers in a U shape that projected out from the walls, giving archers and artillery a wider field of fire. The east tower at Pochlarn, the Roman fort of Arelape, belongs to that period.

Arelape stood at an important spot, where the Erlauf river meets the Danube, and soldiers there controlled river traffic and the road along the south bank. The fort was part of a line that ran through what is now Austria, one of several sections of the Danube Limes listed by UNESCO in 2021. Today the walls lie mostly under fields and houses, but traces of the horseshoe tower have been uncovered, and archaeologists use them to understand how the fort was rebuilt in its later years.

The area is a gentle one for riding. The Danube valley here is wide and green, with orchards and fields, and the B3 runs through small villages with churches and inns. Klein-Pochlarn lies just across the water, and a look back at the town from the far bank is worth the short detour. Traffic on the main road is moderate on weekdays but can build on sunny weekends. Clear days give good views, and autumn mist adds mood.
