Fuel is available in Pochlarn, though it is a small town, and bigger supply is found in Melk a short distance away. Eat at one of the inns along the river, where local freshwater fish such as zander and trout often appear on the menu, with a glass of Gruner Veltliner. The cycle path along the river brings in many visitors in summer, so expect to share the road with them. If you have time, ride up into the hills behind the town for a view across the valley.
t.zeiselmauer kastell zentralbereich@48.3,:
Zeiselmauer is a village of about fourteen hundred people on the south bank of the Danube, between Vienna and Tulln, and under its streets lies a Roman fort. The Romans called it Cannabiaca, and it was one of the forts that guarded the frontier of the province of Noricum and later Pannonia. The fort was built of stone, with a square plan and corner towers, and a small civilian settlement grew up around it. The Danube Limes, of which it was a part, was listed by UNESCO in 2021.

What makes Zeiselmauer interesting is that the Roman fort did not entirely vanish. Parts of the wall survived and were incorporated into later buildings, and the village follows the old street plan. You can see sections of masonry in the village centre if you walk around. The name itself comes from the old German for a wall, and it hints at the Roman remains which later inhabitants recognised as an old fortification. The fort at the centre of the village is the place to start, with signs to guide you.

For riding, this is easy and pleasant country. The B14 follows the river from Klosterneuburg to Tulln, and the hills of the Wienerwald come down to the water on the south side. The roads are well surfaced, the villages are tidy, and there are wine taverns at every turn. The Danube floodplain on the other side is a national park, with wetlands, wild boar and a rich bird life. Cyclists share the roads on summer weekends, and the traffic towards Vienna builds on Sunday evenings.

Fuel is available in the larger towns nearby, such as Klosterneuburg or Tulln, since Zeiselmauer itself is small. The village has a couple of inns and cafes, and at the right time of year the vineyards in the hills are heavy with grapes. Autumn brings the new wine, called Sturm, a cloudy, sweet, barely fermented juice that is served in the taverns. Spring is fresh, with blossoms and green slopes. This is a good place to stop and look at a piece of Roman history that is still part of the village.
t.zeiselmauer kastell kastentor@48.3,16.2:
A Roman fort is built around its gates, and the Kastentor at Zeiselmauer is where the road once entered the fort of Cannabiaca. Gates were the weak point of any fort, so they were guarded by towers and given heavy doors, and the roads that led through them were the arteries of the frontier. This gate faced the main road along the Danube, and soldiers, merchants and messengers passed through it for generations. The excavation of the gate gave archaeologists a close look at how the fort was built and how it changed over time.

The village around it is small, with about fourteen hundred inhabitants, and its neighbour Muckendorf is a little smaller. Together they sit on a gentle terrace above the river, with the Wienerwald rising behind and the flat Danube plain stretching away to the north. This is a landscape of vineyards and orchards, with farm shops selling apples and wine, and the churches are baroque with onion domes.

Riding here is relaxed. The road runs along the foot of the hills, with a little curve and a little climb, and the river is never far away. Greifenstein, a short way east, has a castle perched above the water, and further on Klosterneuburg has a great monastery with an old wine cellar. Tulln, to the west, is a larger town known for its flowers and for its connection to the Nibelungen legend. The area is popular on weekends with cyclists, so watch out for them on the narrow roads.

Vienna is only about twenty kilometres away, so you can use this as a quiet approach or departure from the city. Fuel is better in the bigger towns, and a little planning avoids a detour. In autumn the fog settles in the river valley, and the sun burns through by midday, giving a lovely light on the vineyards. Spring blossom is also fine. If you are interested in Roman history, ask at the local museum or at the town hall about the remains. The people are proud of what lies under their village.
t.wien legionslager umwehrung@48.2,16.4:
Vienna began as a Roman legionary camp called Vindobona, built around the end of the first century on a bluff above the Danube and a small tributary. The camp held a legion, first the Thirteenth and later the Tenth, and it was a large rectangle surrounded by a wall and ditch, with gates on each side. A civilian settlement grew outside it. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius died in this region in 180, and one tradition says he died at Vindobona, though the evidence is not certain.

The camp's outline survives in the street plan of the old city. If you look at a map, you can see how the lanes of the Innere Stadt follow the line of the Roman wall, curving where the corners once stood. Hoher Markt, a square in the middle of the old town, has an underground museum where you can walk through Roman house foundations, and a short walk away, on Michaelerplatz, the excavated remains of Roman buildings are visible in front of the Hofburg. The Danube Limes, which includes Vindobona, was listed by UNESCO in 2021.

Vienna of course has many other layers: the Habsburg palaces, the Ringstrasse, the coffeehouses, the music of Mozart and Beethoven and Strauss. It is a big city, with about one and a half million people, and everything a rider needs is available. Fuel is easy to find on the outskirts, and the centre is compact enough that you will want to park and walk. Parking in the inner districts is regulated by short-term zones, so look for the signs and avoid fines.

To get a sense of the city from above, ride up to the Kahlenberg, a hill on the northern edge of town that gives a fine view over the roofs and the river. The road climbs through vineyards, and on the way you pass wine taverns, a Viennese tradition. In the evening a glass of new wine and a plate of cold meat and bread is a good end to a day. Be careful with tram tracks, which can be slippery when wet, and with cyclists, who are numerous.
t.castle garden and castle@49.3,17.4:
The Archbishop's palace at Kromeriz is a place where a bishop's idea of heaven became a garden. The prince-bishops of Olomouc, who ruled much of Moravia, made Kromeriz their summer residence, and in the seventeenth century they rebuilt the castle and laid out two gardens in the Baroque style. UNESCO listed the palace and the gardens in 1998. The Flower Garden is a formal garden with clipped hedges, fountains, and a long colonnade that is one of the finest in central Europe, while the larger Castle Garden beside the palace is a landscape park of lawns, trees and ponds.

The castle holds a picture gallery with one of the great paintings north of the Alps, The Flaying of Marsyas by Titian, a dark and disturbing work from his last years. The bishop who collected it bought it in the seventeenth century. The castle also has a large library and a music archive, and the rococo Assembly Hall hosted the Austrian parliament during the revolutions of 1848.

In the same ride is Olomouc, the old Moravian capital, whose Holy Trinity Column, a baroque monument over thirty metres high, was listed by UNESCO in 2000. The Haná region, where the two towns lie, is a fertile plain, and the roads run through fields of wheat, sugar beet and rapeseed, with villages of low houses and baroque churches. The riding is relaxed, with gentle bends and moderate traffic. The hills of the Beskydy and the Hostynske vrchy are within reach to the east for more interesting roads.

Kromeriz has about twenty-nine thousand people, so fuel, cafes and shops are plentiful, and the nearby town of Hulin is an alternative. Try a plate of Moravian food, with dumplings and roast pork, or a glass of local wine. Spring is lovely, when the gardens are in flower, and early autumn brings clear light. The gardens are a gentle place to walk after a long ride, so give yourself an hour or two.
t.hazamiyama kofun@34.6,135.6:
South-east of Osaka, in the low country between the Yamato river and the Nara hills, the earth is full of tombs. These are the kofun, great mounds raised for rulers and nobles between roughly the third and the sixth centuries, and the most famous have a distinctive shape, a keyhole, with a round rear mound and a trapezoid front, surrounded by a moat. The Mozu and Furuichi groups, with forty-nine mounds between them, were listed by UNESCO in 2019, and Hazamiyama, as far as I can tell, belongs with the Furuichi mounds.

The scale of the group is the point. These tombs, some of them over two hundred metres long, are built of earth, faced with stones and ringed with clay cylinders and figures called haniwa, which were arranged on the slopes: houses, horses, warriors, shamans and boats. The ruling class that built them had control of workers and resources on a scale that shows in the landscape, and the largest tomb of all, at Sakai, is about four hundred and eighty metres long. They are some of the biggest burial monuments in the world, but because they are mostly covered in trees, at ground level they look like wooded hills in the middle of suburbs.

That is the strangest thing about visiting, and a rider should know it before setting out. The mounds sit among houses, railway lines and rice fields, and many of them are managed by the Imperial Household Agency, so you cannot walk on them, and sometimes only a fenced path along the moat is open. Ponds around the mounds are full of lotus, herons and carp. The best view of the shape is often from above, in a museum or from a nearby building, and you may feel that you are walking round a forest.

The surrounding streets are narrow and busy, and local drivers tend to be cautious. A motorbike is practical for hopping between mounds, with parking at designated places only. Towns around here, including Kashihara and Matsubara, are large and have fuel, convenience stores and noodle shops on every corner. Spring brings cherry blossom along the moats, and the autumn leaves are lovely, while summer is hot and humid, and the rainy season in June makes everything green.
t.nakatsuhime no mikoto ryo kofun@34.6,135:
The name means the tomb of Princess Nakatsuhime, and it is the tradition that she was the consort of Emperor Ojin, one of the early rulers of Japan, whose own tomb, the second largest in the country, stands not far away. She is a name from the chronicles, written down centuries later, so history and legend are tangled.

Like other tombs designated as imperial, it is protected by the Imperial Household Agency, which owns and manages the site and allows no digging and no walking on the mound. You can walk along the edge of the moat, which is wide and full of water, with the green slope of the mound rising behind. It is quiet, a bit mysterious, and in the evening you may see herons standing on the banks. A small ceremonial gateway of wood marks the place where officials make offerings, and a sign explains the identity of the tomb in Japanese.

Archaeologists have made some use of the surroundings. Outside the moat, in the fields and neighbourhoods, they have found rows of haniwa cylinders and the remains of workshops that made them, and small satellite mounds for lesser people, grouped like a family around the main tomb. What they tell us is that these mounds were part of a landscape of ritual and politics, with a power centre on the Osaka plain that controlled trade and iron from the Korean peninsula.

For a rider, this is suburban Japan. The roads are narrow, smooth and slow, with strict speed limits, many traffic lights and small crossings, and local drivers are patient. Parking is difficult, so look for the car parks beside the tomb or in the neighbourhood. Kashihara, about one and a half kilometres away, and Yao, five kilometres, have fuel stations, convenience stores and noodle restaurants. A bowl of udon and a vending-machine coffee are the right sort of lunch, and the cherry trees along the moat in early April are worth the visit by themselves.
t.otorizuka kofun@34.6,135.6:
Otorizuka is a small mound, and its name, which seems to mean the bird mound, is lovely. What I do know is the setting: a plain south-east of Osaka that holds one of the greatest concentrations of burial mounds in the world, in the Furuichi group, and a small mound like this is part of the supporting cast, a tomb for a person of lower rank who wished to lie near a king.

The reason small mounds matter is that they show who was buried near whom. The large keyhole tombs, built for rulers in the fifth century, were surrounded by smaller round or square mounds, perhaps for relatives, officials or servants, arranged around them like a court. Their sizes and shapes reveal a ranking in death, and archaeologists have excavated some of them and found weapons, tools and armour, together with, in some cases, the remains of horses. Otorizuka, a smaller grassy hill near houses and fields, belongs in that picture.

Visiting is easy and a little odd. A sign by the path tells you its name, and you can stand beside it, perhaps with a child cycling past on the way home from school. The mound is covered with pine, bamboo and shrubs, and in spring and early summer the air is full of the smell of cut grass and the sound of cicadas. Because it is small, you can walk around it in minutes, and the surrounding neighbourhood, with its vegetable plots and small shrines, makes the walk more interesting.

For riding, the area around Kashihara, with its flat roads and rural lanes, is pleasant, but the traffic can be dense at rush hour, and some roads are very narrow. Keep to the speed limits, which are strictly enforced. Fuel stations and convenience stores are everywhere, and Matsubara, the larger city to the north-east, has plenty of services. Aim for spring or autumn, when the air is clear and the plain looks its best, and bring a spare hour for the nearby mounds.
t.joganjiyama kofun@34.6,135.6:
Not every great tomb is a mountain. Joganjiyama Kofun is one of the smaller, humbler mounds in the Furuichi cluster in southeastern Osaka, a patch of grass and trees tucked between houses, a rice field's worth of land that happens to be fifteen hundred years old. The ride labels it by a nearest town, Kashihara, but you are really in the Kawachi plain, where the Yamato kings built the huge keyhole-shaped tombs that give Japan's early centuries their name. Together with the Mozu group near Sakai, the Furuichi tombs were inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2019.

The shape is the point: a round mound joined to a square one, from above a keyhole, and the whole thing once ringed with clay figures called haniwa and a moat. Most of that is long gone. What you see today is a green mound with a fence, a signboard and an unexpected hush. Walk around the edge and notice how the neighbourhood has curved itself around it, streets bending out of respect, bicycles parked against the railings.

The riding here is city riding, to be honest. Small roads, narrow lanes, traffic lights, schoolkids on bicycles at three in the afternoon. This is a place for walking and looking, and your bike's job is to get you between mounds. Fuel is easy, since Habikino, Fujiidera and the larger suburbs are all just minutes away, and every other corner has a vending machine for a cold canned coffee.

If you want the grand scale, go and see the nearby tomb of Emperor Ojin, which is far bigger. What this small mound gives you instead is the sense that the big ones were part of an ordinary landscape of lesser tombs, built for family members and retainers, and that ordinary people have lived beside them for centuries. In autumn the leaves turn, and in April the surrounding streets are pink with cherry blossom, which is the best time to come.
t.daikandaiji temple site@34.5,135.8:
Daikandaiji does not exist any more. That is the interesting thing about it. In the seventh century this was one of the biggest temples in the young Yamato state, a royal foundation near Asuka with a vast compound that, according to the old records, ranked among the top few in the country. When the capital moved north to Nara early in the eighth century, the temple went with it, reborn as Daianji, and the original site was left to farmland. What remains is an open field with low foundation stones, a few information boards, and the quiet that follows a big idea.

The setting is classic Nara basin: flat rice fields, small hills at the edges, and the green triangles of Mount Miwa and the Asuka hills not far away. The nearest big towns are Sakura and Kashihara, both with fuel, supermarkets and trains, so there is no pressure to stock up. The roads around here are narrow and agricultural, often one lane and a half, and the speed limit is a polite suggestion that the local tractors enforce for everyone.

You are on well-trodden pilgrim ground. Routes of the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage pass through this region, and the old road to Mount Koya also threads the area. If the ride you are on mentions those, you are following the same line pilgrims have walked for a thousand years, only with more horsepower. The foundation stones are spread out in the grass in a pattern that you can read once you stand on the right spot, and the whole thing takes about ten minutes to understand and fifty to enjoy.

Local food is plain and good. Nara is known for kakinoha-zushi, a pressed sushi wrapped in persimmon leaves, and for tsukemono pickles that appear on every set meal. Autumn is the season for persimmons, which hang orange on bare branches against the paddies, and if you come in May the rice is just planted, fields shining like mirrors. Summer is hot and humid, and the cicadas drown conversation. Go early or late, and plan on a lunch in a small town instead of a view.
t.kumano sanzan seiganto ji@33.7,135.9:
Hardly any approach in Japan is as dramatic as the one up to Seiganto-ji. A temple has been here for well over a millennium, founded according to tradition in the fourth century, but what hits you is how it sits: a vermilion three-storey pagoda in front of a 133-metre waterfall, the tallest single-drop fall in the country, with the cedar forest pressing close on both sides. The temple and the neighbouring Nachi shrine share the mountain and the same story. Together they form one of the three Kumano shrines on the Kii Peninsula, and the pilgrim trails that link them are on the World Heritage list.

The ride to get here is the real prize. Coming down from the north on Route 42 you follow the Kii coast with its sea cliffs, tunnels and tiny fishing harbours, then turn inland at Nachikatsuura and climb a steep, twisting mountain road through plantation cedar to the temple car park. Expect hairpins, damp tarmac and bad visibility in rain, because this part of Japan gets some of the heaviest rainfall in the country. Shingu is the bigger town nearby, with fuel and supermarkets; the coastal strip has stations too, but fill up before you climb.

The pagoda is open for you to climb, and the view from the top, when the weather behaves, shows the waterfall right in front of you and the Pacific beyond. The old stone steps that lead down from here to the falls are part of the Daimon-zaka path, lined with giant cedar trees; even if you do not walk the whole thing, a few minutes on the stones is worth it.

Culturally, Kumano blends Buddhism and the native Shinto faith so thoroughly that the line between them blurs. Three-legged crows appear on amulets here, a symbol of the divine guide who led the legendary first emperor through these mountains. In the early afternoon the tour buses arrive, so aim for first thing in the morning. Winter is quiet and cold but sometimes clear, and spring brings azaleas.

Ask at the temple about the traditional hearty teahouse food nearby; the mountain is well-fed with noodles and mochi.
t.ojin tenno ryo kofun@34.6,135.6:
Emperor Ojin's tomb is the largest in Japan by volume, even if the Nintoku tomb near Sakai is longer, and it feels it. The mound is some four hundred metres long, a keyhole of earth with a double moat that holds water the colour of old jade, and the whole thing is so overgrown it reads from a distance as a wooded hill dropped into a town. Only the imperial household agency decides who sets foot on the mound, which means nobody does. What you get is a path around the outside, a worship platform at the front, and a very particular kind of silence.

It is called Konda Gobyoyama locally, and it sits in the Furuichi group in the eastern part of Osaka prefecture, close to Habikino. The ride labels it by the nearest bigger town, Kashihara, but the real setting is the Kawachi plain at the foot of the Kongo and Katsuragi range, flat, suburban, busy with commuters. There are no wide open roads here, just short hops between traffic lights, but it all happens quickly and fuel is everywhere.

What makes the place special is scale. To grasp it, walk the perimeter path; the walk is long, and the curved wall of trees on your left never seems to end. The moat attracts herons, and in winter ducks gather in the water. Early morning is best, with the low sun flat on the ground and joggers drifting past.

The tomb dates to about the late fourth or early fifth century and belongs to the age when the Yamato rulers had the technology, the labour and the ambition to move thousands of tonnes of earth for a funeral. Archaeologists have found clay haniwa figures, bits of armour and horse gear, and the cluster around it includes dozens of smaller tombs for relatives. Many are tucked behind ordinary houses.

Go in spring when the cherry trees line the nearby lanes or in the gold of November. In summer the heat in this basin is sticky and heavy, and a canned coffee from a vending machine becomes a ritual.
t.aoyama kofun@34.6,135.6:
Aoyama Kofun is a modest tomb among many, one of the Furuichi mounds in southeastern Osaka that together make up a landscape of burials from the fifth century and thereabouts. The ride calls it by a nearer town, Kashihara, but the ground is the Kawachi plain, below the Kongo and Katsuragi hills, and the character is residential: low houses, small shops, canals of traffic on the main roads and quiet lanes that circle the mounds.

What you find is a forested hump of earth, fenced and signposted, set in the middle of ordinary life. Sometimes you see the keyhole outline only from the map; from the ground it is a tree-covered rise that the street goes around. That is the odd charm of the Furuichi group. The tombs were once strikingly bare, with sloping flanks covered in river stones and lines of clay figures. Today they have grown into small forests, and the birds love them: you hear warblers and bulbuls in spring and see herons in the moats.

The riding here is a patchwork. Fuel is trivial to find, because Habikino and Fujiidera and the larger neighbouring cities are close, and the main roads are lined with the usual Japanese convenience stores where you can get a hot coffee and a rice ball for the price of a small coin.

Japan's earliest rulers were not buried in obscurity. They were buried in an enormous show of power, and the scatter of satellite tombs around the big ones suggests a system: relatives and officials were interred near their lord, a kind of political map written in soil. Having seen the grand tomb of Ojin close by, an afternoon among the smaller mounds like this gives you the full picture of the culture.

Come in the cool months; March and April bring blossom, and November is dry and bright. Avoid the midsummer afternoons, when the plain turns into a sauna and the cicadas sound like machinery.
t.kumano sanzan kumano nachi taisha@33.7,1:
Everyone who comes to Nachi comes for the waterfall, and the waterfall earns it. Nachi no Taki drops 133 metres in one clean ribbon, the tallest single fall in Japan, and the shrine of Kumano Nachi Taisha was built to worship it. For well over a thousand years the water itself has been treated as a god. The shrine buildings stand on the slope above, vermilion halls in the cedar forest, close enough that the roar reaches the courtyard when the rains have been heavy.

The mountain road up to the shrine from the Nachikatsuura coast is steep and twisting, with the hairpins you would expect, tight and shaded. In wet weather the tarmac stays slick and the clouds come down; this corner of the Kii Peninsula is one of the rainiest places in Japan. Shingu is the larger town with a full range of fuel and supplies, and the coastal strip near Nachikatsuura also has stations, so fill the tank before the climb, because there is nothing up on the mountain except souvenir stalls and noodle shops.

The pilgrim path is the other draw. The Daimon-zaka slope is a stone-paved lane lined with cedars that are several hundred years old, and it climbs in mossy steps up to the shrine; people in rented kimono photograph themselves there every morning. A short walk up from the shrine is the neighbouring temple of Seiganto-ji, with its pagoda in front of the falls. Pilgrims used to visit both, a reminder that the old religions here did not divide the sacred up neatly.

Look for the three-legged crow, Yatagarasu, the symbol of Kumano. According to legend it guided the first emperor through these mountains; now it adorns amulets and also the badge of Japan's national football team, which delights visitors who spot it.

The best moment is early, before the buses, or after the drizzle in the late afternoon when mist hangs in the cedars. Summer is steamy and spring is mild. Wear grippy boots for the stone steps.
t.nonaka kofun@34.6,135.6:
Nonaka Kofun sits quietly in the town of Fujiidera in southeast Osaka, one of the larger tombs of the Furuichi group, and unlike many of its neighbours it has a story that archaeologists keep returning to. When it was excavated in the 1960s, workers found huge amounts of weapons and armour inside and around the mound: helmets, iron arrowheads, swords and stacks of iron plate. The place seemed to be a kind of arsenal buried beside the tomb of someone powerful. It makes you think about what the fifth-century Yamato court considered precious.

The map labels the nearest town Kashihara, but you are really on the Kawachi plain, a low area between the Yamato river and the mountains, now thickly built up with suburbs. The tomb is a rounded, forested mound, and from above it forms the typical keyhole shape. It is not a showpiece like the giant tombs nearby; you walk around, read the sign and appreciate how the Furuichi group was woven into everyday life.

Riding here is plain city riding. Use the bike to hop between the tombs, and expect traffic, signals and the kind of narrow streets that make a big touring machine feel overdressed. There is no problem with fuel, as Fujiidera and Habikino and the other nearby cities have stations at every turn, and the convenience stores open all night.

Because the tombs lie so near each other, it is easy to build a route that gathers several in an afternoon, going from small to huge. Start with the humble mounds, then finish at the massive tomb of Emperor Ojin; the contrast teaches you more than the signboards.

If you can, come in spring or in late autumn. At the right hour in March the cherry blossoms dust the paths, and the whole district has the calm of a place that has made peace with its own antiquity. Summer is thick with humidity and noise from the cicadas, and the best advice then is to carry a cold drink and visit early.
t.hachizuka kofun@34.6,135.6:
Hachizuka is one of the stranger tombs in the Furuichi cluster, for anyone who has got used to the keyhole shape. The ride labels it by a town called Kashihara, but you are really on the Kawachi plain, below the Kongo and Katsuragi mountains, among the fruit orchards and commuter lines that thread through Habikino and Fujiidera.

What I like about the whole group is how mixed the tombs are. The giants get the headlines, but the surrounding mounds are a social map: round ones, square ones, keyholes, big, small, spread across the plain in a pattern that shows who ranked where in the Yamato court of the fifth century. Hachizuka sits alongside this, reminding you that the tomb builders did not use one template but a whole vocabulary. Walk around it and you will find a small information board, a path along the fence and a surprising number of cats.

Riding between these sites is easy but dull. Narrow lanes, constant traffic lights, kids in uniform on bicycles after school. Park the bike near one of the small lots, and walk. Fuel and food are right there in Habikino and Fujiidera, with their station forecourts and ever-present convenience stores, and Osaka itself has a food culture worth taking seriously: okonomiyaki on the griddle, kushikatsu skewers, takoyaki octopus balls from a street stall.

Habikino is also known for its grapes, and the hillsides above the plain grow them for local wine, which makes an unexpected addition to a heritage day. If it is September, look for the roadside stands.

Come in the cooler months. The plain gets steamy by July, and the afternoon light is flat and hazy. In early April the cherry trees along the nearby lanes bloom and the whole neighbourhood seems to exhale, and a mound that looks like ordinary woodland suddenly feels like part of a very old conversation between the living and the dead.
t.hakayama kofun@34.6,135.6:
Hakayama Kofun is one of the quieter satellites that crowd around the giant tomb of Emperor Ojin in southeastern Osaka. The name is plain enough: Hakayama means tomb mountain, and that is how the neighbourhood treated it for a very long time. The ride calls the nearest town Kashihara, but the ground is the Kawachi plain at the foot of the Kongo range, in the Furuichi district, where the Yamato elite built a necropolis of well over a hundred mounds.

It matters because of its position. When you stand near it you can see how the great tomb and its smaller companions form a deliberate group, with the satellites placed around the main mound like a court around a king. Excavations around Ojin's tomb and its neighbours have turned up horse trappings, clay figures, iron tools and even the remains of ritual objects, and archaeologists read the layout the way a historian reads a seating plan. Hakayama is part of that layout, a small piece of a very large sentence.

The setting is more domestic than monumental. Streets run right up to the moat, a footpath circles the mound, and there is usually a gardener or a pensioner out for a morning stroll. Wildlife is better than you might expect: egrets stalk the moat water, dragonflies hover in summer, and in the woods on the mound there are bush warblers calling in spring.

The riding itself is city traffic, so lower your expectations. This is a place to put on a hat and walk. Fuel is no problem, as the surrounding towns are crowded with petrol stations, and every corner has a vending machine selling hot canned tea in winter and cold in summer.

If you have time, head up to the hills above Habikino and look back across the plain; from a little height you can see the tomb group as a series of dark green patches in a sea of rooftops. Spring cherry blossom and late autumn colour are the best times, with winter mornings clear and cold.
t.suketayama kofun@34.6,135.6:
Suketayama is another of the Furuichi tombs, set in the part of southeast Osaka where the old Yamato elite buried their dead beside the Ishikawa river and the broad Kawachi plain. The ride names the nearest town as Kashihara, but you are within sight of Habikino and Fujiidera and the commuter lines that bind this place to Osaka's centre. The mound here is smaller than the great keyhole tombs but has its own presence, a green hill in a district of tile roofs.

A thing worth knowing about these tombs is how they were treated afterwards. After the age of the great kings the mounds were no longer special, and over the centuries they became wood lots, orchards, paddies and in some cases the base of a medieval fort. Then in the Meiji period the state decided that the biggest were imperial tombs and fenced them off, which is why some are now untouched and silent while others have been dug and measured. Suketayama belongs to the smaller category, the type that archaeologists were allowed to study and local people were allowed to walk beside.

Traffic around here is dense and the lanes are narrow, so bring patience instead of a plan for speed. The riding value is in the context. Use a bike to hop from mound to mound, and enjoy the odd contrast between ancient earthworks and the modern suburb on all sides. Petrol stations are everywhere, and so are bakeries and noodle shops. Try udon in the Osaka style, with a light kelp broth and a soft fried tofu pouch, the kitsune udon that locals defend vigorously.

In the hills above the plain, toward the Kongo range, there are grape growers and small wineries, and the road up toward Kawachi Nagano has views back across the plain. Autumn is the best season, dry and clear, and spring is lovely for blossom. July and August are punishing.

Go on a weekday morning and you will often have the whole place to yourself, apart from a few cats and a gardener raking leaves.
t.nishiumazuka kofun@34.6,135.6:
The name Nishiumazuka means west horse mound, and horses do figure in the story of the Furuichi tombs. Excavations around the giant tomb of Emperor Ojin turned up harness fittings and even buried horses in nearby tombs, and historians read this as a sign of the new cavalry culture arriving in Japan from the Korean peninsula in the fifth century. Horses meant armies, and armies meant a different kind of kingship, which is the story these mounds tell if you read them closely.

Nishiumazuka is a compact tomb in the southeast of Osaka, among the houses of Habikino and Fujiidera on the Kawachi plain. The ride names the nearest town as Kashihara, but you could just as well say you are at the foot of the Kongo and Katsuragi range, with the commuter railway line running through. A fence, a signboard and a screen of trees are most of what the visitor gets, and that is plenty.

Do not expect an empty road. The lanes are narrow, there are traffic lights every few hundred metres and schoolchildren cycle three abreast, so this is slow, polite riding. The consolation is the convenience: fuel, vending machines and bakeries are within a few minutes, and you can be back on the expressway to Nara or Kyoto without trouble. Osaka itself is a magnificent place to eat, so if you plan an overnight, plan for a bowl of kushikatsu or a plate of okonomiyaki.

Look at the moat if you can see it. Water here is often green with duckweed, and in winter you will see ducks on it and grey herons standing like statues. Seasonal contrasts are strong: the plain is shimmering and humid in summer, and the cicadas make a continuous roar.

Autumn is dry, bright and ideal. Late March and early April bring cherry blossom to the lanes that skirt the mounds. If you only have time for one or two tombs, make them the big one and a small one like this, because together they show what the whole thing meant.
t.higashiyama kofun@34.6,135.6:
Higashiyama Kofun is the east hill, and that is how it was named, by neighbours who had no idea what was under the trees. It is another of the Furuichi mounds in the southeast of Osaka, where the Kawachi plain is packed with suburbs and the old tombs of the Yamato kings are tucked between them. The nearest named town on the ride is Kashihara, but you are among the streets of Habikino and Fujiidera, within sight of the Kongo hills.

One thing worth noticing here is how the tombs shaped irrigation and farming. The moats served as reservoirs, and for centuries farmers drew water from them to feed rice paddies, which is part of the reason many of the tombs survived at all. The Kawachi plain has some of Japan's oldest reservoirs, and the sight of still water around a mound is a clue to its long working life, not just a mournful ornament.

The mound is wooded, fenced, and signposted. A path leads around part of it and you can peek at the water. It is a place for twenty minutes, not two hours, and the best way to use it is as a counterpoint to the grander tombs nearby. Climb out of the neighbourhood and look back at the plain from the hills; the dark patches of trees among the rooftops are the tombs.

The roads are as urban as roads can be. Narrow lanes, bicycles, school crossings and endless traffic lights, with petrol stations and convenience stores at every corner. A touring machine feels clumsy here; a small commuter bike is ideal. Fuel is no concern, and Osaka's food culture is a constant temptation, with takoyaki from a street stall at any hour.

The seasons are marked clearly. Spring brings cherry blossom, early summer brings the rainy season, when the moats turn jade green, and autumn brings crisp air and golden light, ideal for walking. Late summer is the worst, humid and loud with insects. If the sun is low, the tomb's shape can sometimes be read from a nearby rooftop or footbridge, which is the closest you get to the aerial view the builders never saw.
t.cave of las mulas de molino@24.7,-105.0:
It is a land of long flat valleys, mesquite and thorn scrub, adobe villages, dry creek beds and low blue ranges on the horizon, with the Sierra Madre Occidental rising to the west.

Durango as a whole has a reputation as film country. Hollywood shot hundreds of westerns on its dusty plains, and John Wayne was a regular. The ride gives that feeling: broad skies, old ranch gates, cottonwoods along the creeks and the occasional dust devil. The area north of Durango city is also home to Mennonite farming colonies, whose families arrived from Canada and Chihuahua in the twentieth century, and you will see their cheese and apple stalls beside the highway, along with fields of beans and oats.

The riding is of the long-distance, open-road kind. Federal Highway 45 runs north to Chihuahua and south to Durango and Zacatecas, with wide shoulders, big trucks and long straight sections where wind is the main hazard. Side roads are good for exploring, but surfaces can be rough, and cattle on the road are common. The usual Mexican advice applies: avoid riding after dark, watch for topes, the speed bumps that appear without warning at village edges, and use toll roads where they exist for smoother tarmac and better safety.

Fuel is available in Nuevo Ideal and in larger towns, but distances are long, so top up whenever you pass a station. Durango city, about a hundred kilometres south, has everything you need.

Winter nights are frosty and spring brings dust and wind, while summer rains in July and August turn the desert green and the creeks run brown. Autumn, with clear skies and warm days, is the best season. If you intend to look for the cave, ask in the village; local knowledge counts more than any map.
t.zona nucleo 01@20.9,-103.8:
The blue agave takes seven or eight years to ripen, and in all that time it does nothing but sit in the red volcanic soil and look like a giant spiky pineapple. Then a jimador arrives with a long-handled blade called a coa, strips the leaves, and cuts out the heart, which looks like a huge pineapple and weighs as much as a small child. The hearts are baked, crushed and fermented, and what comes out of the still is tequila. The landscape that makes this possible, the agave fields and distilleries around the town of Tequila in Jalisco, was listed as a World Heritage site in 2006.

This zone sits near Amatitan, a town of about eleven thousand people that has a long history of distilling. The setting is a plain of dark red earth and blue-grey agave, row after row, against the backdrop of the Tequila volcano, which rises to nearly three thousand metres to the northwest, and the deep canyon of the Santiago river to the north. Old haciendas with whitewashed walls and chimneys stand among the fields. Some of the distilleries have been working since the eighteenth century, and several run tours and tastings, although you should obviously think twice about the tasting if you are on a bike.

The riding is lovely in a gentle way. From Guadalajara, which is about an hour away, you can take the toll road or the older highway through small towns, with agave stretching on both sides, and then explore the back roads between villages. Corners are soft, surfaces mostly good but with Mexico's classic hazards: topes, potholes, stray dogs and slow trucks. Fuel is easy in Amatitan and Tequila, the larger town just up the road, and Guadalajara has everything.

Spend time in Tequila itself, a pretty town with a big church, a main square and a famous old train that takes visitors through the fields. Try a michelada or a plate of carne en su jugo, a Jalisco speciality of beef in broth, and ask your host about the difference between blanco and reposado.

The dry season, from November to May, is the best time. The rains in summer turn the fields green, bringing afternoon storms, and the colours are richer then.
t.cape floral region protected areas@-34.4:
The Cape Peninsula ends in a long, wind-battered headland, and at its tip, Cape Point, the Atlantic and Indian oceans seem to argue. Here the rock plunges to the sea in great cliffs, the sky is huge, and on most days a gale tries to remove your hat. This is the southern part of Table Mountain National Park, set aside to protect the Cape Floral Region, the smallest and richest of the world's six plant kingdoms.

Fynbos, the fine-leaved shrubland, is the star. It includes proteas, ericas and restios, in an astonishing number of species, many of which grow nowhere else. In late winter and spring the slopes colour up in pinks, oranges and yellows. Wildlife includes bontebok, eland, ostriches, Cape mountain zebra and chacma baboons, which are clever and bold, so keep food out of sight and the bike's luggage fastened. African penguins nest on the beach at Boulders, not far away on the False Bay side, and are a quick detour.

For riders, the main road down the peninsula from Cape Town is a delight. The route passes Chapman's Peak, a road cut into cliffs above the sea with views that make you slow down, though it sometimes closes for rockfall or in high winds. Further south the road runs through Fish Hoek and Simon's Town, and then into the park. Wind is the big factor: summer south-easters can be strong enough to shove a bike across a lane. Late spring and early autumn have the best balance of warmth and calm.

A restaurant near the car park does decent meals, and a funicular takes people to the old lighthouse if they do not fancy the climb. Bring layers, since weather changes by the hour.
t.lednice valtice cultural landscape@48.7,:
The Lednice-Valtice landscape is what happens when a very rich family decides to make a whole district into a garden. For centuries the Liechtenstein dynasty owned this corner of southern Moravia, near the border with Austria, and from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century they reshaped it, planting woods, digging ponds and building follies, until castles, parks, canals and farmland were composed into one huge designed scene about two hundred square kilometres in area. UNESCO listed it as a cultural landscape in 1996.

Valtice, a small town of under four thousand people, is the baroque heart, with a large palace used by the Liechtensteins as a summer residence. Lednice, a few kilometres away, has a neo-Gothic chateau with a glasshouse and a minaret, about sixty metres tall, built in the 1790s as a romantic touch. The fanciful buildings scattered through the parkland include a colonnade on a hill, a hunting lodge and a mock ruin, and the whole thing is meant to be found as you wander or ride along tree-lined avenues.

Wine is the local obsession, and Valtice is the capital of Moravian wine, with cellars, tasting rooms and a wine salon in the castle. The surrounding vineyards produce Grüner Veltliner, Riesling and Pálava, a local aromatic grape. Further east the Pálava hills, a limestone ridge near Mikulov, rise from the plain. Riding here is gentle: flat or softly rolling roads, avenues of oaks and poplars, and a few lazy bends past vineyards. Speed limits in villages are strictly enforced. Spring brings blossom, early autumn the grape harvest and golden light, and summers can be hot.

Valtice has a few shops and cafes and a fuel station nearby, and the larger towns of Mikulov and Břeclav have more. Schrattenberg, over the border in Austria, is only a few kilometres away, and the old frontier is now unmarked. Do not drink and ride, a point worth remembering in a wine town, but do buy a bottle for the evening, and try the sweet trdelník pastries.
t.wien canabae sudwest@48.2,16.4:
Vienna sits on top of an older city, and Vindobona was it. In the first century AD, the Romans built a legionary fortress here, on a bluff above the Danube, to guard the northern frontier of the empire. A civilian settlement, the canabae, grew up beside it, with taverns, workshops and homes for the families of soldiers, and the area to the southwest of the fortress was part of that sprawl. Today the streets of the inner city still follow the lines of the Roman camp, and fragments of walls and baths lie beneath cellars and basements.

The Hoher Markt, a square in the old town, has the exposed foundations of two Roman houses, displayed in a small underground museum. Tradition says that the emperor Marcus Aurelius, the philosopher-ruler, died at Vindobona in AD 180 while campaigning on the frontier. The Danube limes, as the line of forts and watchtowers is known, was added to UNESCO's World Heritage list in 2021, and the Wien sites are part of that long chain. Another small fort at Ybbs, further upriver, belongs to the same ride.

Riding in Vienna is a matter of trams, one-way streets and cobbled lanes, with strict parking rules in the centre. The Ringstrasse, the grand boulevard circling the old town, is a pleasure to ride on a quiet morning, passing the opera house, the parliament and the museums. Outside the city, the Danube valley and the Wachau, a wine and apricot region west of the capital, offer excellent riding. Be careful of tram tracks, which are slippery in rain. Spring and autumn are the most pleasant seasons.

Vienna has plenty of fuel stations, particularly on the outskirts, and the central districts are packed with cafes serving coffee and cake, wine taverns known as Heuriger on the city edges, and traditional restaurants where Wiener Schnitzel is the standard order. Leave the bike at a hotel garage and explore the centre on foot, with a stop in a coffee house to read the paper.
t.robben island@-33.8,18.4:
Seen from the beach at Bloubergstrand, Robben Island is a low, flat smudge on Table Bay, with Table Mountain standing up behind it from the other side. It is one of the best known and most difficult places in South Africa to think about. For several centuries the island served as a place of exile and isolation, a prison for political opponents of the Dutch and British, a leper colony and a military base. Between 1961 and 1991 it held political prisoners of the apartheid state, including Nelson Mandela, who spent eighteen of his twenty-seven years in custody here.

Visitors reach the island only by ferry from the Nelson Mandela Gateway at Cape Town's V&A Waterfront, since no private boats or bikes are allowed, and the trip is organised as a guided tour led by former political prisoners or trained guides. The tour takes you through the maximum security prison, past the lime quarry where prisoners worked in blinding glare and the small cell where Mandela was held. It is sober, and many people say it changes the way they think about the country. UNESCO listed the island in 1999.

For riders the useful ground is on the mainland. The R27 coast road north from Cape Town runs along Table Bay, with long open views of the island, wide beaches that attract kitesurfers and, on clear days, Table Mountain at the far end of the bay. Traffic can be heavy in the morning and late afternoon, and the wind in summer, a strong south-easter, blows sand across the road and shakes light bikes. Early morning light on the water is the best time for photographs.

Bookings for the ferry usually need to be made well ahead, especially in the busy season from December to March, and boats can be cancelled when the sea is rough. Fuel and food are easy in Bloubergstrand and Cape Town, and the beachside cafés look straight at the island. If you only see it from the shore, it still tells you something. The island is also a nature reserve, home to African penguins and many seabirds.
t.city of graz historic centre@47.1,15.4:
Graz has a hill in the middle of it, which tells you something about the town. The Schlossberg rises steeply out of the old centre, topped by a clock tower whose big hour hand and small minute hand were swapped, by tradition, so that the time could be read from far away. The fortress that once crowned the hill was dismantled by Napoleon's armies, but the tower was bought back by the citizens, and that act of stubbornness is part of the town's character.

The old town is a UNESCO site, and the reason is that it reads like a layered history of central European building styles, from Gothic to Renaissance to Baroque to modern, all of it in a compact space. The Landeszeughaus, the provincial armoury, is the largest historical arsenal in the world, with thousands of suits of armour and weapons kept in the rows where they were stored for defence against the Ottoman Empire. Nearby there is a blob-shaped modern art museum, locally nicknamed the friendly alien, and an island in the river Mur that floats as a steel and glass platform with a café. Graz is a university city, and in term time the cafés fill with students.

Eating is a pleasure in Styria. The region is known for pumpkin seed oil, dark green and nutty, which is poured over salads, soups and even vanilla ice cream, and for the wines of the south, which are crisp whites grown on steep slopes. You will find a decent meal anywhere. In the evening the squares fill with outdoor tables and the sound of conversation.

The riding is the real bonus. South of town, the Styrian wine roads wind through hills of vines and orchards on narrow, twisting asphalt, and to the north the foothills of the Alps offer plenty of curves around Schöckl and the Mur valley. Inside Graz, trams and cyclists share the streets, and the old centre is partly pedestrian, so park outside and walk. Fuel is available everywhere in the city, which has well over two hundred thousand people. The best months are May and early autumn, when the days are warm and the air is clear. Summers can be hot, and winters are grey and foggy in the basin.
t.vienna@48.2,16.4:
Vienna rewards the rider who parks the bike and walks. The Innere Stadt, the old centre, sits inside the line of the Ringstrasse, the great boulevard laid out in the nineteenth century where the medieval walls once stood, and it is lined with the opera house, the parliament, the university and a procession of grand museums. At the heart is Stephansdom, the cathedral with a roof of coloured tiles and a tall south tower that has been a landmark for centuries. The Hofburg, once the imperial palace, takes up a sizable chunk of the neighbourhood.

The city's culture is a culture of tables. Coffeehouses, with marble tabletops, newspapers on wooden holders and waiters in black, are recognised by UNESCO as part of the intangible heritage, and a single coffee can buy you an afternoon. Wiener schnitzel, thin and crisp and served with potato salad, is the standard meal, and Sachertorte, a dense chocolate cake with apricot jam, is the standard sweet, though locals disagree about where to eat the best one. The Naschmarkt has stalls of olives, spices and fresh produce, and the Prater, with its giant Ferris wheel from 1897, is a cheerful reminder that Vienna once led the world in amusements.

Riding out of Vienna is easier than riding in. The Höhenstrasse climbs through the Vienna Woods to the viewpoint at Kahlenberg, a good road for an evening run with views over the Danube and the city. East of town, the land flattens and opens into the Pannonian plain, where roads run straight through vineyards and fields, and where the shallow, reed-fringed Neusiedlersee waits in the heat, a steppe lake that feels like an entirely different country. Trams, taxis and cyclists make the centre a place for patience, and parking rules are strict, so ask at your hotel.

Fuel is easy at stations around the ring roads and on the main exits, though there are few in the centre. Summer can be hot and humid, winter is cold and grey, and the best months are May, June and September, when the evening light lingers. Be gentle with the cobbles, and mind the tram tracks in wet weather, because they are slick and can catch a wheel.
t.jewish quarter and st procopius basilica:
The basilica of Saint Procopius in Třebíč looks stern from outside, a long and plain Romanesque and Gothic church with massive walls and a squat tower, and it was built in the early thirteenth century as part of a Benedictine monastery founded in 1101. The monks chose a site by the Jihlava river, in the rolling country of the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands, and over the centuries the monastery became rich and powerful before being closed in the eighteenth century. The church survives as a rare and fine example of a style that blended the round arches of Romanesque with the pointed arches of Gothic, with a crypt that is older than the rest.

The surprise is inside. The interior is bright, high and balanced, with a long nave and a fine carved portal, and wall paintings that reveal the faith of the age. Across the river, just a few minutes' walk away, lies the Jewish quarter, one of the best preserved in Europe, and together the two sites are listed by UNESCO as an example of Jewish and Christian cultures living side by side. That is not a romantic phrase here. The two communities lived in neighbouring districts, traded together and sometimes quarrelled, but the town's history is one of constant contact.

The area is a quiet one for riders, a region of low hills, mixed woodland, ponds and fields, with good roads that run between villages with a steepled church and a tavern. The Vysočina, as the highland is called, is not dramatic, but it is peaceful and varied, and there is often little traffic. In summer the fields are golden with wheat and bright with poppies, and in autumn the forests turn orange and brown. Winter brings snow and ice, and roads may be treacherous. Watch for farm vehicles and for deer at dusk.

Třebíč is a town of about thirty-nine thousand people and has all the fuel, food and accommodation a rider needs. Czech beer, goulash and dumplings are the standard, and the cafés in the main square are a good place for a break. There is a small nuclear power station at Dukovany, a short distance to the east, visible as a cluster of cooling towers on the horizon, which gives the pleasant landscape an unexpected edge. A weekday visit in May or September avoids the crowds.
t.kutna hora historical town centre with t:
Kutná Hora was once the second city of Bohemia, and the reason is silver. In the thirteenth century, rich veins were found in the hills here, and within a hundred years the town was producing a large share of Europe's silver, which paid for kings, armies and cathedrals. The royal mint, known as the Italian Court because of the Florentine craftsmen who ran it, struck the Prague groschen, a silver coin that circulated across Central Europe, and the Bohemian king sometimes stayed here. The wealth of the town is written in its buildings, notably the great Cathedral of Saint Barbara, a Gothic masterpiece with soaring, pointed vaults and flying buttresses like the ribs of a ship, dedicated to the patron saint of miners.

The other famous sight is a few minutes away at Sedlec, where the bone church, an ossuary chapel, is decorated with the bones of tens of thousands of people. Skulls form garlands, a chandelier hangs made from every bone of the human body, and a coat of arms is carved in bone. The reason was practical: the cemetery was believed to hold soil from Golgotha, and so many people were buried here that bones had to be dug up to make room. In the nineteenth century a local woodcarver was commissioned to arrange them, with a macabre sense of order. The effect is more thoughtful than frightening.

The ride from here goes on to see the landscape of the Kladruby horses, where an old stud farm breeds the grey and black ceremonial carriage horses of the Habsburg court. The countryside of central Bohemia is gentle, with green fields, ponds and small woods, and roads that run straight for stretches and then bend through villages. Surface quality can be uneven in smaller roads, with patches, cobbles in villages and poor shoulders. Take care in wet weather, because the tarmac can be slippery, and watch for farm vehicles.

Kutná Hora has just over twenty thousand people and offers fuel, shops, restaurants and a good selection of guesthouses. Try the traditional Czech dishes of roast pork with dumplings and cabbage, with local beer, and rest in one of the cafés of the old town. The best time to visit is spring or autumn, when the crowds are lighter. Weekends in high summer bring bus parties from Prague, so an early start helps. Parking in the historic centre is restricted, so leave the bike outside the old town.
t.the jewish quarter@49.2,15.9:
In Třebíč, the Jewish quarter is the part of town that nobody wants to leave. A dense knot of about a hundred and twenty houses, built close together on a slope above the Jihlava river, it survived because the Jewish population had been confined here since the seventeenth century, and because the town's later development took place elsewhere. The streets are narrow and irregular, passing under arches and between buildings of different ages, and the whole quarter has a close, human scale that cannot be built any more. UNESCO listed it in 2003, together with the nearby basilica.

Two synagogues stand in the quarter. The Old Synagogue has painted walls and a carved Torah shrine, and the Rear Synagogue, with a beautiful ceiling of painted plasterwork, is now a place of exhibitions. Above the town, on a hillside, lies the Jewish cemetery, one of the largest in Moravia, with some three thousand tombstones that show the names and symbols of families who lived here for centuries. The Jewish community of Třebíč was destroyed during the Second World War, when almost all its members were deported and murdered, and the memorial in the quarter and the cemetery gives the visit a weight that is hard to forget.

The ride that begins here goes south to the Lednice-Valtice landscape, a vast ornamental park of palaces, follies, lakes and avenues laid out by the Liechtenstein family and also a UNESCO property. Between the two, the road crosses Moravia, with gentle hills, vineyards and villages, and a long tradition of wine. The south Moravian wine region is the most famous in the Czech Republic, with white wines such as Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, and the cellars in the villages serve wine in the evening. Road surfaces are generally good, though country roads can be patchy and cobbled in village centres.

Fuel and food are easy in Třebíč, which has nearly forty thousand people, and in the wine country the pensions and cellars offer simple meals. Take care with alcohol when riding, because the Czech Republic has a zero tolerance rule. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, with warm light and long evenings, and the vintage in September fills the villages with music.
t.guadalajara@20.7,-103.3:
Guadalajara is Mexico's second city in many ways, and the heart of its mariachi and tequila traditions. Mariachi music, the charro horsemanship and the tequila spirit all trace their cultural roots to the state of Jalisco, and the capital is where they come together. The historic centre has big colonial buildings, wide plazas and a cathedral with two towers that were rebuilt after an earthquake in the nineteenth century. Murals by José Clemente Orozco, one of the great Mexican muralists, cover the walls and dome of the Hospicio Cabañas, a vast neoclassical complex that is a UNESCO site.

Tlaquepaque and Zapopan are old towns now absorbed into the metropolis, and each has its own character. Tlaquepaque is known for pottery, glass and handicrafts, with pedestrian streets and open-air restaurants. The city has a reputation for good food, and the torta ahogada, a pork sandwich drowned in spicy sauce, is the local specialty. Birria, a slow-cooked meat stew, is another favourite.

For riders, Guadalajara is both the start and the finish of the road to the tequila country. About an hour northwest, the town of Tequila sits among fields of blue agave, with the volcano of the same name behind it. The agave landscape and the old distilleries in the area are a UNESCO World Heritage site. The road there is mostly a fast highway, with trucks and buses, followed by smaller roads between the plants, rows of spiky blue-grey rosettes stretching to the horizon. Toll roads are well kept, but local roads can have potholes and topes, the sharp speed bumps that appear without much warning.

The metropolitan area has millions of people, and fuel, food and repairs are available everywhere. Out in the country, stations are less frequent, though still regular on the main roads. Pemex, the national brand, has stations along most highways. Be aware that the rainy season runs from June to September, with heavy afternoon storms, and that the city's traffic can be chaotic, with buses, taxis and motorbikes weaving constantly.

Winter and spring bring dry, warm days, and the light on the agave fields in late afternoon is wonderful. Drink the tequila slowly, and not before riding.
t.neusiedler see@48.1,16.9:
Despite the label, you are not on the lake. This point lies on the right bank of the Danube, about thirty kilometres east of Vienna, in Petronell-Carnuntum, and the lake is a good half hour's ride further south. What you have instead is something that most riders miss: the ruins of Carnuntum, once the capital of the Roman province of Upper Pannonia and a military base of the Danube frontier. In its time it held a legionary fortress, an amphitheatre and a city of tens of thousands, and several emperors passed through. Marcus Aurelius is said to have written part of his Meditations while on campaign here.

Most of what was built has been quarried away over the centuries, but a few pieces stand. The Heidentor, the pagan gate, is a freestanding arch of massive stone rising out of the fields, and it has become the symbol of the place. There is a reconstructed Roman quarter, with villas rebuilt using ancient techniques, and an archaeological park where excavations still go on every season. The flat farmland between Petronell and Bad Deutsch-Altenburg is rich in finds, and farmers plough up pottery fragments.

North of the villages lies the Donau-Auen National Park, one of the last intact stretches of floodplain forest in Central Europe. Poplars, willows and oaks stand in the wet ground, with white-tailed eagles overhead and beavers working the backwaters. A stop on the dyke path, with the broad grey river sliding past, shows why the Romans put their frontier here. The Danube cycle route runs right along it, so expect families on bikes.

For the rider, this is a quiet, flat, easy ending to a day on the road. The back roads through Rohrau, birthplace of Joseph Haydn, and the smaller villages are straight and lightly trafficked, with wide fields, wind turbines on the horizon, and a steady breeze that can push you sideways on exposed stretches. The Bundesstrasse into Vienna is faster but busier.

Petronell is small and has limited services, so go for fuel and a proper meal in Hainburg an der Donau, a town of about six and a half thousand with a medieval gate and wall, a few kilometres east. After a long day, a glass of Zweigelt and a plate of Wiener schnitzel at a village inn do the job, and you will still be in Vienna before dark.
t.ostrava@49.8,18.3:
Ostrava smells of coal, or used to, and the memory is part of its charm. For a century and a half this was the industrial heart of Czechoslovakia, a city of mines, coke ovens and steelworks on the border of Silesia, built on rich seams of black coal that ran under the plain. The last mine closed in 1994, and the great Vítkovice ironworks stopped producing iron in 1998, but the buildings were not demolished. Instead, the blast furnaces, gasholders and coking plant of the old works have been turned into a cultural quarter, and the result is among the most interesting industrial heritage sites in Central Europe.

The skyline is the best part. A gasholder, a huge cylinder, has been converted into a concert hall called Gong, and Blast Furnace Number One, a tangle of pipes, stoves and walkways, can be climbed to a viewing platform for a sweeping look over the city and the distant Beskydy mountains. Nearby, the Landek Park museum, on a hill, takes you down a real mine. Ostrava, with about three hundred thousand people, is the third largest city in the Czech Republic, and it hosts an annual music festival, Colours of Ostrava, in the industrial site.

For a rider, Ostrava is a base for two distinct kinds of ride. To the south and east, the road climbs into the Beskydy mountains, a range of long, forested ridges with winding roads, mountain huts and views over Silesia, while the peak of Lysá hora, at 1,323 metres, is the highest in the range. To the north-east, the border with Poland is only a short ride away, and beyond lies Tarnowskie Góry, a historic lead, silver and zinc mining town whose old mine tunnels and drainage system are on the UNESCO list. Both rides start on busy industrial roads, with trams, trucks and lots of lights, before the countryside opens up.

Fuel and food are easy in a city of this size. Look for a pub serving Czech goulash with dumplings and local beer, and the old town's square has cafes with terraces. The Czech Republic requires a motorway vignette, and fines for speeding are firm, with frequent radar checks. Winters are cold and grey, with snow in the hills, and summer is warm and sometimes humid. May to September offers the best conditions for riding, with long days and dry roads.
t.osaka@34.7,135.5:
Osaka runs on appetite. It is Japan's third-largest city, with some two and a half million people, and for centuries it was the nation's kitchen, the place where rice from the whole country was traded and where merchants made fortunes and lived well. The local motto kuidaore, eat until you drop, is not a boast so much as a way of life, and you will see it in the neon crabs and puffer fish along Dotonbori.

The castle gives you the history. Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the commoner who rose to unify Japan, began building it in 1583, and the original was among the largest in the country. It fell in 1615 when the Tokugawa besieged it and ended the Toyotomi line, and the keep standing today is a twentieth-century reconstruction on the old stone base, but the massive walls and moats are the real thing. South of the city, the town of Sakai holds the huge keyhole-shaped tombs of ancient emperors, among them the enormous Daisen kofun, surrounded by moats full of water and reeds.

Riding in Osaka is dense and fast, with elevated expressways stacked above the streets, taxis darting between lanes and big toll costs on the Hanshin Expressway. Parking can be tricky, so use a car park near the edge of the centre. Outside town, the hills of Ikoma and Katsuragi to the east and the Rokko range toward Kobe are good motorcycle territory, with twisty roads and fine views of the bay.

For fuel, the suburbs are well supplied, though stations in the centre are few. For food, you hardly need advice: takoyaki, the octopus balls from street stalls; okonomiyaki, the savoury pancake cooked on a griddle at your table; kushikatsu, fried skewers where you must not double-dip the sauce. Summer is brutally hot and humid, while spring and autumn are lovely. Arrive early, eat well, and let the city's cheerful bluntness work on you.
t.denver colorado rockies@40.4,-105.0:
There the Rockies rise in a long blue wall, with Longs Peak standing out as a notched summit above the rest, and on a clear morning the contrast between the field in front of you and the peaks behind is sharp. Campion is a small, quiet community; Berthoud, about six kilometres away, is a small town of some six thousand people with a historic main street.

Berthoud takes its name from Edward Berthoud, a railroad surveyor and engineer who explored the passes of the Colorado Rockies in the 1860s, and who also gave his name to the high pass on US 40 above Winter Park. The surrounding land is irrigated cropland, with fields of corn, wheat and sugar beets, and the Little Thompson River winds quietly through cottonwoods. Loveland, a bit farther north, is known for its sculpture and for its Valentine's Day postmark.

For a rider, this is the doorstep to the mountains. US 34 runs from Loveland up the Big Thompson Canyon to Estes Park, a beautiful, winding road squeezed between granite cliffs and a rushing river, which was devastated by a flash flood in 1976 and again in 2013. It is a road for caution: tight, shaded, and prone to rockfalls. Colorado 7 and 66 give alternatives into the high country. The plains roads here are dead straight, grid-like, and fast, with the wind blowing hard across the open country, often from the west.

Fuel is easy in Berthoud and Loveland. The weather here can change rapidly: summer afternoons bring thunderstorms off the mountains, often with hail, while spring may bring sudden snow. Early mornings are the best time, with the sun low and the peaks sharp, and the air cold and clear. Set out before the traffic begins, fill the tank, and head west toward the canyons, with the whole range ahead of you.
t.custer@43.8,-103.6:
Custer sits on the southern flank of the Black Hills of South Dakota, a small town in a big forest, and it makes a fine base for some of the best motorcycle roads in the Midwest. It was named for Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer, whose 1874 expedition confirmed gold in the hills, and the rush that followed was one of the sparks of the war with the Lakota, for whom these hills, the Paha Sapa, are sacred. That history is not far below the surface anywhere around here, and it is worth keeping in mind.

The roads are the reason riders come. Needles Highway climbs through granite spires and passes through narrow tunnels cut in the rock, one of them so tight that it is called the Needle's Eye. Iron Mountain Road, part of the Peter Norbeck Scenic Byway, loops through pigtail bridges built of timber so that you spiral down while looking through a frame of pines at Mount Rushmore in the distance. Norbeck, the senator and governor who planned the byway in the 1920s, wanted drivers to feel they were finding the hills at a slow pace. Speed limits are low, the curves are tight, and the surface is good but sometimes gravelly after storms.

Wildlife is a major attraction, and a risk. Custer State Park, just east, holds a herd of about a thousand bison that wander across the roads, along with pronghorn, mountain goats, and the famous begging burros. Give animals plenty of room, and never push past a bison on the road. The Crazy Horse Memorial, an unfinished mountain carving, lies a short ride north of town.

Custer has fuel, food and plenty of motels, and the tourist season runs from May to October, with the Sturgis rally in August crowding every road. Nearest large towns are Hot Springs and Rapid City, both a good distance away, so top up the tank. Summer thunderstorms boil up quickly in the afternoon, and a lightning show over the granite is something to watch from a covered porch with a cold drink.
t.cape point@-34.4,18.5:
Cape Point is where the Cape Peninsula runs out of land: a ridge of sandstone cliffs falling about two hundred metres into the Atlantic, with a lighthouse on top and a wind that can blow your visor shut. People often say it is where two oceans meet and that it is the southern tip of Africa. Neither is quite right. The tip of the continent is Cape Agulhas, a long way east, and the meeting of warm and cold currents is a broad, shifting zone rather than a line, but none of that matters when you stand on the viewing platform and watch the swell come in from Antarctica.

The road in runs through the Cape of Good Hope section of Table Mountain National Park, and you pay an entry fee at the gate. Inside, the tarmac is narrow and rolling, bordered by low fynbos, a plant kingdom that exists nowhere else on Earth in such variety. Ostriches wander the verges, bontebok graze on the flats, and the baboons are famous for opening bags and stealing sandwiches, so keep your panniers shut and never feed them.

Two lighthouses stand here. The older one, completed around 1860, sat so high that it was often wrapped in cloud and useless to ships, and after a Portuguese liner struck the rocks below in 1911 a second, lower light was built. You can walk up from the car park or ride the funicular, which carries the name of the legendary Flying Dutchman, the ghost ship said to haunt these waters.

The best time to come is a weekday morning, when the tour buses have not yet arrived and the light is clean. Winter brings dramatic seas and fewer visitors, while summer's south-easter can be brutal on the exposed road, so grip the bars and expect gusts. The ride down the peninsula, through Kommetjie and past the penguins at Boulders if you have time, is one of the finest short coastal runs in the country.

Bring a windproof layer even in January. The edge of Africa is rarely warm.
t.clarence@-33.9,18.8:
The dot sits well inland of Clarence Drive itself, on the northeastern side of Cape Town where the city thins out toward the winelands, and the ride is on its way home. Kraaifontein, a big working suburb, sits just beside it, while Stellenbosch and Paarl lie a short run to the east. The coast road that gives the ride its name, the R44 between Gordon's Bay and Rooi-Els, is hours behind you by now.

Clarence Drive deserves a few lines anyway, because it is the reason the day exists. It was carved into the foot of the Hottentots-Holland mountains, with the road clinging to the cliffs above False Bay, and it has a reputation among South African riders as the best coastal tarmac near Cape Town. The corners come in a long, rhythmic series, the sea sparkles on your left, and in winter and spring the southern right whales sometimes show up in the bay, close enough to watch from the lay-bys.

By contrast, the final stretch is purposeful. The N1 and the R300 carry fast, heavy traffic, with trucks, minibus taxis and commuters weaving between lanes, and a rider should keep a calm distance and check the mirrors often. Sunday evenings are especially busy. If you have energy left, the Durbanville and Stellenbosch roads are worth a detour, with vineyards laid out on rounded hills and the Hottentots-Holland and Simonsberg ranges standing blue behind them.

Fuel is easy everywhere, with large stations and shopping centres in Kraaifontein, Brackenfell and Bellville. A cold drink and something to eat at a roadside cafe is a good idea after the day's heat, because the Cape sun is strong and dehydration creeps up quietly.

The Winelands also hold an older story. Dutch settlers arrived in the seventeenth century, and the French Huguenots followed a few decades later, planting the vines and building the gabled homesteads that still dot the valleys. A ride through the hills as the light fades, with mountains turning pink behind the vineyards, makes a very satisfying last half hour.
t.franschhoek pass@-33.8,18.6:
By the time the ride finishes, the high ground of Franschhoek Pass is far behind and you are back among the flat, busy suburbs north of Cape Town, in the Kraaifontein and Durbanville region. Tygerberg hill, the low, rounded rise that gave Bellville its backdrop, sits close by. The mountains of the winelands are a faint blue line on the eastern horizon, and Table Mountain stands out to the south-west on a clear day.

The pass itself is the memory worth carrying. The R45 climbs out of the village of Franschhoek in a series of tight bends and then runs along the shoulder of the Franschhoek mountains before dropping toward Villiersdorp and the Theewaterskloof dam. The old road follows a route first used by elephants and later by farmers and traders, and the views over the valley and back toward the vine-covered slopes are some of the best in the Cape. Franschhoek itself, whose name means French corner, was settled by Huguenot refugees in 1688, and the town is now one of the country's food capitals, with a surprising number of serious restaurants for a place of its size.

Between the pass and the finish, the character of the ride changes entirely. The R304 and the N1 carry fast traffic, there are taxis and trucks to watch, and the sun glares off the tarmac. The advice is simple: leave a generous gap, keep your visor clean, and save the sporting riding for the mountains. Late afternoon can be congested as commuters head home, so a stop for a cold drink before the final run is not a bad idea.

Kraaifontein and Brackenfell have plenty of fuel and shopping centres, and Durbanville has cafes and wine farms if you prefer something more civilised. The Durbanville hills are a good place to watch the sun go down over a field of vines, with the sea fog sometimes pouring in over the ridge from Table Bay in the evening.

If you are doing the whole route, it is a good day: mountains, vineyards, history, and a city at the end.
t.grossglockner@48.1,16.1:
The dot lies in the Vienna Woods, the low forested hills just southwest of the capital, near Alland and Heiligenkreuz. It marks the return from the Grossglockner High Alpine Road and the Wachau, a very long way east of the big mountain, and it is the kind of place where the day's adrenaline quietly drains out and the road turns to oak and beech.

Heiligenkreuz is the reason to slow down. The Cistercian abbey here was founded in 1133, and its monks have lived there ever since, which makes it the oldest continuously inhabited Cistercian monastery in the world. The Romanesque and Gothic buildings are impressive, and the monks, who have sung Gregorian chant in recent times to a surprising global audience, run guided tours. Nearby is Mayerling, where Crown Prince Rudolf of Austria died in 1889 in the hunting lodge that was later turned into a Carmelite convent, a mystery that still fascinates Vienna.

The riding is gentle and pleasant. The Helenental road, with its tight curves along a stream and shaded by beech, is a classic local favourite and can be busy at the weekend with motorcycles, cars and cyclists. The Wienerwald is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, so the forest is thick with old trees, and the roads wind from valley to ridge past inns and wine villages.
