Surfaces are mostly good, although leaf litter and damp are a hazard in autumn, and fog can sit in the valleys.

If you have come from the Grossglockner, remember how different the two roads are. The high alpine road rises to about 2,500 metres at the Hochtor, charges a toll, and is closed in winter. This is a lower, softer landscape, where the mountains give way to the Danube plain just beyond.

Fuel is found in Alland, Baden and the towns around, and the area is full of Heuriger, the wine taverns where the year's wine is served with cold cuts and bread. A glass of white and a plate of Brettljause in a garden under the trees is a very civilised end to a long ride.
t.keszthely@46.8,17.2:
The Festetics Palace, built in the eighteenth century by the Festetics family, has a famous library and a large park, and the town has a long academic tradition. The Georgikon, founded in 1797, is said to be the first agricultural college in Europe.

The ride starts here and runs along the north shore, a land of volcanic hills, vineyards and small villages. The lake is shallow, with an average depth of about three metres, and it warms quickly in summer, which makes it popular with swimmers and sailors. The roads along the shore are generally flat, with gentle bends and long views over the water, but the hills rise inland, and the roads there are steeper and twistier. Traffic can be heavy in July and August, especially at weekends, so early starts are wise. In spring and autumn, the shore is quiet and the light is soft.

Nearby, Hévíz has the largest thermal lake in Europe, where visitors bathe in warm water, even in winter, among water lilies. The north shore wine region has a strong reputation, with Badacsony's basalt hills producing white wines from Olaszrizling and the rare Kéknyelű grape. The volcanic cones, with their vertical columns of basalt, stand above the lake like small mountains, and a climb to the top gives a wide view.

Fuel and food are easy in Keszthely, with stations, supermarkets and many restaurants, and the town centre has a pleasant pedestrian street. Local fish, like pike-perch from the lake, are served in many restaurants, and a glass of local wine goes well with it.

Take a stroll on the lakeside promenade before leaving, and watch the light on the water. It is a gentle start to a long day.
t.raftsundet@68.4,15.2:
The cliffs are black and wet, the peaks are jagged, and in winter they hold snow to the shore. The strait is part of the route the Hurtigruten coastal steamer takes, and on a good day a ship can be seen inching between the walls.

The riding in this part of Norway is among the best in Europe. Roads follow the coast, with sea on one side and mountains on the other, crossing bridges and tunnels, with bends, tight and open, and a surface that is usually good. The summer sun does not set from late May to mid-July, which gives endless daylight, while autumn and winter bring the northern lights. Rain and wind are common, and the temperature rarely rises above comfortable, so layers are necessary. In summer, tourist traffic, including campervans, slows progress, so early starts are rewarded.

Off the strait lies the Trollfjord, a short, steep fjord only about a hundred metres wide at its mouth, where cruise boats run in summer. In 1890, a famous battle was fought here, when fishermen in rowing boats blocked the entrance to stop steamers from taking the best cod grounds, and the incident is remembered in local history. Sea eagles nest in the area and are a common sight. Stokmarknes, about twenty kilometres away, is the birthplace of the Hurtigruten, founded there in 1893, and it has a museum devoted to the line.

Fuel is not available at the strait, so fill up in Melbu, eighteen kilometres away, or Stokmarknes, nineteen kilometres, where there are also shops and cafes. Dried cod, called stockfish, and fresh fish soup are local specialities, and fish shops sell prawns, crab and salmon in season.

Stop at a pull-off and watch the water for a while. The stillness between the walls is the heart of Lofoten.
t.zakopane@49.3,19.9:
Zakopane has been the capital of Polish mountain life for more than a century, and it wears the role with a mixture of pride and fatigue. About twenty-eight thousand people live here, right below the Tatra range, and in peak seasons several times that many visitors pour in for skiing, hiking and a stroll along Krupówki, the crowded main street of souvenir shops, grill stands and music. Behind the bustle lies a distinct culture, that of the Górale, the highlanders, with their own dialect, music, costume and wooden architecture, and the Zakopane style of timber building, popularised in the late nineteenth century by the artist Stanisław Witkiewicz, still shapes the best old villas.

The mountains are the point. Giewont, the long ridge above town, carries a steel cross put up in 1901, and legend says the profile of the mountain is a sleeping knight who will wake when Poland needs him. The Wielka Krokiew ski jump stands at the edge of town, and a cable car climbs Kasprowy Wierch for views across the border into Slovakia. The most famous walk is to Morskie Oko, a glacial lake set under sheer rock walls, reached by a road and a long gentle trail from Palenica Białczańska.

As a place to ride, Zakopane is better as a destination than a thoroughfare. The roads approaching it are busy, parking is limited and expensive, and traffic in July, August and the winter holidays can crawl. Go in the early morning, or in June or September, when the town breathes more easily. The surrounding country, especially the road along the foothills toward Kościelisko and the Chochołów valley, rewards a slower pace, with log cottages, wooden churches and shepherd huts scattered across the hillsides.

All services are easy here, with fuel, workshops, restaurants and rooms of every kind. Try a plate of grilled oscypek with cranberry jam, or hot tea with raspberry syrup. Weather in the Tatras changes quickly, and a sunny morning can turn to cold rain by afternoon, so carry a waterproof layer. At night the air smells of woodsmoke, and the peaks glimmer under the stars.
t.chapman s peak drive@-34.1,18.4:
Chapman's Peak Drive is about nine kilometres of road cut into the cliffs between Hout Bay and Noordhoek, and it is among the most famous coastal roads in the world. It was built in the early twentieth century, with convict labour, blasting a shelf into the sheer face of the mountain, and it has been hanging above the Atlantic ever since. The road is carved into sandstone and granite, with the sea hundreds of metres below on one side and the rock wall rising on the other.

The ride is spectacular and quite short. The road drops and rises in tight bends, with ocean views opening at every corner, and a series of retaining walls, galleries and tunnels have been built to protect it from rockfall. Even so, the road is sometimes closed after rockfalls or in strong winds, so check the status before you set out. It is a toll road, and the toll booth takes cards and cash. The surface is good, but gusts can be strong, and the walls are close, so stay alert.

The photo stops are at the lay-bys along the route, where a view of Hout Bay on one side or the long curve of Noordhoek beach on the other opens up beneath you. Late afternoon is the best time, when the sun slants across the water and the cliffs glow orange. Be careful about parking, as there are warnings about theft from vehicles, and keep valuables out of sight.

Fuel is not on the road itself. Constantia, on the way back toward Cape Town, and the villages around Hout Bay have stations, and the city itself is not far. Hout Bay has a harbour with fish and chips, and boats leave to visit a small island where a colony of Cape fur seals lives.

Whether you ride it north or south, take it slowly. The drop is real, the view is huge, and the road is more a ledge than a highway. A few tourists in rental cars will be doing the same, so be patient.
t.noordhoek beach@-34.1,18.4:
Noordhoek Beach is a long, wide, almost empty sweep of white sand on the western side of the Cape Peninsula, about eight kilometres from end to end. The mountains of the peninsula, steep and blue, rise at the northern end, and the lighthouse at Kommetjie marks the south. Behind the dunes, the valley holds a handful of farms, stables and a village with a cluster of cafes. It feels a long way from the city, though it is not.

The sea is the Atlantic, cold and rough. Water temperatures stay low all year, because the Benguela current brings cold water up from the Antarctic, so even in midsummer a swim is brisk, and rip currents are strong. Most people paddle, walk or ride horses along the sand, and swimming should be done only in places with lifeguards. The sound of the surf is constant, and the air smells of salt and kelp.

A small piece of history sits on the sand. In 1900, a steamship called the Kakapo ran aground here, and the rusting remains of the wreck can still be seen, partly buried, when the tide and sand allow. It is a lonely sight, and a reminder of how dangerous this coast was to ships.

For riders, the beach is the end of a good ride, usually coming down Chapman's Peak Drive from Hout Bay. The roads around Noordhoek are flat and pleasant, with views of the mountains and the sea. Traffic is light, apart from weekends, when visitors arrive from the city. Fuel is not at the beach, so use the stations at Constantia or the larger villages nearby, and fill up before you head south toward Cape Point.

Late in the afternoon the light turns gold, and the surf glows. Take off your boots, walk to the water and let the wind clear your head. Watch the horse riders and the dogs running in the waves, and stay a while.
t.piketberg@-32.9,18.8:
Piketberg sits at the foot of a flat-topped sandstone mountain in the Swartland, the wheat and wine country north of Cape Town, and it is the sort of place most people drive straight past on the N7. That is a pity, because the town has an easy, old-fashioned charm. The name is said to come from the piquet, the military guard post the Dutch East India Company kept here in the eighteenth century, and some of the Cape Dutch buildings date from those years.

The mountain behind the town rises abruptly from fields of wheat, which turn gold in late spring and are cut in November. Orchards, vineyards and rooibos plantations appear to the north and east, and in August and September the wildflowers of the West Coast, daisies and bulbs in blazing orange and white, spread across the slopes after good winter rain. The air is dry and clear, the sky enormous, and the light turns everything the colour of honey.

Fuel is easy here. Piketberg has stations and shops, and since the next big town on the N7 is a good distance away, it is an important stop. Cape Town is roughly a hundred and fifty kilometres to the south, and Citrusdal, over the Piekenierskloof Pass to the north, is the gateway to the Cederberg. Many riders going to or from the northern Cape fill up in Piketberg out of habit.

The riding in the area is mostly straight and fast on the N7, with gentle rises and long views. The more rewarding roads run through the Swartland farmland on quieter routes, with big bends and little traffic. In summer, temperatures can climb above thirty-five degrees, with a strong dry wind, so carry water. In winter, the hills are green, and cold, wet fronts can sweep in off the Atlantic.

Stop for a coffee and a pastry in the town, look at the old church and the neat streets, and carry on. A small town, a large landscape and a long day ahead make a good combination.
t.bainskloof and@-34.1,18.3:
The name means wood bay in Dutch, because the early settlers cut timber from the forests in this valley to build and heat Cape Town. Today the harbour is lined with fish-and-chip stalls, and boat trips run out to Duiker Island, a rock covered in noisy Cape fur seals. Behind the village rise the sharp peaks of the Twelve Apostles and the Sentinel, a rock that looks like a sleeping giant.

The coast road from Hout Bay climbs onto the shoulder of the mountain and runs along cliffs high above the sea. Sea mist, called the Cape Doctor on the wind-blown days, rolls over the ridges, and the temperature can drop ten degrees in minutes. Around here, the mountain slopes carry fynbos with proteas and ericas, and in spring the hillsides are covered with colour. Dassies, the rock hyraxes, sun themselves on the stone walls.

This stop belongs to a ride that includes Du Toitskloof, the pass over the mountains east of Paarl, on the route to the interior. The old road over the top winds through granite and fynbos in tight curves, while the modern N1 now passes beneath in a long tunnel, and riders can choose between the two. Here, on the peninsula, the riding is different, with cliff roads, tunnels and sea views. Traffic is heavy on sunny weekends, and parking at viewpoints is hard to find. Strong south-easterly winds in summer can be dangerous on exposed sections, so check the forecast and be ready to turn back.

Practically, Hout Bay has fuel stations, supermarkets and a good selection of restaurants and cafes, many by the harbour, with fresh fish and chips, calamari and crayfish in season. There is also a weekend craft market. Constantia, a short way over the ridge, has more shops and wine estates. For a short break, the beach has a long sweep of white sand and cold, clear water. Parking is limited near the harbour on weekends, and security is wise, so never leave anything on the bike.
t.chapman s peak@-33.8,18.5:
This is the north end of the metropolitan area, where Cape Town runs out into dunes, wetlands and sand-coloured scrub, with the huge Atlantic on the left. Sunset Beach, Table View and Blouberg have sprawling beach suburbs, and the sea wind makes it a favourite spot for kitesurfers.

The land here is flat and sandy, the old floor of the Cape Flats, and beside the road lies a large nature reserve with wetlands that draw flamingos, pelicans and a host of other waterbirds. Further north, on the West Coast Road, the R27, the landscape opens into low scrubland that turns to carpet in spring, when the daisies and other annuals flower in late August and September. The Koeberg nuclear power station, South Africa's only one, sits on the coast a few kilometres north and is a landmark on the skyline.

Riding on the R27 is a different experience from the mountain roads. It is a long, straight, fast road with a view of the sea on the left and the sand dunes beside, and the south-westerly wind can be vicious, so a loaded bike gets pushed around. Traffic is heavy at commuting hours and on weekends. The better riding is on the roads that run inland to Malmesbury and the Swartland, among wheat fields and low hills. Surface quality is good. In spring, the flower season brings crowds, and cars stop suddenly, so ride defensively.

For practicalities, the area has everything, with fuel stations, supermarkets and shopping centres at Table View, and a long line of cafes and restaurants along the beachfront, where seafood and coffee come with a view of the mountain. Parking for bikes is easy. Further north on the coast, Melkbosstrand has a pleasant seafront and small services. The sunset over the Atlantic from here, with the mountain silhouetted across the bay, is one of the best finishes a day can have.
t.hohe@47.8,16.5:
Burgenland lies tucked against the Hungarian border, and it is the youngest of Austria's federal states. The region was part of the Kingdom of Hungary until 1921, when it was awarded to Austria after the First World War, and the town of Sopron, just across the line, chose by plebiscite to stay Hungarian. The composer Joseph Haydn served the Esterházy princes at Eisenstadt for decades, and the palace where he worked still stands.

The land is Pannonian, which means the western edge of the Hungarian plain, with a warm, dry climate, wide skies and light that feels more southern than Alpine. Vines cover the slopes, and the red grape Blaufränkisch, with its spicy dark fruit, is the speciality, alongside sweet wines made near the lake. A few kilometres further east, the Neusiedler See, a huge, shallow steppe lake ringed with reeds, draws birdwatchers and windsurfers. Villages have long, low houses with arcaded courtyards and storks nesting on chimneys.

The Hohe Wand, which gives this stop its label, is a limestone plateau far to the north-west. Here, on the border, the riding is calm and flat, a land of straight avenues of walnut and cherry trees, old churches and the occasional sunflower field. The roads are in good shape, and traffic is light except around Eisenstadt and Mattersburg. Wind can be fierce across the plain. In summer, heat shimmers over the tarmac, and in the vintage season, tractors loaded with grapes cause delays. The Rosalia ridge offers gentle bends through beech and oak woods.

Practically, there are fuel stations in Mattersburg and Eisenstadt, and small villages have a bakery or a shop. Wine taverns serve local wine with cold meats, bread and spreads, and traditional dishes such as goulash and goose, especially around St Martin's Day in November. Remember that Austrian drink-driving limits are strict. The border with Hungary is open under Schengen, so crossing is simple, though carry your documents. Evenings in late summer are soft and golden.
t.salzkammergut@48.0,16.3:
This is the heart of the Thermenlinie, the line of hot springs and vineyards that runs south from Vienna along the foot of the hills, and the sunny south-east slopes grow two local white grapes found almost nowhere else, Zierfandler and Rotgipfler. Together they make a heavy, aromatic wine that has been prized since the Habsburg court. In the village centre, a Renaissance castle and a baroque church stand among the half-timbered houses.

Heurigen are the point of the place. These are family-run taverns that serve their own wine for a few weeks a year, announced by a bundle of pine twigs hung over the door, and the food is cold platters, bread, spreads and roast pork, eaten at long tables under chestnut trees. On a warm evening, the sound of laughter drifts down the lane, and an accordion or a small group sometimes plays. The surrounding slopes are terraced with vines, and above them the forest begins.

The Salzkammergut, named in this stop's label, lies far to the west, but the roads here have their own pleasures. Above the village, the narrow road to the Anninger hill climbs through woods in tight, shaded bends, with views over the plain and the occasional meadow. The surface is generally good, though leaf litter and moss make it slippery. Traffic is heavy on the main road along the foot of the hills, with commuters and truck traffic, so quieter lanes are better. In summer, afternoon heat sits on the basin, and in autumn the vines turn red and gold.

Practically, fuel stations are in Guntramsdorf and Mödling, both close, and every village has a bakery or a shop. Remember that Austrian drink-driving limits are strict, and it is best to taste after the ride is done or to stay locally. Parking is easy near the village centre, and the tram to Vienna runs from Baden. A late afternoon here is hard to beat, with the light on the vineyards.
t.gesause@47.9,16.8:
This one is on the western shore of the Neusiedler See, the great steppe lake on the Austrian-Hungarian border, which is about as far in character from the Gesäuse's limestone walls as you can get without leaving Austria. Where the Gesäuse is vertical, the Neusiedler See is horizontal: a shallow lake, rarely more than a couple of metres deep, fringed by one of the largest reed beds in Europe, with the Hungarian plain vanishing into haze on the far side.

The villages along the western shore, Breitenbrunn, Purbach and Winden, are wine villages in the shelter of the Leithagebirge hills. Blaufränkisch and sweet dessert wines are the speciality, and the local growers have been working this sunny slope since Roman times. Purbach in particular has a charming street of low whitewashed houses and cellar lanes, the Kellergassen, where the wine was traditionally stored away from the village houses to reduce fire risk. Many are open for tasting in season, with a bench, a plate and a view of the vines.

Riding here is a different pleasure. The roads are flat, quiet and wide-open, with little traffic outside summer weekends, and the lake often produces strong wind: this is a famous windsurfing and kitesurfing water for a reason. A crosswind on an exposed section can push a lightly loaded bike around, so keep your grip relaxed. The lake itself is a UNESCO cultural landscape, shared with Hungary, and a national park protects the saline pans and shallow ponds of the Seewinkel to the east. In spring and autumn the sky fills with geese, cranes and waders on migration, and the reed edges hold herons and, if you are patient, the bearded tit.

For fuel and larger shops, Neusiedl am See at the north end is the sensible option, about seven kilometres away and with over eight thousand people. The smaller villages have bakeries and cafés but fewer petrol pumps.

If the weather is warm, plan for a late afternoon stop. The light off the water and reeds goes copper in the last hour before sunset, and the Heurigen come alive. A beer, a plate of bread and smoked pork, and the long straight road home make for an easy end to a hard day in the mountains.
t.szentendre@47.7,19.1:
Szentendre is the artists' town of the Danube Bend, a short ride north of Budapest, with narrow cobbled streets, baroque churches and a mass of little galleries and cafés. It has been a popular day out for people from the capital for generations, and the old centre fills with visitors on any warm weekend. But the town is small enough, and the houses colourful enough, that it keeps its charm, and the riverside promenade on the Danube is a pleasant place to rest.

The town's character comes from its history. In the late seventeenth century, Serbian refugees fleeing the Ottoman Turks settled here, and their merchants built a series of Orthodox churches with onion domes and richly painted interiors. Their baroque houses line the central squares, and the town's many museums include one devoted to the ceramic artist Margit Kovács, and another, rather charmingly, to marzipan. A few kilometres north of the centre is the Hungarian Open Air Museum, a large park of traditional village houses brought from across the country.

Riding here is mostly a matter of getting to and from. The road from Budapest follows the river along the foot of the hills, busy with commuter traffic, and the centre is crowded, with narrow streets and a lot of pedestrians, so park at the edge and walk. On weekday mornings, the town is calmer. The best riding starts beyond the town, where the road runs north along the Danube, with the hills of the Pilis and Visegrád ranges rising to the west and the broad river on the right.

Szentendre has about twenty-four thousand people, so fuel, food and supplies are straightforward, with stations and supermarkets on the approach roads. The centre is full of cafés and restaurants, and a plate of fish soup or a slice of cake in a courtyard is a fine way to pause. Pomáz, the next town along, has about fifteen thousand people and more services. Note that traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, so an early start is wise.
t.visegrad@47.8,19.0:
The Danube makes a sharp turn at Visegrád, squeezing between two ranges of hills in a narrow gorge before swinging south toward Budapest, and the town sits at the point of the bend, below a fortress that watches the whole thing. The citadel stands on a steep hill about three hundred and fifty metres above the river, and its walls look out over the water, the town and the forested slopes across the way. It is one of the best views in Hungary, and it has been used for strategic purposes for more than a thousand years.

The history here is royal. In 1335, the kings of Hungary, Bohemia and Poland met at Visegrád to agree on trade and alliance, a meeting that gave its name, in 1991, to the Visegrád Group of central European states. In the fifteenth century, King Matthias Corvinus built a magnificent Renaissance palace on the river bank, which was destroyed under Ottoman rule and later uncovered and partly rebuilt. The palace, with its fountains and courtyards, gives a glimpse of the court that once filled this small town, and the Solomon Tower beside the river is another relic of the Middle Ages.

The ride to Visegrád along the Danube is among the nicest in the region. The road follows the river from Szentendre through Leányfalu and Tahitótfalu, with the water on one side and the wooded hills on the other, then passes Dömös before reaching the bend. The corners are gentle, the views wide, and the surface is generally good. It is popular with cyclists and motorcyclists, so take care at weekends. The road up to the citadel is steep and narrow, with hairpins, and a good place to test your cornering.

Visegrád is a small town with about seventeen hundred residents and basic services, but fuel is available at Nagymaros, just across the river by ferry, and Vác, about twelve kilometres away, is the larger town with more choice. There are restaurants along the riverside, serving fish and Hungarian dishes, and cafés near the palace. The best time to visit is spring or autumn, when the hills are green or golden, and the crowds are thinner.
t.esztergom@47.8,18.7:
Esztergom was Hungary's capital before Budapest was anything, and the Hungarians still talk about it with a sort of quiet pride. Stephen, the first Christian king, was born here around the year 975, and he was crowned in 1000 or 1001, so in a sense the nation begins on this bluff above the Danube. Kings lived in the castle on the hill until the thirteenth century, when a Mongol invasion pushed them south, and the town became the seat of the Catholic primate of Hungary, which it remains.

The skyline is dominated by the basilica, the largest church in the country, a big neoclassical building with a green dome that you can see from far down the river. Inside is the Bakócz Chapel, a small Renaissance masterpiece in red marble that was taken apart and rebuilt when the cathedral was constructed. From the dome you look across the Danube to Slovakia, to the town of Štúrovo, and the two are connected by the Mária Valéria Bridge, blown up in 1944 in the war and not rebuilt until 2001. Crossing it is a small, strange pleasure, with passport-free travel in both directions now.

The riding up the river is a favourite. Route 11 runs along the right bank of the Danube through Dömös, Visegrád and Szentendre, with the water on one side and wooded hills of the Pilis and Visegrád ranges on the other. It is a gentle, scenic road with steady curves, a good surface and plenty of places to stop for fish soup or a coffee. Sundays are busy with Budapest day-trippers, and the town traffic at the Danube Bend ferry crossings can be slow. For more excitement, turn into the hills at Dömös and take the winding roads over the Pilis toward Pilisszentkereszt, where the forests are deep and quiet.

With nearly thirty thousand people, Esztergom has plenty of fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés, and a good thermal bath at Štúrovo if you cross the river. Parking near the basilica is easy for bikes. If you arrive in the late afternoon, climb to the terrace outside the cathedral and watch the evening light on the water. The Danube here is wide, calm and slow, and you can follow a barge for a long time without seeing it move.
t.tihany@46.9,17.9:
Tihany is a peninsula that pokes into Lake Balaton like a thumb, a hilly, volcanic outcrop in the middle of the largest lake in central Europe, and it narrows the lake almost to a strait. From the top, the water spreads out on both sides, with the vineyards of the north shore on one side and the low southern shore on the other, and on clear evenings the light on the water is unforgettable. The village sits on the ridge, a neat place of white houses and thatched roofs, with a Benedictine abbey at its heart.

The abbey was founded in 1055 by King Andrew I, and the deed of foundation, which survives, contains the oldest known text in the Hungarian language, a few words in a Latin document, so the place has a special status for Hungarians. The present church is baroque, with a pair of towers visible from across the lake, and the interior is richly decorated. Behind it, a path leads to a viewpoint over the water, and nearby are the remains of old hermit cells carved into the volcanic rock.

The peninsula is also a protected landscape, with odd cone-shaped geyser formations, an echo that bounces off the abbey walls, and a lavender-growing tradition that has made the plant a symbol of Tihany. In summer, lavender fields turn the slopes purple, and the shops sell lavender oil, soap and honey. The lake itself has a small ferry between Tihany and the south shore, a short crossing that gives a fine view of the peninsula from the water.

The roads on the peninsula are narrow and winding, with tight bends and short climbs, and in summer they are crowded with visitors, so allow plenty of time, and be careful of pedestrians. The best times to ride are in early morning or in the evening, when the light is soft and the day-trippers have gone. Tihany is small, with about fourteen hundred residents, and fuel is limited, so fill up in Balatonfüred, about six kilometres away, a town with about thirteen thousand people, a lakeside promenade and plenty of cafés, restaurants and shops.
t.budapest@47.5,19.1:
Budapest is two cities that were joined in 1873: hilly Buda on the west bank and flat Pest on the east, with the Danube between them as the main street. The Chain Bridge, opened in 1849, was the first permanent crossing, and the lions on its ends were said to have been made without tongues, a story locals find funnier than visitors do. Above it, on Castle Hill, stand the royal palace and the Matthias Church, with its patterned roof tiles, while on the Pest bank, the Parliament, finished in 1904, sprawls along the water like a Gothic wedding cake. At night it is lit gold, and it is one of the great sights of Europe.

The city sits on hot springs, and bathing is a cultural habit more than a tourist attraction. The big baths, Széchenyi in the park and Gellért under the hill, are places where elderly men play chess in the water and families stay for hours. The city also has the oldest underground railway on the European continent, the little yellow M1 line, opened in 1896. Food is paprika-heavy, with goulash, chicken paprikash and fried bread called lángos with sour cream and cheese, and the old Jewish quarter in Pest is full of bars set up in half-ruined courtyards.

On a motorbike, treat the centre as slow. Tram tracks cut through the streets, cobbles are slick when wet, and drivers are quick and a little impatient. The Buda hills offer some of the best city riding, with tree-lined roads climbing to viewpoints, and you can be out of the suburbs and into the forest in thirty minutes. North along the river lies the Danube Bend, with Szentendre, Visegrád and Esztergom, and it is where most Budapest riders go on a fine weekend. Motorways such as the M0 ring, the M1 and the M3 need an electronic vignette, which is easy to buy online or at a petrol station.

Fuel and food are no problem in a city of nearly two million people, with filling stations on every ring road. Choose accommodation with secure parking, as theft of bikes is not unknown. In winter, snow and ice are possible, and in July the heat on the tarmac can be intense. Go for an evening ride across the bridges, when the lights come on, and you will see why people stay.
t.tromso@69.7,19.0:
Tromsø is unexpectedly lively for a town so far north. It stands on an island, linked to the mainland by a bridge and a tunnel, at nearly seventy degrees north, with snow-covered peaks all around and about fifty thousand people who have built a university, a brewery and a fine collection of bars into the Arctic. It has been called the Paris of the North, partly in jest and partly because it has long had a worldly side, thanks to the polar expeditions that set out from its harbour.

The Arctic Cathedral, finished in the 1960s, is the building you will see in every photograph, a series of tall white triangular panes that evoke ice or sails, and across the water the cable car climbs to a ledge on Storsteinen, about four hundred metres up, where the whole archipelago opens out below. On a clear night in winter the aurora can ripple above it, and in summer the midnight sun hangs in the sky from about the end of May until late July. The polar night, with its blue twilight, runs from late November into January.

The surroundings are dramatic. Fjords cut deep into the mainland, steep peaks rise straight from the sea, and the islands of Kvaløya and Ringvassøya are reached by bridges and tunnels, giving some of the best riding anywhere. Roads are narrow, twisting and often wet, with views of the sea at every turn and little traffic outside the peak weeks. Wind can be strong on exposed bridges and sudden snow showers can arrive even in early summer. Reindeer and sheep graze beside the road, so keep your speed down.

Practical matters are easy here. Tromsø has fuel stations, supermarkets and workshops, and being the largest town for hundreds of kilometres it is the place to prepare thoroughly. Prices are high, as everywhere in Norway, but the fish is very good, and the local brewery claims to be the northernmost in the world. Parking for motorcycles in the centre is simple, and you can leave the bike while you ride the cable car.

Come in summer for riding, and in winter for the lights, but not on two wheels. This is a place where you linger longer than you planned.
t.narvik@68.4,17.4:
Narvik exists because of iron. In the late nineteenth century the huge ore deposits at Kiruna in Swedish Lapland needed an ice-free port, and the Norwegian coast, warmed by the Gulf Stream, offered one. The railway, the Ofotbanen, opened in 1902 and still carries ore trains down the mountains to the quay, where it is loaded onto ships, and the great ore jetty, lit at night, is the most characteristic sight in town.

That industrial importance made it a prize in the Second World War. In April 1940 German forces seized the town, and a series of naval and land battles followed in the fjords and mountains, ending in the first Allied victory on land against Germany. The Allies then withdrew, as the war in France demanded, and the town was left badly damaged. The War Museum tells the story clearly, and the war cemetery, where soldiers of several nations lie side by side, is a quiet place.

Narvik has around fourteen thousand people and sits on the Ofotfjord, with steep mountains rising almost from the shore. A gondola takes you high up the slopes for a view of the fjord and the peaks, and in early summer the midnight sun shines on the water. Ski enthusiasts come in winter, and the aurora sometimes appears over the town.

From here the E10 climbs east through the Rombak valley and up to the Swedish border, passing Riksgränsen and the high lakes and bare mountains of Abisko, which is where this ride goes. The road is well surfaced, with long, easy bends, tunnels and a few tight sections, and it follows the railway for much of the way. Weather can turn quickly, with snow possible in any month at the pass, and strong winds on the exposed stretches. West, the same road leads out to Lofoten. Watch for reindeer on the road in the Swedish part, where they wander freely.

Fuel is plentiful in Narvik, with several stations and supermarkets, and it is wise to fill up here since services thin out quickly towards the border. Sweden, just beyond, has its own prices and rules, but the currency is the krona and cards are accepted almost everywhere.

Leave in the morning, ride into the light, and pause by a lake when the wind drops.
t.cheyenne crossing@44.3,-103.9:
Spearfish Canyon is the kind of place where the road follows the creek and the cliffs close in on both sides. The canyon, cut through the northern Black Hills by Spearfish Creek, has limestone walls hundreds of feet high, covered in pine and spruce, with aspen and birch that blaze yellow in autumn. US 14A runs along the bottom for about twenty miles, and Cheyenne Crossing, near the middle, is a small roadside stop where a store and a cafe serve riders, hikers and passing travellers. The name recalls the old stage route between Cheyenne and Deadwood during the gold rush years.

Gold is the history here. In 1874 Custer's expedition confirmed that there was gold in the Black Hills, which belonged to the Lakota under an 1868 treaty, and the rush that followed led to years of conflict over land that remains unresolved and important to the Lakota. Deadwood, a few miles east, grew into a boomtown, where Wild Bill Hickok was shot in 1876, and the town still has its historic main street. Lead, nearby, was home to the Homestake Mine, once among the deepest gold mines in the world, which closed in 2002 and now houses an underground science laboratory.

The riding is relaxed and rewarding. The canyon road has flowing bends, a good surface and a modest speed limit, and the cool air under the trees is a pleasure on a hot day. Roughlock Falls, a short walk from the road, drops into a pool, and Spearfish Falls lies near the northern end. The scenic byway is busy in summer, so ride in the morning if you can, and watch for deer, particularly at dusk. Autumn is spectacular, but rain and snow can come early, and the road is not always cleared immediately.

Services around the crossing itself are limited, so fill up in Spearfish, about thirteen miles to the north, or in Lead and Deadwood, where fuel, food and rooms are plentiful. A bit further on, Sturgis hosts its famous motorcycle rally every August, when traffic across the Black Hills grows heavy. For a quiet ride, late May to June or September offers the best balance of weather and space.
t.jihlava@49.4,15.6:
Jihlava sits at the heart of the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands, the Vysočina, a plateau of ponds, rye fields and gentle forested hills that rolls on for miles with no big drama but a lot of quiet beauty. The town is small by European standards, about fifty thousand people, but its history is surprisingly rich. In the thirteenth century silver was found in the surrounding hills, and miners and merchants poured in, many of them German speakers. The silver made Jihlava one of the richest towns in the Czech lands, and under the old streets a labyrinth of cellars and tunnels, partly open to visitors, preserves that medieval wealth.

The great central square, one of the biggest in the Czech Republic, is lined with Gothic and baroque houses and a mighty church of Saint James. Gustav Mahler spent his boyhood in the town, and the composer is commemorated with a plaque on the house where his family lived. Every autumn an international documentary film festival fills the cinemas and cafes with film makers and students.

On a bike the Highlands are all about easy, flowing roads. They climb and dip over broad ridges, pass through villages with a church and a pond, and cross the occasional wooded valley. The tarmac varies, with some smooth main roads and a few rough minor ones, and in spring frost heave can leave patches. There are few steep passes; this is relaxed touring, ideal for a long day and a clear head. About forty kilometres to the east, Třebíč has a remarkably well-preserved Jewish quarter and a great Romanesque basilica, both recognised by UNESCO.

Czech cities have plenty of petrol stations along the main roads, and Jihlava is no exception, with several on the ring road. In the town, ask for a pivo and some svíčková, braised beef in a creamy vegetable sauce with bread dumplings, which is a Czech classic.

Early autumn is especially lovely, with mist over the ponds and golden birches, though midsummer brings long light. Winters are cold and snow lingers on the plateau.
t.brezno@48.8,19.6:
Brezno lies in the upper valley of the Hron river, at the southern foot of the Low Tatras, and the mountains dominate the view to the north. The main summits, including Ďumbier and Chopok, rise beyond two thousand metres above the beech and spruce forest, and from late autumn the high ridge is white. The town itself is modest, about twenty-one thousand people, with a pleasant square, a long tradition of mining and metalwork, and an easy, unhurried pace.

The valley has a particular railway curiosity. From nearby Čierny Balog, a narrow-gauge forest railway wound for decades up into the hills to bring out timber, and the line has been preserved as a tourist railway running through woods and over small bridges. Slovak villages in this region keep up many traditions, including folk costume and festivals, and wooden cottages still stand along some valleys.

Riding here is mountain riding at a reasonable scale. To the north the road climbs from Brezno towards the Čertovica pass, around twelve hundred metres, that crosses the Low Tatras to Liptov. The tarmac is mostly good, the bends are smooth and open, and the forest is dense and green. There is a ski area on the slopes with parking and a few huts, and in summer you may meet hikers and cyclists on the road. South of Brezno the valley runs past small villages and open hills toward Banská Bystrica and the Slovak Ore Mountains.

Weather in the mountains can turn quickly. Mist and showers are common in the afternoon, and the pass can feel chilly even in July. In winter it may be closed or icy, so check conditions. The best months are June, July and September.

Fuel is easy in Brezno itself, which is large enough to have several stations. The pass road has few services, so fill up before climbing. For lunch, try halušky with sheep cheese and bacon, the national dish, or a bowl of kapustnica, cabbage soup. Slovakia requires an electronic vignette for motorways, though not for the ordinary roads around Brezno.
t.zvolen@48.6,19.2:
Zvolen is a railway and forestry town in the middle of Slovakia, where the Hron and Slatina rivers meet in a broad basin ringed by the volcanic hills of the Slovak Ore Mountains. It is not a famous place, and it does not try to be. Instead it is practical, with a big university of forestry and technology, trains running in all directions, and a large number of people who work with wood and trees.

The notable building is the castle, a Gothic stronghold founded in the late fourteenth century under King Louis I of Hungary, who used it as a royal hunting residence. Its four corner towers and courtyard are neat and square, and the castle now houses part of the Slovak National Gallery with old masters and decorative art. Nearby, the main square is lined with old buildings, and in the surrounding hills the Borová hora arboretum collects hundreds of tree species from across the world.

For riders, Zvolen is a hub on the way to some of central Slovakia's best country. North-east, the road toward Detva climbs into the foothills of the Poľana, a huge extinct volcano whose forested caldera, now a protected landscape, is quiet and mossy. West lie the old silver-mining towns, with Banská Štiavnica, a UNESCO site of steep lanes and baroque churches, about forty minutes away. The roads are winding, with mixed surfaces, and in places the edges are rough after winter. Traffic is moderate in the valleys and light in the hills.

Spring is green and damp, summer warm, and autumn can be glorious as the beech forests turn colour. In winter snow arrives on the higher roads, and the valleys can hold fog for days.

Fuel is easy in a town of forty-four thousand, with stations at the roundabouts and supermarkets for supplies. Local food centres on hearty dishes like bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep cheese, and smoked sausages, washed down with Slovak beer or a glass of the fruit brandy known as slivovica.
t.bratislava@48.1,17.1:
Bratislava is a capital that you can see across in a glance. The Danube flows past a hill topped by a white, four-towered castle that locals say looks like an upturned table, and the old town lies at its foot, compact and cobbled, a few minutes' walk from the river. Austria is just across the water, and Vienna is only an hour away, which means the city lives under the shadow of a bigger neighbour and has learned to enjoy its own pace.

From 1536 to 1783 the city, then called Pressburg or Pozsony, was the capital of the Kingdom of Hungary, when Buda was under Ottoman rule, and from 1563 to 1830 Hungarian kings were crowned in Saint Martin's Cathedral, whose spire carries a replica of the crown. Germans, Hungarians and Slovaks lived side by side here for centuries, and the street names and the cuisine still carry traces of all three. The blue-painted Art Nouveau church and the peculiar flying-saucer bridge, built in communist times, are other landmarks.

For riders, the city is a place to cross rather than explore, since traffic along the Danube and on the ring roads is heavy. But north-west lie the Little Carpathians, a ridge of forested hills clothed in vineyards, with a wine route linking small villages like Pezinok and Modra. The roads curl gently through the vines and orchards and are best on a weekday morning. To the east, at Devín, the ruins of an ancient castle stand at the confluence of the Danube and the Morava, right on the old Iron Curtain line.

Slovakia uses an electronic vignette on motorways, which must be bought before you use them, and it is wise to check this at the border. Fuel is plentiful and generally cheaper than in Austria, so riders from Vienna often cross the bridge just to fill up.

Late spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the vineyards are green or golden and the new wine called burčiak appears in the cellars.
t.szombathely@47.2,16.6:
Szombathely sits in western Hungary, only a few kilometres from the Austrian border, and it claims to be the oldest city in the country. The Romans founded it around the middle of the first century as Savaria, and it prospered on the Amber Road that carried Baltic amber south to the Adriatic. The ruins of a temple to Isis, the Egyptian goddess, were rebuilt from fragments and stand in the middle of town, a reminder of how cosmopolitan the Roman world was. Saint Martin of Tours, the soldier who famously shared his cloak with a beggar, was born in Savaria in the fourth century, and the town honours him with a pilgrimage and a church.

Later centuries added baroque grandeur. The cathedral and the bishop's palace look over streets of ochre and cream houses, and a good open-air museum on the edge of town preserves farmhouses from the western Hungarian villages. A few of them show the traditional way of living on this border land, which was shaped by Hungarian, German and Slovenian influence.

For riders, Szombathely is the doorway to a gentle, lovely landscape. West and south lie the Kőszeg hills, with the quaint walled town of Kőszeg at their foot, and the Őrség National Park, a land of woodland, meadow and scattered hamlets with thatched or shingled farmhouses. The roads are narrow, with moderate bends and low traffic, and there is pleasure in simply meandering from village to village. Surfaces vary, so watch for patches and farm vehicles, especially in harvest season.

Fuel and food are easy in a town of nearly eighty thousand, and the Austrian border is just a short ride, so prices are worth comparing. Local specialities include pumpkin seed oil, used in salads and soups, and rich cakes from the old Habsburg tradition.

The best months are May to June and September, when meadows are green and the air is clear. Motorways need the Hungarian e-vignette; the minor roads do not.
t.novi sad@45.3,19.8:
Novi Sad is the capital of Vojvodina, the flat, fertile northern province of Serbia, and it lies on the left bank of the Danube, with a fortress on the opposite shore. The Petrovaradin Fortress, a vast eighteenth-century Habsburg bastion, rises on a rocky headland and is sometimes called the Gibraltar of the Danube. The clock tower on its wall has a curious feature: the hour hand is the long one and the minute hand the short one, so that boatmen on the river could read the time from afar. Underground there are miles of tunnels, and from the ramparts you see the whole city and the river curving through the plain.

The city has a calm, polite character, with a pedestrian centre of pastel facades, a neo-Gothic church and cafes that stay open late. It was a centre of Serbian culture in the Habsburg era, a place where writers and scholars gathered when Belgrade was still under Ottoman rule. Its bridges were destroyed in the 1999 bombing and later rebuilt. In summer the city is best known for the EXIT music festival, which began here in 2000 as a student protest and grew into one of the largest in Europe.

For riders, Novi Sad is the gateway to the Fruška Gora, a low forested ridge south of the Danube, protected as a national park. Roads wind up through woods and past vineyards, with sixteen Orthodox monasteries scattered among the hills, many founded after the Ottoman invasions, and charming small wine villages such as Sremski Karlovci. The riding is gentle, with smooth bends and good views over the plain. The wide Vojvodina flatlands elsewhere offer long straight roads and wide skies, with wind a constant.

Fuel and food are plentiful. Serbian cooking is generous, with grilled meats, stuffed peppers and thick cream. Choose between May and early October. Traffic is busy at rush hour around the bridges, and speed enforcement has become more serious, so keep your speed legal and carry your documents, including insurance.
t.krems wachau@48.4,15.6:
Krems sits at the eastern gate of the Wachau, the stretch of the Danube between Melk and Krems that has been protected as a UNESCO World Heritage landscape. The river here runs between steep terraced slopes, where vines and apricot orchards cling to stone walls built by hand over centuries, and medieval villages cluster at the water's edge. Krems itself, with the adjoining old town of Stein, is the biggest place on the stretch, a town of about fifteen thousand with a pretty centre of painted gabled houses, arched gateways and cobbled lanes, and a long tradition of wine and apricot schnapps.

The Wachau is famous for its white wines, especially Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, and for the Wachauer Marille, the apricot, which blossoms in April and is harvested in July. Every cellar and tavern sells apricot jam, dumplings, liqueur and brandy. Across the Danube stands Göttweig Abbey, a vast Benedictine monastery on a hill, whose baroque staircase and terraces look over the whole valley. Upstream is Dürnstein, with its blue and white abbey tower, where Richard the Lionheart was held prisoner in the castle above the village in the twelfth century after quarrelling with the Duke of Austria on his way home from the Crusades.

For riders, the road along the north bank of the river and the one along the south bank offer gentle, scenic riding rather than anything technical. The tarmac is smooth, the bends are wide, and the views of vineyards, castle ruins and the river are the point. In summer and autumn weekends the road is busy with cyclists, tourist coaches and other riders, so ride slowly and patiently, and consider a weekday. A small ferry crosses the river at Spitz, a handy way to switch banks. In April, the apricot blossom is a reason to come early in spring.

Krems has several fuel stations and supermarkets, so it is easy to prepare for a day on the road. Stop at a Heuriger, a wine tavern marked by a branch over the door, for a plate of cold meats, cheese and a glass of local wine, but only if you are not riding on.
t.cederberg pass roads@-32.5,19.3:
The Cederberg is the wild, rust-red country about three hours north of Cape Town, a mountain range of sandstone that wind and water have carved into arches, pinnacles and overhangs. It lies in the Western Cape, inland from Clanwilliam, and it is protected as a wilderness area. The rocks glow orange at sunset, and the formations have names, such as the Maltese Cross, a tall pillar, and the Wolfberg Arch, a natural bridge. The air is dry and clear, smelling of fynbos and dust, and at night the stars fill the sky in a way that city people rarely see.

The name comes from the Clanwilliam cedar, a rare conifer that grows only in these mountains and has been much reduced by fire and the demand for timber. Today, the range is better known for rooibos tea, which grows in the sandy soils of the surrounding valleys, and nowhere else in the world on any scale. Local farms harvest the needle-like leaves, and you may see them laid out to dry in the sun. The San people lived here for thousands of years, and left rock paintings in caves and shelters, including those at Stadsaal, which show animals and human figures in red ochre.

The roads are mostly gravel, and that is part of the appeal. The R364 from Clanwilliam climbs over the Pakhuis Pass, a fine piece of road engineering from the nineteenth century, with views over the valley, and then runs on through the heart of the range. The poet C. Louis Leipoldt, who loved this country, is buried near the top of the pass. The gravel is generally well graded, but corrugations, loose stones and steep drops are common, and a bike needs to be treated with respect. Take it slowly, and give yourself plenty of time.

Weather is extreme. Summers are very hot and dry, and winters can be cold and wet, with occasional snow on the peaks. Fires are frequent in the fynbos. The best seasons are spring, when the wildflowers cover the plains, and autumn.

Carry water, food and a repair kit, because help is a long way off. A few farms and camps offer meals and accommodation, but book ahead.
t.clanwilliam overnight@-32.2,18.9:
Clanwilliam lies in the Olifants River valley, about two hundred kilometres north of Cape Town, at the foot of the Cederberg, a rugged range of orange and red sandstone that rises abruptly from the dry plain. It is a small, sleepy town and a good place to stop for the night, with whitewashed Cape Dutch houses on the old main street, a dam on the river that is popular for sailing and a long tradition of farming, citrus, vegetables and above all rooibos tea. The tea bush grows almost nowhere else in the world except in this region, and the farms around the town process the leaves, which are bruised, left to oxidise and dried in the sun.

The town was founded in 1808 and named after an Irish earl, father-in-law of the then governor of the Cape, which makes it one of the oldest in the country. The Cederberg itself is famous for its rock formations, with arches, pinnacles and a Maltese cross standing in the desert, and for the San rock paintings found in caves, some thousands of years old. The rare Clanwilliam cedar, a conifer that grows only on the highest slopes of these mountains, gives the range its name.

For riders, the Cederberg offers scenery that changes by the hour. The N7 north from Cape Town is a straight, fast highway, and beyond Clanwilliam the roads into the mountains, such as the route over the Pakhuis Pass, wind through stunning rock country, though some of the secondary roads are gravel and can be corrugated or loose, so check conditions with locals and take care. Wind can be strong in the valley, and the summer sun is fierce, with temperatures above thirty-five degrees on many days, so start early and carry water.

Fuel is available in Clanwilliam, a place with several stations and a few shops, and it is wise to fill up here before heading into the mountains, where there is none. In late August and September the wildflowers appear in the valley, a reason to come in spring. Winters are cold at night in the mountains and can bring snow to the peaks.
t.ehrenhausen@46.7,15.6:
Ehrenhausen stands on the Mur river at the very edge of Austria, in the south of Styria, with Slovenia only a few minutes away, and the hills behind it are covered in vines. This is the beginning of the South Styrian Wine Road, a winding route through steep, forested ridges where every south-facing slope is planted, the farmhouses sit on top, and the whole landscape feels like a green, softer version of Tuscany, which is what the locals call it. The village is small and has an old market square with a baroque church and a castle, and a grand mausoleum built by the Eggenberg family, one of the most powerful noble houses in the Habsburg lands.

The local wines are mostly white. Sauvignon Blanc is the star, with a sharp, green character, and is joined by Welschriesling, Morillon, which is the local name for Chardonnay, and a light, tart rosé called Schilcher in the western part of the region. In the small farm taverns, the Buschenschank, which can only sell their own produce, you sit under chestnut trees at wooden tables and eat bread, cold meats, pumpkin seed oil on cheese and Kernöl-flavoured dishes. Pumpkin seed oil, dark green and nutty, is a local delicacy that appears in everything from soup to ice cream.

For riders, the lanes of the Wine Road are a pleasure, with short climbs, tight bends and views over rows of vines that roll down to the valley. The surface is mostly good, but the roads are narrow, with farm tractors and cyclists in autumn, and loose gravel at the edges of corners. Kitzeck, higher up in the Sausal hills, has some of the highest vineyards in Europe. The best time to ride is September and October, when the grapes are harvested, the light is golden, and the new wine, called Sturm, is on sale, but it is also the busiest, so book a table if you want to eat.

Fuel is available in Ehrenhausen or in Leibnitz, seven kilometres north, which is the larger town, and it is wise to fill up before climbing into the hills. Most taverns close in winter, from November to March.
t.gamlitz@46.7,15.6:
Gamlitz is the heart of the South Styrian Wine Road, the string of steep vineyards that runs along the Slovenian border in the south of Austria, and in autumn the whole landscape seems to glow. The hills here are covered with vines in tight, green rows, and little farmhouses and wine taverns perch on the ridges, with the Alps in the far distance. The region is nicknamed the Styrian Tuscany, a fair comparison, though the light is softer and the hills are steeper.

Wine is the focus, and the local specialities are white. The Sauvignon Blanc, crisp and aromatic, has made the region famous, and the Morillon, as Chardonnay is called here, and the Welschriesling are also much grown. The wine is sold in the Buschenschank, a small farm tavern that has the right to sell its own produce, marked by a bunch of twigs hung over the gate. There, you sit on a bench, drink wine from a jug and eat a plate of cold cuts, cheese and bread, and look out over the vines. The local pumpkin seed oil, a dark green, nutty oil, is drizzled over salads, soup and even ice cream.

The roads are a rider's delight, though not for speed. They twist along the crests, dip into hollows and climb again, with a surface that is generally good and traffic that is mostly local. Steep gradients, tight bends and the odd tractor with a wine trailer mean that it is a ride for relaxed enjoyment, and the corner of every hill offers another view. The wine road is busy on weekends in autumn, with cyclists and visitors to the harvest festivals, so choose a weekday if you can. Of course, a rider should be careful about tasting, and the police do check.

The harvest begins in September and continues into October, when the leaves turn red and gold, and the air smells of crushed grapes and woodsmoke. In spring, the hills are green and the fruit trees are in blossom, while in summer the heat can be fierce. Winters are quiet and many taverns close.

Ehrenhausen, three kilometres away, has a few services, and Leibnitz, about seven kilometres away, is the nearest large town, with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Gamlitz itself has some stations, cafes and places to eat. Do book ahead for lunch in autumn.
t.leutschach@46.7,15.5:
Leutschach lies on the Slovenian border at the southern edge of the Styrian wine country, and the roads around it follow the steepest, wildest part of the wine road. This is a place where the hills are so steep that the vineyards are worked by hand, and the border runs along the crests, so that you can look across to the vineyards of Slovenia, which seem exactly the same. The village itself is small and attractive, with a square, a church and a few old houses, and a long tradition of winemaking and farming.

For a long time, the border region was a place of movement and change. For centuries, the area was part of the Habsburg monarchy, and the people on both sides spoke German and Slovene. After the First World War, the line was drawn between Austria and the new Yugoslavia, and from then on, the border divided families and land. Today, since Slovenia joined the European Union, the border is open, and you can cross freely, though you should carry your passport. Slovenian wine country, around Maribor, begins just beyond, and has its own old vines.

The ride here is among the best in Styria for tight twisting roads. The road climbs and falls, with sharp corners, short straights and a rough surface in places. The scenery is the main attraction, with big views over the vineyards and the forest, and the gentle light of the late afternoon turns the leaves gold. Traffic is light on weekdays, though weekends in autumn bring more visitors. Tractors and cyclists share the road, and care is needed on the blind bends.

Nature in the area is gentle. Orchards of apple and pear fill the lower slopes, and the woods are mostly oak and chestnut, with wild garlic in spring. Hares and deer graze in the fields, and in the evening, the sound of church bells carries across the valleys. The air in summer is warm and scented with hay.

Arnfels, five kilometres away, has a small castle and a few shops, and Leibnitz, about fourteen kilometres away, is the closest town with proper fuel and supermarkets. Leutschach itself has some basic services, with a few inns and taverns serving local wine and food. Plan your fuel in advance, and carry some cash.
t.soboth@46.7,15.0:
Soboth sits on a high wooded pass in the south-west corner of Styria, close to the Carinthian border, where the long ridge of the Koralpe sinks into a broad saddle and the road crosses from one province to another. It is a spread-out settlement more than a village, with farms, a church and a lake, the Sobother Stausee, a reservoir held by a dam in the forest, whose dark water reflects the spruce on its banks. The road tops out at well over a thousand metres, and the air is cool and smells of resin, with mist hanging in the hollows on summer mornings.

The surrounding country is a landscape of forest and pasture, wide and thinly populated, with timber and farming the main livelihood. Close by, on the Slovenian side, the little towns of Dravograd and Ravne na Koroškem lie in the Drava and Meža valleys, and the border has been open to riders since Slovenia joined the Schengen area, so the roads form natural loops between the two countries. In the Drava valley, Lavamünd is the small town where the Lavant river joins the Drau, with an old stone bridge and a castle above.

For riders, the Soboth road is the reward. The B69 from Eibiswald on the Styrian side climbs in a series of broad curves through spruce woods, with a smooth surface and fine visibility, and drops on the Carinthian side toward Lavamünd in tighter bends with views of the Drau valley opening up. It is a relaxed, flowing road, well suited to a long day in the saddle, and traffic is light, apart from some timber trucks and holiday traffic in August. Rain and fog come quickly, and in winter there can be ice and snow, though it is usually cleared.

A rest at the reservoir, with a view of the water, is a pleasant stop, and the inns around the pass serve simple Styrian and Carinthian dishes such as Käsnudeln, pasta filled with cheese, and dumplings with sauerkraut. The best months are May to October.
t.badacsony@46.8,17.5:
Badacsony is a volcanic hill that stands over the north shore of Lake Balaton like a lump of dark bread left on a table. It rises to 438 metres, a flat-topped basalt butte, the product of eruptions millions of years ago when the area was a shallow sea. Time has cut the lava into hexagonal columns, and near the top the cliffs form a long wall of organ pipes, with a famous natural gateway, the Kőkapu, or Stone Gate. The slopes below are terraced and planted with vines, and they catch every ray of sun, with the lake adding reflected light and warmth.

The wines here are among the best in Hungary. The volcanic soil gives a mineral edge to the whites, and the local specialities include Szürkebarát, or Pinot Gris, which is rich and full, and Kéknyelű, a rare white grape whose name means blue stalk, grown almost nowhere else. The vineyards are dotted with small stone cellars and press houses, many of them open for tastings, and in summer the hillside is a favourite for visitors. The poet Sándor Kisfaludy built a house here in the early nineteenth century, and his wife, Róza Szegedy, became a local legend, and her house is now a wine museum and a restaurant with a good view.

The road along the north shore, the 71, is a gentle cruise, with the lake on one side and vineyards and volcanic hills on the other. Balaton is the largest lake in central Europe, about seventy-seven kilometres long but only a few metres deep, and the light on it is soft and shimmering. The corners are easy, the surface is generally good, and the pace is unhurried. In July and August, the road is busy, with holidaymakers, cyclists and slow-moving traffic, so come in May, June or September, when the weather is mild and the crowds thinner. On a hot day, a swim in the warm, shallow water is a fine reward.

The surrounding hills of the Balaton Uplands National Park hold other volcanic cones, such as Szent György-hegy and Csobánc, with castle ruins and forests of beech and oak. The shores have reed beds that harbour many birds, from herons to great crested grebes.

Badacsony is a village with cafés, restaurants and wine bars, serving fish from the lake, such as fogas, or pike-perch, and goulash. There is fuel at Badacsonytomaj, close by, and Tapolca, a larger town inland, has supermarkets and services. Fonyód, across the water, is reached by a ferry from Badacsony in summer, and it is also a nearby service town.
t.balatonfured@47.0,17.9:
Balatonfüred has been taking the waters since before anyone thought of calling it a holiday. On the north shore of Lake Balaton, Hungary's inland sea, this town of about thirteen thousand grew up around its mineral springs, which were known for treating heart conditions, and in the nineteenth century it became a fashionable resort for the aristocracy and writers. The old spa park and the promenade are still the heart of the place, and the long line of plane trees along the lakeshore makes a pleasant, shaded walk after a day on the bike.

Balaton is shallow and wide, nearly eighty kilometres long, and the light on it is unlike anything else in the country. The north shore is the hilly side, with vineyards climbing the volcanic slopes behind the towns. This ride ends here, but you should not skip the neighbours: Csopak, a few kilometres west, is wine country with the local Olaszrizling, and Tihany, just east on its peninsula, has an abbey and a famous echo. The roads along the shore are mostly gentle, with the corners saved for the little lanes up through the vines, where the surface can be patchy.

The lake is the reason everyone comes and also the reason traffic is heavy. Summer weekends can be slow, with Hungarians and Germans packing the road 71 and the shore towns. Aim for a weekday, or ride in May, June or September, when the wine festivals begin and the water is still warm for a swim. Afternoon thunderstorms roll across the lake in summer with startling speed, so keep an eye on the sky over the south shore.

As a finish, Balatonfüred is easy. It is large enough to have fuel stations, supermarkets and a pleasant choice of restaurants, with freshwater fish such as fogas, the lake's pike-perch, on the menu, plus paprika-heavy stews and the sweet pastries Hungary loves. Rest in the park, grab a glass of the local white at a terrace on the harbour, and watch the sailing boats tack across a lake that seems to have no far shore.
t.amatitan@20.8,-103.7:
Amatitán is a small agave town west of Guadalajara that sits in the middle of the blue fields you came for. The landscape around it, rows of grey-blue agave plants like spiked rosettes on red volcanic soil, with the cone of Tequila volcano rising behind, is the central picture of the Ruta del Tequila. The plants take six to eight years to ripen before they are cut, so each field is a calendar of the owner's patience. In 2006 UNESCO recognised the agave landscape and the old distilleries and haciendas of the area as a World Heritage Site, and Amatitán is one of the places where you can feel why.

The riding is gentle and varied. The road between here and the town of Tequila runs through the fields, with long, easy curves, farm tracks leading off on either side, and the smell of baked agave on the wind when a distillery is working. Traffic is mixed, with trucks hauling agave hearts, pickups, and the odd tour van. The surface is generally good but can be rough at the edges, and topes, the speed bumps Mexicans love, appear at every village with little warning. Look out for them, and for painted warnings that are faded to nothing.

Amatitán is also home to some famous names in tequila, and the old Herradura hacienda, which lets visitors in for tours, is nearby. If you want to taste, do it after the riding. Tequila here is made with blue Weber agave, the hearts of which are baked in ovens, crushed, and fermented and distilled. The white or blanco is clear and sharp, the reposado has rested in oak, and it is good manners to sip rather than shoot.

The town has about eleven thousand inhabitants, so you will find fuel, a bank machine and a couple of simple places to eat, such as taquerias and torta stands. The market is the place for fresh fruit and agua fresca. Day temperatures in the dry season can reach thirty degrees or more, so bring water and leave early. The wet months from June to September bring afternoon storms that make the red dirt slick, and cooler air that is welcome.
t.tequila@20.9,-103.8:
Tequila is both a town and a drink, and it is rare for the two to be so closely bound. The town, with about thirty thousand people, lies at the foot of the volcano of the same name, and its centre is a tidy grid of low houses painted in strong colours around a main plaza and a parish church. Mexico gives such places the title Pueblo Mágico, and here it fits more honestly than usual, because the thing the town is famous for is still produced a few streets away. The air in places smells of cooked agave, sweet and a little smoky, and the big distillery names, Cuervo and Sauza among them, have their old facilities in town.

If you have never seen the process, there are tours that walk you through the baking ovens, the crushing, the fermentation and the stills, and end, naturally, with a tasting. As a rider, go on the tour and sip, but save the proper tasting for the end of the day. The local way to drink is the cantarito, a clay cup filled with tequila, citrus juice and soda, which you will see sold from stands around the plaza. It goes down easily in the heat, and that is the problem.

The riding to reach it is among the easiest on this route. The road from Amatitán passes through agave fields with long, open bends, and the surface is usually good. Arriving in the town means slow, cobbled or uneven streets, one-way systems, and a lot of pedestrians, and parking near the plaza is tight. If the town is crowded, as it is at weekends, leave the bike a few streets out and walk in. There is a small train that runs tourists out to the distilleries, which tells you how seriously the place takes its visitors.

Tequila is large enough for everything you need: several fuel stations on the main roads, banks, pharmacies and a good range of places to eat, from market stalls to proper restaurants with courtyards. The mornings are the best time, when the light is gentle and the fields glow, and the heat has not yet turned the day sluggish. Rain is likely in the summer afternoons, so plan around it.
t.magdalena@20.9,-104.0:
Magdalena is a small town in the highlands of Jalisco, in the heart of the blue agave country, and it has a quieter, more rural feel than the busy tequila towns nearby. It lies west of Guadalajara, in a landscape of dry hills and fields where rows of spiky blue-grey agave plants run to the horizon. About sixteen thousand people live here, and the town is known for opal and obsidian, which are mined in the surrounding hills and sold in small shops around the plaza. It sits on the Ruta del Tequila, which links Guadalajara with Tequila and its distilleries and haciendas.

The agave landscape of Tequila is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the plants take around seven to ten years to mature before they are harvested by jimadores, who use a sharp tool called a coa to cut away the leaves and expose the piña, the heart. The piñas are cooked, crushed and fermented before being distilled. Tequila can legally be made only in Jalisco and a few other states, and the process is a point of pride. Many distilleries offer tours and tastings, but as always, drinking and riding do not mix, so limit yourself or share a taxi.

The riding in this area is relaxed. Roads cross rolling hills with long, open bends, with agave on both sides, and the surface is usually fair, with potholes appearing on smaller roads. Trucks carrying agave and sugar cane are common, and you should be wary of speed bumps called topes, which appear without warning in villages. The weather is warm and dry for much of the year, with a rainy season from June to September, when afternoon storms are heavy but short. The best months for riding are November to April.

Magdalena has fuel stations, shops and several places to eat, where you can have tortas ahogadas, a Jalisco speciality of pork sandwiches drowned in spicy sauce, or birria, a spicy goat or beef stew. Cold beer is welcome, and so is fresh agua de jamaica. Stay a little, and watch the sun go down over the blue fields. The light turns the agave a deep violet.
t.durango@24.0,-104.7:
Durango is a handsome colonial city in the north of Mexico, set on a high plateau at about 1,900 metres, with a baroque cathedral, tree-lined plazas and a relaxed, small-town pace for a place of half a million people. It was founded in 1563 by Spanish settlers, who came for the silver of the Sierra Madre, and for centuries it was a mining and ranching centre. In the twentieth century, Hollywood found the dry country around the city, and dozens of Westerns were filmed here, with John Wayne among the stars who came. Film sets still stand outside town and are open to visitors.

The roads from Durango head west toward the Pacific, and the most famous is the Espinazo del Diablo, the Devil's Backbone, a stretch of highway 40 that climbs the Sierra Madre Occidental toward Mazatlán. It is a legendary piece of road, with hundreds of bends carved into steep mountain terrain, narrow in places and dropping into huge valleys, with views of pine forest, rock walls and distant peaks. The modern toll highway now bypasses much of it with tunnels and bridges, including the Baluarte Bridge, among the highest cable-stayed bridges in the world, but the old road is still there for riders who want it.

Be careful on the old road: it is narrow, the surface varies, and lorries are slow on the uphills and quick on the downhills. Fog and rain can reduce visibility, especially in summer, and rockfalls occur. Start early and avoid the dark. Fuel is available in Durango and in the larger towns on the way, but gaps exist in the mountains, so keep the tank full and do not rely on small villages.

Durango has a rich food tradition, with caldillo durangueño, a beef stew with chile, and the famous local cheese, and mezcal is made in the region too. Walk the plaza in the evening, when the cathedral is lit and families come out to eat ice cream. The dry season is October to May, with cold nights in winter at that altitude. Pack layers, because the temperature changes dramatically between the plateau and the coast.
t.gryllefjord@69.4,17.1:
Gryllefjord is a fishing village at the north-western end of Senja, Norway's second largest island, and it is about as far as you can go before the road gives out and the Atlantic takes over. It has fewer than five hundred inhabitants, a harbour, a small ferry quay and a handful of buildings, and the ferry runs from here across to Andenes on Andøya, a crossing of a couple of hours that is worth taking in summer. The mountains behind the village are jagged and steep, and the sea is a deep, cold blue. Finnsnes, on the mainland side of the island, is the nearest town of any size, nearly forty kilometres away.

This is Arctic Norway, well above the Arctic Circle, and the seasons are extreme. From late May to late July the sun does not set, and the light at midnight is soft and gold, which is the finest time to ride. In winter, the sun disappears for weeks, and the northern lights are visible on clear nights. The weather is changeable, often windy, and the temperature even in summer can be cool, so pack warm layers and waterproofs.

The scenic route on Senja runs along the outer coast, passing through villages like Mefjordvær and Husøy, with views of peaks that rise sharply from the water. The road is mostly narrow and well maintained, with some tight bends and short tunnels, and traffic is light. Sheep and reindeer wander near the road, and sea eagles circle above the fjords, so keep your eyes open. Along the route are viewing platforms and small art installations that are part of the National Tourist Routes programme.

Fuel is a point to plan for. Pumps exist at Finnsnes and some villages, but not everywhere, and opening hours can be limited, particularly on Sundays. Fill the tank whenever you can, and carry some food. In the harbour you can buy fresh fish, and the local specialty is stockfish, cod dried on racks in the cold air. Gryllefjord is quiet, the sort of place where the sound of the gulls is the main event, and the long evening light does the rest.
t.bergsbotn@69.4,17.4:
Bergsbotn lies at the head of Bergsfjorden, on the north-west coast of Senja, Norway's second-largest island, and it is the place where the island's reputation as Norway in miniature starts to make sense. Steep peaks drop straight into the sea, the fjord runs cold and dark between them, and the lights of a few small houses stand at its edge. A viewing platform reaches out over the water, built as part of the scenic route programme, and from it you can look across the fjord to a wall of jagged mountains whose profile reminds some people of a saw and others of the horns of an ox. Local names say the same thing in Norwegian.

Senja is reached by a bridge from the mainland near Finnsnes, and the road around its outer coast is among the best in the north.
