It twists along the shore, runs over short bridges, cuts through headlands and climbs across low passes with views of open ocean. The road is narrow in places, the surface varies from smooth to patched, and in winter it can be icy and dark. In summer you have the midnight sun, from late May to July, and the light can be golden at two in the morning. In autumn and winter the northern lights make the dark hours worth staying up for.

Weather rules everything up here. A clear, blue morning can become a wall of fog and rain within an hour, and the wind coming across the open sea can be strong enough to push a heavy bike sideways. Pack warm layers even in July, because the sea air is cold. Reindeer and sheep walk onto the road, and elk are not unknown.

Plan fuel carefully. The island is not densely populated, and the villages are small. The nearest town with a proper range of services is Finnsnes, back on the mainland side, and a rider coming out along the coast should fill up there or at the last reliable pump before the outer road. Food is simple: fish, often cod or halibut, fresh bread, and strong coffee. In peak summer, small cafés and campsites open, but in the shoulder season much is closed. Bring snacks, and a little patience for the ferry-and-bridge logistics.
t.tungeneset@69.5,17.3:
Tungeneset is a viewing platform on the west side of Senja, set on a rocky point above the sea, and it offers what is perhaps the most photographed outlook on the island. A path of steel and timber boardwalks leads out over the rock to a viewing point, designed to be unobtrusive but strong enough to stand the weather. In front of you, the mountains rise in sharp, bare peaks straight from the water, and depending on your angle and the cloud, you can pick out the pointed silhouettes that appear in every Senja guidebook. Below, the sea works at the foot of the rock, and in the right light it goes from slate to silver to green.

The riding to reach it is a pleasure. The road along Senja's outer coast winds along inlets and across low saddles, and the bends come in a smooth, steady rhythm that makes it easy to relax. Short tunnels cut through rock, and the road in places runs close to the water, with a barrier and a gravel verge between you and the sea. The surface is mostly good, but frost heave and rough patches turn up with little warning, especially in spring. It is a road that rewards a calm pace. Campervans and tour cars are common in summer, so be patient and use the pull-outs.

This coast faces the open Norwegian Sea, and the weather arrives fast. Wind is common, and so is rain. It can be warm in the sun and bitterly cold in the shade. The light in the shoulder months, late summer and early autumn, is clear and low, and it makes the peaks look sharper and closer. In winter the road may be icy, with limited daylight and snow, and the platform may be closed.

Fuel is the thing to plan for, because this part of the island has none. Finnsnes, on the mainland side, is the nearest town of any size, and smaller villages along the coast may have a pump or may not, so do not rely on it. Take food and a flask, and ride on a full tank. White-tailed eagles hunt over these waters, and a patient observer will often see one drift over the cliff. Take rubbish with you, and keep to the boardwalk, as the thin soil on the rock heals slowly.
t.husoy@69.5,17.7:
Husøy is a fishing village on a small island off the coast of Senja, tied to the larger island by road, and the lanes of its wooden houses are painted in the traditional reds, yellows and whites of the north. It is a working harbour first of all: boats at the quay, nets and crates on the wharf, and the air heavy with the sharp smell of salt, diesel and fish. Racks of drying cod stand in places, the old method of preserving the catch that built the economy of the Norwegian north. Stockfish, as it is called, was shipped to southern Europe for centuries, and the trade shaped places like this.

The ride to Husøy is a gentle one. The road follows the coast, passing small bays and farms, and the island comes into view as a low, green hump against the grey sea. It is a good place to slow down, park, and walk. The lanes are narrow and the speed is low, and there is no hurry. In summer, the light lasts all night, and the village has a calm, outward-looking feel, while in autumn the sea can be rough, with waves thundering on the rocks at the outer edge. A strong wind is common, and a rider on a lightweight bike should be ready for gusts when crossing exposed stretches.

Small places like this live on a few things: fish, tourism in summer, and the stubborn love of those who stay. If you meet someone mending nets on the quay, you may get a story or two, but remember that people are at work. Check what is open before you come, as cafés and shops are few and may keep short hours. Seabirds nest on the cliffs nearby, and sea eagles, with their huge pale wings, sometimes circle over the harbour.

Finnsnes, back on the mainland side, is the nearest town for fuel, supermarkets and repairs, and it is some distance away, so top up before you set out along the coast. Gryllefjord, a small place farther out, is closer, but it offers few services. The best time to be here is a still evening in summer, when the water is calm, and the whole village glows in the long low sun.
t.botnhamn@69.5,17.9:
Botnhamn is a tiny fishing settlement on the north side of Senja, facing the open sea, and it is an end of the road in the best sense. The little harbour is sheltered by rocky headlands, with a handful of houses and boat sheds, and behind it rise steep, jagged mountains that drop straight into the ocean. Finnsnes, over thirty kilometres away, is the closest town of any size, so supplies need to be sorted earlier. The area has been settled for thousands of years, with traces of Sami and Norse inhabitants, and fishing has been the main livelihood for most of that time.

The road from the south follows the fjords and headlands, with a mix of tight bends, tunnels and wide views, and the surface is generally good. It is a quiet road, and in the early morning, you may have it to yourself. Wind can be strong near the coast, and rain showers move through quickly, so waterproofs are wise. In summer, the midnight sun lights the peaks in gold, and you can ride late into the evening. The best months are June to August, though even then it is cool.

Nearby, at the village of Bergsbotn, a viewing platform juts out over the fjord, with a dramatic view of the mountains and the water below, and it is one of the most photographed spots on the island. Senja has a reputation as a smaller, wilder version of Lofoten, with fewer crowds and a similar landscape of sharp peaks and white beaches. Whales sometimes appear off the coast in winter, and sea eagles are common throughout the year. The coast has beaches of pale sand that look tropical until you put a toe in the water.

There are limited services here, so plan accordingly. Fuel should be taken in Finnsnes or another larger village, and there is no guarantee of a cafe, though the occasional roadside kiosk may sell coffee and waffles. In many places, the best meal is a simple one: fresh fish, bread and cheese eaten beside the sea. A flask of hot coffee and a warm jacket are all you need, and the stillness of the evening is the reward.
t.wall south dakota@44.0,-102.2:
Wall is a small town on the edge of the Badlands that has become famous for one of the most successful pieces of marketing in American history. In 1931, a pharmacist named Ted Hustead and his wife Dorothy bought a drugstore here, in a town of a few hundred people, and struggled to make a living. Then Dorothy had an idea: offer free ice water to the travellers crossing the prairie in the heat. Signs went up along the highway for miles, and the customers came. Today Wall Drug is a sprawling complex of shops, with a giant jackalope, a dinosaur, a cafe and an animated cowboy band, and billboards for it appear on roads all over the world.

It is, of course, a tourist trap, but a good-humoured one, and it has doughnuts, five-cent coffee and a very large collection of Western art and souvenirs. Many riders stop for the experience as much as for supplies. The interstate runs past the town, and the main street has the usual motels, diners and gas stations, so it is a convenient base before the loop road.

The Badlands Loop road begins a few miles south, and leads through the national park, a landscape of eroded buttes, pinnacles and canyons painted in bands of pink, yellow and grey. The Lakota called the area mako sica, meaning bad land, because it was difficult to cross, and the early French trappers said the same thing in their own language. The road runs along the edge of the formations, with long views over the prairie, and the surface is generally good, with easy curves and a few steady climbs. You may see bison, bighorn sheep and prairie dogs along the route.

Fill the tank in Wall, since the loop has few services. Summer is hot, with temperatures often above thirty-five degrees Celsius and violent thunderstorms, hail and wind in the afternoon. Spring and autumn are more pleasant, and the low light at dawn or dusk makes the rock glow. Bring water, sunscreen and a windproof layer, and watch for rattlesnakes if you leave the road. Winter can bring snow and closures, and the whole area is far from any large city, so plan ahead.
t.pinnacles overlook@43.9,-102.2:
The Badlands look wrong in the best way. Out of the flat grassland of western South Dakota, the ground suddenly collapses into a maze of striped gullies, spires and ridges in yellow, pink and grey, as though somebody had tilted a wedding cake and left it out in the rain. Pinnacles Overlook sits near the northeast entrance of Badlands National Park, and it gives you the first good look over the edge of the wall, along with the long, flat prairie beyond.

The shapes are young in geological terms. The rock is soft clay, silt and volcanic ash laid down over tens of millions of years, and erosion eats it at something like an inch a year, so the landscape is changing in front of you. Fossils turn up in the layers, from ancient horses and rhinoceros-like beasts to sabre-toothed cats, and paleontologists have been working here since the nineteenth century. The Lakota called it mako sica, land bad, because it was hard to cross, and French trappers called it les mauvaises terres a traverser, and both described it fairly.

The Badlands Loop Road, State Highway 240, is the way to see it. It runs for about thirty miles through the park, with a series of overlooks along the rim, and the riding is gentle: long sweeps and small climbs, with a surface that is usually good, and a speed limit that keeps you attentive. Bison and prairie dogs may wander close to the road, and bighorn sheep appear on the rocks. The wind is a constant, and summer storms can bring hail and sudden gusts. Dawn and dusk are the best hours, when the low light turns the ridges to gold and rose. Midsummer is hot and exposed, with little shade.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Wall, on Interstate 90 a few miles north, is a sizeable stop with fuel, motels and the famous Wall Drug, where free ice water drew early travellers from 1931 and the brand has been drawing them ever since. Inside the park, there is little beyond a lodge at Cedar Pass, so fill up in Wall or Interior. Bring water, sunscreen and a windproof layer. The park entry fee is payable at the gate. Walk a little away from the car park, where the quiet is absolute, and listen to the wind in the grass.
t.panorama point@43.8,-102.1:
Panorama Point earns its name with a view that really does go all the way round. From the overlook at the edge of the Badlands, the ground drops away to the south into the White River Valley, a wide plain of yellow grass and shadowed canyons, with flat-topped buttes standing on the horizon. It is a quiet place, much less visited than the busy overlooks near the visitor centre, and a good place to sit on the bike and let the wind do its work.

The land to the south belongs to the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, home of the Oglala Lakota, and this country has seen some of the most painful chapters in American history. The Stronghold Table, a high tableland in the Badlands to the south-west, was a gathering place for the Ghost Dance in 1890, a spiritual movement that frightened the authorities and led to the massacre at Wounded Knee, a short distance away, in December of that year. Today the land is part of the Oglala Lakota's territory, and the Oglala Lakota run a section of the park jointly. It is worth reading about before you come, and approaching with respect.

The riding here is good, flowing and easy. The Badlands Loop Road passes along the north edge of the formation, through grassland dotted with yucca, and the curves and dips are gentle. The surface is generally good, with a few patches of frost heave. The danger is the weather: wind, heat and thunder come fast on the open plain, and the sky is enormous, so you see storms coming from a long way off. Spring and early autumn are most comfortable, and in October the park is nearly empty, with cool air and clear light.

There are no services at Panorama Point beyond a pit toilet and a few parking spaces. The nearest fuel is at Interior, a small place, or at Wall, to the north on the interstate, and for a larger choice Rapid City is about an hour away. Cedar Pass Lodge has food during the season, and the visitor centre is a short distance east. Carry water, because the dry air and sun take more out of you than you notice, and rattlesnakes sometimes lie in the sun on the paths, so watch your step.
t.ben reifel visitor center@43.8,-101.9:
The visitor centre at Cedar Pass is the park's front door, and it is named for Ben Reifel, a Brule Lakota from the Rosebud Reservation who rose to become a US congressman for South Dakota in the 1960s, one of the first Native Americans elected in that era. It sits at a gap in the Badlands Wall where a road, a creek and a handful of old buildings all squeeze through, and from the car park you can see the first great pinnacles rising behind the lodge.

It is a useful stop for a rider. Inside there is an exhibit on the geology and a collection of fossils, a cafe in the lodge nearby, a bookshop, rangers to ask about the weather and road conditions, and toilets and drinking water that are worth taking seriously in a place with little shade. Outside, trails lead into the formations. The Door, Window and Notch trails are short and each gives a different view of the layered rock, and the Notch includes a log ladder and a drop, so it suits steady feet. Take care on the clay: it is dry and crumbly in sunshine and as slick as grease after rain.

The Badlands Loop Road is a satisfying ride, and this is its midpoint. It is a fairly straight, flowing road with long views, passing from the pinnacles in the east to the open prairie in the west, with a handful of pull-outs. The speed limit is modest and enforced by rangers, and the prairie dogs, bison and bighorn sheep are all quite capable of stepping into the road. Wind from the west can be strong, and summer storms bring hail. Cedar Pass Lodge has cabins and a restaurant, open in season, and the campground is nearby.

Fuel is not available at the visitor centre. Interior, a few kilometres east, is tiny, and Wall, off Interstate 90, has several stations, motels and the famous drugstore with its signs stretching hundreds of miles in each direction. Kadoka, to the west along the interstate, and Philip are smaller. Check your tank before you enter, and carry water. The park is open all year, though winter brings snow and the occasional closure, and the entry fee is payable at the gate. The light at the end of the day, when the ridges turn red and the shadows fill the gullies, is the best reason to stay for sunset.
t.kadoka@43.8,-101.5:
Kadoka is a village of fewer than a thousand people on the high plains of South Dakota, a quiet place of wide streets and grain elevators, and the name is a Lakota word often translated as hole in the wall, which refers to a gap in the Badlands wall nearby. The town sits on the interstate, at the south-east end of the long arc of the Badlands, and it is a handy base for those who want to see the park without paying resort prices.

Around Kadoka the prairie is open and almost treeless, with grass, wheat and cattle as far as you can see. The Lakota lived here for centuries, hunting bison, and the Pine Ridge reservation lies just to the south, where the Wounded Knee massacre of 1890 took place. The history of these plains is one of conflict and loss, and a visit to the memorial and the Lakota cultural centres in the area can provide a more complete picture of the region's past.

The Badlands Loop Road runs through the national park between Wall and the village of Interior, passing the Pinnacles and Yellow Mounds overlooks and the visitor centre at Cedar Pass. The ride is gentle, with views of crumbling spires in stripes of cream, rust and lilac, and the contrast with the flat green prairie on the rim is startling. Wind blows steadily across the plains, so expect a push, and heat in summer can be harsh. Traffic is lightest in the early morning, and the light is best in the evening.

Kadoka has fuel, a few motels and cafes, and a small museum with a collection of vintage cars, a curiosity worth a quick look. Philip, the next town east, is about twenty-six kilometres away, but supplies are modest in this part of the state. Be careful of deer and livestock on the road at dusk, and watch for sudden storms, which build quickly on the plains. If you are lucky, a clear night here shows a dense sky of stars, with almost no artificial light to compete.
t.needles highway@43.8,-103.5:
South Dakota Highway 87 is the road that Peter Norbeck wanted, and he was not a man to leave a line on a map to chance. The governor and later senator, a great lover of the Black Hills, scouted the route on foot and horseback around 1919, and the engineers did their best to follow his choices, blasting through granite where they had to. The result is a narrow road that threads through towering granite spires, the needles that give the highway its name, and passes through tunnels barely wide enough for a car. For a motorcyclist, it is one of the great short roads of the American Midwest.

The granite is the real star. Millions of years of weathering have carved the rock into tall, slender columns and sharply cut domes, some leaning, some balanced, all in shades of grey and pink. Pine and spruce cling to every crack, and at Sylvan Lake the water reflects the boulders and the forest in an almost Japanese composition. The highest point in the Black Hills, Black Elk Peak, is a short distance away, and the country around is thick with deer, bighorn sheep, and mountain goats.

The riding is tight and technical. The road twists and climbs, with sharp bends, narrow lanes, and little room for error. The Needles Eye tunnel is only about eight feet wide, so wide panniers and luggage need care, and the lower tunnels are lower still. Speeds are low, and the real skill is in looking well ahead and keeping the bike steady. Traffic can be heavy in summer, especially during the August motorcycle rally at Sturgis, when the whole area fills with riders. Early morning is the best time to ride it.

Custer, about nine kilometres to the south, is a small town with fuel, food, and lodging, and it is the sensible place to fill up before entering the park. There is an entrance fee for Custer State Park, and the road may be closed in winter after heavy snow. Watch for wildlife on the road, especially buffalo, which wander freely in the park and can be dangerous if provoked. Autumn is a good season, with fewer crowds and the golden aspens against the dark pines, though the weather can turn quickly in the hills.
t.iron mountain road@43.8,-103.5:
Iron Mountain Road is the showpiece of the Peter Norbeck Scenic Byway, and it was designed as such. Norbeck and his engineer, working in the 1930s, wanted a road that would pull travellers slowly through the Black Hills and deliver them to sudden views, and they got it. Wooden pigtail bridges loop over themselves to gain height, tunnels are placed so that a carved presidential face appears in the frame at the end, and the road twists along a ridge with the forest falling away on either side.

The most famous of those views is of Mount Rushmore. Heading north on US 16A, you pass through a tunnel, and as you emerge the granite faces of four presidents appear in the distance, perfectly framed by the rock. Gutzon Borglum began carving the mountain in 1927, and the work, which employed hundreds of local workers, ended in 1941. It is a controversial monument for reasons that include the fact that the Black Hills are sacred to the Lakota, and the land was taken in breach of treaty, a history that is worth knowing as you ride.

The road itself is a pleasure. It is about seventeen miles of tight bends, sudden climbs, and short, curving bridges, and the speed limit is low, around twenty-five miles an hour on some sections. The tunnels are narrow, and the pigtails demand a slow, steady hand. The surface is generally good, though the weather can leave patches of damp, and the traffic can be heavy in summer. Mornings are the best time, when the light is soft and the road is quiet.

Custer, nine kilometres to the south, has fuel, food, and bike-friendly lodging, and Rapid City, to the north-east, is the big town with all the services. Autumn colour is excellent, though snow can come early, and the byway can be closed or icy in winter. Watch for wildlife, particularly deer and bison, and take care of the pigtails, where the road narrows and the drop is steep. The sound of a bike echoing through a tunnel is one of the small joys of the hills.
t.kogel bay@-34.2,18.8:
Clarence Drive is the coast road that South Africans point to when they want to impress visitors, and Kogel Bay is one of its quieter pleasures. The road squeezes between steep mountain slopes and the cold Atlantic, hugging the cliffs for miles, and then dips to a long, pale beach where the dunes roll up against the fynbos. The sea here is rough and the undertow dangerous, so it is a place for walking and watching rather than swimming.

The mountains behind are the Kogelberg, which form the heart of a UNESCO biosphere reserve, and the vegetation is the extraordinary Cape fynbos, a plant community found nowhere else on Earth. Proteas, ericas, and restios cover the slopes, and in spring and early summer they flower in great numbers. Baboons roam the area, and they are bold, so keep your food out of sight and your distance. From June to November, southern right whales come into the bay to calve, and you can often see them from the roadside, rolling slowly in the swell.

The riding is a delight. The road, the R44, runs from Gordon's Bay toward Rooi-Els and Betty's Bay, clinging to the mountainside with sweeping bends and views over False Bay and the sea. It was built by hand in the early twentieth century, cut into steep rock, and the engineers must have enjoyed the challenge. The surface is generally good, though rockfalls and sand can occur, and the road is narrow in places, with cyclists and tourists stopping suddenly. Wind is a major factor, and strong south-easterlies in summer can be hard work.

Fuel is easiest in Gordon's Bay at the western end, or in Grabouw and Somerset West, inland. There is little in the way of services at Kogel Bay itself, apart from a small car park and a few picnic spots. Bring water and sun protection, because the light is strong. The best season is spring, for flowers and whales, though autumn is also pleasant, with calmer air. Winter brings storms and rain, and the sea can be spectacular, but the road is more exposed. Late afternoon is the finest time, when the sun lights the cliffs from the west.
t.rooi els@-34.3,18.8:
Rooi-Els is a handful of houses and a fierce mountain, and the combination is spectacular. The village sits on the shore of False Bay, squeezed between the Atlantic and the cliffs of the Hottentots-Holland and Kogelberg ranges, and the name means red alder, after a tree that grows along the stream. The steep slopes behind the village are covered with fynbos and cut by dark gorges, and the whole place feels like the end of the world.

It is also a favourite haunt of baboons. Troops of chacma baboons roam the Cape peninsula and the coastal mountains, and in Rooi-Els they are used to people. They are clever and can be aggressive, and they have been known to open car doors and raid saddlebags. Do not feed them, keep food secured, and give them room. Rock hyraxes, called dassies, sun themselves on the rocks, and in the sea you may see seals, dolphins, and, in season, whales passing close to shore.

Clarence Drive is the star here. From Gordon's Bay the road climbs along the cliffs, with tight bends, rock overhangs, and views that open to the whole sweep of False Bay, before dropping to the village. At its best it is a rider's road, with a good surface, flowing corners, and the sea at your side. Rockfalls are possible after heavy rain, and sand sometimes drifts across the surface. Traffic is usually light on weekdays but heavier on weekends, and the wind can be strong and gusty.

Fill up in Gordon's Bay, about thirty kilometres to the west, or in Grabouw, inland, before you set off. Bring water, a rain layer, and a sense of patience if you meet a troop of baboons on the road. The best season is spring, when the fynbos flowers and the weather is mild, and the best light is late in the afternoon, when the cliffs glow gold. In midwinter, storms can bring huge swells, and the road is rewarding but must be ridden carefully.
The Ômine Okugakemichi is not a road at all, at least not one you can ride. It is a mountain trail that runs for about a hundred kilometres along the spine of the Ômine range in the Kii peninsula, linking Yoshino in the north with Kumano in the south, over peaks, ridges and rock faces. For more than a thousand years, yamabushi, the mountain ascetics of the Shugendo tradition, have walked it as a spiritual practice, combining Buddhist, Shinto and older mountain beliefs, with rituals at sacred rocks, waterfalls and cliffs along the way. It is part of the UNESCO-listed Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range, inscribed in 2004.

The central peak, Sanjogatake, also called Ômine-san, is still closed to women, one of the last such places in Japan, a tradition that is both revered and contested. The trail is long, steep and demanding, with chains and ladders in places, and should only be attempted by experienced, well-prepared hikers.

For riders, the mountains offer some of the best roads in Japan. National Route 169 runs north-south through the eastern side of the range, along valleys and reservoirs, and Route 168 runs through the western side toward Totsukawa, a remote village with a long suspension bridge and hot springs. Roads are narrow and twisting, with tunnels, landslides and roadworks, and traffic is light. Rain is frequent, and the Kii peninsula is one of the wettest places in Japan, so be prepared for heavy downpours, especially in the rainy season and typhoon season.

Yoshino, at the northern end of the range, is famous for its cherry blossoms, with tens of thousands of trees covering the mountainside in spring, and Kimpusen-ji, the head temple of Shugendo, with its huge wooden hall. Kōya-san, to the west, is the headquarters of Shingon Buddhism, with temples, a vast cemetery and temple lodgings. Fuel is available in towns, but sparse in the mountains, so fill up in Gojō or Yoshino before heading south. Autumn is especially beautiful, with red and gold leaves and clear air.
t.chapel of san nicolas tolentino of the f:
On the high plateau of southern Zacatecas, close to the border with San Luis Potosí, the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro passed through a dry landscape of grassland, yucca and nopal cactus, linking Mexico City with the silver mines of the north. Haciendas grew up along the way, and the former Hacienda of San Nicolás de Quijas, with its chapel dedicated to San Nicolás Tolentino, is one of the sites inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2010 as part of the royal road. The chapel, with its simple façade, bell gable and adobe walls, stands in a small village surrounded by fields and open range.

The haciendas were the economic centres of colonial Mexico, with farms, workshops, chapels and housing for workers, and many have fallen into ruin since the land reforms of the twentieth century. Visiting them gives a sense of the scale and isolation of life on the frontier.

Pinos, about twenty kilometres away, is a mining town founded in the sixteenth century, perched at around 2,500 metres in the hills. It is a Pueblo Mágico, with colonial churches, old mines and cobbled streets, and it has fuel, shops and simple places to eat. The surrounding area is high, dry and windy, with cold nights even in summer, and the light is intense.

Riding here is about wide open spaces and long distances. The roads are mostly paved, straight or gently curving, with little traffic, but watch out for livestock, potholes and speed bumps at village entrances. Fuel stations can be far apart, so plan accordingly. The cities of Zacatecas, with its pink stone cathedral, and San Luis Potosí are both within a couple of hours' ride. Try gorditas, enchiladas zacatecanas and mezcal from the region. Spring and autumn are the best times, as summers bring storms and winters cold nights.
t.historic ensemble of the town of ojuelos:
Ojuelos de Jalisco lies on the high, dry plateau where Jalisco meets Aguascalientes, Zacatecas and Guanajuato, at over two thousand metres, a land of grassland, nopal cactus, mesquite and wide horizons. The town owes its existence to the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road that carried silver north from the mines of Zacatecas and supplies from Mexico City, eventually reaching all the way to Santa Fe in what is now New Mexico. UNESCO listed a series of sites along the road in 2010, including the historic ensemble of Ojuelos.

In the sixteenth century, this stretch of the road was dangerous country, contested during the long Chichimeca War between Spanish settlers and the nomadic peoples of the plateau. Ojuelos began as a presidio, a fortified outpost to protect the caravans, and the old fort still stands near the centre, alongside a stately church and plaza. Around the town, haciendas grew up to raise cattle and grain, and some of them, including Ciénega de Mata, are part of the same listing. The sky here is enormous, with clear dry air and afternoon clouds building into towering thunderheads in the summer rainy season.

The roads across the plateau are mostly long and straight, with gentle grades and wide views, linking towns such as Lagos de Moreno, Aguascalientes and San Luis Potosí. Watch for topes, the speed bumps that guard every village, sometimes unmarked, as well as livestock and slow trucks. Toll roads, the cuotas, are faster and generally safer, while free roads can be rough. Daytime riding is strongly advised, and it pays to check local conditions before travelling.

Ojuelos has around twelve thousand people and fuel, shops and simple restaurants. The region is ranching country, so expect excellent beef, cheese and dairy, and in the plaza you may find birria or tacos al pastor. Evenings are cool even in summer and cold in winter, so bring a warm layer, and if you arrive at dusk, watch the light turn the plateau gold and the church stone pink before the stars come out.
t.yoshino and omine kimpusen ji@34.4,135.9:
Every April, the hillsides of Yoshino turn pink and white as tens of thousands of cherry trees burst into bloom, and the narrow ridge-top town fills with visitors who come to see one of Japan's most famous blossom displays. But Yoshino is more than a flower show. It is the heart of Shugendō, a mountain religion that blends Buddhism, Shinto and ancient nature worship, and the Kimpusen-ji temple, with its enormous wooden main hall, the Zaō-dō, is its spiritual centre. The temple is part of the Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range, listed by UNESCO in 2004.

The Zaō-dō is one of the largest wooden buildings in Japan, and inside, hidden for most of the year, are huge statues of Zaō Gongen, a fierce deity with blue skin and flaming hair. Yoshino was also briefly the seat of the Southern Court in the fourteenth century, when the Emperor Go-Daigo set up a rival imperial court here during a period of civil war. From Yoshino, the Ōmine pilgrimage route runs south along the mountain ridges to the Kumano shrines, a demanding trek through forests and over peaks that ascetics still undertake.

The roads in the Kii mountains are some of the most beautiful in Japan, winding through deep valleys and over passes, with forests of cedar and cypress and villages clinging to the slopes. Many roads are narrow and twisty, with tight bends, tunnels and steep drops, and they can be slippery in rain, which is frequent. Traffic is generally light, except during the cherry blossom season, when Yoshino becomes extremely crowded and access may be restricted. Autumn, with its red and gold leaves, is another beautiful time to visit.

Yoshino has small shops, restaurants and guesthouses, but fuel is better found in larger towns like Gojō, Sakurai or Gose. Try kakinoha-zushi, sushi wrapped in persimmon leaves, a local speciality, and kuzu, a starch made from the arrowroot plant, used in sweets and noodles. Stay overnight in a temple lodging if you can, to experience the morning prayers.
t.former hacienda of penuelas@21.7,-102.3:
South of the city of Aguascalientes, on the high plateau of central Mexico, the former hacienda of Peñuelas stands among fields and scrub, its stone and adobe buildings, chapel and courtyards a reminder of the great rural estates that once dominated the region. It was one of the stops on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road from Mexico City to the silver mines of Zacatecas and beyond to New Mexico, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of sites along the road, inscribed in 2010.

Haciendas like Peñuelas were small worlds of their own, with the owner's house, a chapel, granaries, stables, workers' housing and often a store, where workers were frequently bound by debt. They produced cattle, grain and other goods for the mining towns and travellers on the road. The landscape around is open and dry, with mesquite, nopal cactus and grassland, and the sky is huge, with dramatic thunderstorms in the summer rainy season. The villages around Peñuelas are small and quiet, with churches and plazas where life moves at a slow pace.

The roads here are mostly straight and flat or gently rolling, with good surfaces on the main routes and rougher conditions on smaller roads. Watch out for topes, speed bumps at the entrance to every village, as well as livestock, slow trucks and occasional potholes. The toll roads, cuotas, are faster and generally safer, while free roads pass through more villages. Daytime riding is advisable, and it is wise to check local conditions before travelling.

Aguascalientes, a city of over seven hundred thousand people, has everything you need, from fuel to food and accommodation, and it is famous for the Feria de San Marcos, one of the largest fairs in Mexico, held in spring with bullfights, concerts and cockfights. The region is known for its guava, wine and textiles, and for dishes such as birria and enchiladas. The name of the city comes from its hot springs, and some old bathhouses are still in use, perfect after a long day in the saddle.
t.nisanzai kofun@34.5,135.5:
In the middle of the sprawling city of Sakai, south of Osaka, a large keyhole-shaped mound rises above a ring of moats, covered in dense forest and surrounded by houses, roads and shops. This is the Nisanzai Kofun, a monumental tomb built in the fifth century for a member of the ruling elite of early Japan. It is one of the largest of the Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group, a collection of burial mounds listed by UNESCO in 2019, which includes the enormous Daisen Kofun, traditionally attributed to the emperor Nintoku and one of the largest tombs in the world by area.

The kofun cannot be entered, as they are managed by the Imperial Household Agency, and you can only walk around the outside, along the moats. But the scale is impressive, and the contrast between the ancient wooded mounds and the modern city around them is striking. The best way to appreciate their shape is from above, and the observation floor of the Sakai City Hall offers a view over the mounds that makes sense of what you cannot see from the ground.

Riding in Sakai is urban riding, with heavy traffic, traffic lights, narrow streets and the need to follow Japanese road rules carefully. It is not a scenic ride, but it is a fascinating place to explore, with a long history as a trading port and a centre of craftsmanship. Sakai is famous for its knives, made by skilled smiths for centuries, and many chefs consider them among the best in the world. The tea master Sen no Rikyū, who shaped the Japanese tea ceremony, was born in Sakai in the sixteenth century.

For better riding, head south east towards the mountains of the Kii Peninsula, where winding roads lead to Mount Kōya, the great monastic centre founded by the monk Kūkai in the ninth century, and to the ancient pilgrimage routes of Kumano. The roads there are narrow, twisty and spectacular, through forests of cedar and cypress. Sakai has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants, and the larger cities of Osaka and Nara are nearby. Summers are hot and humid, with typhoons possible in late summer, while spring and autumn are the best times to ride.
t.temple of nuestra senora de los dolores:
Villa González Ortega is a small town on the high plateau of Zacatecas, in north central Mexico, and its church of Nuestra Señora de los Dolores is one of the sites recognised as part of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the Royal Inland Road. This was the great trade route that linked Mexico City with the silver mines of the north and eventually with Santa Fe in New Mexico, a journey of more than two thousand kilometres across deserts, mountains and plains. For almost three centuries, wagons, mule trains, soldiers, priests and settlers travelled this road, and the towns, churches, haciendas and bridges along it tell the story of the Spanish colonisation of the north. UNESCO listed the route in 2010.

The church is a simple, sturdy building with a facade of local stone, typical of the churches of the region. Inside, it holds images of the Virgin of Sorrows and other saints, and the town still celebrates its patron saint with processions, music and fireworks. The town itself is small, quiet and dusty, with a central square, a market and a few shops.

The landscape of the Zacatecas plateau is vast and open, with plains of grass and scrub, cactus and mesquite, and mountains rising on the horizon. The roads are mostly long and straight, with good surfaces on the main highways and rougher conditions on the minor roads. The altitude is high, more than two thousand metres in many places, and the light is intense, with clear blue skies most of the year. Wind can be strong, and the temperature drops sharply at night.

The city of Zacatecas, a little more than an hour away, is a beautiful colonial city built on the wealth of its silver mines, with a pink stone cathedral, narrow streets and a cable car over the town. It is a fine place to spend a night. Villa González Ortega has fuel and basic services, and the larger towns of the region have everything you need. As with any travel in rural Mexico, it is worth checking current safety advice before setting out, and avoiding riding at night, when livestock and unlit vehicles are a real hazard.
t.st lorenz wachtturm@48.4,15.5:
On the quiet south bank of the Danube in the Wachau, opposite the wine village of Weißenkirchen, the little church of St. Lorenz has a secret in its walls. Part of the building stands on, and incorporates, the masonry of a Roman watchtower, one of a chain of small fortifications that guarded the river frontier of the province of Noricum in late antiquity. The Danube was the edge of the empire here, and soldiers in the tower kept watch over the far bank for raiders. Today the site is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Danube Limes listing, inscribed by UNESCO in 2021.

The Wachau itself is a UNESCO cultural landscape too, a stretch of the Danube between Melk and Krems where the river cuts through the hills of the Bohemian Massif, and terraced vineyards climb the steep slopes above medieval villages and castles. Grüner Veltliner and Riesling wines from these terraces are among the finest in Austria, and in spring the valley turns white with apricot blossom; the Wachauer Marille is a protected local speciality. Downriver at Dürnstein, the ruined castle on the cliff is where Richard the Lionheart was held captive in the 1190s on his way back from the Crusades.

The Wachau is a famous motorcycle valley. The road along the north bank through Spitz, Weißenkirchen and Dürnstein is lovely but busy, with cyclists, tour buses and speed limits, while the south bank road through Aggsbach, St. Lorenz and Mautern is quieter and more relaxed. Small ferries link the two banks in several places. Side roads climb into the hills of the Waldviertel to the north and the Dunkelsteiner Wald to the south, with twisty sections and excellent views back over the river. Spring blossom, autumn harvest and early mornings in summer are the best times.

There is fuel in Spitz, Mautern and Krems, nine kilometres downstream. The heurigen, wine taverns run by the winemakers themselves, serve cold cuts, cheese, spreads and their own wines, and they are open at certain times of the year, marked by a bunch of pine twigs hung over the door. Try apricot dumplings in season, and save the wine tasting for the end of the ride.
t.tulln kastell zentralbereich@48.3,16.1:
The Nibelungenlied, the great medieval German epic, sends Kriemhild down the Danube to marry Etzel, king of the Huns, and has her meet him at Tulln, which says something about the town's importance on the river for centuries. Long before that, the Romans built a cavalry fort here called Comagena, and its walls still lurk beneath the town centre. The best survival is the Salzturm, a tower by the river whose lower parts are Roman, among the best preserved Roman structures in Austria. The fort is part of the Danube Limes World Heritage listing.

Tulln's more recent fame comes from art and gardens. The painter Egon Schiele was born here in 1890, in the station building where his father was stationmaster, and the town has a museum dedicated to him in a former prison by the river, as well as a reconstruction of his birth room at the station. Tulln also calls itself a garden town, with a large permanent garden exhibition and flowers everywhere in summer. The Tullnerfeld, the plain around the town, is flat, fertile farmland, with the Wagram, a long terrace of vineyards, rising to the north.

For riders, the Tullnerfeld itself is flat and straightforward, with long straight roads through fields, but it is a convenient base for exploring the Danube valley. West, the Wachau with its vineyards and castles is less than an hour away; south, the Vienna Woods offer winding roads through forests and over hills; and north, across the river, the Wagram and the Weinviertel have quiet roads through vineyards and villages. Traffic is heavier near Vienna, but the side roads are quiet.

As a town of over ten thousand people, Tulln deals easily with fuel, food and a bed for the night, and its riverside promenade is made for an evening stroll with an ice cream. The Schiele museum in the old prison building is small but moving, and if you have time, the garden show grounds are a colourful contrast to a day on the road. The Wagram vineyards to the north produce excellent Grüner Veltliner and the rare red Roter Veltliner, so pick up a bottle for later rather than tasting before you ride.
t.mautern kastell ostbereich@48.4,15.6:
In the fifth century, as Roman authority along the Danube collapsed, a holy man named Severinus lived at a place called Favianis, organising food supplies, ransoming captives and negotiating with barbarian kings on behalf of the remaining Roman population. His biography, written by his disciple Eugippius, is one of the most vivid accounts of the end of Roman rule in central Europe, and Favianis is generally identified with Mautern, a small town on the south bank of the Danube opposite Krems. The Roman fort here, parts of which survive in the town walls, is part of the Danube Limes World Heritage listing.

Mautern sits at the eastern end of the Wachau, where the Danube valley opens out, and above it on a hill stands the huge Benedictine abbey of Göttweig, a Baroque complex that dominates the landscape and offers sweeping views over the valley. Across the river, Krems and its neighbour Stein are old wine towns with narrow streets, Gothic churches and Renaissance houses, and the vineyards on the terraces around them produce excellent Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.

The roads here make the most of the river. The south bank road west into the Wachau is quieter than its counterpart on the north bank, and the climb to Göttweig is a pleasant twisting run with views. South, the Dunkelsteiner Wald offers forested hills and quiet roads, while north, across the bridge to Krems, the roads climb into the Waldviertel, with tight corners and lovely scenery. Traffic is moderate, but watch out for cyclists along the river.

Mautern has a filling station and a few shops, and Krems, just over the bridge, has everything from bike dealers to bookshops. The heurigen of the region, open only at certain times and marked by a bundle of greenery hung over the gate, serve their own wines with cold meats, spreads and bread in courtyards and gardens, and there are few nicer ways to end a day. In July the apricots arrive, and Marillenknödel, apricot dumplings rolled in buttery breadcrumbs, appear on every menu. Göttweig's terrace café has one of the best views on the Danube.
t.the jewish cemetery@49.2,15.9:
On a hillside above the Jihlava river in Třebíč, thousands of gravestones stand among trees, some upright, some leaning, some covered in ivy and moss, their Hebrew inscriptions weathered by centuries. The Jewish cemetery is one of the largest in the Czech Republic, founded in the seventeenth century and used until the Second World War, and it is part of the World Heritage listing of the Jewish quarter and St. Procopius' basilica in Třebíč, inscribed in 2003, the first Jewish monument outside Israel to be listed.

The Jewish quarter of Zámostí, across the river from the town centre, is one of the best preserved in Europe, with narrow lanes, houses built on the slope, two synagogues and the remains of the old community buildings. The community was destroyed in the Holocaust, and the quarter's survival is a poignant reminder of a lost world. The basilica of St. Procopius, on the other side of the river, is a remarkable Romanesque and Gothic building, part of a former Benedictine monastery, with a beautiful crypt and portal.

The riding around Třebíč is a pleasure, through the rolling hills of the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands, with fields, forests and fishponds. The tarmac is decent, the lorries few, and the bends flow gently rather than bite. Telč, with its arcaded Renaissance square, is an easy morning run away, and the Dalešice reservoir, south-east of Třebíč, is a lovely spot for a ride and a swim. Late May, with rapeseed glowing yellow across the hills, is a particularly good moment.

Třebíč is a town of nearly forty thousand people, so fuel, supermarkets and repair shops are no problem, and the Jewish quarter has a few cafés and guesthouses in its restored houses. The cemetery and the rear synagogue, with its painted interior and a model of the quarter as it once was, can both be visited, and men are asked to cover their heads among the graves. Take your time on the slope among the stones; the silence there says more than any guidebook. Afterwards, a plate of svíčková, beef in a creamy root-vegetable sauce with dumplings, and a cold local beer are the classic Czech consolation.
t.sacred sites and pilgrimage routes in th:
The Kumano Kodō, the ancient pilgrimage routes, link it with two other great shrines, Hayatama in Shingū and Nachi with its tall waterfall, and with the sacred mountains of Kōyasan and Yoshino further north. UNESCO listed the whole network in 2004 as one of only two pilgrimage routes on its register, the other being the road to Santiago de Compostela.

What makes Kumano special is its blend of Shinto and Buddhism, nature and devotion. Emperors and aristocrats in the Heian period made the arduous journey here dozens of times, and later ordinary people followed, believing that walking the routes washed away their sins. Hongū shrine originally stood on a sandbank in the river called Ōyunohara, until floods in 1889 destroyed much of it and it was moved to higher ground. A giant torii, one of the largest in the world, now marks the old site, rising above the rice fields like a gate to another world.

The riding here is wonderful but demands attention. National Route 168 follows the Kumano River gorge north and south through steep forested mountains, with cedars and cypress crowding the slopes and the river glinting far below. The road has been much improved, with tunnels and bridges, but side roads are often narrow, single-track and twisty, with blind bends, landslide debris after rain and the occasional sharp drop. Typhoon season, late summer to early autumn, can close roads entirely. Spring and late autumn bring the best weather and colours.

Hongū itself is a small village with a few shops and restaurants; for a proper choice of fuel and services you need Shingū, over twenty kilometres down the river. Nearby, the hot spring villages of Yunomine, Kawayu and Watarase make for a perfect rest stop; at Yunomine, Tsuboyu is a tiny cabin bath on the river that pilgrims have used for centuries. A soak after a day in the mountains is the best reward you could ask for.
t.former hacienda of pabellon de hidalgo@2:
Pabellón de Hidalgo is a small town in the north of the state of Aguascalientes, and its old hacienda has a moment of national drama attached to it. In January 1811, after the insurgent army of Miguel Hidalgo was routed by royalist forces at the Battle of Puente de Calderón near Guadalajara, the retreating leaders met here, at the Hacienda de San Blas de Pabellón. Exhausted and defeated, they stripped Hidalgo of his military command and handed it to Ignacio Allende, who had long resented the priest's leadership. A few weeks later both were captured in the north, and by the summer both had been executed. The War of Independence would go on for another decade without them.

The hacienda buildings, with their thick adobe walls, a chapel and a courtyard, now house a museum of the insurgency, and the whole complex counts as one of the inscribed sites of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road that ran from Mexico City north to Santa Fe in New Mexico, carrying silver, goods and settlers for three centuries. Haciendas like this one were waypoints and economic hubs, with farms, ranches and workshops supporting traffic on the road.

The landscape is high and dry, nearly two thousand metres above sea level, with open plains of grass and scrub, fields of maize and chilli and, on the horizon, low ranges of hills. Aguascalientes is known for its hot springs, as the name suggests, and for its guava orchards in the Calvillo area to the west. The state capital, also called Aguascalientes, hosts the Feria de San Marcos every spring, one of the biggest fairs in Mexico.

The riding here is mostly highway, on the fast toll and free roads that run north towards Zacatecas, with long straight stretches, trucks and buses, and the occasional speed bump, or tope, appearing without warning in villages. Topes are the great hazard of Mexican roads; watch for them everywhere. For supplies, Rincón de Romos is six kilometres up the road, with Pemex and other fuel stations, taquerías and shops. Try the birria, a rich stew of goat or beef, and the local guava sweets. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in the summer rainy season.
t.uxa tequipa@23.1,-101.5:
In the high desert of northern San Luis Potosí, among creosote bush, yucca and endless sky, lies a landscape that is sacred to the Wixárika, the people outsiders often call the Huichol. Every year, pilgrims walk or travel hundreds of kilometres from their homes in the Sierra Madre Occidental of Jalisco and Nayarit to Wirikuta, the place where, in their cosmology, the sun was born. Along the way they stop at a sequence of sacred sites, springs, rocks and hills, each with its own name, offerings and rituals. Uxa Tequipa is one of these places, and the route as a whole has been proposed for the UNESCO list as Huiricuta, the Wixárika sacred route.

To an outsider, the land here may look empty, but it is anything but. The Wixárika leave offerings of arrows, candles, coins and beaded objects, and they gather híkuri, the peyote cactus, which is central to their religion and grows wild in the desert. It is vital to understand that peyote is a protected plant, that picking it is illegal for outsiders and deeply offensive, and that the sacred sites should be approached with respect, if at all. Many have no signs, and local guides are the best way to learn what is appropriate.

The landscape is a high, arid plateau at around two thousand metres, framed by ranges such as the Sierra de Catorce, with dramatic light, huge skies and cold nights even in summer. Mining has been part of the region's history for centuries, and the ghost-town atmosphere of Real de Catorce, reached through a long single-lane tunnel, is a popular stop. Large-scale mining projects in Wirikuta have caused serious controversy, with the Wixárika fighting to protect their sacred land.

For riders, this is remote and empty country. Paved highways give way quickly to dirt, and services are few and far between. The old mining town of Charcas, roughly thirty-five kilometres off, is where you will find fuel and basic shops; La Herradura and Santo Domingo are small villages. Carry plenty of water and fuel, prepare for heat during the day and cold at night, and keep a respectful distance from any ceremony you encounter. The silence of the desert at dawn is unforgettable.
t.huacuri quitenie@23.3,-101.2:
Somewhere in the creosote flats north of Charcas, in San Luis Potosí, the land that the Wixárika people call Wirikuta begins to feel different, even to a visitor who knows nothing of its meaning. The horizon widens, the mountains of the Sierra de Catorce rise to the east, and on a clear morning the whole desert seems to hum. Huacuri Quitenie is one of the sacred places along the Wixárika pilgrimage route to Wirikuta, where pilgrims stop to pray and leave offerings on their way to Leunar, the hill they call Cerro Quemado, where the sun was born.

The pilgrimage itself is one of the oldest living spiritual traditions in North America. Groups of Wixárika, led by a mara'akame, a shaman, travel from their communities in the mountains of Jalisco and Nayarit, a journey of several hundred kilometres that once took weeks on foot. Today many travel by truck or bus, but they still stop at the sacred springs and rocks, taking part in rituals of confession, purification and renewal. The desert is not wilderness to them; it is a living map of their gods and ancestors.

Nature here is tough and surprisingly rich. Barrel cacti, yucca and agave dot the gravel plains, along with the small, button-like peyote that hides in the shade of shrubs. Hawks circle overhead, jackrabbits bolt across the track, and at night the stars are extraordinarily bright. Summer brings heat and sudden afternoon thunderstorms that can turn dry arroyos into torrents in minutes; winter nights can drop below freezing.

For a rider, the important thing is self-sufficiency and respect. Roads are few, mostly unpaved, often sandy or rocky, and signage is minimal; a dual-sport bike and good navigation help. Charcas, a former mining town of about thirteen thousand people, twenty-odd kilometres away, is the nearest place with reliable fuel, shops and food. Bring water and spare fuel for exploring. Do not pick plants, do not disturb offerings and do not intrude on ceremonies; ask a local guide or community member if you want to learn more. Ridden slowly and quietly, this is some of the most haunting country in Mexico.
t.ferto neusiedlersee cultural landscape@4:
The Neusiedler See, Fertő in Hungarian, is a strange lake. It is huge, over three hundred square kilometres of water stretching from Austria across the border into Hungary, but almost nowhere is it deeper than a couple of metres, and a vast belt of reeds surrounds much of it, so that from many places you cannot actually see the water. It has no natural outflow, its level depends on rain and evaporation, and in the 1860s it dried out completely for several years, with farmers ploughing the lakebed. The lake and the villages around it were listed by UNESCO in 2001 as a cultural landscape shaped by thousands of years of human life on the border between Alpine and steppe worlds.

On the Austrian shore, Rust is a little town of baroque burghers' houses where storks nest on the chimneys, and Mörbisch hosts operetta festivals on a floating stage. On the Hungarian side, the Esterházy palace at Fertőd, sometimes called the Hungarian Versailles, was where Joseph Haydn served as court composer for decades. Just south of Sopron, in August 1989, the Pan-European Picnic opened a border gate for a few hours, and hundreds of East Germans ran through to the West, a moment that helped bring down the Iron Curtain.

This is flat country, and the riding is about wind, light and space rather than curves. Roads around the lake run through vineyards, villages and reed beds, with views across the water to the Leitha hills. The area is very popular with cyclists, so expect them in large numbers, especially on weekends; the Seewinkel, east of the lake, is an expanse of small salt lakes, pastures and bird reserves where grey cattle and water buffalo graze. Wind can be strong and gusty, and sudden thunderstorms in summer are not unusual. If you use motorways, remember both Austria and Hungary require a vignette.

Sopron, eleven kilometres away, is a lovely old town with everything you need, as are the larger villages on the Austrian side. This is wine country: Blaufränkisch reds, crisp whites and the sweet Ausbruch wines of Rust. Try fish from the lake, goulash on the Hungarian side, and the local apricot specialities in early summer. Spring and autumn, with migrating birds, are the best times.
t.tatsusayama kofun@34.6,135.5:
Southern Osaka has a secret that is hard to see from the ground: its suburbs are woven around ancient burial mounds, some of them among the largest tombs ever built. In Sakai, these kofun belong to the Mozu group, which, together with the Furuichi group further east, was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 2019. Tatsusayama is one of the smaller mounds, a wooded hill surrounded by houses and roads, but it is part of the same story. Between roughly the fourth and sixth centuries, the rulers of the Yamato court and their elite were buried in tombs shaped like keyholes when seen from above, with moats around them and clay figures called haniwa placed on their slopes.

The largest, the Daisen Kofun attributed to Emperor Nintoku, is close by and is nearly half a kilometre long, so big that you can only appreciate its shape from the observation floor of Sakai City Hall or from the air. The tombs are under the control of the Imperial Household Agency and cannot be entered, so you walk around their moats, with turtles and herons in the water and the dense forest of the mounds rising behind. It is a strangely peaceful experience in the middle of a busy city.

Sakai has another side as an old merchant city. In the sixteenth century it was a rich, largely self-governing port, trading with China and the Portuguese, and it was the home of Sen no Rikyu, the master who shaped the Japanese tea ceremony. The city is still famous for its knives, made by hand in small workshops, and many chefs consider Sakai blades the best in the country.

This is urban riding, plain and simple: traffic lights, expressways, buses and bicycles on the pavements. Do not come here for the corners. Come for the history and as a starting point for better roads, south towards the Izumi mountains and Wakayama, or east into the hills of Nara and the Kii peninsula, where the old pilgrimage routes to Kumano lead through deep forest. Fuel, food and lodging are everywhere in Sakai. Try a bowl of noodles near the station and visit a knife shop; even if you buy nothing, watching the sharpening is a pleasure.
t.ingyo tenno ryo kofun@34.6,135.6:
The tomb attributed to Emperor Ingyo stands in Fujiidera, in the eastern suburbs of Osaka, and it belongs to the Furuichi group of kofun, the other half of the World Heritage site shared with Sakai's Mozu tombs. It is a large keyhole-shaped mound, wooded and surrounded by a moat, and like all imperial tombs it is managed by the Imperial Household Agency and closed to visitors. Scholars debate whether the attributions to specific emperors are accurate, since they were made long after the tombs were built, but the scale of the monuments speaks for itself. Nearby, the tomb attributed to Emperor Ojin, Kondagobyoyama, is the second largest in Japan by volume.

The Furuichi area grew up along the Yamato River, which flows from the Nara basin through a gap in the hills into the Osaka plain, and this was the corridor along which the early Japanese state developed. The city of Kashiwara, right next to the tomb, sits at that gap, and the town of Fujiidera takes its name from a temple that houses an ancient thousand-armed statue of the goddess of mercy, Kannon, one of the oldest of its kind in Japan.

East of here, the Takenouchi Kaido climbs over the Nijo hills into Nara Prefecture. It is said to be the oldest official road in Japan, recorded in the early seventh century, linking the port of Naniwa with the capital of Asuka, and parts of it still have old houses and stone markers. For riders, it is the start of a beautiful route: over the hills to Asuka, then south through the mountains to Yoshino, famous for its cherry blossoms and for the mountain religion of Omine, with its yamabushi ascetics. Once you leave the suburbs behind, the roads become narrow and winding, with forested slopes, small villages and tea fields.

In Fujiidera itself, the riding is purely urban, with narrow streets, traffic lights and a lot of bicycles. Fuel and convenience stores are everywhere, and Kashiwara and Yao are large towns. Kashiwara is known for its grapes and small wineries on the slopes of the hills, an unexpected find in Osaka. Spring and autumn are ideal for riding into the Nara mountains; in summer, the humidity is relentless.
t.cemetery in encarnacion de diaz@21.5,-10:
Encarnación de Díaz is a market town in Los Altos de Jalisco, the high, dry plateau between Guadalajara and Aguascalientes, and its cemetery is a surprising piece of world heritage. It is one of the stops listed as part of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road that once ran from Mexico City to Santa Fe in present-day New Mexico, along which silver went south and settlers, missionaries and goods went north for almost three centuries. The cemetery, built in the nineteenth century, is enclosed by a wall with arched galleries and filled with ornate tombs and chapels, carved in local stone, which reflect the prosperity and piety of the town's families. On the Day of the Dead, at the beginning of November, it fills with flowers, candles and families sitting by their graves.

Los Altos is a region with a strong identity. Its people are known for their fair skin and Spanish ancestry, for horsemanship and the charreada, the Mexican rodeo, and for a deep Catholic faith. During the Cristero War of the 1920s, when the government clashed with the Church, Los Altos was one of the centres of armed resistance, and the memory of that conflict is still present in churches and local stories. The land is red earth, cattle pasture, agave fields and scattered oak trees, and the sky is huge.

The riding is high-plateau riding: the Highway 45 between Lagos de Moreno and Aguascalientes passes right by the town, a fast four-lane road with heavy truck traffic, and it is mainly a way of getting from A to B. The smaller roads that branch off towards villages like Teocaltiche or San Juan de los Lagos, home of one of Mexico's most visited pilgrimage shrines, are quieter, with long, sweeping bends over the hills, though you will have to watch for topes, the speed bumps that appear without warning at the entrance to every village, and for livestock on the road.

Encarnación has fuel, banks, restaurants and simple hotels, so it is a sensible stop. Try birria, slow-cooked goat or beef in a spicy broth, a Jalisco speciality, and the local cajeta and dairy sweets. At this altitude, the sun is strong, and the nights are cool, so pack accordingly.
South of Zacatecas, on the high plateau of northern Mexico, the old Camino Real de Tierra Adentro passes through a landscape of dry hills, maize fields and mesquite. This was the royal road of the interior, the great artery that ran from Mexico City for more than two and a half thousand kilometres north to Santa Fe, in what is now New Mexico, and it was the backbone of Spanish colonial expansion. Wagons and mule trains carried the silver from the mines of Zacatecas and Guanajuato south to the capital and the coast, while settlers, soldiers, priests and goods made their way north. Along the route, haciendas, chapels, bridges and towns grew up, and today sixty sites, including the historic centre of Zacatecas, form a World Heritage route.

Zacatecas itself is the jewel of the region, a city of pink sandstone built in a narrow ravine at an altitude of around two and a half thousand metres. Its baroque cathedral, with a carved façade of astonishing richness, is one of the most beautiful in Mexico, and the hill of La Bufa, which looms above the city, was the scene of a decisive battle in 1914 during the Revolution, when Pancho Villa's troops took the city. A cable car runs across the town to the summit. The old Eden mine, where you can take a small train into the mountain, gives an idea of the silver that made the city rich.

Riding up here is a high-altitude experience. The air is thin, mornings are cool even in summer, and the sun is strong. Roads around Zacatecas, such as federal highways 45 and 49, are generally in good condition, with long straights and open bends through dry hills, but trucks are heavy, and some stretches carry a lot of traffic. Smaller roads lead to villages, old haciendas and the sanctuary of Plateros near Fresnillo, home of the Santo Niño de Atocha, which attracts large numbers of pilgrims. Watch out for topes and animals, and do not ride at night.

Trancoso and the suburbs of Guadalupe and Zacatecas have fuel, shops and restaurants. In Zacatecas, try enchiladas zacatecanas and gorditas, and visit one of the old cantinas in the centre. Mezcal from the state of Zacatecas is also worth trying, preferably after the bike has been parked.
t.huiricuta mucuyahue@23.5,-101.1:
In the high desert of San Luis Potosí, below the mountains of the Sierra de Catorce, lies Wirikuta, the most sacred landscape of the Wixárika people, better known as the Huichol. Every year, pilgrims walk or drive hundreds of kilometres from their homes in the mountains of Jalisco and Nayarit to this semi-desert, following a route they believe their ancestors travelled at the beginning of time. According to their tradition, the sun was born on the hill called Cerro Quemado above Real de Catorce, and the desert is where they come to collect hikuri, the peyote cactus, which they consider a sacred plant and use in ceremonies. The various sacred sites along the pilgrimage, including this one, are on Mexico's tentative list for World Heritage.

The landscape is stark and beautiful: a wide plain of creosote bush, cholla and Joshua-like yuccas under a huge sky, with the bare mountains rising behind. The light at dawn and dusk is golden and soft, and the nights are cold, often near freezing in winter. This is not a place for tourists to pick peyote; the plant is protected, it is only legal for the Wixárika in their ceremonies, and respect for their sacred places is essential.

The riding is the real attraction for many. Real de Catorce, the old silver town in the mountains above the desert, is reached by a long cobbled road climbing from the plain, about twenty kilometres of shaking stones, and then through the Ogarrio tunnel, a single-lane tunnel more than two kilometres long, with traffic regulated in both directions. The town itself, once almost abandoned, is now partly revived with hotels and restaurants, and its stone houses and church, home of a popular image of St Francis, attract pilgrims of their own. On the desert side, dirt tracks lead across the plain, but sand and loose gravel make them hard work on a heavy bike.

There is nothing at all on the plain itself. The nearest fuel is in Matehuala and Cedral, on the plains to the east, and the shops in Real de Catorce cater mainly to visitors. Carry plenty of water, protect yourself from the sun, and do not ride in the desert at night, as cattle and other animals wander freely on the roads.
t.frontiers of the roman empire the danube:
Marcus Aurelius, emperor and philosopher, spent several years at Carnuntum during his wars against the Germanic tribes north of the Danube, and he is thought to have written part of his Meditations here; the third book carries the note that it was written at Carnuntum. In the second century, this was one of the most important places on the Roman frontier: a legionary fortress, an auxiliary fort and a civil town that grew into the capital of the province of Upper Pannonia, with tens of thousands of inhabitants. Today, the archaeological park at Petronell-Carnuntum and Bad Deutsch-Altenburg shows reconstructed houses, a bath and streets built using Roman methods, two amphitheatres, and the Heidentor, a great ruined triumphal arch standing alone in the fields. The Danube Limes became a World Heritage site in 2021.

The Danube flows past just to the north, and between Vienna and the Slovak border it runs through the Donau-Auen National Park, one of the last large stretches of floodplain forest in central Europe, with side channels, gravel banks, willows and poplars, home to beavers, kingfishers and white-tailed eagles. Bad Deutsch-Altenburg is a small spa town with sulphur springs, and the Hundsheimer Berge, low limestone hills to the south, offer dry grasslands and views over the river and the plains of Pannonia.

Riding here is pleasant rather than dramatic. The B9 runs from Vienna to Hainburg and the Slovak border with long straight stretches across farmland and vineyards, and the minor roads into the hills around Hundsheim and Prellenkirchen are narrower and more fun, with views towards the Leitha mountains and Lake Neusiedl to the south. Wind often blows across the flat land from the east, and in summer it can be very hot. Austrian motorways require a vignette, and speed limits on country roads are strictly enforced.

Petronell-Carnuntum and Bad Deutsch-Altenburg have cafés and small inns, and Hainburg, a medieval town with walls and gates on the Danube, has fuel and more choice. Try a glass of wine from the Carnuntum wine region, known for its red Zweigelt and Blaufränkisch, at a Heuriger, the local wine tavern, with a plate of cold meats, cheese and bread, and then head across the border to Bratislava, just a few kilometres away.
t.kofuku ji@34.7,135.8:
In the early eighth century, when Nara became Japan's first permanent capital, the powerful Fujiwara clan moved their family temple here, and Kofuku-ji became one of the great temples of the city, wealthy enough to maintain its own warrior monks. Its five storey pagoda, rebuilt in the fifteenth century after one of several fires, is the second tallest wooden pagoda in Japan and a symbol of Nara, reflected in the Sarusawa pond below. The Central Golden Hall was rebuilt and reopened in 2018, and the National Treasure Museum holds the famous statue of Ashura, a three faced, six armed guardian with a strikingly human expression. Kofuku-ji is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara World Heritage Site. The pagoda is undergoing a long restoration and may be wrapped in scaffolding when you visit.

Nara Park, around the temple, is home to over a thousand sika deer, considered messengers of the gods, which wander freely and bow to visitors in hope of crackers. They are tame but can be pushy, so keep food out of sight. The great Todai-ji temple, with its giant bronze Buddha, and the Kasuga Taisha shrine, with its thousands of lanterns, are within walking distance.

Riding in Nara is city riding, with traffic and narrow streets, but the city is smaller and calmer than Kyoto or Osaka. The roads into the hills east of Nara are more interesting, including the drive up Mount Wakakusa, a toll road with views over the city, and the roads through the Yagyu area toward Iga. South of Nara, the roads through the Asuka region, the earlier capital, pass ancient burial mounds and rice paddies.

Nara has petrol stations on its main roads and a wide choice of restaurants. Try kakinoha sushi, mackerel or salmon sushi wrapped in persimmon leaves, a Nara speciality, and nara-zuke, vegetables pickled in sake lees. Parking a motorcycle in central Nara is possible in designated areas; ask at your hotel. Autumn, when the maples turn, and spring, when the cherry blossoms bloom, are the busiest and loveliest seasons.
t.temples in the town of nombre de dios@23:
Nombre de Dios is one of the oldest Spanish towns in northern Mexico, founded in the 1560s by Franciscan missionaries and settlers on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road that ran from Mexico City north to Santa Fe in New Mexico, carrying silver, mercury, supplies and settlers for nearly three hundred years. The road was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2010, along with a string of towns, churches, haciendas and bridges, and the temples of Nombre de Dios are among them, simple churches in stone and adobe that once served as bases for missions to the north.

The town sits in a green valley southeast of Durango, on the Mezquital river, at around eighteen hundred metres. The surrounding country is a mix of farmland and dry hills, with mesquite and cactus, and the light is clear and bright. Durango state is known for its mezcal, distilled from wild agave, and Nombre de Dios is one of its traditional producing areas; small distilleries, vinatas, may welcome visitors.

The riding in Durango is magnificent, if you go further. The highway from Durango west to Mazatlán, through the Sierra Madre Occidental, once crossed the Espinazo del Diablo, the devil's backbone, a famous road of curves; a modern highway with the Baluarte bridge, one of the highest in the world, now cuts the journey, but the old road is still there for the brave. Closer to Nombre de Dios, Highway 45 runs south toward Zacatecas through open plateau.

Nombre de Dios, a town of around five thousand, has fuel and basic services, and Durango city, about fifty kilometres away, has everything. Durango is also known for western films: Hollywood shot many of them in the deserts near the city, and some of the old sets remain as attractions. Ride in daylight, and check local advice on security.
t.bridge of ojuelos@21.8,-101.8:
The silver carts of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro needed to cross streams on the high plain between Mexico City and Zacatecas, and at Ojuelos, in the northeast corner of Jalisco, a stone bridge was built in colonial times to carry the road. It is part of the World Heritage listing of the royal road, along with the historic centre of Ojuelos, which grew around a presidio, a fort built to protect travellers on the road from the Chichimec peoples who resisted Spanish expansion.

The country here is high and open, at around two thousand two hundred metres, a land of grassland, nopal cactus and mesquite, with fields of maize and beans and wide skies. It is part of Los Altos, the highlands of Jalisco, a region known for ranching, rodeo, charrería and cheese. The winds can be strong, and the nights cold even in summer.

The riding here is about wide horizons rather than curves: long, straight roads across the plateau, with little traffic, few towns and big skies. Highway 70 and Highway 51 link Ojuelos with San Luis Potosí, Aguascalientes and León. Surfaces vary, and topes appear at the entrance of every village. Watch for livestock on the road, especially at dusk.

Ojuelos de Jalisco, eighteen kilometres away, is a town of about twelve thousand with fuel, food and simple hotels. Its colonial centre, with a plaza, a church and the presidio, is pleasant for a stroll. Aguascalientes and San Luis Potosí are large cities a couple of hours away. The area is quiet, but check local advice on security before travelling and ride in daylight.

Spend a moment on the bridge and think about the traffic it once carried: long trains of mule and ox carts, soldiers, friars, merchants and families heading north to the mining frontier, sometimes for months at a time. The presidios along the route were the anchors of that journey, and towns like Ojuelos grew from the need for water, rest and protection. Many of the place names along the old road still remember those stages. Try the local cheeses, birria, a spiced meat stew, and the tortillas made by hand in small restaurants.
t.huahuatsari@22.8,-101.9:
Every year, Wixárika pilgrims, the people often called Huichol, walk or travel hundreds of kilometres from their homeland in the Sierra Madre Occidental to Wirikuta, a sacred desert in San Luis Potosí, where they gather peyote and make offerings at sacred places along the way. Huahuatsari is one of the sacred sites on this route, in the high desert near Villa de Ramos. The pilgrimage route has been placed on Mexico's tentative list for World Heritage, and the sites along it are places of prayer, not tourist attractions.

The landscape is the altiplano, the high plateau of northern Mexico, at around two thousand metres: a vast plain of desert scrub, cactus, yucca and creosote bush, with mountains on the horizon and huge skies. The light is fierce at midday and soft at dawn and dusk, and the nights are cold and full of stars. Wind sweeps across the plain, and dust storms are possible.

Riding here is about distance and space. The roads across the altiplano are long, straight and empty, with few towns and fewer services. Highway 49 from Zacatecas to San Luis Potosí is the main route, and smaller roads lead to villages like Villa de Ramos. Surfaces vary, livestock wander, and fuel stations are far apart.
