Carry water and plan fuel carefully.

The Wixárika tradition sees Wirikuta as the place where the sun was born, and the pilgrimage retraces the path of the ancestors, with fasting, confession and ritual at each stage. In recent years, mining concessions in the Wirikuta area have caused bitter conflicts, as the Wixárika and their supporters have fought to protect the sacred land, and the issue remains sensitive.

Villa de Ramos is a small town with basic services; Los Zacatones, twenty five kilometres away, and the larger towns on the main highways have fuel. Real de Catorce, a former silver mining town in the mountains to the north, reached through a long tunnel, is a magical place to visit. Respect the Wixárika sacred sites: do not disturb offerings, and do not collect peyote, which is protected and sacred.
t.wooden churches of the slovak part of th:
The Church of All Saints in Tvrdošín, at the edge of the town in the Orava valley, is a wooden Gothic church from the fifteenth century, built of larch and fir, with a shingled roof, a tower with a distinctive spire and a painted interior, and it is one of the oldest of the wooden churches listed as a World Heritage Site in Slovakia. Its Renaissance and Baroque decorations, including a carved altar and paintings, were added over the centuries.

Orava is a valley in northern Slovakia, along the river of the same name, surrounded by mountains: the Tatras to the east, the Malá Fatra to the west and the Polish border to the north. Orava Castle, perched on a cliff above the river at Oravský Podzámok, is one of the most spectacular castles in Central Europe, used as a setting for the 1922 film Nosferatu. The Orava reservoir, a large lake near Tvrdošín, is a popular summer destination, and the open air museum at Zuberec shows traditional village life.

The landscape here is green and mountainous, with forests, meadows and wooden villages, and the views of the Tatras are superb on clear days. Winters are long and snowy, summers mild and pleasant.

The riding in Orava is excellent: winding roads through valleys and over passes, with good surfaces and views. The road over the Western Tatras toward Liptov via Zuberec and the Huty pass is particularly good, and the routes along the Orava river are pleasant. Traffic is moderate, heavier on weekends and in summer. The border crossing to Poland at Trstená leads to the Podhale region and Zakopane.

Larch shingles weather to a silver grey, and the church at Tvrdošín seems to grow out of its graveyard among old trees, with a wooden fence around it. Tvrdošín is your fuel stop, and Trstená, five kilometres away, also has everything you need. Local food includes bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep cheese, and Orava cheeses, including smoked oštiepok.
t.pochlarn vicus und kastellbad@48.2,15.2:
Pöchlarn is a small town on the south bank of the Danube, a few kilometres upstream from Melk, where the river is broad and slow and the Wachau valley is about to begin. The Romans called it Arelape and kept a fort here on the frontier of the empire, with a civilian settlement, the vicus, and a bathhouse for the garrison. Not much is visible above ground, but the town is part of the Danube Limes World Heritage site, which traces that long line of forts and watchtowers through Austria.

Pöchlarn has another, more literary claim to fame. In the Nibelungenlied, the great medieval German epic, it appears as Bechelaren, the seat of the noble margrave Rüdiger, who welcomes Kriemhild on her way to marry Etzel. The town plays this up with statues, fountains and a Nibelungen-themed walk. It is also the birthplace of the painter Oskar Kokoschka, and his family's former house is now a small museum dedicated to him.

The riding around here is relaxed and scenic. Roads run along both banks of the Danube, with the B1 on the south side and the B3 on the north, the latter especially popular with riders heading into the Wachau. The corners are gentle, the surfaces good, and the views of vineyards, apricot orchards and monasteries are superb, but summer weekends bring many cyclists, caravans and fellow bikers. Head north into the hills of the Waldviertel or south towards the Ybbstal and the foothills of the Alps if you want twistier roads and less company.

Across the river, the pilgrimage church of Maria Taferl sits high above the valley, its twin towers visible for miles, and the road up to it is short and fun with a fine view at the top. Downstream, Melk Abbey's golden façade is one of the great sights of the Danube.

Pöchlarn itself is small but has fuel, a supermarket and inns serving Austrian classics, from Schnitzel to Wachau apricot dumplings in season. A short break by the river, watching cruise boats and barges slide past, is a pleasant way to rest. The Danube cycle path runs right through town, so keep an eye out for cyclists when you park.
t.hanzei tenno ryo kofun@34.6,135.5:
The Mozu kofun are strange. In the middle of modern Sakai, a heavy industrial and residential city south of Osaka, rise huge forested mounds surrounded by water-filled moats, some of them shaped like a keyhole, and these are the tombs of the rulers of Japan from the fifth century. Hanzei's tomb is one of the smaller ones in the group, though still well over a hundred metres long, and it is easily reached because the moat path runs around it. The giant of the group, attributed to Emperor Nintoku, is nearly five hundred metres long and one of the largest tombs in the world by area.

You cannot go inside, because the Imperial Household Agency maintains the tombs as sacred sites, so what you see is a wall of trees, a stretch of water and a signboard. The Mozu-Furuichi group of mounds was listed as a World Heritage site in 2019, and their significance is in the scale. These mounds took thousands of workers, and they were covered with stones and ringed with clay figures called haniwa, which were placed on the slopes. The effect from the air is extraordinary; on the ground you have to take it on trust.

Riding here is urban, and you should treat it that way. The roads are narrow, congested and full of commuter traffic, with traffic lights every few hundred metres and a lot of cyclists, so the pace is slow, and the best thing to do is park and walk. Early morning is quiet, and the park paths around the moats are good for a stroll. Sakai has long been known for its knives and its tea masters, as well as its bicycle components industry, since Shimano has its headquarters here, which is a bit of wry local pride.

Fuel and food are no problem in a city of this size, and there are plenty of convenience stores and noodle shops. The Sakai City Museum, near the big tomb, explains the group and offers a viewpoint. In spring the moats reflect cherry blossoms, and in autumn the camphor trees turn a deep green and yellow.
t.kumano sanzan nachi no otaki@33.7,135.9:
Water falls a hundred and thirty-three metres in a single drop at Nachi, the highest single fall in Japan, and it is not just a scenic attraction but a god. The Nachi no Ōtaki has been worshipped since long before the shrines were built, as a place where a kami lives, and the Kumano Nachi Taisha, a vermilion shrine on the hillside, was set up to honour it. Next door, the Buddhist temple of Seiganto-ji, with its three-storey pagoda in front of the falls, is one of the most photographed views in Japan, and shows how the two religions lived side by side.

The falls are part of the Kumano Sankeimichi pilgrimage routes, the Kumano Kodo, which cross the wild and wet Kii Peninsula and were walked for a thousand years by emperors, samurai and ordinary people. The routes were inscribed by UNESCO in 2004, and some of the old paths, paved with moss-covered stone steps and lined by tall cedars, are still there. The crow with three legs, the Yatagarasu, is the guide of the Kumano deities, and you will see it on signs and souvenirs.

The ride in the Kii Peninsula is demanding and rewarding. The coastal Route 42 gives sea views, tunnels and fishing towns, and the mountain roads inland are narrow, steep and densely forested, with sharp corners and a lot of moisture. This is one of the wettest parts of Japan, so expect rain and mist, particularly in summer and autumn, and treat the surface with caution after storms, when rockfall can close roads. The road up to the shrine is steep and parking is limited, so allow time at busy periods.

Katsuura, the nearest port, is a major tuna landing and the place to eat it fresh, in a small restaurant near the harbour. Fuel is available in Katsuura and in Shingu, about eleven kilometres away, which also has the Hayatama shrine, another of the three Kumano grand shrines. Bring a rain jacket, and leave extra time, because a visit to the falls is much better when you are not in a hurry.
t.kurizuka kofun@34.6,135.6:
South of Nara city, the plain is flat and green, with rice paddies in every direction and low, rounded mountains standing on its rim, and the first Japanese states grew here. Kashihara, on the southern side of the basin, sits near the old capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara, where the court and the first lasting Buddhist temples took shape in the sixth and seventh centuries. Kurizuka is one of the many kofun, ancient burial mounds, scattered around the district, and it is a modest, tree-covered hump rather than a spectacular monument.

What makes the area interesting is how thickly history is packed into it. The Kawara-dera temple site, listed on our label, is the remains of one of the oldest temples in Japan, with foundation stones and a quiet field where there were once halls. Nearby stand the Ishibutai tomb, an enormous stone chamber uncovered by the removal of its earth mound, and the Takamatsuzuka tomb, famous for its painted walls. Legend places the first emperor, Jimmu, in Kashihara, and a large shrine bears his name.

The riding is calm and gentle. The roads wind between paddies, villages and persimmon orchards, with low gradients, short climbs into the foothills, and plenty of narrow lanes with sudden turns. The surface is generally good, but tight corners, farm vehicles and cyclists are part of the experience, and hire-cycle tourists tend to wander. Autumn is the best time, particularly when the red spider lilies bloom along the paddy edges in September and the rice turns gold in October. Summers are very humid, and mountain roads on the edge of the basin can be foggy.

Kashihara is a sizeable town of seventy thousand and more, so fuel, convenience stores and noodle shops are no problem, and the Kintetsu railway lines mean there are small station cafes everywhere. Be aware that many kofun are protected as imperial tombs and cannot be entered, and that the mounds themselves are often hard to recognise unless you know what you are looking at. A sign, a moat and a stand of old pines are usually the clues.
t.former college of nuestra senora de guad:
Zacatecas was built on silver, and the town next to it, Guadalupe, was built on faith. In the middle of the eighteenth century a Franciscan college was founded here to train missionaries who would go north into the unconquered country, and its big church, cloisters and long galleries still stand on the edge of the city, now serving as a museum of colonial art with paintings, carved altarpieces and religious objects. The college once sent friars as far as Texas and California.

The silver strike at Zacatecas in 1546 started a rush that shaped this part of Mexico. A road, the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, was beaten out to carry the metal south to Mexico City and supplies north, and it ran for more than two thousand kilometres to Santa Fe in New Mexico, in use for almost three centuries. UNESCO listed parts of the road in 2010, and the Guadalupe college is part of that story as one of the places where people on the route stopped to pray, rest and equip themselves.

For a rider, the high plateau around Zacatecas is dry and cold, with big skies and long straight roads, and the town sits at around 2,400 metres, so the air is thin and the nights can be chilly even in summer. Highway 45 between Zacatecas and Aguascalientes is fast, with trucks, and the toll roads are in better condition than the free ones. The old centre of Zacatecas is a tangle of steep, cobbled and sometimes one-way streets, and the cable car up to the Cerro de la Bufa gives a fine view. Rain falls mainly between June and September, in sharp afternoon storms.

Guadalupe is effectively a suburb of Zacatecas, so fuel, food and cafes are all easy. Try local dishes such as asado de boda, a spicy pork stew traditionally served at weddings, and look for the sweets made of fruit and nuts sold in the markets. Opening hours of the museum vary and it tends to close on Mondays, so check ahead.
t.bridge la quemada@21.3,-101.1:
The silver of Guanajuato came with a price, and the price was a war. In the middle of the sixteenth century, as the Spanish pushed north and the roads began to carry wagons of ore, the Chichimeca peoples of this high plateau resisted, and for several decades attacks on convoys made the journey dangerous. The Spanish answered with forts, called presidios, along the road, and with settlements of Indian allies, and the old road, the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, grew up as a fortified corridor.

The bridge at La Quemada is part of that road, a stone structure in the open country of the Bajío, north of Guanajuato, where dry hills, mesquite and cactus alternate with irrigated farmland. UNESCO listed the Camino Real in 2010. The region has more recent history, too: a short ride south is Dolores Hidalgo, where in 1810 the priest Miguel Hidalgo called for rebellion against Spanish rule, an event Mexicans celebrate each September.

Riding here is easy and open, with gently rolling roads and big skies, and traffic is moderate except on the main highway. The roads between towns are generally in decent condition, though village streets are cobbled and often punctuated with speed bumps, and cattle sometimes wander onto the road. Dawn and late afternoon give the best light, and midday sun can be fierce, so a cooling layer under the jacket helps. Rainfall comes in short, intense bursts in summer, and winter nights can be cold at this altitude.

San Felipe, the nearest town of any size, has fuel, shops and food, and it is a calm place with a pleasant plaza. The area around is known for its small chilli-growing farms and goat dishes, and cabrito is a common choice on menus.
t.bridge of el fraile@20.8,-100.8:
Atotonilco is a small village in the hills outside San Miguel de Allende, and its sanctuary is sometimes called the Sistine Chapel of Mexico. The church was founded in the eighteenth century and covered, inside, with extraordinary baroque paintings by a local artist, who filled the walls and ceilings with scenes of the Passion, saints and symbols in a dense, theatrical style. It is still an active place of pilgrimage, and many people walk here from San Miguel, especially during Lent, in a tradition that goes back centuries.

San Miguel itself is a colonial town founded in the sixteenth century, a handsome place with cobbled streets, a pink neo-Gothic church that dominates the main square, and a large population of foreign residents and artists. The town and the sanctuary were listed by UNESCO in 2008. San Miguel was also the birthplace of Ignacio Allende, a leader of the independence movement of 1810, and the town carries his name. The surrounding landscape is a high, dry plateau with low hills, with hot springs near Atotonilco that people have used for generations.

The roads in the area are good, with long straight stretches, gentle curves and some narrow cobbled streets in the villages, though cobblestones can be slippery in the rain. Traffic can be heavy in San Miguel at weekends, when visitors arrive from Mexico City, and the old town centre is best explored on foot. Dry months from November to May are the best time for a ride, and the light at sunset is lovely.

San Miguel de Allende, about ten kilometres off, has fuel stations on its outskirts, and the town is full of cafes, bakeries and restaurants. Take warm clothes for evenings, because the altitude is around 1,900 metres and nights can be cool even in spring. The sanctuary is a place of worship, so dress with respect and be quiet inside.
t.historic town of guanajuato and adjacent:
Guanajuato is a town that has been dug into, built over and tunnelled through, and it has a character all of its own. It sits in a narrow canyon in the highlands of central Mexico, and the silver mines that made it rich lie in the hills around it. In the eighteenth century the Valenciana mine was among the richest in the world, and the profits built grand churches, theatres and mansions, all painted in bright colours and packed into steep, winding streets. UNESCO listed the town and its mines in 1988.

The most distinctive thing about Guanajuato for a motorcyclist is that part of the road network is underground. When the river was diverted to prevent flooding, its old bed became a system of tunnels used by traffic, with stone arches, narrow lanes and a dim, echoing atmosphere that is entirely unlike anywhere else. The tunnels are one-way in places, signs are confusing, and the walls are close, so ride slowly with your headlight on and follow the traffic. Above ground, steep, narrow streets, steps and tiny plazas, such as the Alley of the Kiss, make the town a good place to park and walk.

Outside the centre, the panoramic road above the town gives a view over the rooftops, and the Pípila monument is a favourite viewpoint. The road to the Valenciana church, with its richly carved baroque facade, climbs through the hills, and the roads to Dolores Hidalgo, the cradle of the independence movement, are fast and open. The city is at about 2,000 metres, so it is mild most of the year, with rain in summer. In October the Cervantino arts festival fills the town, and finding a place to stay becomes difficult.

Fuel stations are mostly on the edges of town, and parking in the centre is tight, so it is worth leaving the bike at a secure car park and walking. The town has a large student population, so cafes and cheap restaurants are everywhere. The Mummies Museum is a macabre but popular visit, and the university steps are a good place to sit and watch the town go by.
t.zeiselmauer kleinkastell@48.3,16.2:
Before there was a Vienna, there was a frontier. For some four hundred years the Danube formed the northern boundary of the Roman empire in central Europe, and a chain of forts, watchtowers and harbours kept watch along the south bank. Zeiselmauer, about thirty kilometres upstream from the modern capital, was one of them, and a stretch of Roman wall with a tower still stands in the village, incorporated into later buildings. The Danube Limes in Austria, Germany and Slovakia was listed by UNESCO in 2021.

The fort here was one of the auxiliary forts on the river, and in the middle ages the site was reused, with its walls forming the basis of a church and village. The Roman tower, one of the highest surviving Roman structures in Austria, is the main thing to look for, and a small museum in the village tells the story. The river meanders through wooded floodplains here, and the Wienerwald hills rise to the south, giving a pleasant mix of landscapes.

The riding is gentle and varied. The Danube road, with its long views over the river, is straight and fairly fast, while the roads that climb into the Wienerwald are twisting, shaded and a pleasure, with beech woods, small villages and wine taverns. Cyclists are common, particularly along the Danube cycle path, so give them room. Summer weekends bring crowds from Vienna, and weekdays are quiet. Late September and October are lovely, with the vineyards turning gold.

Zeiselmauer is a small village with a bakery and an inn, and for fuel and shops Stockerau, seven kilometres away, is the sensible choice, with Klosterneuburg and Tulln also close. The Heurigen, wine taverns, serve young wine and cold meats in courtyards and gardens, and a green branch hung over the door signals that they are open. A rider can enjoy the atmosphere over a glass of grape juice or a cup of coffee, and the food, which includes schnitzel and pretzels, is excellent.
t.mautern kastell westbereich@48.4,15.6:
On the south bank of the Danube, just where the river leaves the Wachau gorge and swings out onto the plain, the Romans built a fort called Favianis, and its successor, the town of Mautern, still has the pattern of the Roman streets. The fort was part of the Danube frontier, and in the fifth century, when the empire was crumbling, it became famous because of a monk named Severinus, who came here to help the population and negotiate with the barbarian kings. His life, written by a disciple, is one of the few detailed accounts of life on the Danube at the end of Roman rule.

Parts of the Roman wall and a tower are still visible, and a small museum has finds from the site. Across the bridge is Krems, and upriver is Stein, a pretty medieval town, with the gorge of the Wachau beginning beyond. The Wachau is a World Heritage landscape, listed in 2000, of terraced vineyards, apricot orchards and ruined castles, and it is known for its crisp white wines, Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, and for its apricots, which turn up in jam, schnapps and dumplings.

Riding in the Wachau is a delight, though one that needs a bit of care. The road along the river, the B3, is narrow and winding, with tight bends, a lot of tourists and a lot of cyclists, so keep to a modest pace. In spring, the apricot trees blossom in late March and April and the valley is white and pink, and in late summer the vineyards are green and heavy with grapes. Cooler mornings are best, and midsummer afternoons can be crowded. The steep road up to the Jauerling, the highest hill in the area, gives more space and views.

Fuel is easy at Krems and at the edge of Mautern, and the towns have bakeries and cafes. Local wine estates, called Heurigen or Weingüter, often have simple food and a terrace, and a rider can enjoy the view with a glass of apricot juice. Ferries across the Danube, such as the one at Spitz, are a pleasant way to switch banks, but check the timetable first.
t.carnuntum legionslager@48.1,16.9:
Carnuntum was a Roman city, a legionary base and, for a time, a capital. The Fourteenth Legion, the Gemina, was stationed here from the first century, and the camp, with its great barracks and parade ground, guarded a crossing of the Danube where the Amber Road from the Baltic met the river. By the second century it was the capital of the province of Upper Pannonia, with an amphitheatre, baths and a population of tens of thousands. The emperor Marcus Aurelius is said to have spent part of the German wars here, and tradition holds that he wrote some of his Meditations in the camp.

In AD 193 the legions on the Danube proclaimed their governor, Septimius Severus, emperor at Carnuntum, and in 308 Diocletian and other emperors met here to try to patch together the tetrarchy. After that the city faded, and in later centuries it was a quarry for the villages around it. The Pagan Gate, a ruined triumphal arch standing in the fields, is the landmark, and an archaeological park has reconstructed houses, a gladiator school and the amphitheatre. The legionary camp, on our list, has largely vanished under fields, but the outlines are being revealed by surveys and excavations.

The country around is flat and fertile, with vineyards on the low hills and the broad Danube floodplain, now a national park, the Donau-Auen, with its wetlands, oxbows and sea eagles. Roads along the river are easy and fast, with scenery that is pleasant rather than dramatic, and the busy road to Bratislava, only forty kilometres away, is an alternative route. The Neusiedler See, a huge shallow lake, is a short ride to the south. Summers can be hot, and spring and autumn are best.

Hainburg an der Donau, with its medieval gates and walls, is seven kilometres away and has fuel and cafes. Bad Deutsch-Altenburg is a small spa town with a church on a hill. The Carnuntum wine region produces red wines, such as Zweigelt, that go well with the local food. Tickets to the archaeological park are modest and the park is generally open from spring to autumn, so check before you go.
t.old village of holloko and its surroundi:
Hollókő is a village of about three hundred people in the Cserhát hills of northern Hungary, thirty-odd kilometres south of the Slovak border, and it is one of the few places in Europe where a whole way of life has been kept, not by a museum but by the people still living in the houses. It was one of the first places inscribed by UNESCO, in 1987, as a living example of a traditional village of the Palóc, a Hungarian ethnic group of this region.

The houses are low, whitewashed and roofed with tiles or shingles, with carved wooden porches and small windows, lined up along a single street under the ruin of a thirteenth-century castle on the hill. The older buildings were destroyed by fire in 1909, and the village was rebuilt in the same style, so the look is deliberately old. The Palóc are known for their embroidery, with bright floral patterns on blouses and tablecloths, and for their costumes, which villagers still wear at festivals. The Easter celebrations, with songs, dances and the sprinkling of girls with water, draw crowds from across the country, and the village is busy then, so it is best to avoid it if you want peace. The name comes, according to one tale, from the raven, the hollo, that carried off a young woman's jewels, though the legend is nothing you could check.

The ride from the valley is gentle. Roads here wind over the wooded Cserhát hills, with orchards, small fields of wheat and sunflowers, and views to the Mátra mountains in the east. The main road from Szécsény is in decent shape, but side roads may have patches, potholes and farm vehicles. In spring the cherry and plum blossom is lovely, and in autumn the oaks turn bronze. Winter brings frost, and snow can linger on shaded corners.

Szécsény, about ten kilometres away, has six and a half thousand people, fuel stations, shops and a fine Forgách mansion, now a museum. Hollókő itself has a handful of guesthouses, small cafes serving hearty Palóc dishes such as bean soup and stuffed cabbage, and a few craft stalls. The village is free to wander, though there is a small charge to visit the castle and the museums. Weekdays outside the holidays are best, and an early start helps.
t.pilgrimage routes kumano sankeimichi o@3:
The Kii Peninsula, south of Osaka, is one of the most heavily forested and least populated parts of Japan, a knot of steep, cedar-covered mountains that has been a place of pilgrimage for more than a thousand years. The pilgrimage routes of Kumano, called the Kumano Kodo, were inscribed by UNESCO in 2004 together with the sacred sites of Koyasan and Yoshino and Omine, and the Ohechi route is the long mountain branch that starts near Tanabe, on the coast, about eleven kilometres from the point on your map.

The destination was the three Kumano shrines, Hongu, Hayatama in Shingu and Nachi, where people from emperors to farmers came to pray for healing, rebirth and a good afterlife, believing that the mountains were the pure land of the gods. In the Heian period, retired emperors made the trip dozens of times. Ohechi is the old coastal route over the mountains, a rough path of moss-covered stones, fallen leaves and giant cedar trunks that is now walked by pilgrims and hikers from all over the world, and the path is waymarked with small stone markers. You can walk a few kilometres of it from various trailheads without much preparation, but do not underestimate the steepness or the rain.

By road, the route is a joy. From Tanabe, Route 311 climbs into the mountains by way of narrow valleys and forested gorges, towards Hongu, with bends that follow the river, sudden tunnels, and gaps in the trees opening onto layers of misty ridges. The surface is generally excellent, but the roads are narrow and winding, and rain, fog and fallen branches are common, especially in the typhoon season from late summer to October. Speed limits are low and enforcement is polite but firm. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and winter brings frost in the high places.

Tanabe, with nearly seventy thousand people, has fuel, food and all the services, and it is the last town of any size before the mountains. The area is famous for ume, the sour Japanese plum, which is made into pickles and liqueur, and for hot springs. At Yunomine, near Hongu, a small hot spring bath in a hut by the river is among the oldest in the country, and a night in a ryokan with a bath and dinner is the right way to end the day.
t.tsudo shiroyama kofun@34.6,135.6:
On the plain south-east of Osaka, among suburbs, railway lines and car dealerships, the land is dotted with huge grassy mounds shaped like keyholes, surrounded by water-filled moats, and covered in trees. They are kofun, the burial mounds of Japan's early rulers and aristocrats, and the Tsudoshiroyama Kofun is one of them, in the Furuichi group, about two kilometres from the town of Kashiwara and not far from Habikino and Fujiidera. The group, together with the Mozu group in Sakai, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2019.

The mounds were built between about the late third and the late sixth centuries, when powerful chieftains of the Yamato kingdom controlled the plain, and the largest, the tomb attributed to Emperor Nintoku in Sakai, is one of the biggest burial structures in the world by volume. Tsudoshiroyama is a keyhole mound of about two hundred metres in length, and it sits next to several others, so that the whole area is a necropolis laid out beside the old harbour and road networks. The surface was once covered in stone and decorated with clay figures called haniwa, which stood in rows on the slopes, and many have been found by archaeologists. Because the mounds are imperial or protected property, you cannot walk on most of them, but the moats and the shape are visible from paths at the edge.

It is an odd place for a motorcycle ride. This is dense urban Japan, with narrow streets, one-way systems, traffic lights every hundred metres and little parking, and it is best taken slowly. The old road routes of the Kawachi plain pass through, and the hills of Mount Nijo and the Katsuragi range, a short ride to the east and south, offer much better roads, with winding mountain passes and old temples. Rain is common in the early summer, and the heat and humidity of July and August are punishing, so ride in the morning or choose spring and autumn.

Fuel stations, convenience stores and vending machines are everywhere, and a bowl of udon or a plate of Osaka-style okonomiyaki is easy to find. Several of the surrounding towns, including Habikino, have small museums on the kofun, and the Furuichi group has a visitor information office worth consulting for the best viewing spots.
t.yoshino and omine yoshinoyama@34.4,135.9:
Cherry trees are the whole point of Yoshino, and they are planted by the thousand up the side of a ridge in the mountains of Nara Prefecture, about five kilometres from the little town of Yoshino and an hour or two from Osaka. Over some three hundred years, pilgrims planted the sacred shidarezakura and the mountain cherry as offerings to the god of the mountain, and in the first half of April the slopes turn pink, white and green in four layers from the bottom to the top, a wave of flowering that rises up the hillside over about a fortnight.

The mountain was a holy place long before the cherry. It is the northern end of the Omine pilgrimage trail, the long, hard path of the Shugendo mountain ascetics, who combine Buddhism, Shinto and old nature worship, and who walk to Kumano over the peaks. The temple of Kinpusen-ji, whose main hall, the Zao-do, is one of the largest wooden buildings in Japan, houses three fierce blue statues of Zao Gongen, the deity of the mountain, which are shown to the public only on certain days. Parts of Mount Omine have been closed to women for over a thousand years, and the rule still holds. Yoshino was also a place of refuge: Prince Go-Daigo set up the Southern Court here in 1336, and the warrior Yoshitsune hid with his lover Shizuka after falling out with his brother. In 1594, Toyotomi Hideyoshi held a lavish cherry blossom party here, with thousands of guests. UNESCO inscribed the area in 2004 as part of the Kii mountain sites.

The roads up are narrow. Route 169 follows the Yoshino river from Kashihara and Sakurai through steep, wooded gorges, with tunnels and tight bends, and the last stretch to the village climbs in hairpins that become a car park in blossom season. During cherry time, traffic restrictions apply and the whole valley is busy, so go on a weekday and very early, or come in the green weeks of May or October, when the roads are peaceful and the forest is full of birdsong. Winter can bring snow and ice.

Yoshino has about nine thousand people, but the village at the top is tiny and fuel is not sold there, so fill the tank in the valley, at Gojo or Sakurai. The local specialities are kuzu, an arrowroot starch made into sweets and noodles, and persimmon-leaf sushi, which is salted fish pressed in rice and wrapped in leaves. Takamatsuzuka tomb, in Asuka, is famous for its painted wall figures, found in 1972.
t.stretch of the camino real between ojoca:
The Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the Royal Road of the Interior, ran for more than two and a half thousand kilometres from Mexico City to Santa Fe in what is now New Mexico, and carried silver, mercury, supplies and missionaries for nearly three hundred years. UNESCO inscribed a series of its sections and sites in 2010, and the stretch near Ojocaliente, in the state of Zacatecas, passes through high, dry country at around two thousand metres, with the town of Trancoso eight kilometres away and the city of Zacatecas to the west.

The road was born from silver. In 1546 rich deposits were found at Zacatecas, and mule trains began carrying the metal south, bringing back goods from Spain and the south. Fortified posts, missions and farms called haciendas sprang up along the route to feed and protect the convoys, and the Franciscans founded convents to convert the people of the north. Bandits and the Chichimeca peoples, who resisted the Spanish for decades, made travel risky. The old cobbled sections that survive are short, rough stretches of stone set in the earth, often with walls on either side, and they are quite moving to walk. The Franciscan college of Guadalupe, near Zacatecas, mentioned on your ride, was a centre for training missionaries and now holds a museum of colonial religious art.

The landscape is high desert grassland with nopal cactus, mesquite and scrubby hills, and the sky is huge. The main roads, Highway 45 and Highway 54, are well surfaced but carry heavy truck traffic, and the smaller roads between villages are a pleasure, with long straight stretches and low hills. Winds sweep across the plateau, afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and in winter nights can be freezing. The altitude means sun is strong even on cool days. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Fuel stations are on the main roads at Zacatecas, Guadalupe and Ojocaliente, but are rarer on the minor roads, so top up when you can. Trancoso, with fourteen thousand people, has shops and taquerías. Zacatecas, a superb colonial city with pink stone buildings and a cable car above the old silver mines, is the place to spend the night, and its local mezcal and rich stews are worth finding.
t.protective town of san miguel and sanctu:
San Miguel de Allende is a hill town in the highlands of Guanajuato, a little over two thousand metres above the sea, with cobbled streets climbing between ochre and rose-coloured walls, and in the middle of it the Gothic spires of the parish church rise improbably above the rooftops. The point on your map is in the centre of the town, and the sanctuary of Atotonilco, about fourteen kilometres away on the road to Dolores Hidalgo, was inscribed together with the town by UNESCO in 2008.

The town was founded by a Franciscan friar in the mid-sixteenth century and grew rich on silver and on the supply of the Camino Real to the mines, with Spanish landowners building grand baroque mansions around the central square. It is also the birthplace of Ignacio Allende, one of the leaders of the independence movement of 1810, and the town carries his name. The spire of the parish church, the Parroquia, was rebuilt in the 1880s by a local mason, Zeferino Gutierrez, who is said to have copied postcards of European Gothic cathedrals, which explains its strange beauty. At Atotonilco, a modest pilgrimage church is covered, inside, with paintings from floor to ceiling, an explosion of colour that has given it the nickname of the Sistine Chapel of Mexico. In September 1810, Allende and Miguel Hidalgo stopped here and took a banner of the Virgin of Guadalupe to lead their rebel army.

The surrounding highlands offer good riding, with open roads across plains of agave, corn and mesquite, and curving climbs into the hills. The streets of the town itself are steep and cobbled, with one-way systems that confuse, and the stones can be slippery when wet. Park outside the centre or in a car park and explore on foot. The rainy season is from June to September, with afternoon storms, and the dry months are pleasantly warm, with cold nights in winter. Atotonilco also has natural hot springs.

San Miguel has about seventy thousand people, a large community of foreign residents, and every kind of service, including fuel stations on the ring road. Restaurants range from taco stands to elegant courtyards, and the local mezcal and chocolate are worth a try. Book accommodation well ahead for festivals and weekends, and take care not to ride after dark on the highways, where livestock are common.
t.chapel of san antonio of the former haci:
Nombre de Dios, in the state of Durango, is a small, dusty town on a dry plateau about a hundred kilometres south-east of the state capital, and it carries the distinction of having been the site of the first Franciscan mission in Durango, founded in the 1550s.

Haciendas were the engines of colonial northern Mexico, great estates, often with thousands of hectares, that raised cattle and sheep, grew wheat and maize, and supplied the silver mines with food, leather and mules. Each had a main house for the owner, workers' quarters, granaries, a forge, and a chapel where the priest would say mass. Many have since been abandoned, and their adobe walls are slowly returning to the soil, while a few have been restored as hotels or museums. A small chapel like San Antonio often outlasts the main buildings, a whitewashed room with a bell tower, and still serves as a place of worship on the saint's day.

The road along the Camino Real runs through country that feels timeless, a high desert plain of dry grass, yucca and nopal, with distant blue mountains. Durango is also famous as a film location, with many Westerns shot here since the 1950s, and the plain and rocky hills explain why. The highways are straight and often empty, with long views, and the occasional pothole or cow on the road. Highway 45 connects Durango with Zacatecas through the plateau. Afternoon thunderstorms bring heavy rain in the summer, with flooding on low sections, and winter nights fall below freezing. Spring and autumn give the best conditions.

Nombre de Dios has about five thousand people, with a plaza, shops, and a petrol station on the main road, and Durango city has everything, including a handsome baroque cathedral. Carry water and plenty of cash, because card machines can be rare. For food, try caldillo durangueño, a beef and chile stew, and gorditas stuffed with beans or meat, and drink the local mezcal.
t.huirjcuta raunax@23.7,-100.9:
For the Wixarika people, also known as the Huichol, the high desert of San Luis Potosí is the place where the sun was born, and every year pilgrims walk or travel hundreds of kilometres from their mountain villages in Jalisco and Nayarit to Wirikuta, a sacred landscape around the old mining town of Real de Catorce.

The pilgrimage is a journey of renewal in which pilgrims follow the path of their ancestors, make offerings at springs and hills, and hunt the hikuri, the peyote cactus, which is gathered ritually and has a central role in their religion. Its use by the Wixarika is legally protected, and the cactus itself is endangered, so as a visitor you must not collect or disturb any plants, and you should ask before taking photographs or entering any ceremonial place. The climb to the top of Cerro Quemado at dawn is a significant ritual, and the whole area is part of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro heritage listing.

Real de Catorce itself is one of the strangest places in Mexico. It was a rich silver town in the nineteenth century, with fine stone houses, a mint and a bullring, and after the silver price collapsed in the early twentieth century it was almost abandoned. Today a few hundred people live there, in a half-ruined town with cobbled streets, high in the mountains at about 2,700 metres, reached through the Ogarrio tunnel, a long, narrow, one-lane passage through the mountain, with traffic taking turns. The cobbled road up from the highway is long and bumpy, and parking at the end is limited, so take it slowly and watch for horses and jeeps.

Fuel is the thing to plan. There is none in Real de Catorce, so fill up in Matehuala, the larger town on Highway 57, or at Cedral, a small town of eleven thousand people on the way. The air is thin and cold at night even in summer, so bring a jacket, and a hat and water for the day. The town has simple restaurants serving enchiladas, gorditas and strong coffee, and some small hotels.
t.temple of nuestra senora de los angeles:
The high plateau of central Mexico, known as the Mesa Central, is a landscape of dry grass, mesquite, nopal cactus and low volcanic hills, and the village of Noria de Angeles, in the state of Zacatecas, sits in the middle of it, about eight kilometres from Villa Gonzalez Ortega.

Villages like this were created by the silver economy of the colonial period. After the great strikes at Zacatecas in 1546, wagon roads and mule tracks spread across the plateau, and with them came ranches, haciendas, wells and chapels. Noria means a water wheel or a well, and in a place where rain is scarce, a well was a reason to settle. The church would have served the families of a hacienda and its farm workers, and many such temples were built in the eighteenth century from local stone or adobe, with a plain facade, a bell tower and a small dome. They matter in the landscape as landmarks and as the centres of the village's festivals, with fireworks, dancing and processions on the patron saint's day.

The ride is long, open and somewhat austere. Highways cross the plateau in long straight sections, with distant mountains and almost no trees, and the roads between the villages are narrower, with patches, potholes and cattle. The sky is wide and the sunsets are spectacular, but the air at two thousand metres is thin and dry, and the sun is strong at midday. Wind is constant. From June to September, afternoon thunderstorms can sweep across the plain, and in winter nights drop below freezing. Spring and autumn are the best times.

Villa Gonzalez Ortega, with six thousand people, has a few shops, eating places and a fuel station, and Estancia de Animas is smaller. Zacatecas, the capital, is far larger, and a better stop if you need services or a bed. Local food includes asado de boda, a spicy pork stew traditionally served at weddings, and cheese and sweets made from prickly pear, and cold beers in a shaded plaza make a good end to the day.
t.windstallgraben wachtturm@48.4,15.5:
Between Dürnstein and Mautern, a small gully called the Windstallgraben cuts down toward the Danube, and somewhere along its edge stood a Roman watchtower. The Wachau valley was once the frontier of the empire, and the Danube was the line. The Romans built a chain of forts and watchtowers along the south bank, and Mautern, ancient Favianis, was one of the strongest. The Danube Limes in Austria and Germany is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing, and these modest remains are part of that long, thin story.

What you will actually see depends on the spot. Little of a watchtower survives above ground, so you are mainly standing in a landscape that the soldiers knew: a river bend, terraced vineyards, rocky outcrops and the dark woods that crowd the slopes. The Wachau itself is a UNESCO site as well, famous for its apricots, Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, and for villages like Dürnstein, where the English king Richard the Lionheart was held prisoner in 1192 and 1193 on his way home from the crusade.

The riding is a pleasure. The Danube road along the north bank, with the river on one side and vineyard terraces on the other, offers gentle bends, a few small climbs, and views that make you slow down willingly. In apricot blossom time in spring and during the autumn wine harvest, the valley is at its best, but both periods bring cyclists and tour coaches, so expect to travel at a sociable pace. The small ferries at Spitz and Weißenkirchen offer a charming change of banks.

For fuel, go to Krems or Mautern, where the stations are easy to find; the villages of the valley are tiny, and Dürnstein itself has barely three hundred residents. Food is a delight: look for an Heuriger, a seasonal wine tavern marked by a hung branch, where you can eat cold cuts and bread with a glass of wine, though the rider's version is a glass of apple juice spritzer. Come early on weekdays to beat the crowds.
t.st procopius basilica@49.2,15.9:
Třebíč sits on the Jihlava river in the Vysočina highlands, and the basilica of St Procopius sits above the water on the eastern bank, so close to the old town that the rider's biggest problem is finding somewhere to leave the bike. The building began as part of a Benedictine monastery founded at the start of the twelfth century. What you see now is a mix of Romanesque strength, with a very old crypt, and Gothic ambition, with a tall, airy nave that people tend to find more elegant than they expected from the heavy west front. The monastery was later turned into a castle and then into other uses, which is partly why so much has survived in odd corners.

The other half of the reason this place is protected is just downhill. Třebíč has one of the best-preserved Jewish quarters in Central Europe, a tangle of narrow lanes, shared walls and small courtyards that sits between the basilica and the river, plus an old cemetery climbing the slope behind. Basilica and quarter together were inscribed by UNESCO in 2003, and walking from one to the other takes ten minutes and tells a surprisingly full story about how two communities lived side by side for centuries.

For a rider, the Vysočina is quietly rewarding. This is rolling plateau country of ponds, birch woods and long fields, with roads that go up and down without drama and rarely carry much traffic outside the towns. The corners are gentle rather than dramatic, the surface is usually decent but patched, and the villages come every few kilometres, each with a church tower and a pub. Autumn is lovely here, with mist on the Jihlava in the early hours and the plateau turning gold.

Třebíč has everything a rider needs: petrol stations on the edge of town, plenty of cafés around Karlovo náměstí, which is said to be one of the largest squares in the Czech Republic, and a good number of small guesthouses. If you want a quick pause, a coffee and a slice of something sweet in the square will do the job. If you have time, climb the basilica tower for the roofs, the river bends and the ridge of the Moravian horizon, and then continue to Telč or towards Lednice with the sense of having seen a thousand years from one hillside.
t.yamada dera temple site@34.5,135.8:
South of the modern town of Sakurai, in the Asuka region of Nara Prefecture, the grass and low walls of Yamada-dera mark the ruins of what was once a very grand temple. It was founded in the 640s by Soga no Kurayamada Ishikawamaro, a powerful minister of the Soga clan, who was caught up in court intrigue and is said to have taken his own life at the temple in 649, after being accused of treason. The story gives the quiet site a sad edge. In later excavations, archaeologists uncovered the foundation of the main hall and a long covered corridor whose timbers had collapsed and been buried in place, one of the best-preserved examples of seventh-century temple architecture in Japan.

Asuka is where Japan first took the shape of a state. The Soga, the Prince Shotoku circle, the first great Buddhist temples and the first capital-like palaces were all here, a landscape of small valleys, rice paddies, mysterious carved stones and burial mounds. In autumn, red spider lilies line the rice-field edges, and in early spring rape blossom turns the fields yellow. The nearby sacred mountain of Miwa, with its Omiwa shrine, is one of the oldest cult sites in the country, and Miwa is also famous for its thin somen noodles.

For riding, the roads of Asuka are narrow, winding and quiet. Many are one lane wide, with paddies on both sides, small shrines at the corners and plenty of cyclists in the tourist season. This is a place to ride slowly and take a break. A proper fill-up is easy in Sakurai, a town of sixty thousand people about three kilometres off, and in neighbouring Kashihara, which has more shops and cafes. Both are on the old routes that link Nara, Yoshino and Osaka.

Travel to the Ōmine mountains and Yoshino, the other direction, takes you from the plain up into steep forested country with proper mountain roads. To Himeji, you will take the main routes across the Kansai plain and its congestion. Autumn is the most colourful season here, spring the most delicate, and summer very hot and humid. Early morning is the easiest time for quiet photographs.
t.cuyetsarie@22.4,-103.6:
This is a point on the high plateau where Zacatecas, Jalisco and Durango meet, in the dry country at the edge of the northern Sierra Madre Occidental. The names of the rides, Cuyetsarie, Cacai Mutijé and Xurahue Muyaca, belong to the Wixárika people, whom outsiders call the Huichol, and refer to places in their sacred geography. Wixárika communities live in the rugged canyons of Mezquitic and Huejuquilla and the neighbouring sierra, and they keep a living tradition in which certain springs, hills and rocks are sites of offering, prayer and pilgrimage.

The great Wixárika journey takes pilgrims hundreds of kilometres east to Wirikuta, in the high desert of San Luis Potosí, where the peyote cactus grows, and the route is connected to a web of sacred places across the whole territory. Not all of these are open to visitors, and the best approach is a respectful one: stay on public roads, do not enter ceremonial areas, ask before photographing people, and understand that the places are not monuments but working spaces of belief. Ceremonial calendars follow the rains and the seasons, and some days are closed to outsiders.

The landscape itself is wide and austere, a plateau of pale grass, oak, mesquite and prickly pear at roughly two thousand metres, cut by deep barrancas where the land falls away toward warmer country. Mornings are crisp and clear, with a hard blue sky, and winter nights can be near freezing. The summer rains turn the hills green and make the dirt roads treacherous. The tarmac roads are generally quiet and straight, but they can be patched and have livestock on the surface, and some lonely sections have little traffic and no phone signal.

Fuel is the main thing to plan. Monte Escobedo, with about four thousand people, is the nearest place likely to have a station, and Huejuquilla el Alto, farther north, is the other option; Mezquitic is smaller. Do not count on anything between them. Simple food, such as tortillas, beans, roasted meat and strong coffee, is available in town cafes and taquerias, and a night in the small towns tends to be cheaper and quieter than in the tourist spots. Bring water and a spare layer, and take things slowly.
t.holy trinity column in olomouc@49.6,17.3:
Olomouc is the city Prague forgot to overshadow. For centuries before the Habsburgs shifted their attention elsewhere it was the capital of Moravia, and the proof is on the Upper Square, where the Holy Trinity Column rises out of the cobbles like a stone wedding cake. It was built in the first half of the eighteenth century, roughly between 1716 and 1754, and it is among the largest Baroque sculpture groups in central Europe. The city raised it partly as thanks for surviving a plague, and UNESCO listed it in 2000. Walk round it and the saints keep appearing, each one a little more theatrical than the last.

The square is a morning place. Come before the cafe tables fill and the stone is almost gold; come at noon in July and it is a bright, noisy bowl of tourists and students from the old university. You park outside the historic core and walk in, since the centre is mostly pedestrian and the cobbles are unkind to a loaded bike. Olomouc has fuel on every approach road, and a city of a hundred thousand makes food an easy problem. If you want something local, the town is known for its pungent ripened cheese, tvarůžky, which is an acquired smell and an honest snack with beer.

The riding around Olomouc is a different mood. The city sits on the flat, fertile Haná plain along the Morava river, so the approach is straight and agricultural, with cornfields and long poplar-lined lanes. The fun begins when you head east into the Nízký Jeseník foothills or north toward the Jeseníky range, where the roads begin to roll and bend. Treat the square as the start or the end of a day rather than the middle of one, a place to put the bike down and turn into a pedestrian for an hour.

One more detail rewards the curious. The astronomical clock on the town hall was wrecked in the war and rebuilt in the 1950s in a socialist-realist style, so instead of apostles you get workers, athletes and a cheerful sense of civic duty. It looks nothing like the clock in Prague, and Olomouc is perfectly happy about that. Stand there at noon and watch the figures parade; it is odd, a little endearing, and a proper piece of twentieth-century history hiding in a Baroque square.
t.historic town of banska stiavnica and th:
Banská Štiavnica is a town built into a volcano. A great crater, the caldera of an extinct volcano, surrounds the place, and the streets climb steeply up its inner slopes, so that the whole centre is a tumble of pastel houses, churches and castles on a hillside. Silver and gold were mined here from the Middle Ages, and in the eighteenth century the town was one of the richest in the Habsburg Empire. In 1762 the mining academy was founded, one of the first technical colleges in the world, and its graduates carried mining knowledge to many countries. UNESCO listed the town in 1993, along with its technical monuments.

The landscape is full of ingenious water engineering. Because the town sits high on a ridge, with no large river, the miners built dozens of small reservoirs, called tajchy, in the hills above to power their pumps and stamping mills. Many survive, and on a summer day some of them are used for swimming and boating. The roads around the town climb and dip through wooded hills and quiet valleys, with long bends and the occasional steep section, and they are a delight for riders who like gentle, twisting routes. Sitno, the highest peak nearby, offers a viewpoint over the whole district.

Banská Štiavnica has just over ten thousand people, so fuel, food and rooms are available, though the cobbled streets are steep and slippery in the wet. Svätý Anton, a smaller village a few kilometres off, has a handsome manor house, once the home of an aristocratic family, now a museum. The town is also famous for its traditional crafts, including pottery, wooden toys and gingerbread. Old inns serve hearty fare of dumplings, sheep cheese and smoked meats.

If you can, plan to stay overnight. The town is at its best in the evening, when the day trippers leave and the lamps come on. The stone steps, the Calvary on its hill and the little churches stand out against the sky, and in the cool air, you can hear the church bells ring across the valley. A walk through the old streets in the quiet of the night is memorable.
t.millenary benedictine abbey of pannonhal:
Pannonhalma Archabbey stands on a hill above the Hungarian plain, and it has been standing there, in one form or another, for a thousand years. The Benedictine monastery was founded in 996, during the reign of Prince Géza, and its monks helped to bring Christianity to the young Hungarian state. The abbey is called the Mons Sacer Pannoniae, the holy mountain of Pannonia, and the local tradition holds that Saint Martin of Tours was born in the Roman town that stood nearby. UNESCO listed it in 1996, the thousandth anniversary of its foundation.

The building is a mixture of periods. The Romanesque and Gothic church was built over centuries, the cloister is delicate, and the baroque library, housing hundreds of thousands of volumes, is one of the finest in central Europe. The abbey has survived Tatar invasions, Ottoman raids and the communists, who tried to close it, and it still runs a school and a working community of monks. The monks also make wine and lavender products, and the abbey's estate has become a respected wine producer.

The view from the hill takes in the Little Hungarian Plain, a wide patchwork of fields, and on a clear day the Bakony hills to the south and the Alps in the west. The town of Pannonhalma, at the foot, is small and quiet, with a few shops, bakeries and cafés. Visitors arrive in large numbers on weekends, so come on a weekday if you can.

The roads here are gentle, rolling and easy, a pleasant change from the busy motorway that connects Budapest and Vienna a few kilometres to the north. Surfaces are generally good, traffic moderate, and the corners are mild. Spring brings fresh green and fruit blossom, and autumn offers warm light and the smell of harvest. In winter fog may linger on the plain.

Pannonhalma has four thousand people and offers fuel and food, and Győr, eighteen kilometres away, is a big, handsome city with all services. Check abbey visiting hours, since they vary and guided tours are common.
t.nakayamazuka kofun@34.6,135.6:
From the road you would never know it was a tomb. Nakayamazuka is a keyhole-shaped burial mound in the Furuichi cluster of the great Mozu-Furuichi tomb group in southern Osaka Prefecture, a landscape of ancient mounds built between about the fourth and sixth centuries AD, when the Yamato rulers were consolidating power in Japan. UNESCO listed forty-nine of the tombs in 2019. Each is a hill of earth, once faced with stones and lined with clay figures called haniwa, surrounded by a moat, and many have a shape that can only be recognised from above: a round mound joined to a trapezoid, like the head and body of a keyhole.

The oddity of the place is that the mounds now sit in the middle of ordinary suburbs. Houses, rice fields, schools, and railway lines press up against the moats, and a mound you took for a wooded park turns out to be the grave of someone who ruled the land fifteen hundred years ago. Most are managed by the Imperial Household Agency, which restricts access, so you view them from the path around the moat and from viewing points rather than climbing up. Early morning gives you quiet paths and herons standing on the water.

The riding here is urban. Osaka's southern suburbs are a dense web of one-way streets and narrow roads, so expect slow progress, many traffic lights, and cyclists and scooters weaving everywhere. To the east the Kongo and Katsuragi hills rise, and the roads that climb them are far better for riding, with forests, bends and mountain temples, while to the south lies the Kii Peninsula, where the ride list leads to the pilgrimage mountains of Kumano and Fudarakusan-ji. Spring brings cherry blossoms and a mild wind, and summer is hot and humid with a wet season in June.

Fuel is no problem in this part of Japan, since the towns of Habikino, Fujiidera and Kashihara have stations on the main roads, and convenience stores sell coffee and rice balls. Many local shrines, such as Domyoji Tenmangu, offer a quiet place to rest.

These are graves, so keep to the paths, keep the engine quiet near the moat and walk the last stretch.
t.mozu furuichi kofun group mounded tombs:
Konda Gobyoyama is the name of the great tomb that dominates the Furuichi end of this group, and it is the burial mound attributed to the emperor Ojin, a ruler of semi-legendary standing whom the chronicles place around the end of the fourth century. At over four hundred metres long, it is the second largest tomb in Japan, bigger by volume than many pyramids, and beside it stands the shrine of Konda Hachimangu, whose forest and approach give the place a gentle atmosphere. The pairing is typical of Japan. A shrine to the war god Hachiman, who is identified with Ojin, sits beside an earthen tomb that nobody is permitted to enter.

The wider Mozu-Furuichi group, with forty-nine tombs listed by UNESCO in 2019, was built in the plain of Kawachi in the fourth and fifth centuries, during an age when rulers of the Yamato state were trading with and sending envoys to China and Korea. Chinese records of the time speak of the five kings of Wa, who sought titles from the Chinese court, and the scale of the tombs reflects a state that could mobilise thousands of workers. Archaeologists have found that the mounds were covered with fist-sized stones and rows of terracotta cylinders, so that when new they must have gleamed like stepped hills.

The ride in on this side is tame. From central Osaka you take the commuter roads, which are slow, signalised and full of delivery vans, and the area where the mounds stand is a district of low houses and small factories. The reward, as ever, lies beyond. Within half an hour you can reach the Kongo and Ikoma ranges, and a day ride from here can carry you to Horyu-ji at Ikaruga, the temple that preserves some of the oldest wooden buildings in the world, and the other kofun on the ride list.

Getting around is made easier by the fact that Japan is orderly. Fuel stations are everywhere, with attendants at many, and convenience stores open all night offer coffee and snacks. Parking beside the mound is not always available, so use public car parks and walk.

Look for the moat, where reed and water give the tomb a lonely outline, and walk the path round it slowly. The scale only sinks in when you realise you are still walking after twenty minutes.
t.dogameyama kofun@34.6,135.5:
Sakai is the city of the bicycle, which should please a motorcyclist. The Shimano company, whose gears are on bikes all over the world, began here in 1921, and the city still has a long tradition of cycling, with a museum devoted to the machine near the Daisen Park. It seems apt that the same city should hold the biggest cluster of tombs in Japan. Dogameyama is one of the smaller mounds in the Mozu group, and like most of the small ones it is known more by its position than by any biography.

What I can say is that the Mozu tombs date from the fifth century and are part of a huge cemetery of rulers and their kin. Most are surrounded by water-filled moats, and the smaller companion mounds sit like satellites around the great ones. Some are only a few dozen metres across, with a trimmed grass cover and pine trees, and tucked between houses and railway lines. There is something moving about the way modern Sakai has grown around these ancient places without eliminating them.

The landscape is the plain of Osaka Bay, flat and densely built, with the Yamato river to the north and the city's old harbour to the west. Roads here are busy and run in grids, with bicycles, delivery trucks, and the occasional bus all competing for the lane. Early on a weekend morning, the streets are far calmer, and the moats are alive with ducks. Spring has cherry blossom, while June is the rainy season, and August is oppressively hot and humid.

Fuel is no problem in this big city, and Sakai has stations all over. The city also has a great food tradition, with delicate tea sweets, and Sakai knives, which are prized by chefs across the world. There are plenty of places for a rest near the park, and the old merchant quarter by the harbour has a few historic buildings worth a stroll.

From here, the ride list continues to Hokki-ji, an old temple near Nara famed for its three-storey pagoda, one of the oldest in Japan. The road passes the Kongo foothills and leads through a quiet country of small villages and rice fields.
t.tsukamawari kofun@34.6,135.5:
Tsukamawari is easy to miss, a modest tomb among the larger ones in the Mozu cluster at Sakai, and it makes a good excuse for talking about the city's most famous product, the knife. Sakai has been a centre of blade making for centuries, and its craftsmen are said to have first made their name forging the tobacco knives that came into use in the sixteenth century, then turned to swords and finally to the kitchen blades that professional chefs treasure. Even today, many of the best Japanese kitchen knives carry a Sakai stamp, and the old workshops, some of them family firms, stand in the streets near the old harbour. A knife shop here is the sort of souvenir that you can pack in a pannier, though you will need to wrap it properly for travel.

The burial mounds, meanwhile, are the work of an earlier age. The Mozu tombs date from the fifth century and were built for the rulers of the Yamato state and their families. Small tombs like this one are generally thought to have been for members of the elite who served the great king, and they were often built close to the main mound. You will probably see a small hill covered in pines and a strip of water, with a signboard in Japanese and English that explains the history.

The setting is a city of nearly eight hundred thousand people. The roads are busy with commuter traffic, and the narrow lanes between the tombs and the houses are best taken slowly, with a watchful eye for cyclists, delivery vans and school children. The city is flat, with few views, and the air in summer is heavy and humid. Rain in June and heavy rain in September are typical, so check the forecast.

Fuel, like everything else here, is very easy to find, and convenience stores are open at all hours. For a good lunch, look for kitsune udon, noodles with sweet fried tofu, a Kansai speciality, or a plate of okonomiyaki in one of the casual restaurants.

Leave time to wander the park in the evening, when the streets quieten and the dark water of the moat catches the last of the light.
t.mukohakayama kofun@34.6,135.6:
Satellite tombs are the quiet puzzle of Furuichi. Beside every great mound there seems to be a scatter of small ones, some round, some square, and some keyhole-shaped, and Mukohakayama is one of the mounds clustered around the tomb of the emperor Ojin, a sizeable keyhole in its own right. Archaeologists reckon that the people buried in them were relatives and retainers of the ruler, which would make the whole area a vast family graveyard laid out around the king like a court around a throne. At the larger scale the Mozu-Furuichi tombs were listed by UNESCO in 2019.

The tombs make better sense when you remember how the land looked. In the fifth century this was a fertile plain of rice paddies and rivers between the mountains of Kongo and Ikoma and the sea, and the tomb builders had access to a large workforce and an organised administration. They covered the mounds with stones, lined them with clay cylinders and figures called haniwa, and encircled them with moats, so that from a distance they would have looked like fortresses.

Today the neighbourhood is part of Habikino, a city known for its orchards, with grapes and figs growing on the slopes at the edge of the hills. That is useful to a rider, because the roads on the east side lead up into small rural lanes where farm stands sell fruit in season. The riding in the lowlands is slow, with signals and narrow streets, and the key is to head east early. Summer is hot, with high humidity, and autumn is the best season, with clear skies and the first colour in the leaves.

Fuel is available in Habikino and Matsubara, both with stations on the main roads, and the supermarkets and convenience stores sell cold drinks, which you will need in July. A few modest shops near the station offer a plate of local noodles.

The ride list takes this point on to Daigo-ji, the great temple complex in the hills south-east of Kyoto, famous for its cherry blossoms and its five-storey pagoda dating from the tenth century. The road takes you through Nara's countryside, and the old capital makes a good place for a rest on the way.
t.osamezuka kofun@34.6,135.5:
Osamezuka sits in the same Sakai cluster as its larger neighbours, a small mound whose occupant nobody names with confidence, since tombs of this size are remembered by their shape and position rather than by a story. The city around it has plenty of story to make up for that.

Sakai was, for a few centuries, one of the great merchant cities of Japan. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries it was a free port that ran its own affairs through a council of wealthy merchants, defended by moats and mercenaries, trading with Ming China and later with the Portuguese. The Jesuit missionaries who visited called it the Venice of the East, and the merchants who prospered there turned their money to the arts. The tea master Sen no Rikyu, who shaped the Japanese tea ceremony and served the warlords Nobunaga and Hideyoshi, was born in Sakai, and the city still has a strong connection with tea. A sweet and a bowl of matcha in a local tea room is a very good use of a rest.

The tombs are older than all of that by a thousand years, and the combination makes a good portrait of the region. You pass a ditch full of lotus leaves, a pine-covered mound, a temple, and a convenience store, all in the same view.

Riding here, the main matter is patience. The southern Osaka plain is flat and dense, with grid roads and many lights. The ride list leads to Yamada-dera, the temple site in the Asuka region of Nara, where the old Yamato kings and the first Buddhist temples stood, so you ride from one ancient landscape to another and cross the Kongo hills on the way. The roads over the hills are curving and shaded with cedar, and the temperature drops several degrees on the high ground. Spring blossom and autumn leaves are the high points.

Fuel is easy in this part of Japan, and Sakai has stations on every major road. Bring cash for small shops, and keep rain gear handy, because the weather can turn quickly.
t.nintoku tenno ryo kofun@34.6,135.5:
Nintoku's tomb is the biggest grave in Japan, and by area it ranks among the largest tombs ever built anywhere. It is a keyhole-shaped mound nearly five hundred metres long, ringed by three moats, rising out of the middle of the city of Sakai, and the Imperial Household Agency attributes it to the emperor Nintoku, who is said to have ruled in the fifth century. Archaeologists are less sure about the name, which is why scholars often call it Daisen Kofun, after the neighbourhood. Whatever the truth, the labour that went into it must have been prodigious, with estimates of years of work by thousands of people.

The strange thing is that you cannot really see it. At ground level it looks like a long, wooded park behind water, and the shape that makes it famous only reveals itself from the sky. The best view available to an ordinary visitor is from the free observation lobby on the upper floor of Sakai city hall, which looks across the roofs to the forested hump and its moat. There is also a visitor centre nearby that explains the site, and a path that circles the outer moat in about forty-five minutes of easy walking. Early morning is best, with the water still and the herons fishing.

For a rider the area is easy to reach. The Hanshin expressway runs along the coast from Osaka, and the streets of Sakai are broad and orderly, though busy at rush hour. Parking near the tomb is limited, so check the signs at the visitor centre and be ready to walk. Summer is very hot and humid, with cicadas making a wall of sound in the trees, and the best months are April, May, October and November, when the air is clear and the light is kind.

Fuel is no concern, since Sakai is one of Japan's largest cities and the main roads are lined with stations. For something local, try a kitchen knife shop in the old town, a cup of tea at a Sakai tea room, or a stop at the bicycle museum in the park, which is a small and charming collection and a good place to stay out of the rain.

From here the ride list goes on to Daigo-ji, in Kyoto's south-east hills, a long day's ride through Nara, so start early.
t.kumano sanzan nachi primeval forest@33.7:
Rain made this place, and a lot of it. The Kii Peninsula sticks into the Pacific south of Osaka, steep, forested and very wet, with some of the heaviest rainfall in Japan, and the Nachi river tumbles down its flank in a cascade that has been worshipped for well over a thousand years. Nachi Falls drops one hundred and thirty-three metres in a single plunge, the tallest single-drop waterfall in the country, and the Shinto shrine at its foot, Hiro Jinja, treats the falls themselves as the god. Beside it, on a ridge above, Kumano Nachi Taisha and the Buddhist temple Seiganto-ji sit side by side, with a red three-storey pagoda that frames the white thread of water like a postcard. The two religions here have long lived in the same compound.

This is one of the three great shrines of Kumano, the Kumano Sanzan, which together with Hongu and Hayatama in Shingu form the end of the old pilgrimage trails, the Kumano Kodo. Retired emperors of Kyoto made the journey many times over in the Heian and later periods, with long processions, and the sacred crow with three legs, Yatagarasu, became the emblem of the shrines. UNESCO listed the area as part of the Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range in 2004.

The way is long, and the roads are made for riding. Route 42, along the coast, passes tunnels, headlands and fishing villages with views over the Pacific, and the inland roads, Route 168 and 169, climb through cedar forest with twisting bends. Rain can be heavy and sudden, and mist and landslides are possible after storms, so take wet-weather gear in any season. Spring and autumn are lovely, with clear light and warm days, while the typhoon season from August to October can close roads.

Fuel is in Shingu, a city of over thirty thousand people on the Kumano river, and in Nachikatsuura, close to the falls. Stations are fewer in the mountains, so fill up before heading inland. In Nachi, you can find a simple meal of tuna, which is landed at the harbour in Katsuura, and there is a famous tuna auction in the morning.

Walk up the old stone staircase from the Daimonzaka slope, lined with giant cedars, if you have the time. It is a short and atmospheric taste of the pilgrim route.
t.pilgrimage routes koya sankeimichi@34.3,:
Kōyasan is a city in the sky. In 816 the monk Kūkai, known after his death as Kōbō Daishi, received permission from the emperor to found a monastery on a high, forested plateau in the Kii mountains, and from that start the settlement grew into the headquarters of Shingon Buddhism, with over a hundred temples tucked among the cedars. A few thousand people live in the town, and many of the temples take pilgrims and visitors as guests, serving a vegetarian temple meal called shojin ryori and waking guests for morning prayers. At the far end of the main street begins Okunoin, the great cemetery, where a two-kilometre path winds beneath tall cedars past tens of thousands of moss-covered gravestones to the mausoleum of Kūkai, who is believed to be in eternal meditation rather than dead.

The route that fits this point is the old pilgrimage path, the Choishi-michi. It climbs from the temple of Jison-in, by the town of Kudoyama, for about twenty kilometres, marked all the way by stone posts, one for every chō, about a hundred and nine metres, and a hundred and eighty in all. Pilgrims have walked it for over a thousand years, and today it is a good half-day walk through persimmon orchards and cedar woods. UNESCO listed the pilgrimage routes together with the Kii mountain shrines in 2004.

The road up by bike is a pleasure. From Hashimoto, the road climbs through cedar forest in a series of bends, with views over the valley of the Kino river. The plateau sits at around eight hundred metres, so it is cool when the lowlands bake, and it can be cold and foggy in autumn and snowy in winter, with ice on shaded bends. Spring blossoms are late, and the best time is perhaps October, when the leaves turn.

Hashimoto, with nearly sixty thousand people, is the place for fuel, and Kōyasan town has smaller stations. Book a temple lodging in advance, since there is little else to stay in, and leave your bike in the car park at your temple.

I find the cemetery the most moving place, with mist drifting between the cedars and lanterns lit along the path in the dark.
t.komuroyama kofun@34.6,135.6:
Komuroyama belongs to the dense scatter of tombs on the Furuichi side of the Mozu-Furuichi group, in the part of southern Osaka where Habikino, Fujiidera and Matsubara run into one another. It is a modest mound in a district where the large tombs get all the attention, and most visitors pass it with a glance. That is probably the best way to understand the whole group: not as a set of monuments but as a landscape, where hills of earth, ponds, railway lines and houses all share the same plain.

The interesting question is why the kings of the Yamato state chose the Kawachi plain. It lay at the end of the river system that flowed down from the Nara basin, where the royal court had its earlier seats, and close to the coast of Osaka Bay, where ships from Korea and China arrived. A tomb on the plain, visible from the sea road, advertised the power of the dynasty to every foreign envoy who landed. It is a plausible guess that the great mounds were meant to be read from the water, and that the Furuichi group grew up as a second cluster further inland.

The riding from here has two different faces. To the north and west is the Osaka plain, where the roads are dense and slow. To the south and east, the Kongo range rises and the roads to the Kii Peninsula open out, and the ride list leads that way, to Kumano Hongu Taisha, a pilgrimage shrine deep in the mountains south of here. Take spare layers, and set off at dawn.

Fuel is easy in the lowlands, and stations in Habikino and Matsubara are on the main roads. Once you are climbing into the Kii mountains, they become less frequent, so fill up at the last big town. Convenience stores sell hot canned coffee in cold weather and iced drinks in summer, and the vending machines are everywhere.
