If you have a spare half hour, wander the lanes near the tomb at dusk and watch the commuters on the trains to Osaka, with the old mound in the background.
t.nagatsuka kofun@34.6,135.5:
Nagatsuka is another of the small tombs that dot Sakai's old Mozu cemetery, and it is a place to think about the city as a whole. Before it was a place of keyhole tombs it was already a harbour, and it remained one for centuries. In the sixteenth century Sakai was the greatest port in Japan and a self-governing merchant town, whose leading citizens negotiated with the warlords, imported guns and silk from abroad, and were among the first to meet Europeans. When Oda Nobunaga demanded a large sum of money from Sakai in 1568, the merchants eventually paid up and kept their trade, and the city became a source of firearms for his campaigns. Much of old Sakai was later burned and then flattened again in the Second World War, which is why so little remains.

The tombs, by contrast, survived because they were considered sacred ground, and the modern city has grown right up to the moats. A mound like Nagatsuka often sits quietly between houses and a school ground, with a pine tree or two, a stone marker, and a sign that explains it in two languages. The contrast makes a rewarding walk, and it takes only a few minutes.

The ride list from here leads to Todai-ji in Nara, home of the Great Buddha, a bronze statue nearly fifteen metres high in one of the largest wooden buildings in the world. The way there crosses the Kongo hills and takes you through Nara's quiet streets, where deer roam the park and will sometimes block the road. Plan for slow riding at the park, as the animals are very tame and not at all afraid of motorbikes.

For fuel and food, Sakai has everything, and there are stations on the major roads leading to the hills. A bowl of udon or a plate of takoyaki, the octopus balls of Osaka, will carry you to Nara.

Be there on a quiet morning, when the heat has not yet built and the park is almost empty. The only sounds are birds and the hum of a distant train.
t.xurahue muyaca@22.6,-103.3:
In the high dry country of southern Zacatecas, the land is cut by canyons and spiny with mesquite, nopal cactus and agave, and the names of its places are a trail of Indigenous words. They sit in the region between the villages of Susticacán and Tepetongo, in the zone south-west of Zacatecas city where the highlands begin to drop towards the Juchipila valley, and the world around them is that of the Caxcan and Zacateco peoples who held the area before the Spanish arrived.

What I can say is that this was a frontier. In 1541, a great Indigenous rising known as the Mixtón War, led by Caxcan chiefs, nearly pushed the Spanish out of western Mexico, and it was only suppressed after a hard campaign. A few years later, the strike of silver at Zacatecas started the great mining boom that shaped the region, and the roads, haciendas and chapels that you see on the way are a product of those centuries of silver, cattle and maize.

Riding is a pleasure here, if a quiet one. Highways cross high plains of grass and thorn scrub at around two thousand metres, and the smaller roads wind between adobe villages with a plaza and a church, with goats in the verge and the occasional dog asleep in the sun. The altitude keeps the air fresh, and the days are warm and the nights cool. The rainy season from June to September brings afternoon storms, and the landscape turns green, while the dry months from November to April are clear, with crisp mornings.

Fuel is the thing to plan. The villages of Susticacán and Tepetongo are small, and you should not count on a pump, so fill the tank in Zacatecas or in a larger town on the main road before heading out. Carry water, and in the small tiendas you can buy sweet bread, cold drinks and cheese.

If you can find someone local to point out the site, the hills here are rewarding on foot, with views over the valleys and a sense of a very old country.
t.historic centre of the city of zacatecas:
Silver built Zacatecas, and the city still wears it like a coat. In 1546, a few years after the Spanish crushed the Indigenous rising of the Mixtón War, prospectors found a rich vein in the hills here, and within a generation the town was one of the wealthiest in the Americas, shipping silver across the Atlantic and bankrolling the Spanish crown. The money went into churches and mansions, and the centre, listed by UNESCO in 1993, is a tight, steep tangle of pink-stone buildings in a ravine between two hills, 2,400 metres above the sea.

The cathedral is the showpiece, built in the middle of the eighteenth century, and its main facade is a riot of carved stone, saints and angels and vines, in a baroque so exuberant that it looks poured rather than chiselled. Pink cantera stone, quarried locally, is used throughout the city and takes a rosy colour at sunset. You can ride a cable car, the teleférico, over the rooftops to the Cerro de la Bufa, the rocky crag that overlooks the city and was the scene of a great battle in 1914, when Pancho Villa's army took Zacatecas from federal troops and broke the back of the regime. The view from the top is wide, and the wind whips.

The El Edén mine, in the hillside, offers tours of old silver tunnels, entered by a little train, and a few streets away is the Callejón del Beso, a very narrow alley with a romantic legend. Zacatecas has several fine museums, and the old convent at Guadalupe, in the neighbouring town, holds a big collection of colonial painting.

Motorcycles have a hard time in the city centre. The streets are narrow, steep and cobbled, with one-way systems that confuse everyone, and the surface is slippery after rain. Leave the bike in a hotel garage or a car park on the edge, and take the cable car or walk. At this altitude engines can feel breathless, especially older carburettor machines, and the sun burns faster than you expect. Evenings are cool even in summer.

Fuel is easy in Zacatecas and neighbouring Guadalupe, which together have a quarter of a million people, so fill up before leaving for the long roads across the plateau. Try the local cooking: asado de boda, a pork stew in chilli sauce traditionally served at weddings, and a glass of mezcal or the local colonche, a fermented prickly-pear drink.
t.zona nucleo 02@20.7,-103.8:
The landscape of blue agave around Tequila is the best-known piece of this part of Jalisco, but its deeper story lies in a hillside near the village of Teuchitlán, where a civilisation built circles. Between about 300 BC and AD 900, the people of what archaeologists call the Teuchitlán tradition raised round pyramids with an outer ring of platforms, in a pattern that looks from the air like a target, and the locals call them guachimontones. They did not leave a written record, and no one knows what they called themselves, but the architecture suggests ritual and perhaps astronomy. The site's main group, with several of these circles, has been excavated and restored, and it sits on a lava slope above a small lake with the cone of the Tequila volcano on the horizon.

The agave fields are part of the same landscape. The blue Weber agave, which takes eight to twelve years to mature, is harvested by hand by jimadores, who cut away the spiky leaves with a long-handled blade called a coa and leave a heart like a giant pineapple, which is baked and fermented to make tequila. The old distilleries, the haciendas and the fields were inscribed as the Agave Landscape and Ancient Industrial Facilities of Tequila in 2006. The volcano, which rises to about 2,900 metres, gives the fields their mineral soil, and in the cool of the morning the rows of blue-grey plants stretch out in perfect lines.

The riding around here is excellent. From Guadalajara, the roads wind through the agave country on a fine surface with gentle bends, through small villages with colonial plazas, and the lake road toward Teuchitlán is quiet. Weather is warm for most of the year, and the rainy season, from June to September, brings late afternoon storms. The dry months from November to May are the best for riding.

Teuchitlán itself is a small town with a few thousand inhabitants, and it has a fuel station and cafes. For a bigger choice, head to the towns of Tequila or Ahualulco, or to Guadalajara, a huge city of several million. The ride list leads to the Hospicio Cabañas, the neoclassical orphanage in the centre of Guadalajara, with its murals by José Clemente Orozco, whose figure of a man on fire in the dome is one of the great paintings of Mexico.

Drink tequila politely, and not before you ride.
t.tvrdosin@49.3,19.6:
Tvrdošín lies in Orava, the northernmost corner of Slovakia, where the Orava river has been dammed to form a long reservoir under the dark ridges of the Western Tatras and the Roháče. It is a border country, not far from Poland, and a place of wood, snow and sheep, where for centuries people built in timber. The town has a wooden church that stands among the oldest in Slovakia, the Church of All Saints, built in the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century in Gothic style with a steep shingled roof, and its interior is painted with scenes in a folk style that moves between the grand and the endearing. It is one of the Wooden Churches of the Slovak part of the Carpathian Mountain Area, which UNESCO listed in 2008.

Orava has its own proud identity, with a castle that sits on a high cliff over the river, the Orava Castle at Oravský Podzámok, a place that German film director Murnau used for the 1922 film Nosferatu. The reservoir, built in the 1950s and 1960s, drowned a number of villages, and the water has its own fishing, sailing and bird life. In the hills, villages preserve a way of life with shingled farms and meadows, and the local cheese, the smoked sheep cheese called oštiepok, is a delicacy.

Riding in Orava is a pleasure. The roads climb gently from the valley floor into pine forest, with open meadows, and the views toward the Tatras are some of the finest in Slovakia. The surface varies, and in the villages you will find cattle, tractors and the occasional horse cart. Weather in the mountains changes quickly, and a clear morning can turn into a downpour by afternoon. Summer is mild and the autumn leaves are a feast, while winters are long and snowy, and the roads can be icy.

Tvrdošín is a town of nearly ten thousand inhabitants, with fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and Trstená, a few kilometres north towards the Polish border, has more. In a restaurant, look for bryndzové halušky, small potato dumplings with sheep cheese and crispy bacon, the national dish.

Park near the church and walk, since the gate is small, and the churchyard is a pleasant place to sit for a while.
t.zenemonyama kofun@34.6,135.5:
Sakai is a port city of well over seven hundred thousand people, and yet in the middle of its houses and factory roofs sit green islands with water around them. Zenemonyama is one of those islands: a burial mound from the age of the great keyhole-shaped tombs, built in the fifth century or thereabouts for someone powerful enough to move an entire hillside of earth by hand. You will not see much of the keyhole from the ground. The shape only makes sense from the air, which is rather the point, because it was made for an audience of gods and passing clouds.

Start here and you begin a ride in a very particular frame of mind. The suburban streets of Sakai are flat, grid-like and patient, with traffic lights every few hundred metres and scooters nosing between the cars, so this is not where anybody opens the throttle. Take it as the overture. Within an hour or so the Osaka plain gives way to the foothills of the Kongo and Katsuragi ranges, and the road starts to tilt and twist the way you came for.

The rides that leave from this mound point at the old pilgrim country to the south: the Omine Okugakemichi, the mountain path that ascetics of the Shugendo tradition walk from Yoshino down to Kumano, and the Kumano Sanzan shrines with Fudarakusan-ji by the sea. It is a nice piece of continuity. The people who built this tomb and the monks who tramped through the Kii mountains were separated by a thousand years, but both were obsessed with the idea that the land itself is sacred and that you honour it by going to a lot of trouble. On the Omine route the summit area of Sanjogatake still keeps the old rule that women do not climb it, which tells you how long some customs last in these hills.

Practical matters are easy here. Sakai is a big city, so fuel stations, vending machines and convenience stores with decent coffee and rice balls are never more than a few minutes away. Fill the tank before you head into the mountains, because the stations get sparse and close early once you are deep in the Kii peninsula. Expect heat and humidity in July and August, and the best riding weather in October and November, when the air is dry and the hillsides turn red and gold. Remember that Japan keeps to the left, and that the local drivers are far more courteous than their reputation, as long as you stay predictable.
t.magodayuyama kofun@34.6,135.5:
A heron stands in the moat as if it has been paid to be there. That is the first thing worth knowing about Magodayuyama: like most of the large burial mounds of Sakai, it is surrounded by water, and the water is full of life. Carp, turtles, reeds and a surprising amount of birdsong turn up in a part of Japan that otherwise has plenty of concrete. The mound itself is covered in trees that nobody has felled for centuries, since the Imperial Household Agency looks after many of these tombs and keeps people off them. You walk around the edge, not over it, and you read the shape from the lie of the moat.

These tombs belong to a cluster of fifth-century monuments around Sakai that earned World Heritage status in 2019, a few dozen mounds built when the rulers of Yamato were growing strong and wanted the ocean traffic from Korea and China to see how strong. The biggest, the Daisen Kofun, is nearly half a kilometre long. Magodayuyama is the quiet cousin, handy and unpretentious, tucked among houses, which is just the kind of place where you learn how Japanese towns absorb enormous history without a fuss.

The ride that starts here points inland and then up. Yoshino and the Omine mountains mean cedar forest, tight lanes and shadows, with Ominesan-ji, the temple of the mountain priests, beyond the hot-spring hamlet of Dorogawa. Reaching that area from Sakai usually means working through Nara prefecture, and the road gets narrower and slower the higher you go. In places a car and a motorbike must negotiate who gives way, and the surface can be damp and covered in needles and leaves. Treat it with respect, and go earlier rather than later in the day, because the valleys lose the sun quickly and the temperature drops by the kilometre.

For fuel, take no chances. Sakai has stations on every corner, and the next real choice is down in the valley towns on the Nara side. Dorogawa has onsen and a handful of simple places for noodles, but do not count on anything being open outside the main seasons. Spring brings cherry blossom up the Yoshino slopes in stages, from the foot to the summit across several weeks, and autumn is clear and calm. Midsummer is steamy, and typhoon season, in September especially, can close mountain roads for days.
t.itasuke kofun@34.6,135.5:
Itasuke is a modest keyhole-shaped mound from the same age of burial monuments that gave the city its World Heritage listing. It sits amid ordinary streets, one more piece of green surrounded by tiled roofs, with its moat and trees telling you that something older than the neighbourhood is under there. It is a reason to arrive early, on a quiet weekday morning, and see what a city looks like before the engines warm up.

The reason to start here is the road that follows. Kumano Hongu Taisha lies far to the south in the mountains of Wakayama, one of the three grand shrines of the Kumano region and the spiritual heart of a pilgrimage network that people walked for a thousand years. Emperors and ordinary farmers made the trip. The original shrine stood on a sandbar at the meeting of rivers until a flood in 1889 swept most of it away, after which the buildings were moved to higher ground, and the vast steel torii gate that stands at the old site is the tallest of its kind in Japan. It is a good place to see how Shinto and Buddhism mixed here, with no sharp line between them.

Getting there is the real adventure. From the plain you climb through Nara and then Wakayama on routes that follow rivers and ridges for long stretches, often with a single lane in each direction, and the bends come one after another through cedar plantations and past little villages that are stacked up the hillsides. Landslides and heavy rain have damaged this area repeatedly, notably in the typhoon of 2011, so check the status of roads before you set out. The tarmac is often rough in the shadows, and moss and fallen branches are common.

Keep the tank topped up in Sakai or the first towns on the way, because south of the main valleys the stations are far apart and some close early in the evening. Convenience stores are the reliable source of coffee and food, and a bowl of noodles at a roadside restaurant tastes better than it has any right to. Plan a night in the Kumano area if you can: the hot springs at Yunomine are among the oldest in Japan, and a long soak after a day on the bike is exactly what the legs need.
t.komoyamazuka kofun@34.6,135.5:
On the map, Komoyamazuka looks like a green thumbprint pressed into the urban sprawl of Sakai, and that is not far off the truth. It is one of the keyhole-shaped burial mounds in the great tomb cluster that gives the city its place on the World Heritage list, an old mound, likely from the fifth century, wearing a moat and a crown of trees. Nobody is quite sure who lies inside many of these mounds, since archaeologists have rarely been allowed to dig, and the names we use are often a mix of old tradition and later guesswork.

Sakai has always been a place of stubborn pride. In the late Middle Ages it was a free merchant city, run by a council of wealthy traders and protected by a moat of its own, and it was the port through which Portuguese goods, firearms and Christianity reached the Japanese interior. The city made its name through trade and craft, and the knives you see in kitchens around the world, with their sharp, hand-forged edges, still come in large part from here. If you have a free hour, visiting a knife shop is a lesson in quiet engineering. Sen no Rikyu, the tea master who shaped the whole idea of the tea ceremony, was also born in Sakai, which seems fitting for a city that valued refinement as much as profit.

The ride that begins here heads to Daigo-ji, east of Kyoto. The temple dates to the ninth century and holds a five-storey pagoda that is among the oldest standing buildings in the Kyoto area, finished in the middle of the tenth century. The warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi held a lavish cherry-blossom party on its slopes in 1598, a few months before he died, and the flowering trees still draw crowds each April. To get there you cross the whole urban corridor between Osaka and Kyoto, and it is not a ride to savour. Take the expressways, accept the tolls, and save your energy for the quieter hills beyond Fushimi.

Sakai is a big place, so you will find fuel, food and a bed with no trouble at all. The one thing to watch is the traffic: it is thick on weekday mornings, and parking for motorcycles is less generous than in other parts of Japan, so check that your hotel can host a bike before you arrive.
t.hatazuka kofun@34.6,135.5:
Bicycles are the unofficial emblem of Sakai, and that makes Hatazuka a nicely ironic place to begin a motorcycle ride. The city's most famous modern company, Shimano, which makes gears and brakes for cyclists around the world, was founded here in the 1920s, and on the quiet streets around the old tombs you will see a great many commuters, children and elderly shoppers on two wheels. Hatazuka itself is one of the smaller mounded tombs in the cluster of fifth-century monuments that the city is proud of, its earthen slopes now wooded and its moat quiet, an easy place to pause and look at before the day's engine noise begins.

The ride goes north-east to Hokki-ji, a small temple in Ikaruga, in Nara prefecture, a few steps from the more famous Horyu-ji. Hokki-ji has a three-storey pagoda that dates from the early eighth century, and it is regarded as the oldest of its type in Japan. It stands in a calm compound among persimmon trees and rice fields, and the whole district around Ikaruga has a flat, rural, almost sleepy feel, with low hills in the distance and old farm walls. Prince Shotoku, the early statesman who promoted Buddhism in Japan at the start of the seventh century, lived and worked here, which makes this district one of the cradles of Japanese culture.

Between Sakai and Ikaruga, expect a lot of town riding. You cross the Yamato river basin, then follow urban roads past suburbs, shopping strips and rice paddies in a patchwork that goes on for most of the way. The pace is slow, the junctions are frequent, and speed limits are enforced with cameras and patrol cars. It is a relaxed day for exploring rather than for pushing the machine, and the reward is the surprise of finding a thirteen-hundred-year-old pagoda down a lane between houses.

Everything you need is easy to find. Fuel stations sit on every main road, and you will not go hungry, with bakeries, noodle shops and vending machines all around. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild air and clear light, while the damp heat of summer can be fierce on the plain. Use the long weekend queues as an excuse to leave early, because Nara is popular with visitors and the roads fill up by late morning.
t.shichikannon kofun@34.6,135.5:
Haniwa are the clue to this place. These clay cylinders and figures, shaped as houses, horses, warriors and dancers, were set around the slopes of the great Japanese tombs to guard the dead, and replicas of them now stand in parks and museums in Sakai. Shichikannon is a mound from that world, one of the numerous burial sites in the city that became a World Heritage property in 2019, and as with its neighbours you appreciate it from outside the moat. The lawn, the trees and the water do most of the talking.

What makes the Sakai tomb field remarkable is its scale. The largest, the Daisen Kofun, runs close to five hundred metres from end to end and was probably the work of thousands of labourers over years. The people who ordered such things were shaping a political message. They were declaring a dynasty at the point when contacts with the mainland were bringing iron, writing and Buddhism into Japan, and a tomb that could be seen from ships in the bay of Osaka was a handy form of advertising.

Your ride heads off toward Horyu-ji in the Ikaruga area of Nara, a few dozen kilometres away. The temple was founded in the early seventh century by Prince Shotoku, and its main buildings are considered the oldest surviving wooden structures in the world, which is a bold claim and a fair one. The five-storey pagoda and the main hall stand in a long cloister, quiet and weathered, with a smell of old cedar and incense. The place makes you slow down, and you should. Photographers will like the pale morning light on the wooden eaves, and Nara's deer, famous in the city, are not here, so you can eat your lunch in peace.

The road between the two sights crosses the broad Yamato basin, so the riding is mostly flat and sometimes tedious: lights, crossings, scooters, small trucks. But a little lateral thinking pays off. Look for the quieter prefectural roads that wind between rice fields and irrigation ponds and avoid the national route at commuting times. Fuel and drinks are easy to find in Sakai and along the way, since the area is densely settled. Autumn is the best season, with clear air, harvested paddies and the persimmons glowing orange on bare branches along the farm lanes.
t.minegazuka kofun@34.6,135.6:
East of the great ranges, the Osaka plain narrows toward the Yamato river, and this is where the old tomb country of the Furuichi group begins. Minegazuka is one of the burial mounds scattered through the districts of Habikino, Fujiidera and Kashiwara, all of them tucked into a landscape that is now mostly suburbs, vineyards and small factories. These monuments belong to the same fifth-century family of tombs as the ones around Sakai, and together the two clusters make up a single World Heritage property. The largest mound in this neighbourhood, close by in Habikino, is the tomb traditionally given to the emperor Ojin, one of the largest mounds in the country by volume.

There is another surprise: Habikino and Kashiwara are the heart of Osaka's grape country. The slopes at the foot of the hills carry vineyards of table grapes and some wine grapes, and in late summer you will pass roadside stalls selling the fruit. It is the kind of detail that makes the area feel lived in rather than a museum piece, a place where the ancient mounds simply stand beside the vines.

The ride goes to Todai-ji in Nara, where the Great Buddha Hall shelters a bronze figure that was consecrated in 752, the original centrepiece of the capital's religious life. The present hall is smaller than the first, though still huge, and it counts among the largest wooden buildings anywhere. Next door, the deer of Nara Park bow for rice crackers and will happily steal a map out of your pocket, so keep the bike luggage zipped. To get there you go east over the Kongo-Ikoma hills by one of the old passes, which give a little relief from city riding: some bends, a bit of forest, a view back across the plain.

You can find fuel in every town along the way. Aim to cross the hills outside rush hours and not on a sunny autumn Sunday, when the road to Nara is blocked with traffic. If you want a break before the climb, the grape farms often have little cafes and shops, which is a pleasant change from vending-machine coffee.
t.mounded tomb of emperor temmu and empres:
Under a modest round hill in the rice fields of Asuka lie two people who changed Japan: the Emperor Temmu, who died in 686, and his wife, who ruled after him as Empress Jito. Temmu had come to power by winning a short and bloody civil war in 672, the Jinshin disturbance, after hiding for a while in the mountains of Yoshino. Jito, who died in 702, was cremated, unusually for her time, and her ashes were laid beside her husband's. The tomb is octagonal, an echo of the imperial throne's shape, and a deliberate rank marker in the burial customs of the late seventh century.

Asuka has the feel of a place where Japan found its feet. It was the seat of the court in the sixth and seventh centuries, when Buddhism arrived and Chinese models of government were adopted, and the flat valley is dotted with strange stone monuments: giant granite blocks in tombs, carved stone figures whose purpose nobody quite knows, and the painted chamber of Takamatsuzuka, whose murals of women in colourful robes startled everyone when they were found in the 1970s. The whole region is gentle and green, and in September the paddy banks glow with red spider lilies.

The ride from here goes to the Yoshino and Omine area, which suits the story: you retrace, more or less, the path of an exile heading into the mountains. The road leaves the Asuka basin and rises into the Yoshino hills by roads lined with cedar and persimmon, with climbs that get steadily narrower. Kimpusen-ji, the headquarters of the mountain Shugendo tradition, and its enormous wooden hall of Zao Gongen stand high on the slope above the town of Yoshino, a place known above all for its cherry trees, planted by pilgrims over the centuries and flowering in waves from the lower slopes to the summit in April.

Remember a few practical things. The back lanes of Asuka are tiny, shared with cyclists and farm vehicles, and the village streets are often barely wider than a car, so go gently. Kashihara has fuel stations and food in good supply, but between there and Yoshino the choice shrinks. During the cherry season Yoshino is very crowded, and the road up to it may be restricted, so go in the off-season, or very early. Autumn colour, in November, is also lovely, and much quieter.
t.chuai tenno ryo kofun@34.6,135.6:
Chuai is a name from the mists of early Japanese legend. The Chronicles describe him as the fourteenth emperor, husband of the formidable Empress Jingu, who is said to have led an army against the Korean peninsula while pregnant, and he died on the way in Kyushu. Historians doubt that he existed as described, but tradition places his tomb here, in the town of Fujiidera, in the heart of the Furuichi tomb group, and the Imperial Household Agency treats it as his resting place. The mound is a keyhole shape with a moat, and the trees on it are thick and old, as at the other great tombs of this region.

Fujiidera is the smallest sort of Japanese city, a dense grid of houses, shopping streets and railway lines, wedged between Habikino and Kashiwara. It takes its name from the temple of Fujii-dera, a Kannon temple on the old pilgrimage circuit of western Japan, whose gardens are famed for wisteria in spring, and the name itself means the temple of the wisteria well. You can walk from the temple to the tomb and see, in an easy afternoon, two very different kinds of Japanese sacred ground.

The Furuichi group is the sister of the Mozu group in Sakai, and together they form the World Heritage site of the mounded tombs of the ancient Japanese. The mounds here were built in the fourth to fifth centuries, a time of huge political change, and some of the largest are the tombs of rulers who seem to have commanded the whole plain. Walking around the moat on a quiet morning, you feel how unlikely these mounds are in such a busy region.

Your ride takes you to Todai-ji in Nara, across the Ikoma and Kongo hills, and it is a little more interesting than the urban start suggests. You leave the plain via one of the passes on the east side and climb into a different world of forest, shrine steps and slow bends before dropping into the Nara basin. The hall that shelters the Great Buddha is among the largest wooden buildings in the world, and the surrounding park is full of tame deer.

Fuel and food are plentiful on the Osaka side, and the stations get fewer only if you take the very smallest mountain lanes. Weekends in spring and autumn bring heavy traffic toward Nara, so try to be early. Use the time before the crowds to enjoy the calm of the tomb.
t.koyasan niutsuhime jinja@34.3,135.5:
A hunter with two dogs, according to the legend, is why Koyasan exists. When the monk Kukai, later called Kobo Daishi, returned from studying in China in the early ninth century, he threw a ritual three-pronged object into the air and asked it to land on a site for a mountain monastery. He found it hanging in a pine tree on a high plateau in the Kii mountains, and there he met a hunter, the god Karibamyojin, who led him to the place with his dogs. The hunter's mother, the goddess Niutsuhime, is honoured at the shrine that guards the approach. Kukai founded his monastery in 816, and Koyasan has been the headquarters of Shingon Buddhism since.

Niutsuhime-jinja is part of that mountain world, a Shinto shrine that sits alongside the Buddhist halls in the way that Japan's two religions often do. Koyasan today is a town of temples on a forested plateau about eight hundred metres up, with more than a hundred monasteries, many of which take overnight guests who eat vegetarian monastic meals and join the dawn prayers. Okunoin, the great cemetery that leads to Kobo Daishi's mausoleum, is lined with huge cedars and more than two hundred thousand tombs and memorials, and walking it at dusk is one of the strongest experiences in Japan.

The ride up is half the pleasure. From Hashimoto, on the Kinokawa river, the road climbs through steep forest in a series of hairpins, with the plateau opening out above you. Beyond, the Koya-Ryujin Skyline, a long ridge road, runs south, with views across the folded Kii mountains. It is cool at altitude in summer, and in winter snow and ice are likely, so chains or a decision to wait may be called for. The fog can close in quickly, and sudden showers drift over the ridges, so a rain layer is wise.

Your route heads on to Jisho-ji, better known as Ginkaku-ji, the Silver Pavilion in Kyoto, and it is a long day across the Kii highlands and the Nara basin. Fuel is available in Hashimoto, and in the town of Koyasan there is a small selection, but do not run the tank down. The hill town has little in the way of nightlife, and dinner is early, so plan your arrival for the afternoon. For many riders, a night in a temple lodging, with its silence, its tatami floor and its morning chanting, makes the long ride worth it.
t.temple of the town of san jose de avino@:
Silver built this road, and the old church at San Jose de Avino is one of the buildings that mark it. The Camino Real de Tierra Adentro was the great highway of colonial Mexico, running more than two thousand kilometres from Mexico City north to Santa Fe in New Mexico, used by mule trains carrying silver south and supplies north for nearly three centuries. A section of it, with a number of towns and monuments along the way, was listed as a World Heritage site in 2010. Avino was a mining settlement in the hills of Durango, one of the earliest silver camps of the north, and the temple stands in the village as a reminder of the money and faith that came with the mine.

The country around is high plateau, dry and open, with scrub, yucca and prickly pear, and a sky that goes on forever. In winter the nights can be frosty, and the mornings are sharp and clear. To the east, across the border into Zacatecas, the Sierra de Organos rises from the plain, a set of basalt cliffs in tall columns that look like the pipes of a giant church organ. The rocks are so striking that a number of Western films were shot there, and the walking trails among the pillars are popular.

For a rider, the Mexican plateau offers long, straight, quiet roads, with distant ranges, the occasional village and big skies. Highway 45 between Durango and Zacatecas follows the old trade route, and traffic on it is mixed, with lorries and buses. Watch for cattle, potholes and the sudden appearance of speed bumps, called topes, in villages. Winds can be strong on the open plains, and the distances between towns are long, so do not rely on reaching a station late in the day. Winter mornings can be below freezing at this altitude, which is about two thousand metres.

Ciudad Guadalupe Victoria, twenty kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, with fuel stations, shops and basic hotels. In the smaller villages, services are limited, but you will often find a family kitchen serving beans, tortillas, cheese and strong coffee. Durango is known for its mescal and its beef, and local people are friendly to travellers who stop. Plan your day around the light, because the colours of the plateau are best in the hour after sunrise and the hour before sunset, when the hills glow.
t.historic centre of the city of san luis:
The name Potosi was a marketing decision. When silver turned up in the hills east of the new Spanish settlement in the 1590s, the founders hoped that this town would rival the fabulous silver mountain of Potosi in what is now Bolivia, and so they borrowed the name and added San Luis, after Saint Louis. The mines at Cerro de San Pedro did not match the original, but they were good enough to make the town rich, and the historic centre of San Luis Potosi is full of the buildings that money bought: a baroque cathedral with twin towers, a Carmelite church with a tiled dome, and the arcades of the plazas, all in warm pink and ochre stone.

The city lies at about 1,850 metres on the high central plateau, a dry country of scrub and cactus, with cold winter nights and warm, bright days. The Teatro de la Paz, a nineteenth-century theatre, and a number of old mansions and museums sit within a short walk of each other, and in the evening, people gather in the plazas, with vendors selling fruit and sweets. Local food is a strong point: enchiladas potosinas, made with a dough coloured by chile, are the city's signature dish, and the little cheese-filled pastries and the mineral-rich honey sweets are good, too. Cerro de San Pedro, the old mining town above the city, is now a quiet ghost-like village, with a small museum.

For a motorbike rider, the city is a base and a rest stop. Traffic in the centre is busy, and parking can be hard, so look for a hotel with a secure courtyard. Beyond the ring road, the ride heads south-west toward Ojuelos, passing across high plains of grass and scrub, with long, empty straights, distant ranges, and the occasional hacienda. The road surface is variable, and trucks use the highways heavily, so keep alert. The wind can be strong, and in winter the cold surprises people who expected a southern climate.

San Luis Potosi is a big city of more than seven hundred thousand people, so fuel stations, mechanics and shops are everywhere. The old centre has several pedestrian streets, making it a pleasant place to walk. October to April is the best time to ride, with clear skies, while summer afternoons bring storms. Take a jacket for the evening, because the high plateau cools quickly after sunset.
t.brno@49.2,16.6:
Brno is the second city of the Czech Republic, but it behaves like the first city of Moravia, with its own dialect, its own pride and its own very good wine. About 370,000 people live here, a lot of them students, and the centre has the mixture of old and new you would expect: a medieval core below a hilltop castle, baroque churches, and a serious collection of twentieth-century modern architecture.

Spilberk, the castle on the hill, was for a while a fortress and then a notorious prison under the Habsburgs, and it now holds a museum. Down below, the cathedral of St Peter and Paul stands on the Petrov hill, and at noon its bells ring eleven, a custom said to date from a siege by the Swedes in the Thirty Years War, when a trick with the clock saved the city. Gregor Mendel, the father of genetics, lived and worked at the Augustinian abbey here, doing his pea experiments in the monastery garden. The Villa Tugendhat, designed by Mies van der Rohe and finished in 1930, is on the UNESCO list and is one of the best-known houses of the modern movement.

Motorcyclists know Brno for another reason: its racing circuit, which has hosted the Czech motorcycle grand prix for decades and is a short ride out of town. The old street circuit that ran through the villages outside the city was one of the great road courses of Europe before it closed in 1986. For touring, the wine country south of Brno is the draw. Villages with cellar lanes, vineyards in neat rows, and flat or gently rolling roads toward Mikulov and the Palava hills make a relaxed day.

Fuel is easy, with stations on every major road. Brno is a good place to eat, with solid Czech food and local wines by the glass at reasonable prices. Parking in the centre is limited, so look for a garage or ask your hotel. Traffic in the middle of town is dense during commuting hours, and the tram lines are slippery when wet.
t.traismauer kastell zentralbereich@48.3,1:
Traismauer is a small town of under three thousand people on the Traisen river, a few kilometres from the Danube, and underneath its streets lies a Roman fortress. In Roman times, it was called Augustianis, a cavalry fort on the frontier of the Empire, one of a chain of military posts that ran along the south bank of the Danube. The line of forts, towers and roads was the Danube Limes, and in 2021 UNESCO added its western section to the World Heritage List, with sites in Austria, Germany and Slovakia.

The central area of the fort lies under the old town, and you notice the Roman layout in the street plan, with the main streets running at right angles, and in the old walls that still stand in places. A museum in the area tells the story of the garrison, the soldiers who came from across the Empire, and the settlement that grew up outside the walls. The Roman fort was occupied until the fifth century, and the town carried on from there, through the Middle Ages and into the modern era.

The surrounding landscape is gentle: wide fields of wheat and maize, vineyards on the low hills, the green line of the Danube floodplain to the north. The Traisental is a wine-growing area, and the white Gruner Veltliner from here is worth a glass if you are not riding on. The river valley is also popular with cyclists, and you can share the quiet roads with them.

Riding here is relaxed. The roads are good, with light traffic, and a mixture of long straights and easy bends. The Danube cycle path runs nearby, and the Wachau valley, famous for its terraced vineyards and ruined castles, is a short ride upstream. Fuel and food are available in the town, with a supermarket, bakeries and inns, and the larger town of St. Polten is a short ride south. Spring and autumn are the pleasant seasons, though harvest time can bring tractors on the lanes.
t.city of graz historic centre and schloss:
Graz has the best-preserved old town in Austria outside Salzburg and Vienna, and it is much less crowded than either. The historic centre, a UNESCO site since 1999, sits on the river Mur beneath the Schlossberg, a rocky hill with a clock tower on top, and the roofs of the old town are a sea of red tile punctuated by domes and spires. Add a modern touch, the glass and steel Murinsel, an artificial island in the river, and the Kunsthaus, a blue bubble nicknamed the friendly alien, and the city has a mix of old and new that works.

Schloss Eggenberg, a short tram ride from the centre, is the other half of the listing. It was built in the early seventeenth century for Hans Ulrich von Eggenberg, a powerful adviser to the Habsburg emperor, and designed to represent the cosmos, with its state rooms, windows and towers laid out according to the calendar and the planets. Inside, the sequence of richly decorated state rooms is among the finest baroque interiors in Austria, and the Planetary Room, with its painted ceiling, is the one to see. The park outside has peacocks, which wander about like they own the place.

For riders, Graz is a gateway to Styria, the green heart of Austria, with its hills, vineyards and forests. Roads in every direction offer pleasant riding, including the winding routes of the Styrian wine country to the south, and the Schockl mountain and the Alpine foothills to the north. The city itself is busy, with trams and cyclists, and the old centre is largely closed to cars, so park at the edge.

All services are here: fuel, repair shops, hotels and restaurants. Try the local pumpkin seed oil, dark green and nutty, drizzled on a salad or even on vanilla ice cream, and a glass of Schilcher, a tart rose wine from the west of the region. The city is at its best in spring and early autumn.
At Traismauer, one Roman tower still stands high enough to be seen from the street. The Hufeisenturm, the horseshoe tower, is a rounded corner tower of the old cavalry fort Augustianis, named for its shape, and it was part of a defensive wall that ran for hundreds of metres around the Roman garrison. The brick and stone, laid in neat courses, survived because later builders used it as part of the town's medieval walls, and it has been preserved and restored in recent decades.

The fort stood on the Danube Limes, the northern frontier of the Roman Empire in this region, where the river formed a natural border with the Germanic peoples to the north. Soldiers here patrolled the river, watched for trouble and collected tolls, and they were supported by a civil settlement nearby, where traders, craftspeople and families lived. UNESCO placed the western Danube Limes on the World Heritage list in 2021, and this tower is one of the fragments that shows what the whole system looked like.

The walk around the tower is short, but it gives a good sense of scale. The walls rise several metres, and the pattern of the stones shows where repairs were made. Nearby is the Roman Gate, a surviving medieval structure which incorporates earlier material, and a small museum in the town explains the finds. The setting is quiet, with narrow streets and well-kept houses, and few visitors.

Traismauer lies in the Traisental, a region of orchards, vineyards and farmland, on the doorstep of Lower Austria's wine country. The roads here are quiet and smooth, with easy curves and long views over fields, and cyclists share them in summer. Fuel, groceries and a few inns are available in the town, which has about 2,750 inhabitants, and larger towns like Tulln and St. Polten are within easy reach. The Danube itself is a short ride north, and a ferry or bridge takes you across to the other bank.

Ride in spring, when the fruit trees are in flower, or in autumn, when the grape harvest brings tractors and the smell of must. Midsummer afternoons can be hot, and thunderstorms are occasional.
t.pleasure garden@49.3,17.4:
Kroměříž is a small, handsome town on the Morava in the Haná country, the flat and fertile middle of Moravia, and its Pleasure Garden, the Květná zahrada, is a surprise to anyone who arrives expecting a quiet agricultural place. It was laid out in the seventeenth century for a prince-bishop of Olomouc, Karl Liechtenstein-Kastelkorn, who wanted a formal Baroque garden with clipped hedges, parterres and a long colonnade, and the pattern has been preserved with unusual faithfulness. The garden is on the World Heritage list together with the castle.

What you notice first is the geometry. Paths run straight to a rotunda and the colonnade, which closes the garden like a long screen of arches, and the whole design is meant to be seen from a particular angle, with the eye drawn down the central axis. The planting has been restored, with lawn and flower beds, and in summer the roses and the neat order give it a calm, slightly theatrical feel. It is a good place to sit for half an hour and watch the town go about its day.

The roads into Kroměříž are very pleasant for a relaxed ride. They cross gently rolling farmland with fruit orchards and wheat fields, then run through villages with a church tower at the centre, and the surface is generally good. Corners are easy and traffic is moderate outside the rush hours. If you come from Lednice and Valtice, as this ride does, you cross a good stretch of Moravian wine and farm country and can reflect on how much of this land belonged to a few aristocratic families.

Kroměříž is large enough, with almost thirty thousand people, to have all the fuel, food and beds you need, and you will not struggle to find a good lunch. Czech cooking is generous, with pork, dumplings and cabbage, and the local beer is more than respectable. Park near the old town and walk, because the centre is compact.

Spring and early autumn are the best times to visit, when the garden is in flower or the leaves are turning, and the light across the Haná plain softens. Midsummer is warm but still fine, and the crowds remain modest compared with Prague.
t.gardens and castle at kromeriz@49.3,17.4:
Kroměříž is where Czech parliamentary history briefly came to rest. In 1848, when revolution shook the Habsburg lands, the Austrian constituent assembly moved here from Vienna for safety, and the archbishop's castle housed a group of delegates who tried to write a liberal constitution before the emperor dissolved them. That fact tends to surprise people who come for the gardens, but it fits the place: a small town with an unusually grand residence, built for the bishops of Olomouc.

The castle itself is a large Baroque palace, reconstructed after a fire in the seventeenth century, with rich interiors, a library of rare books and a music archive. Its art gallery contains an important collection that includes Titian's late masterpiece The Flaying of Marsyas, a fierce, dark painting that people rarely expect to find in a Moravian provincial town. Next to the castle lies a landscaped park by the Morava, while the formal Flower Garden lies a little to the north, and together they form the listed ensemble.

The roads in are good for an unhurried day. They cross the Haná plain, one of the most productive farming regions in the Czech lands, and they are lined with fruit trees and fields of grain. Corners are gentle, surfaces mostly good, and you meet the usual Czech mix of tractors and local drivers. The ride from Lednice and Valtice crosses wine country and so gives a nice contrast between the vineyards in the south and the farmland here.

Kroměříž is a proper town of nearly thirty thousand, so fuel and meals present no difficulty. The square is lively, there are cafés where you can sit with a coffee and a slice of cake, and local restaurants serve hearty Moravian dishes. The Haná region is also known for its cheese, which has a strong smell and a loyal following, though it is not for everyone.

Visit in late spring or early autumn if you can, when the parks are at their best and the town is calm. Allow at least a couple of hours, because the interiors reward patience and the park is a fine place to wander once you have looked at the paintings.
t.asuka palace site@34.5,135.8:
Few places in Japan can claim as much early history as the plain of Asuka, in the south of the Nara basin. In the seventh century, before Nara or Kyoto existed, the court moved from place to place, and for much of that century the centre of power was here. The Asuka Palace Site, also called Itabuki, was the residence of several sovereigns, and the building was reworked more than once. In 645, in the audience hall of this palace, the court strongman Soga no Iruka was cut down in front of the empress by Prince Naka no Oe and Nakatomi no Kamatari, an assassination that opened the way to the Taika reforms, the first attempt to build a centralised state on the Chinese model.

Today the site is a large, quiet field, with pale gravel marking the lines of the posts and low platforms showing where the halls once stood. It is not dramatic, and it asks for a little imagination, but the setting does a lot. The hills of Asuka rise on all sides, with small green mountains and neat terraced rice fields, and on a clear day the three Yamato mountains, Unebi, Miminashi and Kagu, appear in the distance. In spring, fields of yellow rapeseed and pink cherry trees appear along the lanes, and in September the red spider lilies bloom along the rice paddies.

The riding is small-scale and slow. The lanes of Asuka are narrow, winding and often shared with cyclists, since renting a bicycle is the favourite way to see the village, and signposts in English are limited. The prefectural roads around the district connect Sakurai and Kashihara, both substantial towns of over sixty thousand and over a hundred thousand people respectively, so fuel, convenience stores and restaurants are available within a short distance. Within Asuka itself, there is little more than a few shops and cafés.

Japanese traffic rules, with driving on the left, strict speed limits and polite but firm enforcement, apply, and farm trucks are common. Rain in the early summer, from June to July, can last for days, and summers are hot and humid. Spring and autumn are the best times.

Many of the places in Asuka are linked by a short loop, and a few hours are enough to cover the main ones, though the best advice is to take your time and let the landscape do its work.
t.asuka pond garden site@34.5,135.8:
In the Asuka district, a stone-lined pond lies below a gentle slope, with a channel feeding it and a neat edge of laid cobbles. The Asuka Pond Garden Site was uncovered in the late twentieth century, and it shows that the aristocracy of seventh-century Japan took water seriously, both as a garden feature and as part of ritual. The pond belongs to a type of formal water garden that was introduced from the Asian continent, along with Buddhism and Chinese court culture, and it was probably part of a palace or an elite residence, though the precise function is still debated.

What I find affecting is how modest it is. A pond, a few stones and a channel, now partly reconstructed, but the care in laying the shoreline stones, each chosen and set in place by hand over thirteen centuries ago, says a great deal about the people who made it. Archaeologists have also found wooden objects, which survive in damp ground, giving a rare glimpse of everyday life, such as writing tablets known as mokkan, used to record messages and accounts.

The surroundings are quintessential rural Japan. Small rice paddies, vegetable plots, persimmon trees and farmhouses with grey-tiled roofs line the lane, and the sound is mostly frogs, cicadas, and the occasional tractor. The roads are narrow, lined with drainage ditches on both sides, and edges are soft, so take care when giving way. The local roads link up with the prefectural routes that lead to Sakurai, about four kilometres away, and Kashihara, only slightly farther, where fuel, supermarkets and restaurants can be found.

Time of year matters. In summer the paddies are bright green and the heat is oppressive, with thunderstorms in the afternoon, and mosquitoes are a nuisance in the evening. In autumn the rice turns gold and the persimmons ripen to orange, which is when the whole district looks its best. Winter is clear and cold, with occasional frost on the fields.

If you visit, remember that the sites in Asuka are mostly free to enter and unstaffed, but they are in farmland and near homes, so be quiet, stay on the paths and leave nothing behind. A local bakery or tea shop in the village makes a good stop, and sweets made from mugwort, a local favourite, go well with green tea.
t.sakafuneishi ritual site@34.5,135.8:
Sitting in a quiet field in Asuka is a carved piece of granite that has puzzled people for centuries. Sakafuneishi, the sake boat stone, is a granite block about five metres long, with a shallow basin and a channel cut into the top, and it looks like a boat, which is where the name comes from. It was carved in the seventh century and probably belonged to a ritual or water-related setting, perhaps used for purification ceremonies or for the supply of water in a nearby garden or palace. Nobody knows for sure, and that is part of its appeal.

Asuka has several of these mysterious stone objects, scattered among the fields, and they have become famous. Besides the boat-shaped stone, there are carved tortoise stones, a stone figure said to represent a man and woman, and another stone with a peculiar curved surface. They are probably the remains of a garden or ceremonial space, built for the court of the time with exotic foreign influences, since stonework like this was rare in Japan then and may reflect contacts with the Korean peninsula and China.

The ride to Sakafuneishi is a slow, local one. The lanes are tiny, with little traffic apart from farm vehicles and cyclists, and the land is gently rolling, with rice terraces, bamboo groves and low wooded hills. Roads can be rough at the edge and there are hidden ditches, so keep to the middle and ride slowly. Sakurai is the nearest large town, and Kashihara is also close, so fuel, food and convenience stores are plentiful there, while the village has little beyond a couple of small shops.

The weather is humid, with a rainy season in June and early July and typhoons in late summer and early autumn. Spring blossoms and autumn colours are the best seasons, and clear winter days give crisp views of the surrounding mountains.

It is worth noting that Asuka is a living village, not a museum, and local residents may be tending their fields near the sites, so a polite greeting goes a long way. Finish with a walk along the field paths to the next stone, and enjoy the quiet, with the scent of earth and hay.
t.kawara dera temple site@34.5,135.8:
Kawara-dera is one of the oldest temples in Japan, though you would not guess it from what remains. It was founded in the seventh century in the Asuka district, and it appears in early records as a significant monastery, linked to the imperial family. In the Nihon Shoki, the early chronicle of Japan, the funeral rites for Empress Saimei were held here in the year 661, and the temple was said to have grown into a great complex with a pagoda and a lecture hall. Over the centuries, as the capital moved to Nara and then to Kyoto, it declined, and today only foundation stones, a smaller modern hall and open fields are left.

What gives the site its character is the scale of the foundation stones, which show how large the original buildings must have been, and the lotus flowers that bloom in the nearby ponds in summer. Walking among the stones you can read the plan of the old temple: the pagoda base, the golden hall, the lecture hall in a line, an arrangement borrowed from the Korean peninsula. Excavations have recovered roof tiles, including some of the earliest examples in Japan, with lotus patterns, and they are shown in local museums.

Riding to the temple is part of a quiet loop. The lanes are narrow and surfaced, with little traffic, and the surrounding rice paddies, vegetable plots and low hills keep a pleasant, unhurried feel. You will often share the road with walkers and cyclists, and a quiet engine and a gentle throttle go well with the setting. Sakurai and Kashihara, both within about five kilometres, offer fuel, supermarkets and a range of restaurants. In the village, there are small cafés and shops selling local produce, but they close early.

Seasonally, summer is hot, humid and loud with cicadas, and the lotus bloom in July and August is worth the heat if you start early. Autumn offers cool air, red leaves and golden fields, and spring brings cherry blossoms. Winter is cold but clear.

Near the temple site, the village of Asuka has a few tea houses where you can sit on tatami and drink green tea with a sweet bean cake, a simple pleasure after a morning on the bike. Remember that the area is used by locals, so keep the engine noise down.
t.asuka dera temple site@34.5,135.8:
Asuka-dera is where Japanese Buddhism first took root in earnest. The temple was started in the late sixth century by Soga no Umako, the most powerful minister of his day, as the first full-scale Buddhist temple in the country, built with the help of craftsmen sent from the Korean kingdom of Baekje. Tile makers, bronze casters and architects crossed the sea, and the layout they used, with a pagoda surrounded by three golden halls, was a new thing on these islands, where until then the gods had been honoured in groves and simple shrines.

What you can see today is a modest hall, rebuilt in the nineteenth century, sheltering a huge seated bronze Buddha, known as the Asuka Daibutsu, cast in the early seventh century by the sculptor Tori Busshi. It is the oldest surviving large Buddhist image in Japan, and the face has an archaic, smiling quality, with almond eyes and a gentle expression that reflect continental styles of the time. The statue has been damaged by fire and repaired, and some parts are later, but the core is original. Photography inside is generally not allowed, and a small entrance fee is charged.

In front of the temple stands a stone memorial to Soga no Iruka, who was killed in 645, and not far away is a small monument that marks the spot where, according to tradition, his severed head came to rest. The history of Asuka was violent and political as well as religious.

On the road, expect a cheerful, slow experience. The lanes of Asuka are narrow and quiet, often with rental bicycles and walkers, and the temple lies in the middle of the village, with a few shops, cafés and tea houses opposite. The ride into the village from Sakurai takes only ten minutes, and you will find fuel, convenience stores and restaurants there, as well as in Kashihara. It is easy to combine this site with the other places in the area, such as the stone monuments, the water clock site and the great tomb of Ishibutai.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons. In summer, the heat is heavy, and in the rainy season the lanes are slippery with leaves and mud. Early morning light is particularly good for photographs of the temple gate. A bowl of noodles or a rice ball with pickles from a village shop makes a simple lunch.
t.nakaoyama mounded tomb@34.5,135.8:
The Nara basin is dotted with burial mounds, called kofun, and they are the oldest big monuments of the Japanese state. Between the third and the seventh centuries, rulers and their clans were buried in earthen mounds, some shaped like a keyhole, some round and some square, surrounded by moats and decorated with rows of clay figures called haniwa. The famous giant tombs are in Osaka, but Nara holds some of the earliest and the later stone-chambered ones, and the area around Asuka and Kashihara has several.

Most of these mounds are now covered in trees and grass, with a path around the moat, and some are protected by the Imperial Household Agency, which restricts access to those it identifies as imperial graves. Others are open and free to visit, with an information board and a quiet walk around the perimeter, often with a pond or reed bed beside it.

The country around is gentle, with fields, orchards of persimmon and pear, and views of the Yamato mountains. Kashihara is a city of over a hundred and twenty thousand people, and the main shrine, Kashihara Jingu, stands at the foot of Mount Unebi, dedicated to the legendary first emperor, Jimmu. The roads here are flat, straight in the modern parts and narrow in the old villages, and traffic can be heavy around the city, with frequent traffic lights and many cyclists. Fuel, convenience stores, restaurants and bike shops are easy to find.

The rhythm of the day suits cycling better than motorcycling, and many visitors hire a bike and pedal from mound to mound. If you are on a motorbike, park carefully, as farm lanes are narrow and soft at the edge, and be respectful of private land, since many tombs lie close to houses.

Autumn is the loveliest time, with clear skies and golden fields, while spring brings blossom. The summer rainy season is wet, and summers are hot and humid. Take water and a hat, and linger at the edge of the moat, where herons and kingfishers fish in the stillness.
t.ancient capitals of asuka and fujiwara@3:
Fujiwara-kyō was Japan's first real city, and the grid that was laid out on this plain in 694 under Empress Jitō was a deliberate imitation of the Tang capital of Chang'an. Until then, the court had wandered from one palace to the next, and each reign built afresh. Fujiwara-kyō fixed the capital in one place, with straight avenues, a walled palace compound, and blocks for officials and temples. It lasted only sixteen years before the court moved north to Heijō-kyō, today's Nara, in 710, but the idea of a planned capital stayed, and Nara and Kyoto followed the same pattern.

What remains today is mostly a very large, very flat field. The palace site covers a wide area, and in summer it is planted with flowers, so that large blocks of cosmos or rapeseed or poppies occupy the space where the great audience hall once stood. Small information boards describe what was found, and the sense of space is the main thing. Three small hills, the Yamato Sanzan, ring the plain, and the best view is from the edge of the site on a clear day. It is a place for a slow walk or a bike ride and not for a rush.

On the road, expect the modest, polite traffic of the Nara basin. The surface is smooth, the speed limits are low, and drivers give way. Kashihara, a city of more than a hundred and twenty thousand, lies only a few kilometres away, so fuel, convenience stores and restaurants are everywhere, and Sakurai is close on the other side. The Asuka district to the south is lovely in a way that requires you to go slowly: tiny lanes, rice terraces, stone monuments scattered among the fields.

Weather matters. Summer is hot and humid, and the rainy season from mid June to July can bring days of steady rain, while typhoons visit in late summer. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the autumn light on golden rice is exceptionally beautiful.

If you want a place to eat, look for a small restaurant serving kakinoha-zushi, sushi wrapped in persimmon leaves, a speciality of Nara, or somen noodles, which come from nearby Miwa. A cup of tea and a sweet from a village shop set the afternoon right.
t.shobuike mounded tomb@34.5,135.8:
Some mounded tombs have a name, a story and a signpost. Shōbuike has a pond. The tomb stands in Kashihara, in the flat, tilled country of the Nara basin, a large earthen mound from the late sixth or seventh century, and it is one of the big monuments of the period when the burial customs of the Yamato rulers were changing from the gigantic keyhole tombs of earlier centuries to smaller, more carefully built mounds with stone chambers. Scholars have suggested different candidates, as is common for these tombs.

What a visitor sees is a large grassy mound with a path around it, a moat with water lilies in summer, and rice fields beyond. It is a calm, rural spot, with the sound of frogs in the evening and, in the early morning, mist on the water. Some excavated finds from tombs of this period include stone chambers lined with massive slabs, wooden coffins lacquered with a dry method, and objects like mirrors and beads, which are held in museums in Kashihara and Asuka. These museums are a good place to see what the tombs held, and they open at set times.

For riders, the area is a quiet network of lanes between towns. The main road through Kashihara is busy, with trucks and buses, but once you leave it, the side roads are narrow and calm. Surfaces are generally good, though edges can be soft and drainage channels deep, and farm vehicles are common in the planting and harvest seasons. Kashihara has fuel, shops and restaurants in abundance, and the neighbouring town of Sakurai, with sixty thousand people, is a base for more.

The seasons shape the experience. Early summer flooding of the paddies makes the fields look like mirrors, reflecting the mountains, and autumn brings the colour of harvest, while spring is a mix of blossoms and haze. Midsummer is hot enough to make riding gear a burden.

It is worth stopping for a while at the water's edge, as egrets and herons are frequent visitors, and the whole setting is a pleasant reminder that these monuments were designed to be seen across water and fields. Take a bottle of water, since there are few vending machines in the countryside.
t.asuka water clock site@34.5,135.8:
In the year 660, according to the Nihon Shoki, Prince Naka no Ōe, who would later become Emperor Tenji, built a water clock, a rokoku, and let the court know the time with it. A few years later, in 671, the same chronicle records that bells and drums were sounded to mark the hours, and the water clock site in Asuka, uncovered in 1981 by archaeologists, is believed to be the foundations of the building that housed it. It is among the earliest timekeeping devices recorded in Japan, a hint that the court was serious about order and the control of time, in the Chinese manner.

What you can see at the site is a set of low stone foundations and a reconstructed model of the water clock in a nearby museum, with its stepped tanks and tubes through which water dripped steadily from one level to the next, measuring the hours by the rise of water in the lowest vessel. Pipes, stone basins and a large waterproofed structure were found beneath the ground, showing that the complex was an engineered system rather than a simple building. The details of how it all fitted together are still debated, and I will leave them to the specialists.

The setting is a green field in the Asuka countryside, with farmhouses, persimmon trees and mountains to the south. Riders arrive along narrow lanes that wind between rice paddies, with little traffic, and the scale is low and intimate. There are no large services nearby, so fill the tank in Sakurai, about four kilometres away, or in Kashihara, both of which have petrol stations, convenience stores and restaurants. The area is popular with cyclists in spring and autumn, and on weekends, tour groups follow the loop.

Spring and autumn are best, and the rainy season in June can be heavy. Winter days are clear, with sharp light on the hills.

The museum of Asuka, nearby, has displays on the water clock, the stone carvings and the tomb finds, and it is well worth an hour, particularly if the weather turns. Afterwards, a cup of local tea or a soft ice cream made from local milk fits a gentle afternoon. Sunset over the western hills turns the fields rose and amber.
t.hinokuma dera temple site@34.5,135.8:
Hinokuma lies on the western edge of the Asuka district, where the land begins to rise toward the Katsuragi and Kongō mountains. The name appears in early records connected with the imperial family and the old clans, and a temple, Hinokuma-dera, once stood here, close to the tombs of rulers of the sixth and seventh centuries.

The landscape is a pleasure. From the edge of the plain, the road climbs gently through orchards and small farms, with views back across the basin and the sweep of the Yamato mountains. Kashihara, about six kilometres away, is the nearest big town, and Gose, to the south-west, is a smaller one of about thirty thousand with a walkable centre. Both provide fuel, supermarkets and restaurants.

The ride heading west into the hills is the best part. The roads toward Mount Katsuragi and the Kongō range are narrow, winding and wooded, with tight bends, cool shade and stretches of cedar plantation, where the light drops dramatically. The surface is variable, sometimes broken by roots or leaves, and rain can make it treacherous. In winter, the higher roads can be icy, and some close for the season. Traffic is light apart from weekends, when hikers and cyclists drive in.

The area is steeped in older stories. Mount Katsuragi is associated with ancient shamanistic practices and with the mountain ascetics known as yamabushi, and the shrines at its foot are among the oldest in Japan. The line between myth and history is blurred here, and the legendary first emperor Jimmu is said to have passed through the region.

Spring brings blossom, early summer brings thick green, and autumn adds red and gold to the hillsides. Food is simple: fresh vegetables, tofu, pickles and persimmon leaf sushi. If you stop, take a moment to listen. The only sounds are likely to be birds and wind in the cedars, a rare quality in a country as densely populated as Japan.
t.ishibutai mounded tomb@34.5,135.8:
Ishibutai is the skeleton of a tomb. The massive granite blocks of its burial chamber, now exposed to the open sky, form one of the most astonishing sights in Asuka, a giant stone room that was once buried under an earth mound, and it is generally thought to be the tomb of Soga no Umako, the minister who built Asuka-dera and dominated the court until his death in 626. The mound has long since been stripped away, probably by looters and by the passage of centuries, leaving the stones standing in a grassy square like the bones of some enormous animal.

The scale is what grabs you. Around thirty stones make up the chamber and its passage, and the largest of them weigh in the region of seventy tonnes each, hauled in without wheels or modern machinery from quarries some distance away. You can walk into the chamber through the passage and stand beneath the huge roof stones, which is a strange, slightly claustrophobic experience, and be amazed at how precisely the surfaces were cut and fitted. A modest admission fee is charged and there is a small stall selling tickets and souvenirs.

Around the tomb lies a landscape of persimmon orchards, small paddies, farmhouses with black-tiled roofs and a patchwork of narrow lanes. It is a lovely area to ride gently, with little traffic and sudden glimpses of the hills. Take care on corners where fields come close to the road and farm machinery may be parked, and keep an eye out for cyclists. The town of Sakurai, four kilometres off, has fuel, shops and cafés, and Kashihara is not much farther.

In spring the setting is lush with blossom, in summer it is humid and green, and in autumn the whole district turns gold, with the red spider lilies in September adding spots of crimson along the paddies. Winter is quiet.

Nearby, you can find the tombs of Takamatsuzuka, famed for the brightly painted murals of women in colourful robes found inside, and a museum that explains the finds. Allow time to wander slowly, since the real pleasure of Asuka is in noticing how many layers of history can sit within a short ride.
t.historic centre of the city of guanajuat:
Guanajuato sits at the bottom of a steep, narrow ravine in the central Mexican highlands, at around two thousand metres, and the colour of the city is the first surprise. Houses in ochre, rose, turquoise and yellow climb the hillsides in tiers, with domes and bell towers rising among them, and the streets twist in all directions. The city grew rich from silver, with mines such as La Valenciana, which in the eighteenth century produced a large share of the world's supply, and the wealth paid for baroque churches, mansions and theatres. UNESCO listed the historic town and the silver mines in 1988.

The most unusual feature is underground. When floods threatened the city in the twentieth century, the river was diverted into tunnels, and the old riverbed became a series of road tunnels, so that cars and bikes drive beneath the houses on streets that were once mining galleries. It is wonderfully confusing for a rider. Signs are limited, the tunnels are narrow, with sharp turns and sometimes steep slopes, and a GPS tends to lose its signal. The surface streets are cobbled, steep and often one-way, so do not expect to ride through the centre. Park outside, in one of the garages on the edge or around Marfil, and walk. Scooters and small cars nip about confidently.

The city is full of stories. The Alhóndiga de Granaditas, a grain store, was the scene of one of the first great battles of the independence war in 1810, and the Teatro Juárez is a nineteenth-century opera house with a classical facade and a lavish interior. The narrow Callejón del Beso, the Alley of the Kiss, has balconies so close that lovers on opposite sides could, according to the legend, exchange a kiss. The university gives the town a youthful feel, and in October the Cervantino festival fills it with music, theatre and dance. The Museum of the Mummies, with its naturally preserved bodies, draws crowds.

Fuel, food and lodging are easy, with a city of over seventy thousand and larger suburbs such as Marfil. Local food includes enchiladas mineras, a regional dish of corn tortillas and chilli sauce, and cajeta, a caramel of goat milk. October to May is dry and pleasant.
t.cave of avalos@22.6,-102.4:
The nearest settlements are tiny, such as Piedra Gorda and Cerrito de la Cruz, and the most reliable town for fuel and supplies is Trancoso, a fast-growing town of about fourteen thousand, some fourteen kilometres away, so it makes sense to fill the tank there before wandering the back roads.

The region was opened up by the Spanish after silver was found in the 1540s. The city of Zacatecas, a short drive away, became one of the richest in New Spain, and its historic centre, climbing a ravine with a baroque cathedral covered in carved pink stone, is a UNESCO listing. Haciendas, great fortified estates which processed silver or raised cattle, sprang up across the plateau, and their ruins and restored buildings are scattered through the countryside, with high walls, chapels and arched gateways. The Hacienda de Peñuelas is among those that carry the old story.

Riding the plateau is gentle and open. The roads are long, straight and wide, with distant mountains on the horizon, and the surface is variable, sometimes smooth and sometimes broken at the edges. Cattle and goats cross unpredictably, and dust and wind can be a nuisance in spring. Distances between towns are large, and cellular signal can be patchy, so carry water, cash and a spare layer. The dry season brings clear skies and cold nights, with frost possible in winter, while the rainy season from June to September brings dramatic thunderstorms in the afternoon.

Local food is rooted in ranch life, with carne asada, asadero cheese, gorditas, and prickly pear fruit, called tuna, in season. In a small village shop a cold drink and a bag of roasted pumpkin seeds will do nicely.

If you intend to enter any caves, check access beforehand, as many are on private land, and never explore alone.
t.worcester@-33.6,19.4:
Worcester, in the Western Cape, is the largest town in the Breede River Valley and the traditional beginning of the Route 62 for many travellers, a place of about a hundred and twenty-seven thousand people at the foot of the Hex River Mountains. It sits at the edge of the Cape winelands and it feels it. Vineyards climb the slopes behind the town, irrigated fields spread across the valley floor, and the peaks above turn pink and purple at sunset. In winter they carry snow, a surprise to anyone who thinks of South Africa as permanently warm.

The town is a centre of the brandy industry and of fruit and wine farming, and its streets hold Cape Dutch buildings, old churches and a number of museums. The Kleinplasie Living Open-Air Museum shows how Afrikaner farmers lived in the nineteenth century, with working demonstrations of bread baking and soap making, and the Karoo National Botanical Garden, on the edge of town, displays the extraordinary succulents and wildflowers of the dry interior, which burst into colour after spring rains.

Route 62 is the alternative to the N2, a long, quiet road that runs east through Robertson, Montagu, Barrydale, Ladismith and Oudtshoorn, tracing the line of the Little Karoo between two mountain ranges. It has a reputation as one of the finest roads in the country, and it earns it. The bends are gentle, the views are huge, and the little towns have a character that has been preserved through distance and neglect. On the way you cross rocky passes, cut through red-walled kloofs and pass farm stalls selling dried fruit, biltong and fresh figs. Take care with livestock, which wander across the road, and with the blinding sun, which can make the afternoon glare hard on the eyes.

With a population this size, Worcester has all the fuel, food and accommodation you could want, so use it, because the next town of any size is a long way off. Late spring and early autumn are the best times to ride, when the weather is mild and the wildflowers are out. Summer is hot and dry, with temperatures that regularly pass thirty-five degrees, and the mountains can be stormy in winter. Leave early and keep water on board.
t.hout bay@-34.0,18.4:
Hout Bay is a fishing harbour tucked under steep mountains on the Atlantic side of the Cape Peninsula, and it is the right place to eat before or after Chapman's Peak.
