The Afrikaans name means Wood Bay, because early Dutch settlers cut timber from the forests in the valley behind it, and the harbour has been a fishing base ever since. Today the working boats share the quay with restaurants and market stalls, and on a clear afternoon you can order fish and chips on the water while seals bob around the jetty hoping for scraps.

Chapman's Peak Drive is the reason most riders come. It runs for about nine kilometres between Hout Bay and Noordhoek, cut into the sheer face of the mountain, with the road hanging above the sea on one side and rock walls on the other. There are more than a hundred bends, most of them wide and clean, and the surface is generally excellent, but the drive is a toll road and is sometimes closed after rockfalls or in strong wind, so check before you commit. Early morning light on the water is the best, and later in the day the sea haze turns the cliffs a soft grey.

Out in the bay sits Duiker Island, a small rocky islet crowded with Cape fur seals, and boats leave from the harbour to take visitors close. A little inland, the Constantia valley holds some of South Africa's oldest vineyards, planted by Dutch governors in the seventeenth century, and the wine route there makes a fine finish to a day. The town itself has a lively market at weekends, with food from several continents, though parking can be a trial.

Fuel is easy in Hout Bay, with several stations on the main road, and Constantia has more. The mountain here makes its own weather, with fog and wind arriving suddenly off the Atlantic, so keep a windproof layer. The nearest big town is Retreat, but you will not need it.
t.cape town western cape@-33.3,18.4:
The name Swartland means black land, from the dark renosterbos scrub that once covered the hills, and the landscape is rolling farmland, with wheat fields that turn from green to gold and then to stubble as the year goes on. In spring, particularly in August and September, the roadside verges and fallow fields explode into yellow and orange with daisies and other annuals, and the little town holds a wildflower show to celebrate it.

The coast lies about twenty kilometres west, at Yzerfontein, where the cold Atlantic washes onto long beaches and small rocky coves, so a swim is possible but bracing. Water along this coast comes from the Benguela current and is rarely above fifteen degrees Celsius, so do not expect warmth even in January. Inland, the ground rises to a ridge of granite hills, and the farm roads are mostly gravel or tarmac patched by the heat, with light traffic and long clear views.

Darling has a small claim to cultural fame. A satirical performer here, who made his name mocking apartheid-era politicians in drag, runs a theatre and cafe at the old railway station, and the town also has its own craft brewery and small wine farms on the hills above. The pace is slow and the people are friendly, which makes it a good place to stop for breakfast.

On a motorbike the roads are open and mostly straight, with gentle undulations and wind that can build in the afternoon. Surfaces are fair, though some farm roads are gravel and corrugated. Fuel is available in Darling and Malmesbury, which is the larger town about thirty-five kilometres east. The nearest city of any size is Atlantis, about thirty kilometres away. Carry water, since shade is rare, and expect cool mornings and hot afternoons even in the middle of winter.
t.cape town western cape@-33.5,18.2:
Dassen Island is the nearest land to this marker, a flat, rocky island about ten kilometres to the north-west, and the water around it is some of the coldest and richest on the African coast. The Benguela current sweeps up from the Southern Ocean and brings nutrients that feed a huge web of life. Cape fur seals, cormorants, gannets and African penguins all use the island, though penguin numbers have fallen sharply over the past century, partly because of overfishing of the sardines and anchovies they depend on. The island has a lighthouse from the end of the nineteenth century, and it is a nature reserve not open to casual visitors.

If you want to swim anywhere near here, the coast offers sandy beaches at Yzerfontein, Silwerstroom and Bloubergstrand, but expect shocking cold. The water temperature rarely rises above fifteen degrees, and a few minutes is plenty for most people. Locals in wetsuits dive for crayfish and surf the waves, and on hot days the beaches are crowded, so go in the morning. Yzerfontein is a small village, with a few hundred permanent residents that swell in summer, a harbour for fishing boats, and a long beach where whales can sometimes be seen in spring.

The roads on the way are flat and exposed. The R27 along the coast offers sea views, and in the evening the light on the water is very fine. Gusts from the south-east can be hard on a loaded motorcycle. Inland, the Swartland wheat fields roll away, and there are wildflowers in season. The landscape is open and bare, which makes it a good place to see raptors, and flocks of Cape sugarbirds appear among the flowering shrubs.

Practical needs are straightforward. Fuel is available in Atlantis, Malmesbury and at the larger villages, but is not found at every settlement, so check your range. Bring a windproof jacket and sun protection, and consider a towel for a quick swim.
t.route 62 and swartberg pass photo pull o:
Honestly, the marker for this pull-off has landed in the Atlantic, a hundred kilometres west of Cape Town, so I will write about the place the ride is really after: the Swartberg Pass, one of the great mountain roads of southern Africa. It crosses the Swartberg range between Oudtshoorn and Prince Albert, and it was built between 1881 and 1888 under the direction of the engineer Thomas Bain, using convict labour and little more than picks, shovels and dry-stone walling. Those walls still hold up the road today, and they are astonishingly neat.

The pass is gravel, graded and generally passable on a sensible bike, but steep, narrow and without protection at the edges. It climbs in tight switchbacks to a summit of about fifteen hundred metres, then drops on the northern side into the dry Karoo. At the top, a sign marks the high point, and the view stretches over folded rock layers like the pages of a giant book. It is often closed after snow or heavy rain, and ice can lie in the shade in winter, so check conditions. Riders should take it slowly, use low gears and watch for oncoming vehicles on blind bends.

The route leading to it, Route 62, is a long road through the Little Karoo that has become a kind of legend. It passes through wine villages, ostrich farms and dusty towns such as Montagu and Barrydale, where the pub, with its quirky name, has become a pilgrimage point for bikers. The valley between the mountains grows apricots, peaches and grapes, and farm stalls sell dried fruit, jams and brandy. The Meiringspoort pass, a gorge with waterfalls, offers another dramatic route.

Fuel can be scarce, and it makes sense to fill up in Oudtshoorn and Prince Albert, and carry extra. Summers are fiercely hot, and winters can be freezing at altitude, so check the weather and carry water.
t.cape town western cape@-33.3,19.1:
The valley is a quiet pocket of the Winelands ringed by the Witzenberg and Winterhoek ranges, and the town has the longest row of preserved Cape Dutch buildings in the country on Church Street. On the night of the twenty-ninth of September 1969, an earthquake of magnitude six-point-three shook the town, damaging most of those buildings. Restoration took years, and the street today looks as it did in the eighteenth century, a remarkable act of collective repair.

For the Route 62 ride, Tulbagh is a handsome place to start or finish. The way out leads east through Mitchell's Pass, a steep gorge near Ceres built in the 1840s by the engineer Charles Michell, with cliffs close above the road and a good surface. Ceres lies in a high valley that grows apples, pears and stone fruit, and in winter the surrounding peaks often wear snow, which brings visitors from Cape Town to throw snowballs. Beyond Ceres, the road crosses the Karoo, with big skies and dry hills.

The valley around Tulbagh is full of small wineries, including some of the oldest in the region, along with olive groves and a few farm stalls. The colours change dramatically through the seasons, from the bright green of spring to the gold and red of autumn. On the road, the bends are gentle, the surface is good, and traffic is light except on summer weekends. Mornings can be cold, especially in winter, so wear a warm layer.

Fuel is available in Tulbagh, Wolseley and Ceres, but not on the quiet roads in between, so plan your tank. A swim in the valley means a farm dam or a pool at a guesthouse, since there is no beach. Evening light on the mountains is outstanding, with the cliffs turning from orange to purple as the sun sets, and the air smells of dry fynbos.
t.vienna eastern alps@48.8,17.2:
The border here is the Morava river, which runs through flat meadows and woods, and it forms part of the frontier of the Záhorie, a region of sandy plains and pine forests between the Small Carpathians and Moravia. Until 1993 this was not an international border at all, since Czechs and Slovaks lived in a single state, and the crossing is now invisible, a bridge and a sign.

The town is known for a sweet, a spiral pastry called trdelník, baked over an open fire and rolled in sugar and walnuts, which has become famous across central Europe as a tourist treat. The version made in Skalica has protected status in the European Union, and bakeries around the main square sell it hot. The square itself is pleasant, with a Baroque church, a plague column and a Romanesque rotunda dedicated to Saint George, one of the oldest buildings in the region.

The land around is wine country too, and Skalica has its own small vineyard area, though it is better known for its Moravian neighbours across the river. The Baťa Canal, a navigable waterway built in the twentieth century by the Czech shoe magnate, runs close by on the other side, and boats and cyclists use it. For a swim, small lakes and gravel pits around the town offer bathing in summer, and the water is mild.

Riding here is easy, with flat roads through farmland and forest, mostly in good condition. Slovakia uses the euro, and fuel is generally priced a little lower than in Austria. Motorways require an electronic vignette, so buy one online before using them. The towns are well supplied with stations and shops, and Skalica has several. The nearest big city is Bratislava, about eighty kilometres south. Late summer is the best season, when the vineyards are heavy with grapes and the evenings are warm.
t.denver colorado rockies@40.4,-104.2:
The ride's name points to Pikes Peak, which is far to the south; the country here is Weld County, a vast plain of wheat, cattle and oil derricks stretching away north-east of Denver. Weld County is among the largest agricultural counties in the United States, and the roads here carry grain trucks, tanker lorries and the occasional horse trailer.

The South Platte River crosses the district, and its valley has fed the region since the nineteenth century, when irrigation ditches turned dry ground into farmland. Sugar beets, corn and onions grow along the river, and cattle feedlots stand on the plains behind. Further north-east, the Pawnee National Grassland, with its low sandstone buttes, is among the best remaining areas of shortgrass prairie in Colorado, and its skies are loud with larks in spring. The lark bunting, the state bird, nests in the grass, and the males perform fluttering song flights above the fields.

The riding is wide, flat and quiet. Roads follow a strict grid and run for miles without a bend, and the surface is usually good, though truck traffic has chewed some of the edges. Wind is a constant companion, and in summer thunderstorms build quickly, with big hail. In winter, blizzards can close roads, and ground blizzards reduce visibility to nothing. A rider should expect big skies and little else, and plan fuel carefully.

Fuel is available in Keenesburg and Kersey, as well as at Fort Lupton, but between them are long gaps, so take on fuel whenever you can. Small cafes serve a plain meal of eggs, burgers and coffee, and the owners are friendly to passing riders. Mobile coverage is good in most places, and patchy in the deepest country.

The ride begins and ends in the same area, and the quiet is the main thing: a place to hear the wind in the grass, watch hawks on the fence posts and see the stars at night.
t.lednice@48.8,16.8:
Lednice is a palace, a park and a surprising piece of luxury in the south of Moravia. The palace belonged to the princes of Liechtenstein, who ruled these lands for centuries and turned them into a vast landscaped estate, and the building that stands at the end of the village today is a neo-Gothic confection of towers and pinnacles, rebuilt in the nineteenth century in the English style. Around it lies a huge park with ponds, avenues and follies, and together with the neighbouring Valtice, the whole area is a UNESCO World Heritage site, listed in 1996 as the Lednice-Valtice cultural landscape.

The park is full of curiosities. One is a minaret, around sixty metres tall, built in the early nineteenth century as a romantic folly, a strange sight in the middle of Moravian fields and one that visitors can climb for a view across the park. There are also a Chinese pavilion, a hunting lodge, a romantic ruin and a huge greenhouse, all part of a composition planned over generations. Water runs through the park in channels, and swans, herons and kingfishers live along them.

The countryside around is flat and fertile, a place of vineyards, orchards and fields of corn and sunflowers, with the Thaya river wandering through. Cyclists are everywhere, because the area has a network of paths, and drivers have to be patient. The roads are straight and the corners gentle, and a motorbike here is a way of linking sights rather than an exercise in cornering. The hot summer sun can be strong, and the flat land offers little shade, so the early morning and evening are best.

Lednice has a couple of thousand people, and fuel is better found in Břeclav, a bigger town about seven kilometres away. There are cafes and restaurants in the village, and the wine cellars of the surrounding area offer tastings, though a rider will want to keep it to a sip. South Moravia produces most of the Czech Republic's wine, with whites such as Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, and the local reds are improving.

Visit in late spring, when the park is green and the lilacs bloom, or in September during the grape harvest, when the vineyards are busy and the new wine appears.
t.valtice@48.7,16.8:
Valtice is the wine capital of the Czech Republic, and it looks the part. A large baroque palace dominates the town, built by the Liechtenstein family, who held the estate for centuries and made it a showpiece of their wealth. The palace has a grand courtyard, a riding hall and enormous wine cellars beneath it, and part of the cellars now houses the National Wine Centre, where visitors can taste a hundred of the best Czech wines, chosen in an annual competition. For anyone who enjoys wine, this is the place to learn about the country's vineyards.

The town centre is compact and pleasant, with a baroque square, a church with twin towers and a number of wine shops and taverns. Valtice lies just a few kilometres from the Austrian border, and in the days of the Iron Curtain the border zone here was closely guarded; today the line is open, and cyclists and walkers pass freely into the Austrian wine villages across the fields. A few kilometres to the south stands the Rendez-vous, a small colonnaded hunting pavilion, and the Colonnade at Reistna, a long curved structure on a hill, both part of the estate's park.

The region is the heart of Czech wine country. Vines cover the low hills in neat rows, with small cellars and presses scattered among them, and in autumn the villages smell of fermenting grapes. A local tradition is the burčák, a cloudy, partly fermented young wine sold in the early autumn, sweet and fizzy and stronger than it tastes. The food is hearty, with duck, goose and dumplings.

The roads in the area are flat and quiet, often lined with cherry or apricot trees, and they are well suited to a relaxed ride between cellars and castles. Drivers are used to cyclists, but patience is needed in summer and on weekends, when visitors fill the lanes. With under four thousand people, Valtice has food and small shops, but fuel is better taken in Břeclav, about ten kilometres to the north. Keep an eye on your own limit when tasting, and remember that the Czech Republic has a strict zero tolerance policy for alcohol on the road.
t.mikulov@48.8,16.6:
Mikulov stands beneath a white limestone ridge, the Pálava hills, and from a distance its castle on the rock and the pale church tower on the Holy Hill look like a stage set. It is the southernmost town in Moravia, a few kilometres from the Austrian border, and it has been a crossroads for centuries, a place where Czech, German and Jewish cultures lived together. In German it was Nikolsburg, and for a long period it was one of the most important Jewish communities in central Europe.

The old Jewish quarter and the cemetery on the edge of town, with thousands of gravestones in the grass, are still there, and the synagogue is open as a museum. The castle, a large complex of Renaissance and baroque buildings, was held by the Dietrichstein family, whose tombs lie in a chapel nearby. Walking uphill from the main square, past tall painted houses and stone steps, brings you to the castle terrace, with a wide view over the vineyards and the plain toward Austria.

The Pálava hills behind the town are a protected landscape, a UNESCO biosphere reserve, with dry meadows, rock steppes and scattered oak forest, home to many rare plants and insects. They are a limestone outcrop tied to the Alpine and Carpathian chain, standing out from the plain, and the vineyards on their slopes produce some of the best wine in the country. At the foot of the hills, the village of Dolní Věstonice is where the Venus figurine, a small ceramic statuette some twenty-nine thousand years old, was found in 1925, one of the oldest ceramic objects ever made.

For riders the roads around Mikulov are a mixture of straight farm roads and a few curves on the hill. The surface is good, the traffic is moderate, and in summer the heat and the visitors can be intense. Mikulov has about seven and a half thousand people and everything a traveller needs, including fuel and several good restaurants. A glass of local wine in the square is a fine finish to the day, so long as the bike stays parked. The wine festivals in September bring music and crowds.
t.needles eye@43.8,-103.5:
The Needles Eye is a rock needle, a pillar of weathered granite with a slot through it, and the road beside it passes through a tunnel so narrow that riders have a story to tell about it. The tunnel is a little over eight feet wide, and wide handlebars and panniers need a steady hand and a slow approach. It forms part of the Needles Highway, South Dakota Highway 87, which the South Dakota politician Peter Norbeck laid out on foot and horseback in the early 1920s, choosing the line himself through the granite spires of Custer State Park.

The rock here is extraordinary. The Black Hills are an island of ancient granite and forest rising out of the surrounding plains, and the Needles are tall, slender spires of grey stone, weathered into fingers and towers that poke up through the pines. The Lakota call the hills Paha Sapa, and they hold a deep spiritual meaning. Sylvan Lake, a short way south, is a small lake ringed by boulders, popular for photographs at sunrise. Black Elk Peak, at 7,242 feet, is the highest summit in the state and rises beyond.

For the bike, the Needles Highway is slow, tight and magical, with hairpins, short tunnels and views that open without warning. The speed limit is low and wise, and the road is crowded in summer, particularly in the middle of the day, so go early or late. Tunnels are dark, and oncoming traffic must be watched. Rain can make the surface greasy, and the road is closed in winter, usually from late autumn until spring.

Services are in the towns around the edge of the hills. Custer and Hill City have fuel, food and lodging, and Rapid City, thirty-six kilometres to the north-east, has everything else. Park entry has a fee, and the weather in the hills can change fast, with summer thunderstorms and cold mornings. Look out for bison and burros along the roads in Custer State Park, since they have no respect for traffic.
t.mount rushmore@43.9,-103.5:
Mount Rushmore is the sort of landmark that people expect to be smaller, and then they stand beneath it and find that it is larger than they imagined. The faces of Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Lincoln, each about sixty feet high, were carved into the granite between 1927 and 1941 under the sculptor Gutzon Borglum, with the help of around four hundred workers who drilled, blasted and hand-finished the stone. The monument draws millions of visitors a year, and a small fee is charged for parking.

It is also a deeply contested place. The Black Hills were promised to the Lakota in the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie and taken after gold was found, a seizure the United States Supreme Court later found illegal. For many Lakota, the carving is a desecration of sacred land. A few kilometres away, the Crazy Horse Memorial, a vast mountain carving begun in 1948 and still unfinished, was started at the invitation of Lakota elder Henry Standing Bear as a counterpart. Hearing both stories gives the day more depth.

The route to the monument is part of the fun. Iron Mountain Road, US 16A, was designed by Norbeck with the monument in mind, and its pigtail bridges, curling timber spirals, and narrow granite tunnels were laid out to frame the faces as you approach. One tunnel lines up exactly with the sculpture. The road is tight and steep, with a low speed limit, and it demands both attention and patience, but it is among the great short roads of the American West.

Services are at Keystone, a lively tourist strip a few minutes away, with cafés, fuel and gift shops, and Rapid City, twenty-nine kilometres north-east, has more. The monument is busiest from late morning to mid-afternoon, so arrive early or stay for the evening lighting ceremony in summer. Bring a jacket, since the hills can be cool even in July.
t.hashimoto@34.3,135.6:
Hashimoto is the last real town before the mountains of Wakayama, and for anyone riding out from Osaka toward Koyasan it is where you take on fuel, a hot drink and a deep breath. The Kinokawa River flows through the town, wide and gravelly, with the first folds of the Kii Peninsula rising behind. The trains of the Nankai line run from Namba up the valley to Hashimoto and then climb the mountains on a rack-and-cable stretch, so the place has the busy, practical air of a changeover point, with a supermarket, a few cafés and a good number of petrol stations.

Above the town the road rises through cedar forest into a different Japan. Koyasan, the great monastic centre of Shingon Buddhism, was founded by the monk Kukai, known as Kobo Daishi, in 816, on a high plateau ringed by eight peaks. More than a hundred temples cluster there today, many of them taking in guests, who sleep on tatami, eat a vegetarian temple meal and rise before dawn for the morning chanting. Okunoin, a vast forest cemetery of moss-covered gravestones and giant cedars leading to Kukai's mausoleum, is among the most atmospheric places in the country, and walking its lantern-lit paths feels like moving through another century.

The ride up is the pleasure. The mountain road twists through tunnels and tight bends, often shaded by cedars so thick that daylight is dim, with a rural surface that varies. Weather is changeable, and fog and rain can be sudden. Summer is hot and humid at Hashimoto and pleasantly cool on the mountain, while autumn brings red maples and winter may bring ice on the upper stretches, so check before you set off. The roads are narrow, with local drivers at their own pace, and a calm approach pays off.

Fuel is straightforward in Hashimoto, a city of fifty-seven thousand, but stations are rare once you climb, so fill up before leaving. Convenience stores, a Japanese staple, sell hot coffee and rice balls, and are a fine breakfast on a cold morning.
t.myslenice@49.8,19.9:
Myślenice is a small, sturdy town in the foothills south of Kraków, on the Raba river, and for generations it has been the first place on the road to the mountains where travellers draw breath. The old market square has a pleasant, unhurried look, with a town hall in the middle and a handful of cafés and ice-cream shops around the edge. It sits in the Beskid Wyspowy, the Island Beskids, a landscape of separate, rounded, forested hills that stand like islands among the valleys, and the shapes in every direction give the place a soft, rolling character.

The road running through town is the Zakopianka, the old highway that carries Poles to Zakopane and the Tatra Mountains, and anyone who has driven it on a summer Friday or a winter Sunday will have a feeling about it. Traffic has long been heavy, and a new expressway has relieved much of it, though the old road still jams on busy weekends. Timing matters, and an early start or a weekday ride makes a big difference. On the old roads, the lanes are narrow, with trucks, tourists and the occasional horse cart, and overtaking needs care.

From here the landscape grows steadily more mountainous. The Gorce range lies to the south-west, with beech and spruce forest and high meadows, and beyond it the Tatras rise as a jagged, grey wall, snow-capped into early summer. Along the way, villages of wooden houses with steep roofs give a hint of highland culture, with carved gables and roadside chapels. In the foothills the surface is generally good, the bends are gentle and the scenery changes with every kilometre.

Myślenice has more than seventeen thousand people, with plenty of fuel stations on the main road, and the best strategy is to fill the tank here before the climb. Bakeries sell fresh bread and poppy-seed pastries, and a bowl of żurek, a sour rye soup, is a good way to start. Kraków is about thirty kilometres north, so it makes a handy start or end point.
t.durnstein@48.4,15.5:
Dürnstein is the best-known village on the Wachau stretch of the Danube, and it is easy to see why. The river bends below a ridge, the vineyard terraces climb the slope in neat rows, and the blue-and-white tower of the abbey church rises above the roofs like a piece of confectionery. A ruined castle crowns the cliff above, and the whole scene appears on postcards, in films and in the memory of anyone who has taken a boat down the river.

The castle is the key to the story. In 1192, on his way home from the Third Crusade, Richard the Lionheart of England was captured near Vienna by Duke Leopold V of Austria, who held a grudge from a quarrel at Acre, and the king was imprisoned at Dürnstein for some months before being transferred to German custody and ransomed. The ruin you can climb to today is that same castle, destroyed by Swedish troops in the Thirty Years' War, and the walk up the hill takes about twenty minutes and rewards you with a wide view over the river and vineyards.

Dürnstein is also famous for apricots. The Wachau's apricot, the Marille, is protected by name and appears in jam, schnapps, liqueur, dumplings and cakes, and in late July the orchards are heavy with fruit. A glass of the local apricot brandy at the end of a ride is a wonderful way to be slightly more relaxed than the speed limits recommend. Grapes are the other business: the terraces behind the village produce Riesling and Grüner Veltliner of real quality, and the Wachau has its own wine classification, Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd.

The riding is a pleasure of a different kind than in the Alps. The B3 follows the Danube, with small bends, a flat gradient and a surface that is mostly good, but traffic can be heavy in summer, cyclists are everywhere on the river path and coach parties often block the village lanes. Choose a weekday in April, May or October, when the light is soft and the vines are colourful.

Krems, about ten kilometres east, is the nearest larger town, with several stations and supermarkets. The riverside cafes and wine taverns, or Heurige, are better than the fuel, so plan to eat, and perhaps not rush.
t.weissenkirchen@48.4,15.5:
Weissenkirchen is the Wachau as the wine-growers see it: a village of old houses and cellars squeezed between the Danube and a hillside of terraced vineyards. It is slightly less famous than Dürnstein, and a good deal less crowded, which gives it a more natural feel. The streets are narrow, the gateways lead into courtyards with walnut trees, and the smell of fermenting must hangs in the air in early autumn.

The village takes its name from a white church, and the fortified church on the hill above the houses still dominates the place, protected by walls and a tower built when the Turks threatened Lower Austria in the sixteenth century. A covered stairway climbs to it from the village, and the effort is worth it for the view down onto the red roofs and the river. In the old Teisenhoferhof, a wine-growers' house with an arcaded courtyard, the district keeps a museum about the Wachau's history and its trade, a gentle half hour if the weather turns.

This is a village to taste in. The wine here is graded by the growers' association by weight, from light Steinfeder through Federspiel to rich Smaragd, named after the green lizards that bask on the terrace walls. Many families run Buschenschenken or Heurige, simple wine taverns with a pine branch hung outside to show that they are open. They serve cold cuts, cheeses, pickles and bread with their own wine, and you can sit under a tree and watch the barges on the river. For a rider this calls for restraint, so the glass of Grüner Veltliner should be a small one, or the next stop should be a hotel.

The road is the B3, hugging the north bank of the Danube, and it is a simple, charming, relaxed ride. The bends are gentle, the traffic is mixed with cyclists and tourists, and the surface is generally in good shape. Early on a May morning, with blossom on the apricot trees and the river still, it is lovely. Autumn brings gold in the vineyards and a hint of woodsmoke.

The village has fewer than a thousand people, so there is only limited fuel. Krems is the usual choice, about ten kilometres away, and has everything. A coffee on the terrace beside the river will cost less than you expect and last as long as you wish.
t.spitz@48.4,15.4:
Spitz stands at the western end of the Wachau, where the Danube bends and the valley opens out a little. It is a small town in name and in size, about thirteen hundred people, but it carries itself like a place that has always known its worth. Painted houses front the main street, a medieval gate called the Rotes Tor stands at one end, and above the town the ruin of the Hinterhaus castle looks down from a wooded crag.

Behind the town, a vineyard called the Tausendeimerberg, the thousand-bucket hill, rises in a spectacular set of terraces. It is said to be the largest single vineyard terrace in Austria, and the name refers to the harvest it could produce in a good year, a thousand Eimer, an old measure of wine. Walking among the vines in September, with the grapes heavy and the wasps lazy, is a quiet pleasure. The wines from Spitz have a reputation for crisp, mineral Rieslings, and local cooperatives and family estates are happy to pour a glass.

A small passenger ferry crosses the river here, linking Spitz with the village of Arnsdorf on the south bank, and it is a delightful way to see the Danube at water level. The river is wide, slow and brown, and the barges and cruise ships pass at a stately pace. On the south side, the road runs through orchards and small villages, so a loop crossing the river by ferry and returning over a bridge makes a good short ride.

The riding on the B3 is calm and agreeable. It is a road to be enjoyed at an unhurried pace, with slow, wide bends and views of terraced slopes above the river, and in spring the apricot blossom adds a touch of pink. Weekend traffic is heavy, with convoys of cyclists and tour coaches, so a weekday is better, and a morning start gives you cool air and good light.

For fuel, Spitz may have limited options, so Krems, about fourteen kilometres away, is the more certain stop. In the town, a small bakery or cafe will serve you a Marillenkuchen, apricot cake, made with the local fruit, which is exactly what a rider needs before the long run back down the river.
t.bleik@69.3,16.0:
Bleik is a fishing village on the north-west coast of Andøya, the northernmost of the Vesterålen islands, and it is famous for two things: a long, white beach and a small, steep island just off it. The beach is wide and pale, with dunes behind and a sea that, in summer, glows an improbable turquoise, though the water is bitterly cold. The island, Bleiksøya, rises straight out of the sea like a loaf of dark bread, and in summer it is home to a huge colony of puffins, along with kittiwakes, razorbills and many other seabirds. Boat trips run from the village to see the puffins up close, and it is one of the great wildlife experiences in northern Norway.

Behind the village the mountain slopes rise, and a path climbs to a viewpoint with a wide look over the sea and the island. It is a short walk, and a good one. The village itself is small, a few dozen houses scattered along the coast, with a harbour and a few places to eat. In the summer the midnight sun gives light all night, and the beach is a fine place for a late evening walk. In winter it is a dark and wild place, with storms and northern lights.

The road to Bleik leaves the main route and runs down to the coast through low, open country, with mires, small lakes and a wide sky. It is easy riding, with a good surface and gentle bends, but the wind is a constant factor, and gusts across the open ground can be strong. Traffic is light. Rain and mist arrive fast, and in autumn the roads may be wet and slippery. A long road trip on Andøya is a pleasure for those who like space and light.

Andenes, at the northern tip of the island, is the nearest town, with about 2,800 people, and has fuel, shops and restaurants. It is also the base for whale-watching safaris, which go out to see sperm whales in the deep water just off the coast, a unique thing in Europe. Myre, to the south, has services as well. Pack warm clothes, and book boat trips in advance in summer, as they fill up. The puffin season runs roughly from May to August, and the birds leave in late summer.
t.bukkekjerka@69.1,15.7:
Bukkekjerka sits on the west coast of Andøya, where the road runs close to the open sea and a short walkway leads out over the rocks to a viewing point. The name means something like the goat church, and the story behind it is nothing more than the shape of a rock that someone once thought looked like a church, with goats grazing nearby. The platform that now stands here, part of the scenic route programme, is a simple piece of design, set low in the landscape, with a place to sit and watch the sea. It is the sort of place where you do not need much to enjoy yourself: a flask, a windproof jacket and a quiet half hour.

The coast here is rough and exposed, with waves breaking on dark rock and white foam running up the shore. Beyond the shore, the sea stretches to the horizon, and on a clear day the light on the water is dazzling. Andøya is an unusual island, with large areas of peat bog, called mires, that are home to cloudberries, which ripen in late summer and are the pride of the north. The island also has a patch of unusually young sedimentary rock for this part of Norway, and it is known for fossil finds. A rocket range operates on the island too, and it is used for launching research rockets into the northern sky.

For a rider, the road along the coast is a delight. It is a long, quiet stretch, with open views, a smooth surface and easy bends, and you can ride for long periods without seeing another vehicle. The wind is the chief problem, as there is nothing to stop it, so be prepared for strong gusts, especially near the coast. In autumn and winter, storms can make the road wet or icy. On a clear summer evening, the midnight sun turns everything to gold, and the experience is hard to forget.

Andenes and Myre are the nearest towns with fuel and services, and both are a short ride along the coast. Food is available in both, and a coffee and a waffle in a local café is a good way to warm up. Carry a layer for the wind, and take care not to leave the boardwalk, as the thin soil and vegetation are fragile. In the long light of late summer, it is a good place to watch the sun slide slowly toward the horizon.
t.bridal veil falls@44.4,-103.9:
Spearfish Canyon feels as if somebody lifted a piece of the Rockies and set it down in the Black Hills, and Bridal Veil Falls is its tidiest corner. The falls pour over a ledge right beside the road, perhaps sixty feet of white water falling into a rocky pool under spruce and aspen. You park, you walk about forty steps, and you are standing in cool spray. Some travellers expect more drama, and that is rather the point: here the falls are an excuse to get off the bike beside a creek, not a trek.

The surrounding canyon is the real show. Limestone walls rise a thousand feet or so on both sides, painted in reds and creams, and Highway 14A follows the creek along the bottom in a series of easy, flowing bends. It is a road for relaxing into rather than attacking: speeds are low, the trees close overhead, and the light comes down in slanted columns that make the afternoon ride glow. In October the aspens and birch turn gold and the canyon becomes extremely popular, so expect a procession of cars. Mid-week mornings are best, and early summer gives you the most water.

The history here is mostly mining and movies. The Black Hills gold rush of the 1870s drew prospectors to Deadwood and Lead just over the ridge, and the canyon later fed hydroelectric works for the Homestake gold mine, whose remains you can still spot among the trees. Spearfish Canyon was also part of the backdrop to Dances with Wolves, which put the place on a lot of people's lists.

Practicalities are simple. Spearfish, about twelve kilometres to the north, is a proper town with plenty of petrol, motels and cafes, so top up there before entering the canyon. Lead and Deadwood are the sources at the other end. Deer step onto the road at dusk, and the surface is usually good, though it can hold dampness in shade after rain. Swing past the falls, take a few photographs, and carry on up the canyon to Roughlock.
t.roughlock falls@44.4,-103.9:
Roughlock gets its name from the wagon days. Freight drivers coming down steep Black Hills grades would jam a roughlock, a kind of drag shoe, under a wheel to stop it turning, and the name stuck to a creek that lots of those wagons must have crossed. What I can say is that the falls are good: Little Spearfish Creek drops over a wide limestone lip into a pool, and the whole thing is framed by evergreens and the sort of damp rock that smells faintly of minerals.

From the road you reach it by a short side lane up toward the nature centre, then a gentle walk down to a viewing platform. It is a more serious waterfall than Bridal Veil, and in spring runoff it throws up a roar and a fine mist. Late summer can see it reduced to a modest pour. Autumn, when the aspens go butter-yellow, is the postcard season, and it also brings the heaviest traffic, so aim for an early start.

The Spearfish Canyon Scenic Byway itself is about twenty miles of mellow riding, and this is its high-water mark for me. The curves are gentle and flowing, the surface is usually kind, and the canyon walls make the thing feel enclosed in a way open prairie roads never do. The temperature can swing sharply: you may leave Spearfish in shirtsleeves and want a liner by the time you reach the upper canyon. Rain squalls tend to arrive quickly from the west. Watch for tourists in rental cars stopping without warning, and for deer at dusk.

The Black Hills around here were taken from the Lakota after gold was found in 1874, a history that remains painful and legally unresolved, and the Hills are sacred to the Lakota people. That is worth keeping in mind as you ride through pine-scented country that looks like an easy holiday backdrop.

Fuel is not available at the falls. Spearfish, about seventeen kilometres north, has plenty, and Lead and Deadwood are close at the southern end. If you want a sit-down meal after the walk, either end of the canyon is a better bet than hoping something will turn up in between.
t.koyasan approach@34.2,135.6:
The road to Kōyasan is a climb out of the modern world and into the Japan of the pilgrim. For more than twelve hundred years, this mountain plateau in Wakayama has been the headquarters of Shingon Buddhism, founded in 816 by the monk Kūkai, known after his death as Kōbō Daishi. He is said to be not dead but in eternal meditation at Okunoin, the great forest cemetery at the end of a cedar-lined path, where thousands of lanterns and countless moss-covered tombstones stand in the shade. The complex of temples is a UNESCO World Heritage site, part of the sacred routes of the Kii Mountains.

The approach is part of the experience. From the Kinokawa plain, the roads climb into steep mountain forest of cedar and cypress, with tight bends, stone walls, and views over folded ridges. The old pilgrim path, the Chōishi-michi, climbs from Kudoyama with stone markers every hundred metres or so, and parallel roads follow the same valleys. The mountains here have been revered for centuries, and the air at altitude, cool and fragrant with cedar, seems to change the pace of everything.

Riding up is a pleasure, though a demanding one. The road is narrow, with many curves and blind corners, and it can be damp and slippery under the trees. Traffic is usually light but can be heavy in the autumn colour season and on holiday weekends, when tour buses and cars are numerous. Take care on the hairpins, and watch for fallen leaves and rocks. Snow falls at this altitude in winter, so check conditions between December and March. Mornings are best, when mist hangs in the trees.

Kōya has a small town of temples, cafes, and shops, though fuel is not something to rely on at that altitude. The sensible place to fill up is Hashimoto, about twelve kilometres away, on the plain below. Many temples offer lodging for visitors, with vegetarian monastic cuisine, shōjin ryōri, that includes sesame tofu and seasonal vegetables, and an early morning prayer ceremony. If you stay, it is an experience quite different from a hotel. Dress modestly in the temples, remove your boots at the entrance, and be quiet in the cemetery.
t.kinokawa food@34.3,135.4:
The Kinokawa is the main river of Wakayama, rising in the mountains of Nara and flowing west across a broad, fertile plain to the sea at Wakayama city. The valley is a fruit basket: orchards of mikan oranges, persimmons, peaches, and plums cover the terraces, and in autumn, the roadside stalls sell sacks of fruit for a few hundred yen. The air smells of citrus in November, and the colours of the orchard slopes are the most striking thing about the landscape.

Near Iwade, a short distance from the river, stands Negoro-ji, a large temple complex that was once one of the most powerful in Japan. In the sixteenth century, thousands of monk-soldiers lived here, armed with muskets, and the temple was a political and military force until the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi burned most of it in 1585. A few buildings survived, including a great two-storey pagoda, a national treasure, and the complex now lies quiet among old trees, a place of moss, fallen leaves, and a peaceful kind of grandeur.

For a rider, the area is easy and rewarding. The roads along the river and through the orchards are gentle, with a good surface and plenty of small towns, and the traffic is light outside the commuter hours. The Kinokawa valley is also the route to the mountains of Kōya, so it is a natural place to gather yourself before the climb. Take care at the many small crossroads, where cars appear without much warning, and remember that traffic in Japan drives on the left.

Food is a delight. Wakayama is the home of a particular style of ramen, with a rich pork bone and soy broth, often served with pickled mackerel sushi on the side, and it is hard to find a bad bowl. Iwade has fuel, convenience stores, and restaurants, and Izumisano, farther west, is a much larger city. Look for farm stands selling fresh fruit and juice, and consider a small bag of mikan as a snack for the ride. Autumn is the best season for the harvest, and spring for the blossom, while summer can be hot and humid.
t.zakopane food@49.3,19.9:
Zakopane is where Poland goes to feel like it lives in the mountains. It lies at the foot of the High Tatras, the only truly alpine range in the country, and it has been a resort since the late nineteenth century, when writers, painters and doctors found the thin air and the clear light. The town grew around the culture of the górale, the highlanders of Podhale, whose wooden houses, sheepskin waistcoats, fiddle music and dialect still define the place. Look at the carved timber villas and you are seeing the so-called Zakopane style, an architecture invented here in the 1890s by Stanisław Witkiewicz as an attempt at a national style.

Food is why you are stopping, and the menu is hearty without apology. The cheese to try is oscypek, smoked sheep's milk cheese pressed into spindle shapes, often grilled and served with cranberry jam. Kwaśnica, a sour cabbage soup with pork, will warm you if the day has turned cold. The better places are the ones tucked up side streets or at the edge of town, in timbered rooms with a stove and a menu that does not need translating into six languages. Krupówki, the main pedestrian street, is lively, loud and a bit kitsch, worth a stroll but not the best table.

The ride in from Kraków follows the foothills through Rabka and Nowy Targ, and the final run on the main road is famous for its traffic. At weekends and in holiday seasons the road to Zakopane clogs badly, so an early start or a late arrival makes a real difference. Once you pass Nowy Targ, the Tatras begin to appear on the skyline, a serrated grey wall that makes you forget the slow lorries in front.

Zakopane is a big town of over twenty-seven thousand people, so fuel, parking and repairs are no problem. The practical challenge is parking a motorcycle in the centre. Look for side streets slightly away from Krupówki, and do not leave luggage on the bike. In summer evenings the town buzzes until late. In autumn and winter it is quieter and cheaper, and the stove-heated rooms come into their own.

If the weather turns, mountain storms can arrive quickly. Check the sky over the Tatras before you head out, and keep a rain layer handy.
t.guba owka view area@49.3,19.9:
Gubałówka is the ridge that stands between Zakopane and the open Podhale plain, and it exists for one reason, which is to look at the Tatras. From the top, at a little over eleven hundred metres, the whole range spreads along the southern horizon in one go: Giewont with its cross, the long saw-edge of the High Tatras behind, and the town laid out in the valley like a model. It is the view that people on postcards mean when they say Zakopane.

Most visitors ride up on the funicular, which has been hauling people up from the edge of town since the 1930s. At the top there is a market of wool socks, sheepskin and smoked cheese, a handful of restaurants, and a long ridge walk with every bench facing south. It is commercial, but it is also cheerful, and on a clear morning the commerce hardly matters because the view does all the work.

For riders, the ridge is more about the approach than the summit. The roads around the north side of Zakopane and toward Poronin and Kościelisko link villages of wooden farmhouses with steep shingled roofs, small chapels and hay meadows. The surface varies, and in the hills the corners can be tight and sudden. Take it slowly. In the foothills you get a feel for the old highland life, with shepherds still driving flocks in summer, and the smell of woodsmoke in the cooler months.

The light here changes everything. Early morning gives you clean air and sharp peaks, while afternoon haze flattens the distance. Clouds often gather on the Tatras by midday, so if a clear view matters, go early. In summer, thunderstorms build over the mountains in the afternoon and can sweep across the valley in a matter of minutes.

Fuel, food and repairs are all in Zakopane, a few minutes away, and Poronin and Kościelisko have smaller services. There is no need to carry spare fuel. But do bring a warm layer, because the ridge catches the wind, and in shoulder seasons the temperature at the top can be several degrees below the town.

Photographers should walk a little along the ridge away from the lift station. The crowds thin out within a few minutes, and the angle to the Tatras gets cleaner.
t.melk abbey@48.2,15.3:
Melk Abbey sits on a rock above the Danube like a ship that has run aground in gold. The Baroque monastery, built in the early eighteenth century to designs by Jakob Prandtauer, dominates the town and the river from its crag, with a long, ochre-yellow facade, two spires on the church and a roofline of terraces and pavilions. Benedictine monks have lived on the site since the eleventh century, and the monastery has been a school, a library and a scriptorium for most of that time. Its library holds tens of thousands of volumes, including medieval manuscripts, and the ceiling is covered in painted allegories.

The abbey also has a place in literature. In Umberto Eco's novel The Name of the Rose, the narrator is Adso of Melk, a young Benedictine novice who recalls the events of a monastery murder in old age, and the title of the book has made Melk better known to readers who have never visited. In real life, the town is quiet and old-fashioned, with a main street of painted houses, a few cafes and a handful of guest houses, and the abbey above it, floodlit at night.

Melk is the western gateway to the Wachau, the finest stretch of the Danube valley, where the river runs between steep hills covered with terraced vineyards and apricot orchards, past ruined castles and medieval villages. The valley is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and in spring, when the apricots blossom, it is white and pink. The wines, especially the dry, peppery Grüner Veltliner and the Riesling, are famous, and the apricot, the Marille, appears in jam, schnapps, dumplings and cakes. The road along the river is a fine ride, with gentle bends, views across the water and a surface that is mostly smooth, though in summer and on weekends it fills with cyclists, coaches and cars, and a bike can spend a lot of time in a queue.

Melk has fuel and a good choice of restaurants, with a population of about four thousand, and the larger towns of St Pölten and Krems are within reach. Parking near the abbey is limited, so allow time and take the walk uphill. The best times are May, September and early October, when the weather is mild and the vines are green or turning gold. Early morning light on the facade is wonderful, with the river often covered in mist.
t.mariazell mountain town@47.8,15.3:
Mariazell has been a place of pilgrimage for more than eight hundred years, and you notice it from a long way off, when the green spire of the basilica appears above the forest. According to tradition, a monk named Magnus brought a wooden statue of the Virgin here in 1157, and the town grew up around the chapel built to hold it. Over the centuries the shrine became the most important in the Habsburg lands, visited by emperors and by pilgrims on foot from Vienna, Hungary, Bohemia and as far as the Balkans. The basilica today is a Baroque church built around the older Gothic one, and the little statue stands in a silver chapel at the heart of it.

The town is set in a bowl of mountains in Styria, on the edge of the Alps, with spruce forest and limestone peaks around it. Nearby, the Erlaufsee, a small, clear lake, and the high plateau of the Hochschwab massif offer walking in summer, and in winter, the town has a modest ski area. The local speciality is honey gingerbread, made by bakers who have been at it since the days of the pilgrims, and the streets around the basilica are lined with shops selling candles, carved wood and sweet things.

The roads leading to Mariazell are what a motorcyclist hopes for. From the north, the route climbs through the Lower Austrian hills over passes such as the Annaberg, with a long series of bends through forest and meadow, a good surface and views of the pre-Alps. It is a popular route with Viennese riders and with day trippers, so on fine weekends it is busy, with plenty of motorcycles. Tight bends alternate with open stretches, and the road is well signed, with speed cameras and police checks. Expect mist, rain and cold in the high sections, even in summer, and ice in the early and late season.

Mariazell has fuel and a good range of restaurants, serving traditional Austrian and Styrian food, such as Schnitzel, dumplings and strudel, and the town has a wide range of guest houses. In summer and at the major pilgrimage dates, the place is crowded, so book accommodation ahead. Kindberg, thirty-two kilometres to the south-east, is the next larger town, and St Pölten is the main city to the north. The best months are May, June and September, when the air is clear and the roads are drier.
t.semmering pass@47.6,15.8:
Semmering is where Lower Austria hands over to Styria, and it does so at a saddle of roughly 985 metres in the last eastern bulge of the Alps. The Rax and Schneeberg massifs stand to the northwest, the Hirschenkogel rises right above the village, and the whole place has the faintly faded air of somewhere that was once the most fashionable thing in the empire.

That fashion came with the railway. Carl von Ghega drove the Semmering line through here in the early 1850s, the first true mountain railway in Europe, with viaducts stacked in two tiers and fourteen tunnels clinging to the slopes. It now carries UNESCO status. Vienna's wealthy followed the track and built villas, grand hotels and sanatoria among the beech and spruce, and you can still read that era in the woodwork and the tall verandas along the lanes. Long before the railway, the old road over the pass was the way south to Graz and the Adriatic, and in the early twentieth century the climb served as a famous hill-climb course for racing cars.

On a bike the old pass road is the point of the exercise. From Schottwien on the Lower Austrian side it climbs in a run of tight hairpins through woodland, with the viaducts of the railway visible across the valley as you go. The surface is generally decent, the bends are properly tight rather than merely suggestive, and the gradient never stops being interesting. Beyond the top it drops more gently toward Spital am Semmering and Mürzzuschlag. The modern expressway burrows under all of this, which is exactly why the old road is quiet on a weekday and why the lorries are somewhere else.

Practical matters are simple. Semmering village itself is small, with a few cafés and hotels but no reliable fuel, so tank up before the climb or in Mürzzuschlag, the nearest real town about twelve kilometres away on the Styrian side. Early autumn is lovely, with mist in the valleys and cool, clear air at the top, but even in May a shaded hairpin can be damp, and in winter snow turns the pass into a problem for two wheels. Stop at the top for a coffee and look at those old hotels. Some are lovingly restored, some are still waiting for somebody with a great deal of money.
t.andrassy avenue and the underground@47.5:
Andrássy Avenue is Budapest at its most confident. It was laid out in the 1870s as a grand boulevard from the city centre to the City Park, lined with neo-Renaissance mansions, embassies and the State Opera House, completed in 1884, and it runs straight and wide under rows of plane trees. UNESCO listed it in 2002, together with the first underground railway on the European continent, the Millennium Underground, which opened in 1896, a few years before the Paris metro, and runs just beneath the avenue.

The little yellow trains still run, with the stations kept in their original tiled style, and a ride of a few stops is a delight. At the northern end of the avenue stands Heroes' Square, with its colonnade of Hungarian kings and the statues of the seven Magyar chiefs, and beyond it the City Park, with a castle that seems out of a fairy tale, and the Széchenyi thermal baths, where old men play chess in the steaming water. The avenue also holds sadder memories, notably the House of Terror, which documents the era of fascist and communist rule.

For a rider, Budapest is a lively and often hectic city. Trams, rails and cobbles demand attention, and the traffic on the big ring boulevards moves in waves. Be careful of wet tram tracks, which are slippery. The city's bridges over the Danube are the best part: crossing the Chain Bridge at dusk, with Buda Castle lit up on the hill, is a ride worth taking. The roads out of town toward the hills of northern Hungary are quick and pleasant, and the ride that begins here heads for Hollókő, a preserved village of the Palóc people, and the Roman fort across the Danube in Slovakia.

Fuel is easy throughout the city, and the avenue itself is full of cafes, many of them in old coffee houses with marble tables and chandeliers. A slice of Dobos torte, a layered sponge with caramel on top, is the proper way to rest. In summer, evenings stay warm and the terraces are packed. Leave the bike in a guarded car park, since street parking can be tricky, and enjoy a walk beneath the plane trees.
t.tuapurie@22.3,-104.1:
Tuapurie is the Wixarika name for Santa Catarina, one of the main communities of the Wixarika, whom outsiders know as Huichol, in the Sierra Madre Occidental of northern Jalisco. It is a high, remote, rugged landscape of pine and oak forest cut by deep barrancas, and it is one of the places where the Wixarika have kept their religion and customs alive more fully than most Indigenous peoples in Mexico. The community's centre includes a ceremonial building and a temple, and the seasons are marked by pilgrimages, in particular the long journey to Wirikuta in San Luis Potosi, where the sacred peyote grows. The route from here to the sacred sites is the subject of the ride, and it touches places that have deep meaning for the people who live here.

A visitor should come with humility. This is not a tourist stop but a living community, and many places are sacred and not open to outsiders. Photography may be forbidden or require permission, and it is usual to ask before entering a village or ceremonial area. The community's art, yarn paintings and beaded figures of animals, is made with great skill and can be bought directly from the makers, which is the best way to support the people who create it.

The riding is demanding. Much of the way to the sierra is paved, but the last stretches are on dirt tracks with rocks, ruts and steep gradients, and rain can turn them to slippery mud. Distances are long, mobile signal is patchy, and the nearest services are far away. San Andres Cohamiata, sixteen kilometres off, is a small settlement with basic supplies at best. The sensible approach is to fill the tank in the larger towns in the valley before climbing, carry spare fuel, and have a plan for a breakdown.

The weather swings from warm days to cold nights, and heavy rain falls from June to September. The best time to go is the dry season from November to April, when the tracks are firmer. Autumn light falls golden on the pine slopes. Check the local situation before you set out, as road conditions and community access can change from one season to the next, and respect whatever decisions the community makes about visitors.
t.bratislava@48.2,17.1:
Bratislava has been a border town for most of its history, and it still feels like one. The Danube flows past below a castle on a rocky hill, with Austria visible a few kilometres to the west and Hungary to the south, and the city has been Pressburg, Pozsony and Bratislava at different times. For nearly three centuries, from 1563 to 1830, Hungarian kings were crowned in St Martin's Cathedral, in the old town, so that this modest place was the coronation city of a kingdom. The cathedral spire carries a gilded replica of the crown. Maria Theresa was crowned here in 1741, Mozart played here as a boy, and the old town reflects that Habsburg past in its pastel-coloured baroque palaces.

The old centre is small, car-free and very pleasant, with squares, cafes and quirky bronze statues, including a man peeping out of a manhole, a Napoleonic soldier leaning on a bench and the paparazzo. The castle, rebuilt in the 1950s, is a white block with four corner towers, nicknamed the upturned table, and the view over the river is fine. The UFO Bridge, with its flying-saucer restaurant on a tall pylon, is a relic of the communist era.

The ride toward Vienna is only sixty kilometres, on a motorway that crosses into Austria with almost no formality, as both countries are in the Schengen area. Motorway vignettes are required in both Slovakia and Austria, and the easy way to buy them is online before you start. The road passes the site of Carnuntum, a large Roman legionary fortress and city on the Austrian side, whose reconstructed buildings and amphitheatre are well worth a stop. It was the capital of the province of Pannonia, and the emperor Marcus Aurelius is said to have written part of his Meditations while on campaign nearby.

Within Bratislava, traffic is manageable, though the tram tracks and the cobbles of the old town are slippery when wet. Fuel stations are plentiful on the outskirts. Local food is hearty, with bryndzove halusky, potato dumplings in sheep's cheese with bacon, as the national dish, and cheap, good wine from the Little Carpathians, which begin just outside town. Spring and autumn are the best times to visit, and the vineyards turn gold in October.
t.zilina@49.2,18.7:
Zilina sits where three rivers meet, the Vah, the Kysuca and the Rajcianka, in a basin of northwestern Slovakia surrounded by the Mala Fatra, the Javorniky and the Kysuce hills. That position at a crossroads made it an important trading town, and its old square, with arcaded houses and a Renaissance bell tower, is among the most handsome in Slovakia. The Burian Tower, a tall free-standing belfry in the old town, can be climbed for a view over the roofs. The cathedral next to it, dedicated to the Holy Trinity, is baroque.

Today Zilina is a modern industrial city, partly because of the Kia car factory nearby, and its people are mostly practical and busy. The square is lively on Saturday mornings. Behind the city, the Mala Fatra National Park offers some of the best mountain scenery in Slovakia, with deep gorges, rocky ridges and forests. The castle at Strecno, a short ride along the Vah, stands on a spur above the river, and Orava Castle, a famous medieval fortress on a rock, lies a good way farther northeast.

The riding in this part of the country is varied and rewarding. Roads follow river valleys and cross passes, with long bends and views of wooded hills. The surface is generally good on main roads, though patched on minor ones. Traffic can be heavy on the main route between Zilina and Bratislava, especially trucks, so side roads are often better. The ride to Hronsek takes you south through the Turiec basin and over low hills to the Hron valley, near Banska Bystrica, where a small wooden church stands in a village.

The church at Hronsek is an articular church, built in 1726 entirely of wood without a single iron nail, with a separate bell tower, because the Habsburg authorities allowed Protestants to build only under strict conditions. It is one of several in Slovakia on the UNESCO list, and its interior is lovely, with a painted gallery and warm, pale wood.

Fuel is plentiful in Zilina and in Kysucke Nove Mesto, nine kilometres away. Try halusky with sheep's cheese, or a bowl of kapustnica, a sauerkraut soup with sausage, in a pub in the old town. Summer is warm, and the best months are May to September.
t.stellenbosch@-33.9,18.9:
Stellenbosch is the second-oldest European settlement in South Africa, founded in 1679 by the governor Simon van der Stel, who named it after himself and his wife's family, and it has the look of a town that has been carefully looked after. Oak trees line the streets, white Cape Dutch houses with curved gables stand behind them, and the mountains rise on every side, purple at dusk. It is also a university town, home to the Afrikaans-speaking Stellenbosch University, which gives the centre a young, lively atmosphere.

The wine country surrounds it, and the roads out are among the loveliest in the Western Cape. Head east on the R310 up the Helshoogte Pass toward Franschhoek, a village founded by French Huguenot refugees in the late seventeenth century, and the road climbs through vineyards and pine plantations, with views over the valley as it twists around bends. Other options include the Jonkershoek valley, a quiet dead-end valley full of fynbos, and the long loop over Sir Lowry's Pass to the coast. Traffic can be heavy on weekends and in the harvest season, and the Cape's winter, from June to August, is cold and wet, so spring and autumn are best.

The nearby mountains are part of the Cape Floral Region, a World Heritage site that covers a tiny fraction of Africa and contains an astonishing share of its plant species. Fynbos, the heathland of proteas, ericas and restios, grows on the poor sandy soils and is bright with flowers in the late winter and spring. Baboons live on the slopes, and you may meet them on the passes, where they are wise to steal food from open bike luggage. Wine is the other great crop. The Cape's Mediterranean climate suits grapes, with Pinotage, a South African cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut, as the signature red, and Chenin Blanc as the pride of the whites. Many estates offer tastings, though a motorcyclist should obviously treat them with great caution.

Practical matters are easy, and the town has fuel stations, repair shops and every kind of lodging. Drive carefully through the town centre, where students, cyclists and delivery vans share narrow streets, and park in guarded areas. Paarl, farther north-east, and Kraaifontein, close to Cape Town, are the bigger towns nearby. Take sun protection in summer, because the valley can be hot, and lunch at a vineyard restaurant is a wonderful way to spend a long afternoon.
t.cederberg@-34.0,18.8:
Stellenbosch is the second oldest town in South Africa, founded in 1679, and the heart of the Cape winelands, and this start and finish lies on its western edge, on the way to the Helderberg and Somerset West. The old town has oak trees, whitewashed Cape Dutch buildings and a university with a large student population, and the surrounding hills are covered in vineyards. The grapes grown here, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinotage and Chenin Blanc among them, have made the district famous, and many estates have tasting rooms and restaurants.

The Cederberg, however, is far away, a wilderness about two hundred kilometres to the north, and the road there is a journey into a different landscape. The mountains are a rugged range of orange-red sandstone, shaped by wind and water into arches, pinnacles and caves, including the Wolfberg Cracks and the Maltese Cross. The rock art of the San people is preserved in shelters, some many thousands of years old, showing animals and human figures. The Cederberg is the home of rooibos tea, grown on the slopes and harvested by hand, and the town of Clanwilliam is its centre. The Clanwilliam cedar, the tree that gives the range its name, is now rare and survives in a few high places.

Riding in the Cederberg means mountain passes and gravel. The Pakhuis Pass, near Clanwilliam, is a good tarmac road that climbs through rock formations, and beyond it, many tracks are unsealed, with corrugations and loose sand. Summer is very hot, with temperatures often above forty degrees in the valleys, while winter brings snow on the peaks and cold nights. Spring, from August to October, has wildflowers, and autumn is mild. Clear nights give extraordinary stars.

Fuel is easy near the start, with stations around Stellenbosch, Somerset West and Kraaifontein, the larger towns nearby. In the north, stations are in Citrusdal and Clanwilliam, but nothing lies in the mountains between, so fill the tank and carry water. Mobile coverage fades away from the towns, so tell someone your plans.

Stop at a farm stall on the way for rusks and biltong, and enjoy the sense of the country opening out as the vineyards are left behind.
t.hospicio cabanas@20.7,-103.3:
The Hospicio Cabañas is one of the great buildings of Guadalajara and arguably of the whole of Latin America, a neoclassical complex of low, long wings and twenty-three courtyards that covers more than two hectares. Bishop Juan Cruz Ruiz de Cabañas founded it at the turn of the nineteenth century as an orphanage, hospital and home for the poor, and the architect Manuel Tolsá designed it, with construction between 1805 and 1810. For nearly two hundred years it sheltered thousands of children and the elderly.

The reason people queue is the chapel, whose dome and walls were painted in the 1930s by José Clemente Orozco, one of the Mexican muralists. His masterpiece, Man of Fire, shows a figure of burning energy rising through the centre of the dome, and the surrounding murals tell of the conquest and the clash of cultures in swirling, violent colour. Lying on a bench or the floor looking up is the accepted way to view it. UNESCO listed the hospicio in 1997.

Guadalajara is a big city, of about one and a half million in the centre and many more in its metropolitan area, and the cultural capital of Jalisco, home of mariachi music and tequila. The Plaza Tapatía, a pedestrian square with fountains and a statue of the Hospicio's founder, leads to the cathedral, with its two yellow spires. Tlaquepaque, a neighbouring town, is known for pottery and crafts, and has a lively evening scene.

Riding in the city demands patience, with one-way streets, buses and roundabouts, and parking can be tricky, so use a guarded car park. Fuel is easy. Food is the highlight: birria, a spicy slow-cooked goat or beef stew; tortas ahogadas, pork sandwiches drowned in chilli sauce; and cold glasses of tejuino, a fermented maize drink. Go on a weekday for smaller crowds, and give the murals at least an hour.
t.agave landscape and ancient industrial f:
Rows of blue-grey agave stretch across the red volcanic hills of Jalisco in lines so regular they look drawn with a ruler, and they climb the slopes of the Tequila volcano as far as the eye can see. This is the heart of the agave landscape, where the blue Weber agave has been grown for tequila for more than three hundred years, and UNESCO recognised it in 2006 with the old distilleries and towns around it.

The plant takes seven to ten years to mature, and when it does, field workers called jimadores cut away the long spiky leaves with a sharp tool called a coa, leaving a round heart, the piña, that looks like a giant pineapple. The pinas are baked, crushed and fermented, and the juice distilled. Haciendas, brick chimneys and stone ovens still stand, and the old distilleries at Tequila, such as the one whose founding dates to the eighteenth century, welcome visitors for tours and tastings.

Tequila, the town, lies about six kilometres from Amatitán, in a valley beneath the volcano, with a cheerful plaza, a handsome church and painted houses. A train runs from Guadalajara on weekends, with tasting on board. The riding around is a pleasure. Roads are curving and quiet, among fields and old stone walls, and the colours of red earth, blue plants and green hills in the rainy season are extraordinary. Summers are warm with afternoon storms, and winters are dry and pleasant.

Fuel is available in Tequila and Amatitán, and so are restaurants serving birria, carne en su jugo and fresh tortillas. If you taste, do it sensibly, with a designated non-rider or an overnight stay, since a motorbike and tequila do not mix. Take time to learn the difference between blanco, reposado and añejo, and buy a bottle from a small producer. Late afternoon light turns the fields golden.
t.laponian area@67.3,17.6:
They fall in the heart of the Laponian Area, the huge World Heritage landscape of northern Sweden that takes in Sarek, Padjelanta, Stora Sjöfallet and Muddus, and most of it is roadless wilderness of glaciers, braided rivers, birch forest and bare peaks above two thousand metres. The Sami have herded reindeer through it for thousands of years, following the seasons from the high pastures down to the forests, and the protection of the area is as much about that living culture as about the nature.

What you can ride is the edge of it. From Jokkmokk, a town just north of the Arctic Circle, a road runs west along the Lule river valley to Kvikkjokk, about a hundred kilometres of good surface through spruce and bog where moose step out of the trees at dusk. From Gällivare a road leads up past Porjus and its old hydropower station to the great dammed lakes near Stora Sjöfallet and on to Ritsem, where the tarmac ends beside the mountains. Both are long dead-end rides, which means you retrace your wheel tracks, but the northern light on the water and the open birch slopes make the return feel different.

Jokkmokk holds a famous winter market in early February, a tradition going back to the seventeenth century, when the Sami traded here. In summer it is quieter, and the Ájtte museum is a good place to understand the mountain people and their land. The air smells of resin and cold water, and mosquitoes in July are fierce, so bring repellent and keep your visor down at stops. In the autumn the colours on the hillsides are astonishing and the bugs are gone.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Stations are in Jokkmokk and Gällivare, and the distances between them and the dead-end roads are real, so top up before you turn off the main road and carry a little spare. Reindeer wander freely on the roads and often stand in the middle of a bend, so slow down in the open country and be ready to stop. Sweden's right of public access lets you camp and walk almost anywhere, which is lovely, but respect the reindeer fences and the herders at work.
t.spearfish@44.5,-103.9:
Spearfish stands at the northern edge of the Black Hills, where the prairie of South Dakota lifts into a dark, forested dome of ancient rock and pine. The town, with about eleven thousand people, is a university town as well as a gateway, and its old brick main street, its trout stream and its neat tree-lined blocks give it a calmer feel than the more touristy places further south. The Black Hills themselves are sacred to the Lakota, who call them Paha Sapa, and the land was the subject of a long and bitter dispute after gold turned up in 1874.

That gold rush brought thousands of settlers, and Deadwood, only sixteen kilometres away, became one of the wildest towns in the West, the place where Wild Bill Hickok was shot dead at a poker table in 1876. Today its historic streets are lined with casinos and period buildings, and the Mount Moriah cemetery above town holds Hickok's grave and that of Calamity Jane.

Spearfish Canyon, however, is the real reason riders come. The scenic byway, US 14A, runs about forty kilometres through a limestone gorge, with tall pale cliffs rising above Spearfish Creek and dense stands of spruce, aspen and birch on the slopes. The road is a calm run of smooth bends that follows the creek, with waterfalls beside it, including Bridal Veil Falls, which drops right next to the road, and Roughlock Falls, a short walk off the main route. Parts of the film Dances with Wolves were shot in the Black Hills. Autumn, with golden aspens against the dark pines, is spectacular.

The canyon road can get busy in summer, particularly in August when the huge Sturgis motorcycle rally takes over the region and hundreds of thousands of riders arrive. Traffic then is thick, and it is much more peaceful in June or September. Watch for deer and for the occasional rockfall, and stay within the limit, as the canyon is patrolled.

Fuel, food and rooms are all easy in Spearfish. The historic fish hatchery on the edge of town, dating from the nineteenth century, has a small museum and pleasant grounds. Services in the canyon are sparse, so fill up before you go.
t.cerro gordo@23.2,-104.9:
Cerro Gordo lies in the high country of Durango, on the western side of Mexico's central plateau, where the land rises toward the Sierra Madre Occidental in long, bare ridges. The landscape is a mix of grassland, mesquite and scattered oak and pine, with dry riverbeds that flood after summer storms, and the sky is huge and very blue.

The ride is named for the temples of Nombre de Dios, a town founded by Franciscan friars in the sixteenth century as one of the first Spanish settlements in the region. Its church and convent, built of stone and adobe, speak of the missionary push into the north, when friars and soldiers followed the silver routes. The mining towns of Zacatecas and Durango grew from the same impulse, and the colonial road, the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, ran through this country. Today Nombre de Dios is a quiet town where the plaza is shaded by old trees and the streets are lined with low houses.

The state of Durango has a particular fame in cinema, since many Westerns were shot among its dry hills, with stars such as John Wayne passing through, and the landscape still looks like the backdrop of those films. The state capital, Durango, is a handsome colonial city and a good base. The roads here are generally good, though they can be rough on the edges, with long straights, gentle climbs and wide views. Cattle roam freely and may be on the road, particularly at dusk, so keep your speed under control.

Fuel is a matter of planning. Durango city, about sixty or seventy kilometres away, has everything, and Nombre de Dios has a small station, but the villages in the hills may have none, so fill before you leave and carry a spare can. Carry water, since shade and shops are scarce. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm days and cool nights, while summer brings storms and winter brings frost at night.
t.gordons bay@-34.2,18.9:
Gordon's Bay is a small harbor town at the northeastern corner of False Bay, with the Hottentots Holland mountains rising abruptly behind it and the Atlantic-facing bulk of the Cape Peninsula far away across the water.
