It is the start of Clarence Drive, the coastal road that clings to the cliffs along the eastern shore of False Bay, and for many riders it is the gate to one of the best short rides in the Western Cape. The town itself is a laid-back place with a marina, a few restaurants and a beach that fills up in summer.

The road ahead is the reason to come. Clarence Drive, the R44, climbs out of town along the mountainside with the sea far below and a sheer drop on one side, then sweeps past the bays of Kogel Bay and Rooi-Els, where the mountain falls into the water. The bends are generally open and the surface is good, so it rewards a smooth rhythm rather than speed, and the views across False Bay to Cape Point are wide and dramatic. In spring and early summer, fynbos covers the slopes in a patchwork of pink, yellow and green, and from about August to November southern right whales are often visible close to the shore.

The weather is a factor. The Cape's famous south-easterly wind, the Cape Doctor, can blow hard in summer and make the road demanding on a motorcycle, especially in the exposed sections, and rockfalls after winter storms occasionally close sections for repair. Early morning is calm and the light is lovely, but weekends bring cyclists, tourists and a good deal of traffic, so go early or on a weekday.

Practical things are easy. The town has fuel stations, small supermarkets, bakeries and seafood restaurants, and the nearby town of Somerset West has everything else. Stock up here, because the villages along the coast are small and the next fuel is at Betty's Bay or Hermanus. The harbor is a good place for breakfast, and the coffee shops open early for the cyclists.

If you have the time, the climb up Sir Lowry's Pass, just to the north, offers another view of the bay and a route toward the apple valleys of Grabouw.
t.bettys bay@-34.4,18.9:
Betty's Bay lies about midway along Clarence Drive, a scattering of low houses between the mountains and the sea, and it is the part of the coast where nature takes over. It lies within the Kogelberg Biosphere Reserve, a UNESCO-recognized area that holds one of the highest concentrations of plant species anywhere on earth, with fynbos shrubs such as proteas, ericas and restios covering the slopes in a bewildering variety. In spring, the colors are wonderful, and in winter the mountains are sharp with cloud and rain.

The town is most famous for its penguins. At Stony Point, a short walk along a boardwalk leads to a colony of African penguins, which nest among the rocks and bushes with Cape cormorants and rock hyraxes for company. The birds are endangered, and the colony here is one of the few on the mainland, so it is worth watching quietly and keeping a respectful distance. Nearby, the Harold Porter National Botanical Garden climbs a stream valley behind the beach, with waterfalls and walking paths beneath the cliffs, and is a very pleasant stop.

For a rider, Betty's Bay is the heart of the drive. The R44 continues along the foot of the mountains, with the sea alongside, passing coves and rocky points and, from August to November, whales cruising offshore. The road is wide and well surfaced, with gentle bends and long views. Wind can be strong, especially in summer when the south-easterly blows, and sea mist rolls in on cool mornings, reducing visibility. It is a good road for a relaxed run rather than a hard ride.

Facilities are modest. The village has a small shop and a handful of cafes and guesthouses, but fuel is not reliably available, so top up in Gordon's Bay before you set off or continue to Hermanus or Grabouw. Weekends can be busy at the penguin colony and the garden, and a modest entrance fee applies at both.

Plan a slow day. The place rewards walking, watching and a long lunch, and the light in the late afternoon turns the mountains a deep gold.
t.komsomolsk on amur@50.6,137.0:
Komsomolsk-on-Amur is a city with a founding myth. In 1932, volunteers from the Komsomol, the Communist youth league, were sent to a spot on the Amur River, deep in the taiga, to build a new industrial city, and they arrived to find almost nothing. The city that grew has about 276,000 people today, laid out on a neat grid of broad avenues, and it remains one of the great industrial centres of the Russian Far East, with a steel works, shipyards and an aircraft factory. Solnechny lies a short way to the northeast.

For a rider it is a proper stop. Fuel, food and mechanics are all easy to find, and the city has hotels and cafes of every type. The ride in from Khabarovsk crosses long stretches of forest and marsh, with a surface that can be good in places and punishing in others, and trucks make up much of the traffic. Distances here are big and settlements small, so fill the tank whenever you can. The best season is late summer to early autumn, when the roads are dry and the forest turns gold, while winter is bitterly cold and spring brings mud.

The history of the city is more complicated than the cheerful story suggests. Much of the early construction was carried out by prison labour, and the city stands on the Baikal-Amur Mainline, the great railway built across Siberia in the later Soviet decades. The aircraft factory, which produces Sukhoi jets, is a big employer, and you will see the shapes of aircraft on display in parts of the city. The long Amur embankment is a pleasant place for an evening walk, with the huge, slow river flowing past, a kilometre or more wide in places.

The surrounding landscape is the typical taiga of the Far East, with larch, fir, birch and wetlands, and the Amur itself dominates everything. In summer, mosquitoes and midges are fierce, and repellent is essential. In autumn, the light is lovely and the air smells of damp leaves and woodsmoke. Salmon and sturgeon run in the river, and the local cuisine includes fish soups and salted roe.

From here the road continues toward Sovetskaya Gavan on the Tatar Strait, through even emptier country, so carry spare fuel and food. Good tyres and patience are the main tools.
t.clanwilliam@-32.2,18.9:
Clanwilliam is where the dry West Coast plain meets the first wall of the Cederberg, and the town has been shaped by that meeting. It sits beside a big dam on the Olifants River, among orange orchards and fields of rooibos, the red bush that grows nowhere else in the world as a crop and that locals brew strong and sweet. It was founded in 1808 and named after the Earl of Clanwilliam, the father-in-law of the then governor, which is a very Cape way of choosing a name.

For a rider it is the gateway to the Cederberg, a wilderness of strangely sculpted sandstone, and a place to refuel, shop and eat before the climb. The town has fuel stations, supermarkets and simple restaurants, and it is the last reliable supply point for a good while. From here the road to the east climbs the Pakhuis Pass, a historic mountain road built in the 1870s, with tight bends, rocky walls and views back across the valley. Beyond the pass, the road continues through a landscape of orange rock and fynbos, with gravel tracks leading to remote farms. Early mornings and late afternoons give the warmest colours, while midsummer heat can be fierce and winter can bring cold rain and occasional snow on the peaks.

The Cederberg takes its name from the Clanwilliam cedar, an endangered conifer that grows only in these mountains and was heavily logged in the past. The area is also famous for its rock art. San people painted elephants, antelope, human figures and handprints on the sandstone shelters, and some of the images are thought to be thousands of years old. The poet and doctor C. Louis Leipoldt, who loved this country, is buried near the top of the Pakhuis Pass, and a small memorial marks the spot.

Nature here is spectacular. The sandstone has been eroded into arches, pinnacles and caves, such as the famous Wolfberg Arch and the Maltese Cross, and in spring, from August to September, the plains and valleys explode into colour with wildflowers, particularly daisies. Leopards live in the mountains, though few people ever see one, and the night sky is incredibly clear. The air is dry and aromatic, smelling of buchu and sun-warmed rock.

Fill the tank here, buy water and food, and check road conditions for the gravel stretches. Carry spare tyres or repair kits if you plan to head deeper, and expect to share the road with farm vehicles.
t.krems@48.4,15.6:
Krems is where the Wachau starts, if you come from the east. The Danube turns from a wide, brown, businesslike river into something more intimate here, squeezed between terraced vineyards and forested hills, and the town sits right at the gate. Krems an der Donau has about fourteen thousand people and its twin Stein is a few minutes along the bank, with a medieval gate and a narrow main street that feels more like a film set than a place to buy groceries. You can find fuel, food and a bike-friendly hotel without effort.

The Wachau is a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, and it earns it. The vineyards climb in dry-stone terraces up to the rocky ridges, and the wines here, especially Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, have a mineral snap that comes from the granite and loess soils. The valley is also famous for its apricots, the Wachauer Marille, which have protected origin status; in spring the orchards bloom white, and in July the roadside stalls sell jam, schnapps and fresh fruit. If you are here on a warm afternoon, order a glass of Grüner at a Heuriger, the traditional wine tavern, and don't plan anything strenuous afterwards.

Across the river stands Göttweig Abbey, a Benedictine monastery on a hill, which you can see from the road for miles and which is worth a short detour if you like baroque stairs. Further along, the Danube road passes the village of Dürnstein, with its blue baroque tower and the ruined castle above, where legend says Richard the Lionheart was held captive in 1192 on his way home from the Crusades. The story is half history, half romantic legend, but the castle ruin is real enough.

For riding, the Wachau is more about the pleasures of a steady pace than about corners. The road follows the north bank in gentle bends, with the river on one side and the vineyards on the other, and it is rarely steep. On sunny weekends it fills with cyclists, tour buses and other riders, so go early or on a weekday if you can. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with blossom in April and golden vineyards in October, and the light along the river in the late afternoon is as good as any in Austria.
t.melk@48.2,15.3:
Melk is dominated by one thing, and you can't miss it. The Benedictine abbey stands on a rock above the Danube like a yellow-and-white ship, with twin towers and a baroque dome, and it has watched over this stretch of river for nearly a thousand years. The monks took up the site in 1089, when Leopold II of Babenberg gave the hilltop to the order, and the building you see today is the product of an eighteenth-century rebuilding in full baroque style. It is still a working monastery with a school, and the library, with its painted ceiling and thousands of old volumes, is as handsome a room as you will see in Austria. Umberto Eco gave the name to his narrator in The Name of the Rose, Adso of Melk, which tells you something about the abbey's reputation.

The town below is small, about four thousand people, with a pastel main street and a few cafés that serve decent coffee and a slice of torte. It is a good place to end a day on the Wachau road, since you can find fuel, supper and a bed without any fuss. The Danube bike path runs right past, so expect a good number of cyclists in yellow rain jackets, and treat them with the usual courtesy.

From the abbey terrace the view takes in the river, the bridge and the forested hills of the Dunkelsteinerwald. If the light is low and the Danube is still, the effect is something close to a painting. The Wachau begins just upriver, and it is hard to find a better way to finish a ride than to come in from the west with the abbey slowly growing in front of you.

The riding in the area is mellow rather than dramatic, a matter of long river bends, vineyard slopes and the occasional brief climb. Summer weekends can be busy, and the narrow lanes around the old town do not suit a big touring bike, so use the car park below the abbey. In spring and autumn you will have more room, and the mist rising off the river in the morning is something worth getting up early for.
t.znojmo@48.9,16.0:
Znojmo is a town on a bluff above the Dyje river, on the southern edge of Moravia, with Austria just over the hills, and its character is that of a place that has been on a frontier for a thousand years. The old town is a pleasing muddle of cobbled lanes, Gothic towers and baroque façades, with a tall town-hall tower, a castle on the cliff and a rotunda from around 1100, whose Romanesque wall-paintings are among the oldest in the country. With about thirty-five thousand people, it has full services, so fuel, food and repair are all easy.

The surrounding landscape is the main reason to come. The slopes around Znojmo are wine country, with vineyards of Grüner Veltliner, Riesling and other white varieties, and the cellars of the old town are connected by an extensive underground labyrinth, which you can tour. Along the river, the Podyjí National Park protects a deep, wooded meander of the Dyje, with ruined castles and rare plants. The town is also famous for its pickled gherkins, which are sold in jars across the country and celebrated in a festival each year, which says something about the local sense of humour.

For the end of the South Moravian wine route, Znojmo is a very satisfying finish. The route passes through villages with rows of low wine cellars, called sklepy, in painted yellow and white, and in some places the whole village seems to be made of them. The riding is gentle, with rolling hills, quiet roads and small bends, with an eye out for tractors, farm vehicles and, in September, harvest traffic. The surface is generally reasonable, though patched in places.

If you finish in the evening, have a glass of local wine at one of the cellar bars, but arrange a bed first and leave the bike parked. Czech food here is generous: roast pork, dumplings, goulash, and fruit dumplings. In spring, the blossom turns the fields white, and autumn brings golden light and the smell of new wine. Winter can be cold, with mist over the river, but the old town is cosy then, and the cellars warm.
t.raftsundet@68.4,15.0:
Raftsundet is the narrow strait between the islands of Hinnøya and Austvågøya, and it is the gateway to Lofoten from the east. The strait is about twenty kilometres long and in places only a few hundred metres wide, with steep mountains rising on both sides, and it is the route taken by the Hurtigruten coastal ferries. The famous Trollfjord, a short, narrow side fjord with sheer walls, opens from the strait, and ships sail in to turn around. The nearest towns are Melbu, Stokmarknes and Svolvær, each a short ride away, so fuel and food are not a worry.

The riding in this part of Nordland is superb. The road crosses the Raftsund bridge, a graceful, slender structure, and then runs along the edge of the island with views of the peaks of Lofoten across the water. The surface is good, the bends are frequent but gentle, and the scenery is among the finest in Europe: jagged, snow-streaked mountains rising straight out of the sea, reflected in calm water on still days. Weather can be wild, with rain, wind and low cloud, but when it clears, the light is spectacular. In summer, the midnight sun lasts from late May to mid-July.

The history of the strait is bound up with fishing. For centuries, the cod fishing season, from January to April, drew thousands of fishermen to Lofoten, and the fish was dried on racks and exported to Italy, Spain and Portugal, where stockfish remains a delicacy. The old fishing villages, with their red rorbu huts, are a feature of the landscape. The sea eagle is the largest bird of prey in Europe, and you can see them in the strait, sometimes in numbers.

Fuel is available in the nearby towns, and the road is well served, but in the quieter areas, plan carefully. Svolvær has everything from supermarkets to restaurants, and in smaller villages, you will find small shops and cafes. In summer, the roads are busier with campervans, so ride early or late. A stop to look at the water, in the long evening light, is the best plan for this stretch.
t.andenes@69.3,16.1:
Andenes sits on the northern tip of Andøya, the northernmost island in the Vesterålen archipelago, and it is where the Arctic Ocean begins to feel close. The town is small, with about 2,700 people, a harbour, a lighthouse and a collection of low houses on a flat spit of land, and its main claim to fame is whales. Just off the coast, the continental shelf drops steeply, bringing deep water close to shore, and sperm whales feed there in summer, so boat trips run daily from the harbour. The Whale Safari is a well-established business, and sightings are common, though never guaranteed.

The town has a long history of fishing, and the old lighthouse, built in 1859, still stands on the shore. Andøya was also the site of a Norwegian rocket range, built in the 1960s for research into the northern lights and the upper atmosphere, and it is now being developed for small satellite launches. A museum, the Arctic Whale Centre, explains the whales, and the Polar Museum tells of Arctic exploration. In autumn and winter, the northern lights are bright over the sea, and in summer, the midnight sun reigns.

The Andøya route runs along the west coast of the island, a quiet, open road that follows the shore of the Norwegian Sea, past sandy beaches, bog land and low hills. The surface is good, and the curves are gentle, with the open sea on one side and mountains on the other. Wind can be strong, and in winter, snow and ice are likely. Traffic is light, and you can ride for kilometres with no other vehicle. Look out for sea eagles, whooper swans and, if lucky, elk on the moors.

Andenes has fuel stations, shops and restaurants, so it is a good place to prepare. Myre, further south, also has services, but beyond that, the road is quiet. Local cafes serve fish soup, waffles and coffee, and in summer the quay is lively with boats coming and going. The ferry to Gryllefjord on Senja leaves from here in summer, and it is a nice addition. Rest by the lighthouse in the evening, and watch the sea turn golden.
t.risoyhamn@69.0,15.6:
Risøyhamn is a small village on the eastern side of Andøya, set on a sheltered bay with a view over the Risøysundet strait, and it feels very different from the exposed western coast. The settlement is a scatter of fishermen's houses, boat sheds and a few shops, with a harbour that serves as a base for local boats. The Risøyhamn Church and the old trading post recall the days when the village was a centre of the herring trade, and the area is quiet and peaceful. Myre, about twenty kilometres away, is the nearest place with fuel and shops.

The east coast of Andøya is greener and softer than the west, with farms, birch trees and gentle hills, and the water in the sound is often calm. The island's interior is peat bog, and the high ground has cloudberries in late summer, which locals pick in great quantities. Andøya is also known for its fossils, because the island has some of the oldest rock in Norway and traces of Jurassic life. The Andøya Space Centre, a short distance from Andenes, also holds exhibitions.

The road from Andenes to Risøyhamn follows the coast and then passes through the central part of the island, a mix of bog, lakes and low hills. The route is mostly smooth, with long straight sections and gentle curves. Wind is common, and rain showers pass quickly, but when the sun comes out, the colours are bright. Reindeer do not live on Andøya, but sheep and the occasional elk do, so keep an eye out, particularly at dusk. The road continues to the bridge to Hinnøya, which leads to the rest of the Vesterålen islands.

Be prepared with fuel, since the village has few services, and the nearest pumps are at Myre or Andenes. A small shop may sell coffee and snacks, but options are limited. In summer, the midnight sun allows long evenings, and in autumn, the northern lights may appear above the water. Stop on the quay, watch the boats come in, and listen to the gulls. It is a peaceful place to end a ride.
t.hout bay@-34.0,18.3:
Hout Bay is a fishing harbour wedged into a bowl of mountains on the Atlantic side of the Cape Peninsula, and it keeps a stubborn, salty independence from the city just over the ridge. The name is Dutch for wood: early settlers cut the forests that once stood in the valley for timber, long before the suburbs, and today the slopes of the Sentinel, a rock peak that guards the mouth of the bay, are covered in fynbos and houses with fine views. Constantia, about seven kilometres away over the pass, is the nearest big suburb.

The harbour is where things happen. Fishing boats unload crayfish and snoek, a long, silvery fish that locals braai and eat with apricot jam, and fish and chips are served on the quay to people watching the seals that hang about the wharf in hope of scraps. Boats leave from the jetty for Duiker Island, a rocky islet crowded with Cape fur seals, which you smell before you see. A weekend market in a converted warehouse offers local food, music and crafts.

For a rider, Hout Bay is the hinge of the best coastal loop in the country. From the harbour, you go south on Chapman's Peak Drive, one of the world's great roads, or climb over Constantia Nek into the wine country. The road in from Cape Town goes over the shoulder of the mountain with great views of the bay, and on a clear day the whole waterfront lies below like a map. Summer brings southeasterly winds that whip down the slopes, and in winter cold fronts bring rain and big swell, so check conditions, and be careful with sand and wet patches on the road by the beach.

There is no problem finding fuel, food or a coffee, with petrol stations on the main road and many cafés along the waterfront. Sunsets from the harbour wall, with the mountains turning pink, are very fine, and local restaurants serve seafood with a glass of Cape wine. Weekends in summer are busy, so go early to find parking and enjoy the road before the traffic builds.
t.chapmans peak@-34.1,18.4:
Nine kilometres of road hang on the cliffs between Hout Bay and Noordhoek, and the Cape Peninsula has nothing better. Chapman's Peak Drive was cut into the sheer face of the mountain in the early twentieth century, opening in 1922 after years of work, and it clings to the rock a hundred metres or more above the Atlantic with 114 corners, so people say, in a short, spectacular ride. Between bends there are galleries and shelters built over the road to protect it from falling rock, which is a fact of life here.

The name comes, according to the usual story, from John Chapman, a pilot on an English ship who put into the bay in the seventeenth century. Whatever its origin, the drive is a toll road, with a gate where you pay a modest fee, and it can close without warning for rockfall, high winds or fires, so check the status before you set off. When it is open, it is a joy, with a perfect surface, a view down to the water, and traffic that is usually well-behaved, though tourists stop at the viewpoints and cyclists use it on weekends.

Direction matters for the best view. Ride from Hout Bay toward Noordhoek and the sea is on your left, with the cliff on your right, and the sweep of Noordhoek Beach, one of the longest on the peninsula, unrolls ahead. Winds can be strong, gusting across the cliffs, and in winter the spray from heavy swells can reach the road, so take it easy in rough weather. Morning light is soft, and the late afternoon turns the rock gold, though by then more traffic is out.

At the top of the drive, there is a parking area where you can get off the bike, take in the view over the bay and watch the paragliders sometimes launching from above. The route continues to Noordhoek, with cafés and a farm village, and on toward Cape Point. Constantia and Bergvliet are suburbs to the north, and Retreat is a bigger one, but the best place for fuel is Hout Bay at one end or Noordhoek at the other. Bring a windproof layer even in summer.
t.hermanus@-34.4,19.2:
In Hermanus, one of the town's municipal employees blows a horn made from kelp to announce the whales. The whale crier is a local tradition, and it makes sense, because between roughly June and November southern right whales come into Walker Bay to calve and play, and from the cliff path that runs along the shoreline you can watch them from a few metres above the surf. Mothers and calves roll in the shallows, males breach and slap the water with their tails, and you hear their breath carried across the bay. It is among the best land-based whale watching in the world.

The cliff path follows the coast for about twelve kilometres, passing the Old Harbour, a small museum with fishing boats, and rocky coves with natural pools. The town began as a fishing village in the nineteenth century and takes its name from Hermanus Pieters, a schoolteacher who herded his flock here, and today it has about twenty-five thousand people, a handsome main street of galleries, cafés and seafood restaurants, and a wine valley in the hills behind. Fynbos flowers cover the slopes, with proteas and ericas in bloom through winter.

The riding on the way is among the best of the Western Cape. Clarence Drive, the R44 coast road between Gordon's Bay and Rooi-Els, hugs the cliff above False Bay, with bends, dramatic sea views and rocky coves, and there is hardly a bad stretch. The Kogelberg Biosphere Reserve runs along the inland side, with mountains tumbling down to the water. Winds are strong, especially in summer when the south-easter can make the bike lean, and in winter fronts bring rain and mist, so look at the forecast. The best hours are early morning, when light is soft and the road is quiet.

Fuel is plentiful in Hermanus, and a number of garages sit on the main roads. If you push on, Caledon and Grabouw are the next towns, though they are smaller and further apart. Many restaurants serve fresh fish, calamari and crayfish, and a glass of Hemel-en-Aarde wine from the valley behind town is an excellent way to end the day. Book accommodation in advance during the whale season and school holidays, when the town fills up and prices rise.
t.wellington sa@-33.6,19.0:
Wellington is a farming town at the foot of the Groenberg mountains, and it sits at the start of one of the most beautiful passes in the Cape. It is known for wine, brandy and dried fruit, and long avenues of oak trees lead into its centre, with fields of vines and orchards beyond. Originally called Wagenmakersvallei, the Wagon-makers' Valley, it was renamed in the nineteenth century for the Duke of Wellington, and it grew into a centre of education and trade, with an old girls' seminary and a handsome Dutch Reformed church that give it a dignified air.

The wine estates around the town are quieter than those of Stellenbosch, and many have a family feel, with tastings on the porch and views over the vineyards to the mountains. Dried fruit stalls sell raisins, apricots and figs, and local biltong is excellent. Paarl, about eleven kilometres away, is a much bigger town, and with Wellington it forms part of the winelands of the Boland.

For motorcyclists, the town is the gateway to Bainskloof Pass, the winding road that climbs through the mountains toward Ceres and the Breede River valley. From Wellington, you ride out between vineyards and fruit trees, with the mountain walls rising ahead, and the road narrows and begins to climb into a gorge. Early morning is lovely, with mist in the vineyards and the peaks turning pink, and the traffic is light. Summer heat can be strong, and in winter the mountains get snow, so check the weather.

The town itself has all that you need, with several petrol stations, banks, restaurants and workshops, and a population of more than fifty thousand people when the surrounding areas are counted. The cafés on the main street offer good coffee and breakfasts, and the farm stalls sell fresh bread and jam. Malmesbury, about thirty kilometres to the north-west, is the next sizeable town in that direction, in wheat country. Plan to leave early, with a full tank, before you tackle the mountain road.
t.bainskloof pass@-33.6,19.1:
Andrew Geddes Bain, a Scottish-born road engineer, built this pass in the middle of the nineteenth century, and a surprising amount of his work is still what you ride on. Bainskloof, completed in the early 1850s with the labour of convicts, links Wellington with Wolseley and the Breede River valley by cutting through the Limietberg mountains, and it was designated a national monument long ago. The stonework is the thing to notice: dry-packed retaining walls, culverts and bridges that have outlived most modern roads.

Riding it is a sequence of tight bends in a gorge of rock and fynbos, with the Witte River running far below and rock faces rising close on one side. There is not much run-off and not much width, so keep to your lane, slow down for blind corners, and expect the odd oncoming car in the middle of the road. Baboons sit on the walls and sometimes on the tarmac, and they are bolder than they look, so do not feed or approach them. Ride on a dry day, since the surface can be slippery when wet, and mist and rain make the walls feel closer than ever.

The best moment is a quiet morning in spring or early summer, when the mountains are green and the flowers are out, with proteas and ericas on the slopes and the smell of wet rock. In winter the peaks above the pass may carry snow, and the road can be damp for days, so look up the conditions. Pools in the river below, reached by short paths, are lovely for a swim after a hot ride, if you do not mind the cold. The sun comes late to parts of the gorge, so some bends stay in shade and may hold ice on frosty mornings.

There are no services on the pass itself, so take what you need. Wellington, fourteen kilometres away with a population above fifty thousand, has fuel and restaurants, and Paarl and Ceres are the larger towns on either side. Cell reception can vanish in the gorge, so tell somebody your route, and keep to a steady pace. A flask of coffee and a view are all you need at the top.
t.ceres@-33.4,19.3:
Ceres is fruit country, and the signs on the road say so, with apples, pears and peaches grown in the high valley of the Warm Bokkeveld. The town lies in a bowl surrounded by the Cape fold mountains, and the name is that of the Roman goddess of agriculture, which suits it. Orchards cover the floor of the basin, packing sheds and juice factories line the edges, and in blossom time in early spring the valley turns white and pink. Around forty thousand people live here, a mixture of farming families and seasonal workers.

Winter is the surprise. The Matroosberg, the high peak that closes the valley to the east, collects snow every year, and when it does, cars arrive from Cape Town to throw snowballs and take photographs, turning a sleepy road into a small traffic jam. This is one of the few places in the Western Cape where the cold is real, with frost on the orchards and ice on the roads in the early hours, so check conditions in July and August.

The riding in is a pleasure. From Wellington, the Bainskloof Pass brings you down through the mountains toward the Breede valley, and from there you approach Ceres through Mitchell's Pass, a narrow cut in the rock engineered in the 1840s. The road bends along the river through a gorge, with the walls rising above you, before opening into the broad, green valley. Heading north, the Gydo Pass climbs steeply out of the basin toward the open Karoo plateau, with views back over orchards and the rows of trees, and the world turns dry and empty.

The town has all the usual services, with fuel stations on the main road, banks, workshops and supermarkets, and Worcester, thirty kilometres south-east and a good deal larger, is the next big centre. The farm stalls along the road sell fresh fruit, juice and dried fruit, and the cafés in town are a good place for pie and coffee. Late summer and autumn bring harvests and the smell of ripe fruit, and the light on the mountains in the late afternoon is excellent. Take warm gear if you are riding in winter, because the evenings are sharp.
t.paarl@-33.7,19.0:
Paarl is named after a rock. In 1657, an explorer saw a huge granite dome glistening after rain and called it the Pearl, and the town grew up beneath it, along the Berg River at the heart of the Cape winelands. The Paarl Rock, which locals say is one of the largest granite outcrops in the world, rises above the valley in a smooth grey whaleback, and you can walk or drive up to its base for views over vineyards and the distant peaks of the Drakenstein range.

The town stretches for a long distance along one main street, lined with oaks and Cape Dutch buildings, with wine estates on every side. Brandy and wine are the main business, and the headquarters of a famous wine cooperative are here. The Taal Monument, built in 1975 on a hill above town, celebrates the Afrikaans language with a tall concrete tower and a curved wall. The Huguenots, French Protestant refugees, settled in the valley in the late seventeenth century and left their names on farms such as La Provence and Picardie.

Paarl also carries heavier history. At the Victor Verster prison on the outskirts of town, Nelson Mandela spent the last months of his twenty-seven years in captivity, and it was from its gates that he walked out a free man in February 1990, hand in hand with Winnie Mandela. A bronze statue marks the spot. It is a sober place to stand, beside a highway lined with vines.

For riders, Paarl is the base for several fine mountain roads. The Du Toitskloof old road climbs east toward Worcester in a series of hairpins, Bainskloof lies to the north, and Franschhoek Pass is a short ride to the south-east. The town is a big place, almost two hundred thousand people in the wider municipality, so fuel, parts, repairs and food are no problem, with good coffee and farm breakfasts. Wellington and Stellenbosch are both a short ride away. Summers are hot and dry, with the south-easter wind blowing hard in the afternoons, so ride early, and take a long lunch under the oaks.
t.du toitskloof pass@-33.7,19.1:
For decades, every vehicle crossing from Cape Town to the interior had to climb the Du Toitskloof Pass, and there are drivers who still talk of the queues and the fog. In the late 1980s, a long tunnel was bored under the mountain on the N1 highway, and the old road was given up to riders, cyclists and anyone prepared to spend a little more time. It is now one of the quietest great roads in the Cape, with the traffic thundering through the tunnel below.

The old pass leaves Paarl and climbs the western face of the Du Toitskloof mountains in a series of hairpins and long curves, with granite cliffs overhead and the valley dropping away behind you. The surface is paved and generally good, but rock falls and water can leave debris, and the corners tighten without much warning, so take care in the damp. At the top, a viewpoint offers a wide look back over the Paarl valley, with vineyards, dams and Table Mountain on the far horizon on a clear day, and then the road falls into the Breede valley on the other side.

Cloud sits on the summit more often than not. Cold, thick fog can reduce visibility to a few metres, and in winter snow dusts the peaks and ice forms on the road, so choose a clear day, switch on your lights and slow down. Spring brings wildflowers and rushing streams, while summer is warm and dry, with strong wind funnelling through the gaps. Baboons are seen along the road, and rock rabbits sun themselves on warm stones.

There are no services on the pass, so make use of the nearby towns. Paarl, about sixteen kilometres away, has everything, and Wellington is a similar distance in a different direction, while Worcester, nearly thirty kilometres on the far side, is the next big centre. A drink and snack at one of the farm stalls at either end are a fair reward for the climb. Early morning is the best time, when the road is empty and the light on the cliffs is soft.
t.franschhoek@-33.9,19.1:
Franschhoek means French corner, and the story behind the name is one of the Cape's founding tales. In 1688, a group of Huguenot refugees fleeing religious persecution in France were granted land in this high valley by the Dutch East India Company, and they brought vines and winemaking skills with them. Their descendants still carry names like Du Plessis and Malherbe, the farms have French names, and a monument at the head of the village commemorates them with three tall arches and a statue.

The setting is a sheltered, steep-sided valley enclosed by mountains, with lines of oaks and poplars, whitewashed Cape Dutch gables and rows of vines turning gold and red in autumn. Today the village is known more for its food than its history, with a great number of restaurants for a place of its size, and for wine estates offering tastings. A vintage tram runs between farms in summer, and many visitors come from Cape Town for the day.

The riding is the other reason to come. The road from Stellenbosch runs between farms and vineyards in gentle bends, and from the village the Franschhoek Pass climbs steeply toward the east, with hairpins and wide views over the valley. Traffic can be heavy at weekends and on summer holidays, so a weekday morning is much better. In winter the mountains are often draped in cloud, and rain can make cobbles and painted lines slippery in the village.

The village has fuel stations, cafés and a few small shops, though a larger range of workshops and supplies is found in Stellenbosch, about twenty-four kilometres away, and Paarl nearly the same distance in the other direction. The best time for a visit is spring, when the vineyards are green and the weather is mild, or autumn, when the leaves change colour and the harvest is over. Book a table if you want to eat at one of the better restaurants, and watch your alcohol intake before you ride, since the roads are narrow and there are police checks on weekends.
t.franschhoek pass@-33.9,19.2:
Long before there was a road, elephants walked this route, and the earliest track was known as the Olifantspad, the elephant path. The animals found the easiest way across the mountains between the Franschhoek valley and the high plains of the Theewaterskloof, and later hunters, traders and farmers followed them, until a proper pass was built in the nineteenth century. Today the R45 climbs the same line, and the thought of elephants lumbering up it gives the mountain an extra dimension.

From the village, the road climbs on the south side of the valley in a series of bends, with Franschhoek spread out below among the vineyards. At the top, a viewpoint and monument look down over the valley and the winding road, with the great mass of the Groenberg and Wemmershoek ranges beyond. Then it drops steeply on the far side toward the Lebanon forestry area and the Theewaterskloof dam, a huge reservoir that supplies Cape Town with water. The surface is good and the corners well engineered, with some tight hairpins, but mist and wind can strike on the summit, and in the rain the climb needs respect.

Cyclists and sightseers use the pass heavily at weekends, so go early on a weekday for the clearest road. Fynbos covers the slopes, and in spring and early summer there are proteas, ericas and watsonias in flower, while baboons and rock hyrax appear at the roadside. Fog is common in winter, and the temperature drops sharply near the top, so a spare layer is sensible. The light in the late afternoon turns the mountains deep blue.

Grabouw, nearly thirty kilometres away, is the main town on the eastern side, famous for apples, and Stellenbosch and Paarl are the large centres to the west. Farm stalls and cafés in the valley are a good place to stop for lunch, while the dam on the far side is a pleasant spot for a break, with water, birds and an open sky.
t.villiersdorp@-34.0,19.3:
Villiersdorp is a small fruit town in a valley that remains out of most travellers' plans, which is part of the point. It lies in the Overberg region beyond the mountains from Franschhoek, near the large Theewaterskloof dam, with orchards of apples, pears and stone fruit stretching along the road, and a main street of low buildings and gardens. The town was laid out in the mid-nineteenth century and named for Pieter de Villiers, a local landowner, and it has kept the quiet, orderly air of a farming centre.

The valley is walled in by mountains on both sides, and in spring the orchards are in blossom, with a haze of white and pink against dark rock. In summer, the fruit is harvested and packed, and the roadside stalls sell peaches, plums and nectarines at prices a city dweller will envy. The dam nearby, one of the main water sources for Cape Town, provides a focal point for fishing, birdwatching and sailing, though its level drops in dry years, leaving a wide ring of pale shoreline.

For riders, the town is the eastern end of the Franschhoek Pass run, and a pleasant destination in itself. The road drops from the pass through farmland and pine plantations, with views over the water and the hills, then flattens into rolling country. It is a quiet, rural road, with little traffic, a few long bends and a surface that is good for the most part, though farm vehicles and animals on the road deserve attention. Winds can be strong in the open, and cold fronts bring rain from the west in winter.

The town has a few fuel stations and a couple of simple cafés and bakeries, and Grabouw, about thirty kilometres to the west, is the larger centre with more services, while Caledon, a small town to the south-east, is another option. Tea rooms and farm stalls offer pies, pancakes and jam, and the country markets are a good place to buy local produce. Plan a leisurely lunch before heading back over the mountain, and keep an eye on the weather, since afternoon cloud can gather over the pass.
t.cederberg@-32.5,19.3:
The Cederberg is a place where rock has been sculpted into shapes that seem to belong to another planet. This wilderness of sandstone peaks lies north of Citrusdal in the Western Cape, about two hundred kilometres from Cape Town, and wind and rain have carved it into arches, pinnacles and caves, in red, orange and gold. The Wolfberg Arch, the Maltese Cross and the Stadsaal Caves are among the best known, and in the caves, San rock paintings of animals and people, thousands of years old, can still be seen.

The mountains take their name from the Clanwilliam cedar, a rare conifer that once grew in large stands and is now confined to a few high ridges, after centuries of logging and fires. Down in the valleys, the land is dry and dusty, with fynbos on the slopes, and the surprising thing is that the area is the home of rooibos, the red bush tea, which is grown here on small farms and has been drunk by the local people for generations. In spring, wildflowers cover the slopes, and in winter, snow sometimes whitens the peaks.

The roads are mostly gravel, though the main route over the Pakhuis Pass, another work of Thomas Bain, is a pleasant ride. Gravel surfaces vary with weather and grading, so be ready for corrugations and loose stones, and keep your speed under control, especially on bends and through dry river crossings. Summer is hot, with temperatures over thirty-five degrees, so mornings are best, and winter nights can be freezing. Distances between services are long, and mobile coverage is patchy, so plan carefully.

There is no town in the heart of the mountains, only a few farms and campsites, so fill the tank in Citrusdal or Clanwilliam before you go, and carry water, food and a basic repair kit. Many farms offer simple accommodation and meals, often with a braai in the evening, and the stars here, far from any city, are astonishing. Cederberg wines are made on some farms, at an altitude that gives them a distinct character. Take sunscreen and a hat, and allow yourself time to walk to the rock formations.
t.koyasan temple town@34.2,135.6:
Koyasan is a mountaintop monastery town that has been welcoming pilgrims for more than twelve centuries. In 816, the monk Kukai, posthumously known as Kobo Daishi, received permission from the emperor to found a retreat on this plateau in the Kii mountains, south of Osaka, and it became the headquarters of Shingon Buddhism. Over a hundred temples now stand among the cedar forest at around 800 metres above sea level, and the whole area is part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing for the sacred sites and pilgrimage routes of the Kii mountain range.

The most remarkable place is Okunoin, a cemetery of vast, mossy cedars where more than two hundred thousand gravestones, lanterns and memorials line a long path to the mausoleum of Kukai. Tradition says he is not dead but in eternal meditation, and monks still bring him meals each day. Walking the path in the early morning mist, with the soft light through the trees and the smell of incense and damp moss, is one of the most atmospheric experiences in Japan. Many visitors stay overnight in a temple lodging, called shukubo, where guests eat vegetarian monastic cuisine and can join the dawn prayers.

The road up to Koyasan is a fine one. It climbs from the Kii river valley in tight, well-banked bends through dense forest, with excellent tarmac and almost no traffic outside the holiday seasons, and the air gets cooler as you rise. Autumn colours in late October and November are splendid, and snow can arrive in winter, making the road icy. In the town, speeds are slow and pedestrians are plentiful. Parking is organised near the main temples, and it makes sense to walk once you have arrived.

For services, Koyasan has cafes, small shops and several restaurants serving shojin ryori, the meatless temple cuisine of tofu, vegetables and sesame. Fuel is hard to find in the area, so fill up in Hashimoto, about twelve kilometres from town, before the climb. If you are staying in a temple, check in times and dinner hours, because they tend to be strict, and be ready for early mornings and cold rooms. The silence in the evening is a rare pleasure, broken only by a distant bell.
t.chocho ow wooden village@49.4,19.8:
Chochołów is a village that is better than a museum because people still live in it. A single long street, running through the Podhale region of southern Poland, is lined with log houses of dark, weathered timber, their gables facing the road, with carved decoration, small windows and steep roofs. Most date from the nineteenth century, built by highland families, the Górale, from spruce and fir, and the whole street is protected as a monument. Behind them, on a clear day, the white ridge of the Tatra mountains fills the horizon.

The village has a place in Polish history, too. In 1846, a peasant uprising broke out here against Austrian rule, part of a wider revolt in Galicia, and it was quickly suppressed. The local tradition of independence and pride has never gone away, and the region is known for its highland culture: music played on fiddles, intricate costume, dialect and a strong sense of identity. The Górale are also known for their smoked sheep's cheese, oscypek, sold in small spindle shapes at roadside stalls and grilled on the spot.

The ride from Kraków to this area is a pleasant run through the foothills of the Beskids and the Gorce, with rolling farmland, hay meadows, wooden churches and steep-roofed barns. The main roads can be busy, especially on summer weekends, when traffic heads for Zakopane, and the road through Chochołów is slow, with pedestrians, pedestrian crossings and sometimes tourists photographing houses. A weekday morning or a late afternoon is far calmer. Weather can change quickly in the foothills, with sunshine, storms and clouds spilling off the mountains, so a waterproof layer is wise.

As a stop, it is a short and rewarding one. Cafes and small restaurants serve żurek, a sour rye soup, pierogi and kwaśnica, a hearty sauerkraut stew, and you can walk the length of the street in half an hour. Fuel is available at Czarny Dunajec, about eight kilometres away, and in Zakopane, around twelve, where the traffic is heavier. Park the bike at the side of the road, respect the residents' privacy, and look closely at the carved gables and doors.
t.lofoten norwegian scenic route point 1@6:
North of the Arctic Circle the road to Lofoten starts to feel like the end of the world. This part of Nordland and Vesterålen is a land of fjords, long islands and steep, sharp mountains rising straight out of the sea, with low sun and big weather. The nearest places of any size are Melbu, Stokmarknes and Sortland, small towns on the islands of Hadsel and Langøya, and each has a garage, a supermarket and somewhere to eat. Fuel is thin on the ground farther out, so top up here.

Stokmarknes has a place in coastal history, because it was from here that the first Hurtigruten steamer set out in 1893, on a coastal route that was the start of the famous coastal express. The ship was run by Richard With, a local skipper, and the line proved that the dangerous northern sea route could be sailed in winter. A small museum in town tells the story. The coastal steamers still serve these communities today, and passing ships are a familiar sight.

The riding is the main draw. The E10 and the connecting roads wind along the shores of the fjords, across long bridges and through tunnels, with sharp peaks above and the sea on the other side. Surfaces are generally excellent, and traffic is light, though lorries and campervans are common in summer. Wind can be strong on the bridges, and the weather swings between sun, rain and low cloud in an hour. Speed limits are low and strictly enforced, and the fines in Norway are steep.

In summer, the midnight sun shines here from about late May to mid-July, so the light is endless and golden, and a ride at midnight is an unforgettable experience. In winter, the northern lights dance, though the roads can be icy. The smell is of sea, pine and drying fish. Stockfish, cod hung on wooden racks to dry in the cold wind, is the local product, exported for centuries to Italy. Wear warm layers, even in July, because the evening can be chilly.
t.norwegian scenic route andoya point 4@69:
By now Andøya's boggy flatlands have given way to something more dramatic. The mountains of Vesterålen and the neighbouring island of Hinnøya crowd the view, and the road threads between water and rock, with fjords cutting in from the coast. The scene changes with every turn: bright blue water, steep scree slopes, pastures dotted with farm buildings, and above it all the cloud, which can sit low on the peaks or break open to show a sudden stripe of snow.

Vesterålen is a fishing region and has been for a thousand years. The sea here is rich with cod, and fishermen once rowed out in open boats from small settlements along the shore, the fish being dried on wooden racks to make stockfish for markets as far away as Italy. White-tailed sea eagles are common, and in spring and summer you may see them hunting over the water. In the fjords, porpoises and seals also appear, and the occasional orca is spotted from the road.

For riders this is a satisfying part of the route. The road is mostly well surfaced, with gentle climbs, long views and curves that follow the shore, and there is little traffic outside the summer months. The weather is the main variable: wind and rain can arrive suddenly, and temperatures stay modest even in July, so waterproofs and warm layers are essential. The long summer light means you can ride late into the evening, and the low sun on the water is something you will remember.

Villages along this stretch are small, with a few shops and cafés, but fuel should be planned. Myre is about twenty kilometres away, and Borkenes is about thirty, so it makes sense to top up the tank before a long section. Norwegian roads are well maintained, but speed limits are low and enforced, and cameras are common in towns. Pull over when you see a good view and let faster traffic go by; the point of the ride is not to arrive, but to look.
By now you have crossed to the eastern, more sheltered flank of Senja, and the character of the riding shifts. The mountains are still sharp, but the fjords are broader and the weather often a notch kinder than on the exposed western coast. The mainland town of Finnsnes lies about thirty kilometres away, linked to Senja by a long bridge that crosses the sound, and it is the natural hub of the area with shops, services and a proper selection of places to eat.

The road here has a gentler rhythm. You get long, easy bends along the water, short climbs through birch forest and the occasional stretch where the surface has been recently renewed and feels like silk. Traffic picks up a little near the bridge and the main settlements, so overtaking becomes a question of patience rather than nerve. Evening light on the sound is superb, and a pause at any viewpoint can turn into a longer stay when the water goes flat and the sky turns apricot.

Senja has been inhabited for thousands of years, and the sea has always been both larder and highway. Coastal people here fished cod and herring, farmed small plots and traded with merchants who came by boat long before roads existed. The bridge is a recent change; until it was built, the island's connection to the mainland was by ferry, and a sense of island independence still lingers.

For wildlife, moose browse in the birch forest and are a real hazard at dusk, particularly in autumn, and sea eagles hang over the sound. Salmon rivers run down from the mountains and are popular with anglers in summer. The air smells of resin and salt in equal measure.

Nothing here is far from help by Arctic standards, yet remember that Finnsnes is the reliable fixed point, so plan your shopping and meals around it rather than hoping a small settlement has what you need. Late summer and early autumn are the best seasons, with warm light, fewer insects and the first hint of aurora in the sky after dark.
If you want to understand Senja, wait for the weather to change. Up here at nearly seventy degrees north the sky does most of the work, and a single afternoon can deliver sun, hail, a rainbow and a bank of cloud that rolls down the mountainsides like spilled milk. The fjords on this part of the island are deep and dark, and the peaks above them wear a skirt of low cloud more often than not.

Riding the scenic road here is a lesson in patience and reward. The tarmac is narrow and usually damp somewhere, the corners are blind enough to keep you honest, and there are sheep in the verge and sometimes on the road itself. Then the cloud lifts, and the view opens across a fjord to a wall of rock plastered with snow, and you forget the damp in your gloves. Mornings are generally calmer than afternoons, when the wind picks up off the sea.

The seasons here are extreme, and that shapes everything. From late May to late July the sun stays above the horizon around the clock, and riders can cover a lot of ground at night in an astonishing low gold light. In deep winter the sun disappears altogether, and the northern lights dance over the same peaks. From September into spring the aurora is a real prospect on clear nights, though ice and snow make riding impractical, and the narrow roads are best left to local drivers with studded tyres.

The communities in this part of Senja live from the sea, with cod, herring and now salmon farming driving the economy. Many of the houses are bright wooden buildings with steep roofs, and fish drying racks stand empty or full depending on the season. Sea eagles patrol the coast.

Gryllefjord and Finnsnes are both more than thirty kilometres away, so this is not a spot where you pop out for something, and it is sensible to carry food and a flask with you. Bring gloves you can feel your fingers in, and a flask. The coffee tastes better at the viewpoints.
t.constantia@-34.0,18.4:
Constantia is where wine began in South Africa, and it still has the air of a place that knows it. The valley lies on the eastern side of the Table Mountain chain, sheltered from the Atlantic, with old oak avenues, whitewashed Cape Dutch farmhouses and vineyards climbing toward the steep slopes of the Constantiaberg. It is one of Cape Town's leafiest and wealthiest suburbs, but the farms are open to visitors and the roads around it are some of the most beautiful in the city.

The story starts with Simon van der Stel, the Dutch East India Company governor, who was granted the land in 1685 and built Groot Constantia, whose gabled manor house is now a museum. A century later the farm's sweet wine, Vin de Constance, was famous across Europe: Napoleon had it shipped to him in exile on St Helena, and Jane Austen mentions Constantia wine in Sense and Sensibility as a cure for a broken heart. The style was revived in modern times and you can taste it today, along with the region's sauvignon blanc, which loves the cool breezes from False Bay.

For riders, the best road begins at the top of the valley. Constantia Nek is the saddle between the mountains, and the road drops from it through forest and down to Hout Bay, which leads to Chapman's Peak Drive, the toll road cut into the cliffs above the Atlantic. Rhodes Drive runs the other way, under trees along the slope past Kirstenbosch Botanical Garden to Newlands. Both are twisty, shaded and slow enough to keep you honest, with cyclists and walkers on weekends. For the longer rides east, to Clarence Drive, the winelands or the passes beyond, you leave on the M3 and the N2, which are busy but quick.

The weather is a factor. In summer the southeaster, the Cape Doctor, can blow ferociously across the Cape Flats and the N2, while winter brings rain and the mountains catch the clouds. Spring and autumn are lovely, with green vines and long, clear light.

Constantia has shopping centres with fuel, cafes and supermarkets, and the wine farms have restaurants, though booking is often necessary at the popular ones. Taste with discipline: South Africa enforces drink-driving limits and the roads out of the valley are not the place for a heavy head.
t.retreat@-34.1,18.5:
Retreat sits on the flat land between the mountains of the Cape Peninsula and the sandy plains that run down to False Bay, a busy, working suburb on Main Road and the railway line south of the city. It is no beauty spot, but it lies right at the foot of some of the finest short rides in Cape Town, and its petrol stations and shops are useful when you are about to climb into the hills or head out along the coast.

The road that makes Retreat worth knowing is Ou Kaapse Weg, the M64, which starts in nearby Tokai and climbs steeply over the mountains to Noordhoek and the Atlantic side. It is a proper mountain road, with long sweepers, tight bends near the top and wide views back over the southern suburbs and False Bay. At the summit you ride through the Silvermine section of Table Mountain National Park, with fynbos on every side, and the descent to Noordhoek reveals the long white beach of Long Beach and the cliffs of Chapman's Peak. The road is popular, policed and occasionally closed for fires or accidents, so ride it with respect.

The other good option is Boyes Drive, which hangs on the mountainside above Muizenberg and Kalk Bay, with False Bay below, surfers in the water and, in winter and spring, the chance of whales offshore. Muizenberg itself, with its colourful beach huts, was where Cecil Rhodes had his cottage, and the coast road south leads through Kalk Bay, a fishing harbour with good fish and chips, to Simon's Town and the penguins at Boulders.

Nature here is fynbos country, part of the Cape Floral Kingdom, the smallest and richest of the world's plant kingdoms, with proteas, ericas and restios that flower at different times of year. Tokai Forest, near Retreat, has old plantations and walking trails, and the Steenberg and Constantia wine farms are just to the west.

The weather matters. Summer brings the southeaster, which can blow riders around on the flats and over Ou Kaapse Weg, while winter fronts bring rain and low cloud on the mountains. For the long rides to the Cederberg or Clarence Drive, you head out onto the M5 and the N2 or N7. Retreat has fuel and supermarkets, which makes it a sensible place to fill the tank and grab water before the long road out.
t.atlantis@-33.6,18.5:
Atlantis is not a postcard town, and nobody here pretends it is. It was built from scratch in the 1970s on the sandy plains north of Cape Town, part of the apartheid government's plan to move coloured families out of the city and to create an industrial centre far from the suburbs. The result was a planned town of factories, schools and housing estates, some forty-five kilometres from the city, which still struggles with unemployment and crime. It is worth understanding that history as you ride through.

What the area offers is landscape. Around the town lie the Atlantis dunes, a great sea of white sand that has been used for sandboarding, quad biking and, of course, filming. The flat sandveld here is covered in tough, low scrub, part of the fynbos and strandveld vegetation of the West Coast, and in late winter and spring, roughly August and September, the plains burst into colour as wild flowers bloom after the rain.

Just north of Atlantis lies Mamre, an old Moravian mission village founded in the early nineteenth century, with whitewashed thatched cottages, a church and a mill, one of the most charming places on this coast. To the west lies the coast itself, with Silwerstroomstrand and other beaches where the Atlantic is cold, clear and sometimes rough, fed by the Benguela Current from the Antarctic. The Koeberg nuclear power station, the only one in Africa, stands on the coast to the south.

The rides from here are straight and open rather than curvy. The R27, the West Coast road, runs north toward Langebaan and the West Coast National Park with long straight stretches, while the R307 heads inland toward Darling and Malmesbury, through wheat fields and vineyards. Wind is the main challenge, especially in summer when the southeaster blows hard and the sand can drift onto the road. For the Clarence Drive and Bainskloof rides, the route leads back south and east, past Cape Town toward the mountains.

Atlantis has fuel, supermarkets and fast food, and it is a sensible place to fill up before heading north or into the hills. Stick to the main roads and busy places, keep your bike in sight, and avoid wandering into residential areas. For a calmer stop, ride to Mamre or the coast, where a picnic with a view of the ocean is a better reward.
t.near constantia@-34.0,18.4:
The wooded eastern flank of Table Mountain rises right above this point, a few kilometres from Constantia, where the southern suburbs meet the forests and the mountain. This is Cape Town's green side: oak avenues, pine and gum plantations, old estates and the cool, shaded slopes that catch the clouds when the southeaster blows. Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden lies along the same slope, and on its terraces you can walk among proteas, ericas and other plants of the Cape Floral Kingdom with the mountain towering overhead.

The roads here wind through the trees. Rhodes Drive runs along the mountain from Constantia Nek past Kirstenbosch toward Newlands, a narrow, curving road shaded by old trees, with glimpses of the mountain through the branches. It is slow, often busy and shared with cyclists, but beautiful, especially in the early morning light. The forests of Cecilia and Newlands have walking trails up toward the mountain, and the air smells of pine, damp earth and fynbos.

The rides from here head east into the winelands and beyond. The Franschhoek Pass ride takes you through Stellenbosch and Franschhoek, the valley settled by French Huguenot refugees in the late seventeenth century, whose names still appear on many of the wine farms. The pass climbs out of the valley on a road said to follow an old elephant trail, with tight bends and spectacular views back down over the vineyards. Clarence Drive is the coastal road from Gordon's Bay to Kleinmond, clinging to the mountains above False Bay, where whales can be seen in winter and spring.

The weather shapes everything. In summer the southeaster blows hard and the tablecloth of cloud spills over the mountain, while winter fronts bring heavy rain and cold. The best riding months are often spring and autumn, when the air is clear and the light is golden. Bush fires are a real danger in the hot, dry months, and roads may be closed when they flare up.

For fuel, food and supplies, Constantia's shopping centres are close, and there are cafes at Kirstenbosch and in the nearby suburbs. Leave yourself time for a walk in the garden or the forest; it is one of the most peaceful places in the city, and a fine way to begin or end a long ride into the mountains.
t.near constantia@-34.0,18.3:
Hout Bay sits in a deep green bowl on the Atlantic side of the Cape Peninsula, a short hop over the mountains from Constantia, and this point lies in that valley or on the slopes above it. Steep peaks surround it on three sides: the Sentinel guarding the harbour mouth, the Karbonkelberg to the west and the long ridge of Table Mountain's back table to the east. The fishing harbour, the beach and the village spread out along the valley floor.

The harbour is still a working one, with fishing boats, a fish market and stalls selling snoek, the local fish, as well as boats taking visitors to see the Cape fur seals on Duiker Island, just off the coast. The beach is broad and pretty, but the water is cold, fed by the Benguela Current, and swimming here is bracing even in summer. In the forests and on the slopes above the village, tracks lead up toward the peaks, with views out over the ocean.

The famous road here is Chapman's Peak Drive, a toll road cut into the cliffs between Hout Bay and Noordhoek, with tight bends, rock overhangs and sheer drops to the sea. It is one of the most spectacular coast roads in the world, and is sometimes closed because of rockfall or bad weather, so check before you go. The road over Constantia Nek, the saddle between Hout Bay and Constantia, climbs through forest on a series of curves, offering an alternative route into the city's southern suburbs.

The rides from here head north and east to some of South Africa's most famous roads. The Cederberg ride goes north up the N7 to a wilderness of red sandstone, rock art and rooibos tea farms around Clanwilliam. The Route 62 and Swartberg Pass ride heads east through the Little Karoo, the semi-desert of ostrich farms and wine towns, to the Swartberg Pass, a gravel road built in the late nineteenth century by the road engineer Thomas Bain, with dramatic views over the mountains. Both are long journeys, demanding preparation and plenty of time.

Hout Bay has fuel, shops, cafés and restaurants, and the harbour has fish and chips with a view. The weather is changeable: the southeaster can blow ferociously in summer, and winter brings rain. Start early, check the forecast and enjoy the view of the bay from the road as you leave.
t.grabouw@-34.2,19.0:
Apples built Grabouw. The town lies in the Elgin valley, a high basin in the mountains east of Cape Town, where cool nights, good soil and plentiful water make ideal conditions for fruit. Orchards of apples and pears cover the valley floor and the lower slopes, and in spring the trees are white and pink with blossom. In recent decades vineyards have joined them, producing some of South Africa's best cool-climate wines.

The valley is surrounded by mountains, part of the Kogelberg Biosphere Reserve, one of the richest areas of fynbos in the Cape, with proteas, ericas and restios covering the slopes. The Palmiet River flows through the valley toward the sea, and the Theewaterskloof Dam to the north is one of the largest reservoirs supplying Cape Town's water. Baboons are common on the passes, so keep food out of sight and do not feed them.

The riding into Grabouw is the main attraction. From the west, the N2 climbs Sir Lowry's Pass from Somerset West, a long, steep ascent with sweeping bends and spectacular views back over the Cape Flats, False Bay and Table Mountain. The viewpoint at the top is worth a stop. To the east, the N2 continues over the Houw Hoek Pass, a smaller pass through the mountains toward Bot River and the Overberg. The R321 north to Villiersdorp and the Franschhoek Pass offers a quieter route with curves and views. Wind can be fierce on the passes, especially in summer when the southeaster blows, and fog sometimes rolls over the mountains.

The rides from here go in two directions. The Route 62 and Swartberg ride heads east into the Little Karoo, with its dry landscapes, ostrich farms and the gravel climb of the Swartberg Pass. The West Coast Flower Road heads north to the plains of Namaqualand, where in a good year the spring flowers carpet the land in orange, yellow and purple. Both are long rides, so start early and plan for fuel stops.

Grabouw has fuel, shops and fast food, and the farm stalls along the N2 sell fresh fruit, juice, pies and coffee. Elgin's wine estates offer tastings and lunches with views over the orchards. In spring, when the blossom is out, the valley is at its loveliest, and a slow ride through the orchards with the mountains around you is a pleasure in itself.
t.evans@40.4,-104.7:
There is a small irony in stopping at Evans on the way to Mount Evans. The town, on the South Platte River just south of Greeley, and the mountain west of Denver were both named for John Evans, the second territorial governor of Colorado. The mountain was officially renamed Mount Blue Sky in 2023, partly because Evans was governor when the Sand Creek Massacre took place in 1864, when US troops killed more than two hundred Cheyenne and Arapaho people, most of them women, children and old men. The town has kept its name.

Evans itself is a growing town of over twenty thousand people on the flat plains of Weld County, one of the richest agricultural counties in the country, with fields of corn, sugar beets and onions, cattle feedlots, and oil and gas wells. When the wind blows from the feedlots, you will know it. The South Platte runs along the eastern edge of town, lined with cottonwoods, and offers a bit of green in an otherwise dry and open landscape.

As a food stop, Evans and neighbouring Greeley offer a mix of American and Mexican food, from diners and burger joints to taquerias and family-run Mexican restaurants, reflecting the large Hispanic community that has worked in the region's farms and meatpacking plants for generations. A breakfast burrito smothered in green chile is a Colorado classic, and it will keep you going for hours.

The ride from here to Mount Blue Sky is a long one, across the plains to Denver and then up into the mountains. The road to the summit of Mount Blue Sky is the highest paved road in North America, climbing past timberline to over four thousand metres, with tight switchbacks, no guardrails in places and thin air that affects both rider and engine. It is usually open only from late spring to early autumn, and reservations have been required in recent years. Squaw Pass Road, now known by its new name, Juniper Pass Road, is another beautiful ride through forest.

Evans has fuel, supermarkets and all the services of a growing town. Fill up here, eat well and drink plenty of water; the altitude and the dry air at the top will dehydrate you quickly.
t.near greeley on the way back@40.4,-104.7:
The label says pass, but you will not find one here. Greeley sits on the high plains of northern Colorado, a little over fifty kilometres east of the foothills, where the land is flat or gently rolling and the Rockies rise as a long, jagged wall on the western horizon. On a clear morning, Longs Peak and the peaks of Rocky Mountain National Park stand out sharp and white, and on the ride back from Guanella Pass, they are a reminder of where you have been.

Greeley has an unusual story. It was founded in 1870 as the Union Colony, a planned settlement organised by Nathan Meeker, the agricultural editor of the New York Tribune, and named after Horace Greeley, the newspaper's famous editor, who is linked with the advice "Go West, young man". The colonists dug irrigation canals from the Cache la Poudre River, turned the dry plains into farmland, and banned alcohol, a rule that lasted in one form or another for nearly a century. The novelist James Michener studied and taught here, and his huge novel Centennial, about the history of the plains, was inspired by this region.

The landscape is big and open, with fields, feedlots and grain elevators, and east of town the Pawnee National Grassland stretches towards the Nebraska border, with the Pawnee Buttes rising from the prairie like lonely towers. It is a place of huge skies, thunderstorms that build over the mountains in summer afternoons, and wind that blows hard and often. Watch for crosswinds on the open roads, and for hail in summer storms.

The ride back from Guanella Pass, near Georgetown, takes you across Denver and up the Front Range, either on the interstate or on smaller roads through the farming towns. Guanella Pass itself is a beautiful paved road over the mountains between Georgetown and Grant, at over 3,500 metres, with views of Mount Bierstadt and alpine lakes, and it is usually closed in winter.

Greeley is a city of about a hundred thousand people, home to the University of Northern Colorado, and it has fuel, food and every service. Stop for a coffee downtown, where old brick buildings line the streets, and watch the sun set behind the mountains.
t.near andenes@69.3,16.0:
A few kilometres south of Andenes the road along the west side of Andøya drops to the shore at Bleik, and the view changes from flat bog to something close to the edge of the world. A long white beach curves away under steep peaks, the sea is a cold, startling turquoise on a bright day, and just offshore sits Bleiksøya, a steep pyramid of an island that holds one of the busiest puffin colonies on the Norwegian coast. In summer the birds wheel around it in thousands, and the boat trips from Andenes go out to see them.

Andøya is the northernmost island of Vesterålen, and its northern tip is low and open, with bogs where cloudberries ripen in late summer and a sky that seems far too big. Andenes itself is a working fishing town with a red lighthouse, a harbour, a rocket range down the coast that launches scientific sounding rockets into the aurora, and whale safaris that head out to the deep Bleik Canyon, where sperm whales feed close to the shelf edge. That canyon is the reason this small town has a big name among people who want to see whales.

The riding on the west coast is gentle in shape and wild in mood. The road hugs the shore, squeezed between mountain and sea, with long open views and a handful of tight bends where it rounds a headland. The surface is generally good, but the wind off the Norwegian Sea can be fierce, pushing hard in gusts on the exposed stretches, and the weather can turn from glittering sun to driving rain in an hour. Sheep wander onto the road. In midsummer the sun never sets, and riding this coast at midnight, with the light low and gold across the water, is the thing people remember for years.

Andenes, a few minutes north, has the shops, cafes and fuel for this end of the island, and a summer ferry crosses from there to Gryllefjord on Senja, which makes a fine way to link two scenic routes. Down the island, Risøyhamn and Sortland are the next larger places. Bleik itself has a small community and the beach, which is a lovely place to walk on firm sand and listen to the surf. Bring layers, even in July.
t.near myre@69.1,15.7:
Down the outer coast of Andøya, between the bird cliffs of the north and the fishing village of Myre, the scenery gets quieter and more intimate. The road runs past a string of small settlements like Stave and Nordmela, each a cluster of houses, a few boats and a fish rack or two, and between them a coast of pale beaches, rocks polished by the surf and mountains that rise abruptly from the shore. It is one of those stretches where you want to stop every few minutes, and nobody minds if you do.

The geology here is unusual. Andøya contains rocks and fossils from the age of the dinosaurs, which is rare in Norway, where most of the bedrock is far older, and there are layers of coal and shale on the island that once raised hopes of mining. The island was also one of the few places in northern Scandinavia that stayed partly free of ice in the last glaciation, and scientists come to study the old lake sediments and bogs for that reason.

The riding is a pleasure of the slow kind. The road is narrow in places, with blind crests and a few tight bends where it squeezes past cliffs, and the surface varies from good to patched. There is little traffic outside the summer weeks, but you will meet camper vans, cyclists and the odd tractor. The wind is the factor that matters most: on a calm day the sea lies flat and reflects the peaks, and on a windy one it hurls spray across the road at the exposed points. The best light, especially in the endless days of June and July, is late in the evening, when the sun swings north and lights the beaches from the sea side.

Myre, on the eastern side of the island near the Andfjord, is the main fishing village of the area and the place for shops, a cafe or two and fuel. It has a busy harbour where boats land cod and other whitefish, and in late winter the fish racks around the village fill with drying stockfish. Andenes, at the northern tip, is the other base. Between them there is little except small settlements, so plan accordingly, and remember that even in summer the temperature here can stay in single figures.
t.near melbu@68.4,15.0:
Here the islands of Lofoten and Vesterålen almost touch. The narrow strait of Raftsundet separates Austvågøya, the big eastern island of Lofoten, from Hinnøya, and the water between them runs between steep mountains that rise straight from the sea, some of them over a thousand metres. It is a wild, dramatic landscape, with fewer people than the famous western islands and plenty of space to ride and look.

The Trollfjord, a narrow side branch off Raftsundet, is one of the famous sights of the region: only about a hundred metres wide at its mouth, with sheer walls on both sides, it is visited by boats from Svolvær and by the Hurtigruten coastal ships, which turn around inside it. In 1890 the fjord gave its name to a battle, when fishermen in small open boats fought with the crews of steamships that had blocked the entrance to keep the fish for themselves. The fishermen won, and the event became a symbol of the struggle between traditional fishing and big capital.
