Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany visited this area on his summer cruises in the late nineteenth century and climbed a hill above Digermulen, at the southern end of Raftsundet, that still bears his name. The view from the top over the islands is among the finest in Lofoten. The E10, which links Lofoten to the mainland via tunnels and bridges, passes nearby, and the Raftsund bridge carries a side road across the strait.

The riding here is a mix of main road and narrow side roads, with tunnels, bridges, tight bends along the shore and some spectacular views. Traffic on the E10 can be heavy in summer, with camper vans and tour buses, but the side roads are quieter. The weather can change fast, and the wind can funnel strongly through the straits. The light in the midnight sun is extraordinary, especially when the mountains catch the low sun.

Melbu and Stokmarknes, on Hadseløya to the north, are small towns with fuel and services, and Svolvær, the main town of Lofoten, is about twenty-five kilometres southwest. Between them the settlements are small, so plan your stops.
t.near skaland@69.4,17.4:
Senja is Norway's second-largest island, and its outer coast is the closest thing the country has to Lofoten without the crowds: steep peaks rising straight out of the sea, small fishing villages tucked into the bays, beaches of pale sand, and a road that threads between them through tunnels and along ledges. The village of Skaland sits on the Bergsfjord on that outer side, and the road east of it climbs toward Bergsbotn, where a long wooden viewing platform reaches out from the hillside over the head of the fjord.

Skaland is unusual in having an industry most people would not expect in such a setting: a graphite mine, one of the richest deposits of crystalline graphite in the world, which has been worked here since the early twentieth century. The mine buildings are part of the village, and it is a reminder that this beautiful coast has always been a working place, where people made a living from fish, rock and whatever else the land offered.

The road is the Senja National Tourist Route, which follows the outer coast from Gryllefjord in the south to Botnhamn in the north, and it is a fantastic ride. Expect narrow sections, single-lane tunnels, tight bends around headlands, some steep climbs and descents, and views that keep stopping you in your tracks. The surface varies from good to rough, and frost damage is common. Traffic is light, though camper vans and tourist cars are increasingly common in July. The wind on the exposed sections can be strong, and the weather changes fast. The midnight sun, from late May to mid-July, means you can ride at any hour, and the light at night is extraordinary.

The Bergsbotn platform is worth a stop, with a view over the fjord and the peaks around it. There are small shops in some villages, but services are limited. Finnsnes, on the mainland side, is the main town for Senja, with fuel, shops and hotels, about thirty kilometres away, and Gryllefjord has a summer ferry to Andenes on Andøya. Plan fuel carefully, and carry warm clothes, because even in July it can be cold.
t.near skaland@69.5,17.3:
North of Skaland the outer coast of Senja gets wilder still. The road works its way along the shore between steep, bare peaks, cutting through tunnels where the mountains drop straight into the sea and emerging into small, sheltered bays where a handful of houses, a boat shed and a fish rack make up a village. Steinfjorden and Ersfjorden lie along this coast, each with its own narrow inlet and its own wall of mountains, and further north the road reaches Tungeneset, where a jagged ridge of peaks known as the Devil's Teeth rises from the sea.

The landscape here is the result of ancient rock and recent ice. The mountains of Senja are among the oldest in Norway, made of hard gneiss and granite, and the glaciers of the last ice age carved them into sharp peaks and deep fjords. The sea has since rounded the shoreline into coves and beaches, and on the beaches the sand is pale and the water clear. In summer the sea can look almost tropical, although it remains cold enough to make your breath catch.

People here have always lived from the sea, fishing for cod and other species, and the villages still have the feel of working places rather than tourist resorts. Life was hard, and during the Second World War this coast, like the rest of northern Norway, was occupied and suffered heavy losses. Today tourism has added to the old way of life, but the villages remain small and quiet.

Riding here is about patience and attention. The road is narrow and twisting, with blind bends, single-lane tunnels, steep pitches and a surface that varies from good to poor. Traffic is light, but camper vans can make passing difficult, and the tunnels can be dark and wet. The wind can be very strong on the exposed sections, and the weather changes fast. On a clear evening in summer, the light on the peaks and the sea is unforgettable.

There are small shops in some villages, but no towns of any size until you reach Finnsnes on the mainland side. Make sure your tank is full before you start the outer coast, and take a break at Ersfjord, where there is a fine beach and a rest area.
t.badlands loop state scenic byway point 1:
The prairie lies to you here. For mile after mile around Wall, South Dakota, the land rolls flat and grassy, with wheat fields, cattle and the long, straight line of Interstate 90, and nothing suggests that a few kilometres to the south the ground is about to fall away into a maze of eroded spires and canyons.

Wall is famous for one thing: Wall Drug, a sprawling roadside store that began in the 1930s by offering free ice water to thirsty travellers, and advertised it on signs for hundreds of kilometres in every direction. It worked, and the drugstore grew into a tourist attraction in its own right, with shops, restaurants, a chapel and an animated dinosaur. It is kitsch, but it is also a slice of American road-trip history, and the coffee is famously cheap. During the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally in August, the town is packed with bikes.

The ride south from Wall is short and easy, with gentle curves across the grassland. Then, quite suddenly, the road reaches the edge of the Wall, a long escarpment that gives the town its name, and the badlands appear below you. The first view is stunning: a vast expanse of jagged ridges, buttes and gullies, striped in bands of white, grey, pink and gold, stretching to the horizon.

The weather on the prairie is extreme. Summers are hot, with temperatures often above 35 degrees, and violent thunderstorms can sweep across the plains in the afternoon, bringing hail, lightning and strong winds. Winters are bitterly cold, with blizzards and icy roads. Late spring and early autumn are kinder, when the temperatures are milder and the light is softer.

Wall has fuel, food, lodging and all the basic services, and it is the best place to fill up before entering the park. Inside the park, services are limited, and fuel is not always available. Philip, about forty-five kilometres to the east, and Kadoka, further east along the interstate, have the basics, but Rapid City, about ninety kilometres to the west, is the nearest large town with everything you might need.
t.badlands loop state scenic byway point 2:
From the Pinnacles Overlook, at the western end of the Badlands Loop, the earth looks as if it has been clawed open. Below the viewpoint, ridges and spires of soft rock drop steeply into a wide basin, their sides scored with gullies and streaked with bands of colour. The rock layers are sediments laid down over millions of years by ancient seas, rivers and volcanic ash falls from eruptions far to the west, and the badlands are eroding at a rate of about an inch a year, which in geological terms is lightning fast.

The badlands are one of the richest fossil beds in the world. The rocks contain the remains of ancient mammals that lived here more than thirty million years ago, including early horses, rhinoceroses, sabre-toothed cats and strange pig-like creatures called oreodonts. Palaeontologists have been digging here since the mid-nineteenth century, and new fossils are still being found, often exposed by the rains. If you see a fossil, leave it where it is and report it to a ranger.

The Lakota people, who lived on the surrounding prairies, called this land mako sica, meaning bad land, and early French fur traders called it les mauvaises terres à traverser, bad lands to travel across. The names were apt: the terrain is rough, water is scarce, and the summers are scorching. The southern part of the park lies within the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation and is managed jointly by the Oglala Lakota and the National Park Service.

Near the overlook, the Sage Creek Rim Road heads west along the edge of the badlands on gravel toward the Sage Creek Wilderness, where bison, bighorn sheep, pronghorn and prairie dogs roam. It is a beautiful ride, but the surface can be rough and dusty, and it becomes slippery and impassable after rain. On a road bike, stick to the paved loop.

The overlook is just a parking area and a railing. The road continues east along the edge of the badlands, with frequent viewpoints and short trails. Fuel and food are available in Wall, about fifteen kilometres to the north, and at Cedar Pass, near the eastern end of the loop. The best light is early morning and late afternoon, when the colours glow and the shadows bring out the shapes of the formations.
t.badlands loop state scenic byway point 3:
Halfway along the Badlands Loop the colours change. Around the Yellow Mounds Overlook the grey and buff spires give way to low, rounded hills of bright yellow and ochre, some streaked with red and purple, looking more like a painted desert than a prairie. They are a fossil soil, formed when the dark shale of an old sea floor, the oldest rock in the park, lay exposed to the weather after the water retreated, and they glow in the late afternoon sun.

Beyond the mounds the road crosses a wide, grassy basin, the Conata Basin, with buttes and ridges rising on either side. This is mixed-grass prairie, one of the most endangered ecosystems in North America, and it is home to a remarkable variety of wildlife. Prairie dog towns are common, and you will often see these chubby rodents standing upright beside their burrows, barking warnings to each other. The prairie dogs, in turn, support the black-footed ferret, one of the rarest mammals in North America, which was reintroduced here after being thought extinct.

The road through this section is gentle and scenic, with long, straight stretches and wide curves across the basin. The asphalt is good, and traffic is usually light, especially early in the morning. There are frequent pull-outs and viewpoints along the road, and it is easy to stop and take photographs. Watch out for wildlife on the road, especially bighorn sheep, which often graze on the shoulders.

A little further east, the Fossil Exhibit Trail is a short boardwalk with replicas of fossils found in the area and displays explaining the geology and palaeontology of the badlands. It is a good introduction for anyone curious about the strange creatures that once lived here.

There are no services in this part of the park. The nearest fuel and food are at Cedar Pass to the east and in Wall to the north. The weather can be extreme, with very hot summers and sudden thunderstorms. Carry water, wear a hat, and be careful on the trails, which can be slippery and crumbly. Rattlesnakes are present, so watch where you put your feet.
t.badlands loop state scenic byway point 4:
At Cedar Pass, the eastern end of the Badlands Loop, the road drops through a gap in the Wall in a series of tight curves, from the high prairie down to the White River valley below. It is the most dramatic piece of riding on the whole loop, with sharp spires and cliffs rising on both sides and wide views out over the lower land to the south. The Ben Reifel Visitor Center sits at the bottom of the pass, along with a lodge, a campground and an amphitheatre for evening ranger talks.

The visitor centre is named after Ben Reifel, a Lakota man born on the Rosebud Reservation who became a US congressman, and it is the main information centre for the park. Inside there are exhibits about the geology, fossils and wildlife of the badlands, and a fossil preparation lab where you can watch palaeontologists cleaning and preparing fossils found in the park.

The Door Trail and the Window Trail, both short and easy, start from a parking area just north of the pass. The Door Trail leads through a gap in the Wall into a strange landscape of eroded formations, while the Window Trail leads to a natural opening in the rock with a view over a deep canyon. The Notch Trail, a little further, is more challenging, with a log ladder and a narrow ledge, and the reward is a view over the White River valley.

The town of Interior, just south of the park boundary, is a handful of buildings on the prairie with a very grand name. Beyond it, the road continues south toward the Pine Ridge Reservation and the site of the Wounded Knee Massacre of 1890, a sombre reminder of the violent history of the region.

Fuel can be scarce in this area, and you should plan carefully. Cedar Pass has a lodge and a restaurant, but fuel is limited, and there are only a few stations in the small towns nearby. Kadoka, about thirty-five kilometres east along the interstate, and Wall, to the northwest, have fuel and basic services. The best time to ride is early morning or late evening, when the light is warm and the formations glow.
t.peter norbeck scenic byway point 4@43.9,:
Iron Mountain Road is the reason many riders come to the Black Hills, and it was designed to be exactly that kind of road. When South Dakota's governor and later senator Peter Norbeck laid out the route in the 1930s, he insisted that it should be a road to enjoy, not to hurry along, and he personally scouted much of it on foot and horseback. The result is a twisting, turning ribbon of asphalt through ponderosa pine forest, with pigtail bridges, narrow tunnels and constant changes of direction.

The pigtail bridges are the signature: wooden trestle bridges where the road loops over itself in a tight spiral to gain or lose height in a short distance. There are three of them on Iron Mountain Road, and riding them is a unique experience, like going around a corkscrew. The tunnels are even more remarkable. Norbeck had them aligned so that, as you approach from the south, each one frames a view of Mount Rushmore in the distance, with the four presidential faces perfectly centred in the rock opening.

The road runs between Custer State Park and Mount Rushmore National Memorial, and it is part of a loop that includes the Needles Highway and the Wildlife Loop Road. The Needles Highway, another of Norbeck's creations, winds through a forest of granite spires and squeezes through tunnels so narrow that large vehicles cannot pass. The Wildlife Loop is famous for its herds of bison, which often block the road, and the begging burros, descendants of pack animals, that wander up to cars looking for treats.

Riding these roads is a pleasure, but it requires care. The speed limits are low, the corners are tight, and the traffic can be heavy in summer, especially during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally in early August, when hundreds of thousands of bikes descend on the Black Hills. Watch out for bison, which are large, unpredictable and dangerous, and do not approach them.

There are no services along Iron Mountain Road itself, but Keystone, the touristy town at the foot of Mount Rushmore, is close by and has fuel, food and lodging. Custer, about seventeen kilometres to the southwest, has more services, and Rapid City, about thirty kilometres to the north, is the largest city in the area. A pass is required to enter Custer State Park.
t.near spearfish@44.4,-103.9:
Spearfish Canyon cuts down through the northern Black Hills in a deep, narrow gorge of limestone cliffs, and US 14A follows it for about thirty kilometres from the town of Spearfish up to Cheyenne Crossing. It is one of the most beautiful canyons in the American Midwest.

Bridal Veil Falls is the first landmark as you head up the canyon from Spearfish, a delicate waterfall that drops down a cliff right beside the road. There is a small viewing area, and it makes a good first stop. The canyon walls are made of limestone, formed from the shells of tiny sea creatures in an ancient ocean, and they are full of caves, crevices and overhangs. In autumn the aspens, birches and oaks turn gold and red, and the canyon is ablaze with colour.

The road through the canyon is a delight to ride, with smooth asphalt and long, gentle curves following the creek. The speed limits are moderate, and there are frequent pull-outs for photographs. Traffic can be heavy in summer and during the autumn colour season, and there are often cyclists and slow-moving vehicles. Watch out for deer and for rocks on the road, especially after storms.

Spearfish, at the mouth of the canyon, is a pleasant college town with a historic downtown and a long-running fish hatchery that has been raising trout since the end of the nineteenth century. The town is a good base for exploring the northern Black Hills, and it has all the services you might need.

Spearfish has fuel, food, lodging and motorcycle shops, and it is the best place to fill up before heading into the canyon. There are few services in the canyon itself, apart from a lodge and a small store near Savoy. Lead and Deadwood, just to the east, have more services, and Rapid City is about an hour's ride to the southeast. Ride it early, when the light is soft and the canyon is quiet.
t.near lead@44.4,-103.9:
At Savoy, the midpoint of Spearfish Canyon, a narrower side canyon branches off to the west, and a short road leads up it to Roughlock Falls. This is Little Spearfish Canyon, a more intimate and secluded place than the main canyon, with spruce and pine forest, mossy boulders and a clear stream tumbling over a series of limestone ledges. The falls are reached by a short, easy trail from a picnic area, and they are particularly lovely in spring, when the water is high.

The name Roughlock comes from the days when wagons came down this canyon on their way to the mining camps. The road was so steep that the drivers had to lock the wheels of their wagons with chains, a technique known as roughlocking, to stop them running away. The canyon was also used as a location for the final scenes of the film Dances With Wolves, which was shot in South Dakota in 1989, and the winter camp in the movie was set up here.

The area around Savoy is a junction of canyons, with Spearfish Creek and Little Spearfish Creek meeting nearby. The canyon walls here are steep and dramatic, with limestone cliffs rising high above the road. The forest is thick and green, and in autumn the colours are spectacular. There is a lodge at Savoy, which has a restaurant and accommodation.

The road up Little Spearfish Canyon is narrow and winding, with good asphalt but tight curves and limited visibility. Beyond the falls the road gets rougher and quieter as it heads west into the forest. On a road bike it is best to turn around at the falls and return to the main canyon, which continues south toward Cheyenne Crossing and east toward Lead and Deadwood.

Fuel and basic services are limited in the canyon, and the nearest towns with fuel are Lead, about fourteen kilometres away, and Spearfish, about seventeen kilometres to the north. Lead and Deadwood, the historic mining towns in the hills to the east, have more services, including casinos and hotels. The canyon is quiet and peaceful, and it is a good place to stop for a picnic or a short walk.
t.near lead@44.3,-103.9:
The top of Spearfish Canyon is a different world from the bottom. Around Cheyenne Crossing, where US 14A meets US 85, the canyon opens out into high, rolling country of spruce and pine forest, meadows and small streams, at around 1,800 metres. From here, the road heads east over the hills to Lead, a historic mining town clinging to the steep slopes of a gulch, and Deadwood, its more famous neighbour, a few kilometres further on.

Lead was built around the Homestake Mine, which operated for more than 125 years and became the largest and deepest gold mine in the Western Hemisphere, reaching depths of more than 2,400 metres. The mine closed in 2002, but its deep tunnels are now used for scientific research, as the Sanford Underground Research Facility, where physicists study neutrinos and dark matter far beneath the surface. The Open Cut, a massive open-pit mine on the edge of town, can be seen from a viewing platform.

Deadwood, just down the hill, is one of the most famous towns of the Old West. It sprang up during the gold rush of 1876, when prospectors poured into the Black Hills in violation of a treaty with the Lakota, and it quickly became a lawless boom town. Wild Bill Hickok was shot dead in a saloon here while playing poker, and Calamity Jane is buried beside him in Mount Moriah Cemetery, overlooking the town. Today Deadwood is a lively place with casinos, saloons and historic buildings, and it is a major stop during the Sturgis Rally.

The road from Cheyenne Crossing to Lead is a fine ride, with long curves through the forest and a steep, twisting descent into the town. The asphalt is good, but the gradients are steep, and there can be heavy traffic in summer. The weather in the hills can be cool and wet, with snow in winter, and fog sometimes settles in the valleys.

Cheyenne Crossing has a small store and café, but services are limited. Lead and Deadwood have fuel, food and lodging, and Spearfish, about twenty kilometres to the north, has more services. The roads around here are some of the best in the Black Hills, and it is worth taking the time to explore them.
t.near cape town@-33.9,18.4:
Few cities give you a finish line like this one. You roll into central Cape Town with Table Mountain standing over the whole bowl of the city, flat-topped and close enough to feel personal, Devil's Peak on one side and Lion's Head and Signal Hill on the other. The point on the map sits in the old centre near the Company's Garden, the patch of land the Dutch East India Company planted in the seventeenth century to supply its ships with vegetables on the way to the East.

The rides that end here, over Bainskloof and Du Toitskloof or up the West Coast to see the spring flowers, are long days, and the approach back into town is usually the N1 or N7, busy and fast. Bainskloof Pass deserves a word: it was built by Andrew Geddes Bain in the 1850s and still runs on his stone walls, a narrow, slow, beautiful road above a river gorge where you should expect gravel on the inside of bends and baboons on the parapet. Du Toitskloof is the wide modern alternative over the same mountains, with a long tunnel option for when the weather turns.

Weather is the local obsession, and for good reason. In summer the south-easter, known as the Cape Doctor, can blow with startling force, especially around the mountain and on the False Bay side, and a laden bike on an exposed stretch will feel it. When the wind is up, the tablecloth of cloud pours over the top of Table Mountain. Winter brings rain from the north-west. The best riding months for most people are spring and autumn, roughly from September to November and from March to May.

If you have a little left in you, the short climb up Kloof Nek and along Signal Hill gives the classic view over the city and harbour at sunset. Fuel in South Africa is attendant-served, and a small tip is customary. Use attended or secure parking for the bike overnight and do not leave gear on it; that is simply standard city sense here. Then go and eat: the city is full of good food, from Cape Malay curries in the Bo-Kaap to seafood by the harbour.
t.semmering@47.6,15.8:
Semmering is where Lower Austria meets Styria on a saddle of a little under a thousand metres, and it has been a place of passage and of pleasure for a long time. The pass itself is not high by Alpine standards, but the name carries weight: the Semmering Railway, engineered by Carl von Ghega and opened in the 1850s, was the first true mountain railway in the world, and it is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its viaducts and tunnels thread through the valleys below the road, and if you stop at one of the lookouts you may see a train crawling across a stone arch far below.

Once the railway arrived, Vienna came up for the air. The grand hotels that still stand on the slopes, some restored and some waiting, belong to the era when the capital's bourgeoisie took the train up for the summer season and for winter sport. There is something wistful about the place now, a resort that peaked long ago, wrapped in dark spruce forest with views out over the Rax and Schneeberg.

The modern expressway sweeps through tunnels below the pass, which is excellent news for anyone on two wheels, because it leaves the old road over the top relatively quiet. Coming up from Gloggnitz and Schottwien, the climb has a run of tight bends that are a lot of fun if the surface is dry, though they can be greasy in the shade on cool mornings and you will meet cyclists and the odd bus. Over the top, the road drops down the Styrian side towards Mürzzuschlag in gentler curves. The Wechsel and Bucklige Welt to the east offer an endless supply of smaller roads for the rest of the day.

As a food stop, Semmering is a village of a few hundred people, so options are modest but pleasant: a couple of guesthouses and cafés where a coffee and a slice of cake on a terrace feel exactly right. For fuel it is wiser to rely on Gloggnitz below on the eastern side or Mürzzuschlag on the western. Autumn is lovely here, with larches turning gold and clear views, but be prepared for fog in the hollows and occasional ice early or late in the season.
t.mariazell@47.8,15.3:
According to legend, in 1157 a Benedictine monk named Magnus was travelling through these forests with a small wooden statue of the Virgin when a rock blocked his path; he prayed, the rock split, and he settled on the spot, placing the statue on a tree stump and building a cell around it. That cell became Mariazell, Austria's most important place of pilgrimage. The great basilica that now dominates the little town, with its Gothic tower flanked by two Baroque ones, still houses the statue, and every year hundreds of thousands of pilgrims come, many on foot from Vienna.

Pilgrims need sustenance, and Mariazell has a long tradition of making gingerbread and honey-based liqueurs, sold in shops around the basilica square. A slice of gingerbread with a coffee on the square, under the towers, is a good way to spend half an hour. The narrow-gauge Mariazell Railway, one of the earliest electrified mountain lines in Austria, climbs up from St. Pölten through tunnels and over viaducts, and if you see one of its trains on the way in, you will understand why rail enthusiasts love it.

The roads to Mariazell are what bring riders here. From the north, the route over the Annaberg and the Josefsberg winds through dense forests and over modest passes, with tight bends and long views of the Ötscher massif. To the south, the Seeberg Saddle leads into Styria, with another series of curves through forests and meadows. The roads are generally well surfaced, but there can be gravel, wet patches and cattle grids, and on summer weekends they are popular with motorcyclists, so expect company and occasional speed checks.

Mariazell is small, with around 1,200 inhabitants, but it has restaurants, cafés and hotels catering to pilgrims and tourists. For fuel, it is worth planning ahead, as the surrounding area is sparsely populated and the larger towns lie a good distance away. Nearby, the Erlaufsee is a lovely mountain lake for a short break or, in summer, a cold swim. The weather in the mountains can change quickly, with afternoon thunderstorms common in summer, so keep an eye on the sky.
t.perchtoldsdorf@48.1,16.3:
Perchtoldsdorf lies on the very edge of Vienna, where the city's southern suburbs meet the first hills of the Vienna Woods, and it has the relaxed atmosphere of a wine village rather than a suburb. The hills behind the town are covered in vineyards, and the old streets are lined with Heurigen, the traditional wine taverns where producers serve their own new wine with simple cold food. When a Heuriger is open, it hangs a bunch of pine branches over the door, a sign that has been used for centuries.

The town's history has a darker side. Its massive defensive tower, the Wehrturm, rising next to the parish church, was built in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries to protect against Ottoman raids. In 1683, during the second Ottoman siege of Vienna, the people of Perchtoldsdorf were massacred after surrendering to Ottoman troops, an event still remembered in the town. In more peaceful times, the composer Hugo Wolf lived and worked here, and his house is now a small memorial.

As a starting point for rides south and east, Perchtoldsdorf is excellent. It sits right at the start of the Thermenlinie, the line of wine villages and spa towns that runs south along the edge of the Vienna Woods towards Baden, and the roads through the vineyards and into the woods are pleasant, with gentle curves and views over the Vienna basin. Further afield, the rides head east to the Neusiedler See, a vast, shallow steppe lake on the Hungarian border, or west to the lakes and mountains of the Salzkammergut.

There is fuel and food in Perchtoldsdorf and the neighbouring towns, and the coffee houses in the centre are a civilised place to start the day. Traffic in the Vienna area can be heavy, especially on weekday mornings, so it pays to leave early. At the end of a long ride, sitting in a Heuriger garden with a glass of local white wine, under the chestnut trees, watching the sun set over the vineyards, is a very Viennese way to finish.
t.near moorreesburg on the way back@-33.2,:
North of Cape Town, the Swartland stretches out in long, low waves of wheat, golden in early summer and green in winter, broken by farmsteads, gum trees and the occasional rocky hill. Moorreesburg, about ten kilometres from the point, is one of the main towns of this wheat belt, and it has a small museum devoted to the wheat industry, a modest but fitting tribute to the crop that shaped the region.

The name Swartland, black land, is thought to come from the renosterbos, a native shrub that turns dark grey after rain, giving the hills a dark colour before they were ploughed. The region was settled by Dutch farmers in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, and it has been a breadbasket for the Cape ever since. More recently, the Swartland has become known for its wines, particularly bold Chenin Blancs and Rhône-style reds, made by a new generation of winemakers around the villages of Riebeek-Kasteel and Malmesbury.

Being honest about the swimming: the Swartland is dry farming country, and natural swimming spots are few. The Berg River flows to the east, and farm dams dot the landscape, but most are private and some are unsafe. If you want a proper swim, the West Coast beaches, at Yzerfontein or Langebaan, are within reach, though the Atlantic here is cold, fed by the Benguela Current, and many people find the sheltered Langebaan Lagoon more comfortable.

On the way back to Cape Town from the Cederberg, the N7 highway runs straight and fast through the Swartland, with long views and little shade. It can be windy, and in summer the heat can be intense. In late winter and spring, from about August to September, the fields and verges come alive with wildflowers. Moorreesburg and Malmesbury have fuel, supermarkets and farm stalls, which are a good place to buy rusks, biltong and cold drinks.
t.near grabouw on the way back@-34.1,19.0:
Grabouw is the heart of the Elgin valley, the apple-growing capital of South Africa, a high, cool basin surrounded by mountains about an hour east of Cape Town. Orchards of apples and pears cover the valley floor, and in recent decades vineyards have been planted too, producing crisp cool-climate wines. This stop is a few kilometres from the town, in the hills and forests on the western side of the valley, near the Palmiet River.

On the way back to Cape Town, the N2 climbs out of the valley and crosses Sir Lowry's Pass, with one of the great views in the Western Cape: the whole sweep of False Bay, from the Hottentots Holland mountains to Cape Point, spread out below. There is a viewpoint at the top where most people stop. Be aware that the pass is steep and busy, with heavy trucks, and the wind can be ferocious, especially when the south-easter is blowing in summer.

For a swim, the area has rivers and dams. The Palmiet River runs through the Kogelberg, a nature reserve of fynbos and mountains, with clear, tea-coloured pools, though access is controlled and you may need a permit. Many people prefer to head to the coast, where the lagoon at Kleinmond and the beaches along the coast offer safer swimming. The Atlantic and False Bay can be cold, and the surf can be dangerous, so swim only where it is safe.

An alternative route back to Cape Town follows the R44, Clarence Drive, along the coast from Kleinmond to Gordon's Bay, one of the most beautiful coastal roads in the country, with cliffs plunging into the sea and the mountains rising above. Watch out for baboons, which are common here, and for rockfalls. Grabouw has fuel, supermarkets and farm stalls selling apples, juice and pies. The weather can change quickly, with mist and rain in the mountains.
t.near hustopece on the way back@48.9,16.7:
South Moravia is the warmest corner of the Czech Republic, and in summer the plains around Hustopeče shimmer in the heat, the vineyards and orchards dusty under a hard blue sky. The point lies near Šakvice, close to the Nové Mlýny reservoirs, a chain of three large artificial lakes on the Dyje river, and on the way back to Vienna it is a natural place to cool off in the water.

Above the reservoirs rise the Pavlov Hills, or Pálava, a sudden limestone ridge with cliffs, ruined castles and steppe grassland, rich in rare plants and insects. At the foot of the hills, at Dolní Věstonice, archaeologists found the Venus of Věstonice, a small ceramic figure of a woman about thirty thousand years old, one of the oldest known ceramic objects in the world. To the south, Mikulov is a beautiful town with a castle on a rock, a Jewish quarter and a hill of chapels.

Hustopeče itself is known for its almond orchards, a rarity this far north, and in spring the trees blossom pink and white on the hillsides, celebrated with a festival. The whole region is wine country, with cellars, sklepy, dug into the hillsides, where local winemakers serve their wines, and in late summer and early autumn, burčák, a partially fermented young wine, is sold everywhere.

The reservoirs have beaches and campsites, and at Pasohlávky there is a large thermal water park. The water in the lakes is warm in summer, though algae blooms can occur in hot weather, so check the local water quality reports. The roads in the area are flat to gently rolling, with good surfaces and little traffic, passing through vineyards and villages. Hustopeče and Mikulov have fuel and services. Remember that the Czech blood alcohol limit is zero, so save the wine for the evening, or take a bottle home.
t.bergvliet@-34.0,18.5:
Bergvliet itself is a quiet grid of suburban houses and jacaranda trees in Cape Town's southern suburbs, but look up and you see why the ride starts here. Directly above it, the Ou Kaapse Weg climbs the flank of the Steenberg mountains in a series of long, fast bends, crosses the saddle at Silvermine and drops down the far side towards Noordhoek and the Atlantic. It is the old wagon route across the peninsula, and on a clear morning it is one of the best ten minutes of riding in the city.

Right next door is Constantia, the oldest wine-growing area in South Africa. Simon van der Stel, the Dutch governor, founded his estate here in 1685, and a century later the sweet wine of Constantia was famous across Europe; Napoleon had it shipped to him in exile on St Helena. The old Cape Dutch homesteads, white-gabled and thatched, still sit among the vines at the foot of the mountain.

The slopes above are covered with fynbos, the extraordinary shrubland of the Cape, with proteas, ericas and restios, and the Silvermine section of Table Mountain National Park has walks to viewpoints and a reservoir. Fires sweep these mountains in hot, windy summers, and you may see blackened slopes regenerating with fresh green growth.

Ride the Ou Kaapse Weg with respect. It is fast and well surfaced, but the south-easter can blow hard across the top, baboons sometimes sit on the verge, and traffic police take an interest in speed here. In winter, rain and mist can roll in quickly.

Retreat and Constantia have fuel and every kind of supply, and Constantia's wine farms have restaurants with views over the vineyards, ideal for a long lunch on the way back from Franschhoek, provided someone else does the tasting.
t.near pama on the way back@48.0,17.1:
Wind is the first thing you notice here, and the last. This stop lies on the Parndorf plateau in the far north-east of Burgenland, close to the point where Austria, Slovakia and Hungary meet, and the land is flat, open and swept by a near-constant wind that turns hundreds of turbines on the horizon. On a bike it pushes you around, especially on the open roads between villages, so expect to ride with a lean even on the straights.

Pama and Deutsch Jahrndorf are quiet villages of long, low farmhouses with gates opening onto courtyards, a style typical of the Pannonian plain. Deutsch Jahrndorf sits near the tripoint of the three countries, where a small monument marks the spot, and for decades this was the edge of the Iron Curtain, with watchtowers and barbed wire. Today you can walk from Austria to Slovakia to Hungary in a few minutes.

Bratislava is only fourteen kilometres away, its castle visible on a clear day. The Danube floodplain to the north is a national park, a wild world of side channels, gravel banks and riverine forest.

For a swim, the nearest big water is the Neusiedler See, to the south-west, a shallow steppe lake surrounded by reeds, with bathing areas and beaches at several villages. The water is warm in summer, shallow enough to stand far from shore, and brownish from the fine sediment. It is famous for sailing and kitesurfing, thanks to the same wind that pushes you around on the plateau.

The roads are flat and straight, and the surface is generally good. Watch for farm vehicles and cyclists, and for gusts at junctions and gaps in hedges. The villages have little in the way of shops; fuel and supplies are best found in Parndorf, Kittsee or across the border in Bratislava.
t.purkersdorf@48.2,16.2:
Purkersdorf sits at the eastern edge of the Wienerwald, where the Vienna Woods roll down into the city, and it is the last stop before the motorway delivers you back to Vienna. The town follows the narrow valley of the Wien river, and the hills around are covered with beech forest, meadows and small villages, a landscape of gentle curves and green shade.

The town has one great building. The Sanatorium Purkersdorf, designed by Josef Hoffmann in 1904, was one of the first buildings of modern architecture, a white, cubic structure with geometric details that broke with the ornament of the past. It was a key work of the Wiener Werkstätte, and it still stands, restored, on the edge of town.

For riders, the Wienerwald offers some of the best roads near Vienna. The Riederberg, on the B1 between Gablitz and Sieghartskirchen, is a long, winding climb through forest, popular with bikers on weekends. Small roads lead to Mauerbach, with its old Carthusian monastery, and over the hills to the Danube. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for cyclists, wildlife and police checks.

The forests are home to deer, boar and a rich variety of birds, and in autumn the beech woods turn gold and copper. The Wienerwald is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, protecting a landscape that has inspired Viennese composers and painters for centuries.

Before the city takes you back, look for a green bush or a wreath hung over a doorway: in this part of Austria it means a Heuriger is open, serving the producer's own young wine with bread, cold meats and cheese. One small glass, a long plate, and the last kilometres into Vienna feel shorter.
t.near fort morgan on the way back@40.1,-1:
The eastern plains of Colorado do not do subtle. The sky is enormous, the horizon dead flat, and on summer afternoons thunderheads build into towers that can drop hail the size of golf balls within minutes. This stop lies on the South Platte river, near Fort Morgan, a farming and ranching town on I-76 whose grain elevators are the tallest things for miles.

Fort Morgan began as an army post on the Overland Trail in the 1860s, protecting stagecoaches and wagon trains on their way to Denver. Its most famous son, the bandleader Glenn Miller, grew up here and graduated from the local high school, and the town holds a festival in his honour. The countryside around is sugar beet, corn, cattle feedlots and irrigated fields, with cottonwoods marking the line of the river.

Jackson Lake State Park, north-west of town, is a reservoir in the middle of the prairie, with sandy beaches and a swimming area in summer. On a hot day, it is a welcome break, and the lake attracts pelicans, herons and ducks. The Pawnee National Grassland, further north, is shortgrass prairie with buttes, pronghorn and prairie dogs, and it feels like the old West.

Riding here is all about distance. The roads are long and straight, and the wind can be brutal, blowing across the plains with nothing to stop it. Crosswinds and gusts from passing trucks can push you around, so keep a firm grip and a steady line. Watch for deer and pronghorn at dawn and dusk.

Fort Morgan has fuel, motels and diners strung along the old main street and the interstate exits. Out here the rule is simple: never pass a pump with less than half a tank, because the next town may be fifty miles away and the wind will have been drinking your fuel all afternoon.
t.near custer@43.8,-103.5:
The Needles Highway was laid out in the 1920s by Peter Norbeck, governor of South Dakota and later senator, who scouted much of the route on foot and on horseback, and it threads between granite spires so close together that the road squeezes through a tunnel barely wider than a car. The Iron Mountain Road, the other half of the scenic byway that bears his name, has pigtail bridges, where the road loops over itself to gain height, and tunnels aligned to frame Mount Rushmore in the distance. Together they make one of the most remarkable rides in America.

This stop lies in the Black Hills, near Custer, a small town on the edge of Custer State Park, where herds of bison roam the grasslands, along with pronghorn, elk and the famous begging burros, descendants of pack animals that stop cars to beg for food. The bison are wild and dangerous; keep your distance.

Sylvan Lake, at the start of the Needles Highway, is a small lake surrounded by granite boulders, with a swimming area and a trail around the shore. It is a beautiful spot, especially in the early morning.

Crazy Horse Memorial, north of Custer, is a giant sculpture of the Lakota leader being carved out of a mountain, a project begun in 1948 and still far from finished. Mount Rushmore is a short ride further.

This is slow riding by design: tight bends, single-lane tunnels where you may wait your turn, and bison or burros standing in the road as if they own it, which they do. A park entrance fee applies. In early August the Sturgis rally brings hundreds of thousands of riders to the Black Hills, and the byway becomes a slow parade. Custer is the place for fuel and a motel bed, and its main street of old false-fronted buildings has a few decent diners.
t.near kraaifontein@-33.8,18.6:
Kraaifontein lies on Cape Town's northern edge, where the suburbs give way to wheat fields, vineyards and the first ranges of the Boland. Its name means crow's fountain, a reminder of a time when this was a farm with a spring rather than a busy suburb on the N1. For riders, it is the threshold between the city and the Winelands.

From here, a short ride takes you into some of the most celebrated countryside in South Africa. Durbanville's wine valley is just to the west, with cellars on rolling hills. To the east, the R304 and other roads lead towards Stellenbosch and Paarl, with the great granite dome of Paarl Mountain standing over the vineyards. Beyond lies Franschhoek, founded by French Huguenot refugees in the late seventeenth century, and the Franschhoek Pass, which climbs in sweeping bends over the mountains with views back over the valley.

Roads around Kraaifontein are generally good, but traffic is heavy in the urban belt and minibus taxis stop unpredictably. Keep alert at intersections and traffic lights, keep valuables out of sight and avoid stopping in isolated places after dark, as you would anywhere in a big city. The wind deserves respect too: the south-easter, known locally as the Cape Doctor, can blow ferociously in summer, especially on exposed stretches and passes.

Fuel stations are plentiful along the main roads, usually attended, and it is customary to tip the attendant. Malls and coffee shops abound. In the Winelands, farm stalls sell biltong, fresh bread and fruit, and many wine estates have restaurants. From Kraaifontein the scenery only improves, so fill the tank, grab a coffee and head for the mountains.
t.near hodonice@48.9,16.2:
Hodonice lies in the vineyards and fields just east of Znojmo, in the southernmost corner of Moravia, a few kilometres from the Austrian border. The village is small and quiet, with a church and rows of houses, but the surrounding landscape is one of the most famous wine regions of the Czech Republic. The Znojmo area produces crisp white wines, and the cellars in the villages are often open for tasting.

Znojmo itself, a short ride away, is a lovely old town perched above the gorge of the Dyje river. Its castle complex includes a Romanesque rotunda with remarkable wall paintings, and beneath the town lies a labyrinth of medieval cellars and tunnels. Znojmo is also famous across the Czech Republic for its pickled gherkins, a speciality since the sixteenth century. To the west lies the Podyjí National Park, where the Dyje has carved a deep, wooded valley along the border, matched on the Austrian side by the Thayatal park.

The riding around Hodonice is gentle and pleasant. Roads wind through vineyards and fields, with long views over the rolling countryside. The surfaces can be variable, and the villages often have narrow streets and sharp corners. Traffic is light, but be careful of tractors and cyclists, especially on weekends. The climate is warm and dry, and summer can be hot.

Hodonice has limited services, so for fuel and supplies head to Znojmo, which has everything you need. A stop at a local wine cellar is a classic experience, but leave the tasting for when the riding is done. After this stop the ride crosses into Austria and heads towards the Neusiedler See, Central Europe's great steppe lake.
t.near japons@48.7,15.5:
Japons lies on the high granite plateau of the Waldviertel, the forest quarter of Lower Austria, north-west of Vienna, a land of rolling hills, fields, forests and scattered villages, where the climate is harsher and the pace slower than in the Danube valley below. The village is small and quiet, with a church and farms, and the surrounding landscape is open and airy, with long views over the plateau.

The Waldviertel is known for its castles, monasteries and quiet roads. A short ride east lies Horn, a pleasant market town, and beyond it the baroque Altenburg Abbey, with a magnificent library and frescoes. The Rosenburg, a Renaissance castle on a rock above the Kamp valley, hosts falconry displays in its tournament courtyard. The Kamp itself winds through a deep, wooded valley with reservoirs, a lovely ride with curves and views.

As for the riding, it is excellent. The roads roll over the plateau and plunge into the valleys, with gentle curves, good surfaces and very little traffic. The landscape changes constantly, from open fields to dense forests and rocky valleys. The weather can be cooler and windier than in Vienna, and in winter, snow is common. In spring and autumn, fog can sit in the valleys.

The nearest dependable fuel and food are in Horn, which has everything you need; Japons is a place to look, not to shop. The Waldviertel is known for its potatoes, poppy seeds and carp, and local inns serve hearty dishes such as roast pork with dumplings, Waldviertel style. Hohe Wand and Puchberg lie far to the south, beyond the Danube and Vienna.
t.petronell carnuntum@48.1,16.9:
Marcus Aurelius is said to have written part of his Meditations at Carnuntum, while campaigning against the Germanic tribes across the Danube in the second century. The city was then the capital of the Roman province of Upper Pannonia, a sprawling legionary fortress and civilian town of tens of thousands of people on the frontier of the empire. Today, the village of Petronell-Carnuntum sits on part of the site, and the archaeological park has reconstructed a Roman quarter with houses, baths and streets, built using ancient techniques, a remarkable way to imagine life on the frontier.

The most striking monument is the Heidentor, the heathens' gate, a massive ruined arch standing alone in the fields south of the village, built in the fourth century, possibly to commemorate a victory. It is a haunting sight, especially in the evening light. The amphitheatres and the museum in nearby Bad Deutsch-Altenburg complete the picture of a great Roman city.

The landscape here is the Danube floodplain, protected as the Donau-Auen National Park, one of the last large wetland forests in central Europe, with side arms, gravel banks and dense riparian woods. The riding is flat and relaxed, with roads along the river and through the fields and villages. Traffic can be heavy on the main road towards Bratislava, and wind is common on the open plain.

Fuel and food are most easily found in Hainburg an der Donau or Bruck an der Leitha. Hainburg has impressive medieval walls and gates and a castle ruin on the hill above the river. A visit to the Roman sites and a meal in a local Heuriger, a wine tavern, make a satisfying day. The Neusiedler See lies to the south.
t.near wilhelmsburg@48.1,15.5:
Porcelain with a lily trademark was once found in almost every Austrian kitchen, and much of it came from Wilhelmsburg, a small industrial town in the Traisen valley south of St. Pölten. The Lilien porcelain works were famous for their simple, practical designs, and the town has a museum devoted to the history of ceramics. Today, Wilhelmsburg is a quiet place, with a church and old factory buildings, set in a valley of meadows and forests.

The Traisen flows north from the Alps to the Danube, and its valley is a gateway to the mountains of the Mostviertel and the Pre-Alps. A short ride south lies Lilienfeld Abbey, the largest Cistercian monastery in Austria, with a magnificent church and cloister. Beyond it, the roads climb into the mountains towards Mariazell, the great pilgrimage town of Austria, through forests and over passes. To the north, St. Pölten, the capital of Lower Austria, has a baroque old centre and a modern government quarter.

The riding here is excellent. The roads follow the valley and climb into the hills and mountains, with curves, gradients and views. The roads towards Mariazell and the Annaberg are classics, with tight bends and steep climbs. Traffic is moderate, but the roads can be busy on weekends, and the weather in the mountains can change quickly. Watch for gravel and for cyclists.

Wilhelmsburg has fuel, shops and inns, making it a good stop. A Mostviertel speciality is pear cider, Most, and the local inns serve hearty Austrian dishes, such as Wiener Schnitzel and roast pork. The Neusiedler See lies to the east, beyond Vienna.
t.bad sauerbrunn@47.8,16.3:
Bad Sauerbrunn is named after its acidic mineral spring, which has been used for healing since the nineteenth century, and it remains one of the smaller spa towns of Austria. It lies in northern Burgenland, at the foot of the Rosalia hills, a wooded range that marks the border between Lower Austria and Burgenland. The town is quiet and green, with villas, parks and a spa centre, and it has an air of gentle relaxation.

The Rosalia hills are a pleasant surprise in this region of plains and vineyards. Covered in forests of beech, oak and chestnut, they rise above the surrounding countryside, with views over the Vienna basin to the north and the plains of Hungary to the east. Forchtenstein Castle, the great fortress of the Esterházy family, stands on a spur of the hills, housing a treasure chamber and an armoury. In the Middle Ages, this border region was contested between Austria and Hungary, and Burgenland only became part of Austria in 1921.

On the bike, things are a pleasure. The roads climb into the Rosalia hills, with curves, gradients and views, and wind through the vineyards and villages of the plain. Traffic is light on the minor roads, but the main roads towards Vienna and Wiener Neustadt can be busy. The weather is generally mild and sunny, with hot summers, and wind can be strong on the plain.

Bad Sauerbrunn has a few shops and restaurants, and fuel is easily found in Mattersburg or Wiener Neustadt. A visit to Forchtenstein Castle and a meal in a local wine tavern make a satisfying day. The Neusiedler See lies to the east, with its reed beds and wide views.
t.near sopron@47.7,16.5:
Sopron calls itself the most loyal town, Civitas Fidelissima, because in 1921, when the region was being handed from Hungary to Austria after the First World War, its people voted in a plebiscite to remain Hungarian. The town became a Hungarian peninsula reaching into Austria, and its medieval centre, with the Firewatch Tower rising above the old walls, is one of the best-preserved in the country. The tower offers sweeping views over the rooftops and the surrounding hills.

Sopron has another claim to history. In August 1989, at a meadow near the border, a Pan-European Picnic was organised by opposition groups, and during the event a border gate was opened for a few hours. Hundreds of East Germans, holidaying in Hungary, rushed through to Austria, one of the first cracks in the Iron Curtain, a few months before the Berlin Wall fell. A memorial park marks the spot today.

The high ground around Sopron is the Lővér hills, the foothills of the Alps, covered in forests of oak, beech and chestnut, with walking trails, lookout towers and villas. To the east, the land drops to the Fertő, the Hungarian part of the Neusiedler See, with reed beds and vineyards. The riding is varied, with winding roads through the hills and flat roads across the plain. Traffic can be heavy at the border crossings, and the roads in Hungary may have different speed limits and rules.

Sopron has plenty of fuel stations, shops and restaurants, and fuel is often cheaper than in Austria. Hungarian motorways require an electronic vignette, so plan accordingly. A meal of Hungarian dishes, such as goulash or paprika chicken, with a glass of local Kékfrankos later, rounds off the day.
t.asparn an der zaya@48.6,16.5:
Asparn an der Zaya is the kind of Weinviertel village you could ride through in forty seconds and never suspect it holds one of Austria's best windows onto the deep past. The old castle in the middle of the village houses MAMUZ, the museum of prehistory for Lower Austria, and behind it an open-air area of reconstructed houses from the Stone Age to the Iron Age. If you have ever wondered who lived on these loess hills before the vineyards, this is where to find out.

The landscape is quietly beautiful rather than dramatic. The Zaya is a small river winding east through a wide, gentle valley, and around it the Weinviertel rolls away in long waves of vines, sunflowers and wheat. Cellar lanes, the Kellergassen, cut into the hillsides on the edge of many villages: rows of little pressing houses with doors set into the loess, where wine was made and stored for centuries. On a warm evening the light goes golden over the fields and the whole region seems to slow down.

For riding, think open, flowing back roads rather than hairpins. The lanes between Mistelbach, Asparn and the villages north towards the Czech border are lightly trafficked, mostly decent tarmac, with crests and long bends that let you settle into a rhythm. Watch for farm machinery in harvest season and for gravel carried onto corners from field tracks. Wind can be a factor here; this is open country with little shelter.

As a start and finish, it works well. Mistelbach is only a few minutes away and is the local market town, with fuel, shops and places to eat. Vienna is roughly an hour south, which makes Asparn a calm place to begin or end a longer day towards the Alps, away from the city's traffic. If the museum is open when you pass, give it an hour; otherwise a slow lap of the village and a look at the castle walls is a fine way to bookend the ride.
t.dogashima@34.8,138.8:
Dogashima is the finish, and it earns it. On the western coast of the Izu Peninsula, the sea has carved the soft volcanic rock into a scatter of small islands, arches and stacks, with pale cliffs dropping into water that turns from emerald to deep blue. A short boat trip runs out to a sea cave called Tensodo, whose ceiling has a hole that lets light fall onto the water, and at low tide a sandbar appears between the shore and a nearby island, letting people walk across on the sea floor.

The scenery is the product of volcanic ash laid down under water and then lifted and eroded, which is why the rock is light, layered and easy for waves to shape. Along the coast the cliffs of Sandanbeki, a short drive away, add a darker drama in the form of columnar basalt. Sunset is the moment people come for here: the sun sinks into Suruga Bay, with Mount Fuji sometimes visible in silhouette across the water, and the whole shoreline turns orange.

Reaching this far-western stretch means a long ride along the coastal road, with curves that follow the cliffs, small fishing harbours and views that open and close between headlands. The road is not fast, but it is rewarding, and traffic is light outside holidays. It can be wet and misty, especially in the rainy season and when a typhoon is passing offshore, and the sun glare at the end of the day can be fierce, so a clean visor is worth carrying.

The nearest town of any size is Shimoda, about nineteen kilometres to the south, and it is the sensible place to plan fuel and a bed, although small inns and shops can be found locally. Seafood here is fresh: sea bream, squid, and the local specialties of the Izu coast, with dried fish and seaweed on sale in the harbour shops. Sit by the water with a drink, watch the boats go out and the light go down, and let the day's ride settle quietly.
t.near kraaifontein@-33.9,18.8:
Kraaifontein lies on Cape Town's northern edge, where the suburbs give way to wheat fields, vineyards and the first ranges of the Boland. Its name means crow's fountain, a reminder of a time when this was a farm with a spring rather than a busy suburb on the N1. For riders, it is the threshold between the city and the Winelands.

From here, a short ride takes you into some of the most celebrated countryside in South Africa. Durbanville's wine valley is just to the west, with cellars on rolling hills. To the east, the R304 and other roads lead towards Stellenbosch and Paarl, with the great granite dome of Paarl Mountain standing over the vineyards. Beyond lies Franschhoek, founded by French Huguenot refugees in the late seventeenth century, and the Franschhoek Pass, which climbs in sweeping bends over the mountains with views back over the valley.

Roads around Kraaifontein are generally good, but traffic is heavy in the urban belt and minibus taxis stop unpredictably. Keep alert at intersections and traffic lights, keep valuables out of sight and avoid stopping in isolated places after dark, as you would anywhere in a big city. The wind deserves respect too: the south-easter, known locally as the Cape Doctor, can blow ferociously in summer, especially on exposed stretches and passes.

Fuel stations are plentiful along the main roads, usually attended, and it is customary to tip the attendant. Malls and coffee shops abound. In the Winelands, farm stalls sell biltong, fresh bread and fruit, and many wine estates have restaurants. From Kraaifontein the scenery only improves, so fill the tank, grab a coffee and head for the mountains.
t.near constantia@-34.1,18.3:
The wooded eastern flank of Table Mountain rises right above this point, a few kilometres from Constantia, where the southern suburbs meet the forests and the mountain. This is Cape Town's green side: oak avenues, pine and gum plantations, old estates and the cool, shaded slopes that catch the clouds when the southeaster blows. Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden lies along the same slope, and on its terraces you can walk among proteas, ericas and other plants of the Cape Floral Kingdom with the mountain towering overhead.

The roads here wind through the trees. Rhodes Drive runs along the mountain from Constantia Nek past Kirstenbosch toward Newlands, a narrow, curving road shaded by old trees, with glimpses of the mountain through the branches. It is slow, often busy and shared with cyclists, but beautiful, especially in the early morning light. The forests of Cecilia and Newlands have walking trails up toward the mountain, and the air smells of pine, damp earth and fynbos.

The rides from here head east into the winelands and beyond. The Franschhoek Pass ride takes you through Stellenbosch and Franschhoek, the valley settled by French Huguenot refugees in the late seventeenth century, whose names still appear on many of the wine farms. The pass climbs out of the valley on a road said to follow an old elephant trail, with tight bends and spectacular views back down over the vineyards. Clarence Drive is the coastal road from Gordon's Bay to Kleinmond, clinging to the mountains above False Bay, where whales can be seen in winter and spring.

The weather shapes everything. In summer the southeaster blows hard and the tablecloth of cloud spills over the mountain, while winter fronts bring heavy rain and cold. The best riding months are often spring and autumn, when the air is clear and the light is golden. Bush fires are a real danger in the hot, dry months, and roads may be closed when they flare up.

For fuel, food and supplies, Constantia's shopping centres are close, and there are cafes at Kirstenbosch and in the nearby suburbs. Leave yourself time for a walk in the garden or the forest; it is one of the most peaceful places in the city, and a fine way to begin or end a long ride into the mountains.
There the Rockies rise in a long blue wall, with Longs Peak standing out as a notched summit above the rest, and on a clear morning the contrast between the field in front of you and the peaks behind is sharp. Campion is a small, quiet community; Berthoud, about six kilometres away, is a small town of some six thousand people with a historic main street.

Berthoud takes its name from Edward Berthoud, a railroad surveyor and engineer who explored the passes of the Colorado Rockies in the 1860s, and who also gave his name to the high pass on US 40 above Winter Park. The surrounding land is irrigated cropland, with fields of corn, wheat and sugar beets, and the Little Thompson River winds quietly through cottonwoods. Loveland, a bit farther north, is known for its sculpture and for its Valentine's Day postmark.

For a rider, this is the doorstep to the mountains. US 34 runs from Loveland up the Big Thompson Canyon to Estes Park, a beautiful, winding road squeezed between granite cliffs and a rushing river, which was devastated by a flash flood in 1976 and again in 2013. It is a road for caution: tight, shaded, and prone to rockfalls. Colorado 7 and 66 give alternatives into the high country. The plains roads here are dead straight, grid-like, and fast, with the wind blowing hard across the open country, often from the west.

Fuel is easy in Berthoud and Loveland. The weather here can change rapidly: summer afternoons bring thunderstorms off the mountains, often with hail, while spring may bring sudden snow. Early mornings are the best time, with the sun low and the peaks sharp, and the air cold and clear. Set out before the traffic begins, fill the tank, and head west toward the canyons, with the whole range ahead of you.
t.skalica on the way back@48.8,17.2:
The border here is the Morava river, which runs through flat meadows and woods, and it forms part of the frontier of the Záhorie, a region of sandy plains and pine forests between the Small Carpathians and Moravia. Until 1993 this was not an international border at all, since Czechs and Slovaks lived in a single state, and the crossing is now invisible, a bridge and a sign.

The town is known for a sweet, a spiral pastry called trdelník, baked over an open fire and rolled in sugar and walnuts, which has become famous across central Europe as a tourist treat. The version made in Skalica has protected status in the European Union, and bakeries around the main square sell it hot. The square itself is pleasant, with a Baroque church, a plague column and a Romanesque rotunda dedicated to Saint George, one of the oldest buildings in the region.

The land around is wine country too, and Skalica has its own small vineyard area, though it is better known for its Moravian neighbours across the river. The Baťa Canal, a navigable waterway built in the twentieth century by the Czech shoe magnate, runs close by on the other side, and boats and cyclists use it. For a swim, small lakes and gravel pits around the town offer bathing in summer, and the water is mild.

Riding here is easy, with flat roads through farmland and forest, mostly in good condition. Slovakia uses the euro, and fuel is generally priced a little lower than in Austria. Motorways require an electronic vignette, so buy one online before using them. The towns are well supplied with stations and shops, and Skalica has several. The nearest big city is Bratislava, about eighty kilometres south. Late summer is the best season, when the vineyards are heavy with grapes and the evenings are warm.
t.near stellenbosch@-34.0,18.8:
Stellenbosch is the second-oldest European settlement in South Africa, founded in 1679 by the governor Simon van der Stel, who named it after himself and his wife's family, and it has the look of a town that has been carefully looked after. Oak trees line the streets, white Cape Dutch houses with curved gables stand behind them, and the mountains rise on every side, purple at dusk. It is also a university town, home to the Afrikaans-speaking Stellenbosch University, which gives the centre a young, lively atmosphere.

The wine country surrounds it, and the roads out are among the loveliest in the Western Cape. Head east on the R310 up the Helshoogte Pass toward Franschhoek, a village founded by French Huguenot refugees in the late seventeenth century, and the road climbs through vineyards and pine plantations, with views over the valley as it twists around bends. Other options include the Jonkershoek valley, a quiet dead-end valley full of fynbos, and the long loop over Sir Lowry's Pass to the coast. Traffic can be heavy on weekends and in the harvest season, and the Cape's winter, from June to August, is cold and wet, so spring and autumn are best.

The nearby mountains are part of the Cape Floral Region, a World Heritage site that covers a tiny fraction of Africa and contains an astonishing share of its plant species. Fynbos, the heathland of proteas, ericas and restios, grows on the poor sandy soils and is bright with flowers in the late winter and spring. Baboons live on the slopes, and you may meet them on the passes, where they are wise to steal food from open bike luggage. Wine is the other great crop. The Cape's Mediterranean climate suits grapes, with Pinotage, a South African cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut, as the signature red, and Chenin Blanc as the pride of the whites. Many estates offer tastings, though a motorcyclist should obviously treat them with great caution.

Practical matters are easy, and the town has fuel stations, repair shops and every kind of lodging. Drive carefully through the town centre, where students, cyclists and delivery vans share narrow streets, and park in guarded areas. Paarl, farther north-east, and Kraaifontein, close to Cape Town, are the bigger towns nearby. Take sun protection in summer, because the valley can be hot, and lunch at a vineyard restaurant is a wonderful way to spend a long afternoon.
t.near atlantis@-33.5,18.5:
Atlantis is not a postcard town, and nobody here pretends it is. It was built from scratch in the 1970s on the sandy plains north of Cape Town, part of the apartheid government's plan to move coloured families out of the city and to create an industrial centre far from the suburbs. The result was a planned town of factories, schools and housing estates, some forty-five kilometres from the city, which still struggles with unemployment and crime. It is worth understanding that history as you ride through.

What the area offers is landscape. Around the town lie the Atlantis dunes, a great sea of white sand that has been used for sandboarding, quad biking and, of course, filming. The flat sandveld here is covered in tough, low scrub, part of the fynbos and strandveld vegetation of the West Coast, and in late winter and spring, roughly August and September, the plains burst into colour as wild flowers bloom after the rain.

Just north of Atlantis lies Mamre, an old Moravian mission village founded in the early nineteenth century, with whitewashed thatched cottages, a church and a mill, one of the most charming places on this coast. To the west lies the coast itself, with Silwerstroomstrand and other beaches where the Atlantic is cold, clear and sometimes rough, fed by the Benguela Current from the Antarctic. The Koeberg nuclear power station, the only one in Africa, stands on the coast to the south.

The rides from here are straight and open rather than curvy. The R27, the West Coast road, runs north toward Langebaan and the West Coast National Park with long straight stretches, while the R307 heads inland toward Darling and Malmesbury, through wheat fields and vineyards. Wind is the main challenge, especially in summer when the southeaster blows hard and the sand can drift onto the road. For the Clarence Drive and Bainskloof rides, the route leads back south and east, past Cape Town toward the mountains.

Atlantis has fuel, supermarkets and fast food, and it is a sensible place to fill up before heading north or into the hills. Stick to the main roads and busy places, keep your bike in sight, and avoid wandering into residential areas. For a calmer stop, ride to Mamre or the coast, where a picnic with a view of the ocean is a better reward.
