t.near spitz@48.4,15.4:
Spitz stands at the western end of the Wachau, where the Danube bends and the valley opens out a little. It is a small town in name and in size, about thirteen hundred people, but it carries itself like a place that has always known its worth. Painted houses front the main street, a medieval gate called the Rotes Tor stands at one end, and above the town the ruin of the Hinterhaus castle looks down from a wooded crag.

Behind the town, a vineyard called the Tausendeimerberg, the thousand-bucket hill, rises in a spectacular set of terraces. It is said to be the largest single vineyard terrace in Austria, and the name refers to the harvest it could produce in a good year, a thousand Eimer, an old measure of wine. Walking among the vines in September, with the grapes heavy and the wasps lazy, is a quiet pleasure. The wines from Spitz have a reputation for crisp, mineral Rieslings, and local cooperatives and family estates are happy to pour a glass.

A small passenger ferry crosses the river here, linking Spitz with the village of Arnsdorf on the south bank, and it is a delightful way to see the Danube at water level. The river is wide, slow and brown, and the barges and cruise ships pass at a stately pace. On the south side, the road runs through orchards and small villages, so a loop crossing the river by ferry and returning over a bridge makes a good short ride.

The riding on the B3 is calm and agreeable. It is a road to be enjoyed at an unhurried pace, with slow, wide bends and views of terraced slopes above the river, and in spring the apricot blossom adds a touch of pink. Weekend traffic is heavy, with convoys of cyclists and tour coaches, so a weekday is better, and a morning start gives you cool air and good light.

For fuel, Spitz may have limited options, so Krems, about fourteen kilometres away, is the more certain stop. In the town, a small bakery or cafe will serve you a Marillenkuchen, apricot cake, made with the local fruit, which is exactly what a rider needs before the long run back down the river.
t.near retreat@-34.2,18.5:
Retreat sits on the flat land between the mountains of the Cape Peninsula and the sandy plains that run down to False Bay, a busy, working suburb on Main Road and the railway line south of the city. It is no beauty spot, but it lies right at the foot of some of the finest short rides in Cape Town, and its petrol stations and shops are useful when you are about to climb into the hills or head out along the coast.

The road that makes Retreat worth knowing is Ou Kaapse Weg, the M64, which starts in nearby Tokai and climbs steeply over the mountains to Noordhoek and the Atlantic side. It is a proper mountain road, with long sweepers, tight bends near the top and wide views back over the southern suburbs and False Bay. At the summit you ride through the Silvermine section of Table Mountain National Park, with fynbos on every side, and the descent to Noordhoek reveals the long white beach of Long Beach and the cliffs of Chapman's Peak. The road is popular, policed and occasionally closed for fires or accidents, so ride it with respect.

The other good option is Boyes Drive, which hangs on the mountainside above Muizenberg and Kalk Bay, with False Bay below, surfers in the water and, in winter and spring, the chance of whales offshore. Muizenberg itself, with its colourful beach huts, was where Cecil Rhodes had his cottage, and the coast road south leads through Kalk Bay, a fishing harbour with good fish and chips, to Simon's Town and the penguins at Boulders.

Nature here is fynbos country, part of the Cape Floral Kingdom, the smallest and richest of the world's plant kingdoms, with proteas, ericas and restios that flower at different times of year. Tokai Forest, near Retreat, has old plantations and walking trails, and the Steenberg and Constantia wine farms are just to the west.

The weather matters. Summer brings the southeaster, which can blow riders around on the flats and over Ou Kaapse Weg, while winter fronts bring rain and low cloud on the mountains. For the long rides to the Cederberg or Clarence Drive, you head out onto the M5 and the N2 or N7. Retreat has fuel and supermarkets, which makes it a sensible place to fill the tank and grab water before the long road out.
t.near purkersdorf@48.2,16.2:
Purkersdorf sits at the eastern edge of the Wienerwald, where the Vienna Woods roll down into the city, and it is the last stop before the motorway delivers you back to Vienna. The town follows the narrow valley of the Wien river, and the hills around are covered with beech forest, meadows and small villages, a landscape of gentle curves and green shade.

The town has one great building. The Sanatorium Purkersdorf, designed by Josef Hoffmann in 1904, was one of the first buildings of modern architecture, a white, cubic structure with geometric details that broke with the ornament of the past. It was a key work of the Wiener Werkstätte, and it still stands, restored, on the edge of town.

For riders, the Wienerwald offers some of the best roads near Vienna. The Riederberg, on the B1 between Gablitz and Sieghartskirchen, is a long, winding climb through forest, popular with bikers on weekends. Small roads lead to Mauerbach, with its old Carthusian monastery, and over the hills to the Danube. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for cyclists, wildlife and police checks.

The forests are home to deer, boar and a rich variety of birds, and in autumn the beech woods turn gold and copper. The Wienerwald is a UNESCO biosphere reserve, protecting a landscape that has inspired Viennese composers and painters for centuries.

Before the city takes you back, look for a green bush or a wreath hung over a doorway: in this part of Austria it means a Heuriger is open, serving the producer's own young wine with bread, cold meats and cheese. One small glass, a long plate, and the last kilometres into Vienna feel shorter.
t.near perchtoldsdorf@48.1,16.2:
Perchtoldsdorf lies on the very edge of Vienna, where the city's southern suburbs meet the first hills of the Vienna Woods, and it has the relaxed atmosphere of a wine village rather than a suburb. The hills behind the town are covered in vineyards, and the old streets are lined with Heurigen, the traditional wine taverns where producers serve their own new wine with simple cold food. When a Heuriger is open, it hangs a bunch of pine branches over the door, a sign that has been used for centuries.

The town's history has a darker side. Its massive defensive tower, the Wehrturm, rising next to the parish church, was built in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries to protect against Ottoman raids. In 1683, during the second Ottoman siege of Vienna, the people of Perchtoldsdorf were massacred after surrendering to Ottoman troops, an event still remembered in the town. In more peaceful times, the composer Hugo Wolf lived and worked here, and his house is now a small memorial.

As a starting point for rides south and east, Perchtoldsdorf is excellent. It sits right at the start of the Thermenlinie, the line of wine villages and spa towns that runs south along the edge of the Vienna Woods towards Baden, and the roads through the vineyards and into the woods are pleasant, with gentle curves and views over the Vienna basin. Further afield, the rides head east to the Neusiedler See, a vast, shallow steppe lake on the Hungarian border, or west to the lakes and mountains of the Salzkammergut.

There is fuel and food in Perchtoldsdorf and the neighbouring towns, and the coffee houses in the centre are a civilised place to start the day. Traffic in the Vienna area can be heavy, especially on weekday mornings, so it pays to leave early. At the end of a long ride, sitting in a Heuriger garden with a glass of local white wine, under the chestnut trees, watching the sun set over the vineyards, is a very Viennese way to finish.
t.near soboth@46.7,15.0:
Soboth sits on a high wooded pass in the south-west corner of Styria, close to the Carinthian border, where the long ridge of the Koralpe sinks into a broad saddle and the road crosses from one province to another. It is a spread-out settlement more than a village, with farms, a church and a lake, the Sobother Stausee, a reservoir held by a dam in the forest, whose dark water reflects the spruce on its banks. The road tops out at well over a thousand metres, and the air is cool and smells of resin, with mist hanging in the hollows on summer mornings.

The surrounding country is a landscape of forest and pasture, wide and thinly populated, with timber and farming the main livelihood. Close by, on the Slovenian side, the little towns of Dravograd and Ravne na Koroškem lie in the Drava and Meža valleys, and the border has been open to riders since Slovenia joined the Schengen area, so the roads form natural loops between the two countries. In the Drava valley, Lavamünd is the small town where the Lavant river joins the Drau, with an old stone bridge and a castle above.

For riders, the Soboth road is the reward. The B69 from Eibiswald on the Styrian side climbs in a series of broad curves through spruce woods, with a smooth surface and fine visibility, and drops on the Carinthian side toward Lavamünd in tighter bends with views of the Drau valley opening up. It is a relaxed, flowing road, well suited to a long day in the saddle, and traffic is light, apart from some timber trucks and holiday traffic in August. Rain and fog come quickly, and in winter there can be ice and snow, though it is usually cleared.

A rest at the reservoir, with a view of the water, is a pleasant stop, and the inns around the pass serve simple Styrian and Carinthian dishes such as Käsnudeln, pasta filled with cheese, and dumplings with sauerkraut. The best months are May to October.
t.near guadalajara@20.7,-103.3:
Guadalajara is Mexico's second city in many ways, and the heart of its mariachi and tequila traditions. Mariachi music, the charro horsemanship and the tequila spirit all trace their cultural roots to the state of Jalisco, and the capital is where they come together. The historic centre has big colonial buildings, wide plazas and a cathedral with two towers that were rebuilt after an earthquake in the nineteenth century. Murals by José Clemente Orozco, one of the great Mexican muralists, cover the walls and dome of the Hospicio Cabañas, a vast neoclassical complex that is a UNESCO site.

Tlaquepaque and Zapopan are old towns now absorbed into the metropolis, and each has its own character. Tlaquepaque is known for pottery, glass and handicrafts, with pedestrian streets and open-air restaurants. The city has a reputation for good food, and the torta ahogada, a pork sandwich drowned in spicy sauce, is the local specialty. Birria, a slow-cooked meat stew, is another favourite.

For riders, Guadalajara is both the start and the finish of the road to the tequila country. About an hour northwest, the town of Tequila sits among fields of blue agave, with the volcano of the same name behind it. The agave landscape and the old distilleries in the area are a UNESCO World Heritage site. The road there is mostly a fast highway, with trucks and buses, followed by smaller roads between the plants, rows of spiky blue-grey rosettes stretching to the horizon. Toll roads are well kept, but local roads can have potholes and topes, the sharp speed bumps that appear without much warning.

The metropolitan area has millions of people, and fuel, food and repairs are available everywhere. Out in the country, stations are less frequent, though still regular on the main roads. Pemex, the national brand, has stations along most highways. Be aware that the rainy season runs from June to September, with heavy afternoon storms, and that the city's traffic can be chaotic, with buses, taxis and motorbikes weaving constantly.

Winter and spring bring dry, warm days, and the light on the agave fields in late afternoon is wonderful. Drink the tequila slowly, and not before riding.
t.near ceres@-33.4,19.2:
Ceres is fruit country, and the signs on the road say so, with apples, pears and peaches grown in the high valley of the Warm Bokkeveld. The town lies in a bowl surrounded by the Cape fold mountains, and the name is that of the Roman goddess of agriculture, which suits it. Orchards cover the floor of the basin, packing sheds and juice factories line the edges, and in blossom time in early spring the valley turns white and pink. Around forty thousand people live here, a mixture of farming families and seasonal workers.

Winter is the surprise. The Matroosberg, the high peak that closes the valley to the east, collects snow every year, and when it does, cars arrive from Cape Town to throw snowballs and take photographs, turning a sleepy road into a small traffic jam. This is one of the few places in the Western Cape where the cold is real, with frost on the orchards and ice on the roads in the early hours, so check conditions in July and August.

The riding in is a pleasure. From Wellington, the Bainskloof Pass brings you down through the mountains toward the Breede valley, and from there you approach Ceres through Mitchell's Pass, a narrow cut in the rock engineered in the 1840s. The road bends along the river through a gorge, with the walls rising above you, before opening into the broad, green valley. Heading north, the Gydo Pass climbs steeply out of the basin toward the open Karoo plateau, with views back over orchards and the rows of trees, and the world turns dry and empty.

The town has all the usual services, with fuel stations on the main road, banks, workshops and supermarkets, and Worcester, thirty kilometres south-east and a good deal larger, is the next big centre. The farm stalls along the road sell fresh fruit, juice and dried fruit, and the cafés in town are a good place for pie and coffee. Late summer and autumn bring harvests and the smell of ripe fruit, and the light on the mountains in the late afternoon is excellent. Take warm gear if you are riding in winter, because the evenings are sharp.
t.near grabouw@-34.2,18.9:
Apples built Grabouw. The town lies in the Elgin valley, a high basin in the mountains east of Cape Town, where cool nights, good soil and plentiful water make ideal conditions for fruit. Orchards of apples and pears cover the valley floor and the lower slopes, and in spring the trees are white and pink with blossom. In recent decades vineyards have joined them, producing some of South Africa's best cool-climate wines.

The valley is surrounded by mountains, part of the Kogelberg Biosphere Reserve, one of the richest areas of fynbos in the Cape, with proteas, ericas and restios covering the slopes. The Palmiet River flows through the valley toward the sea, and the Theewaterskloof Dam to the north is one of the largest reservoirs supplying Cape Town's water. Baboons are common on the passes, so keep food out of sight and do not feed them.

The riding into Grabouw is the main attraction. From the west, the N2 climbs Sir Lowry's Pass from Somerset West, a long, steep ascent with sweeping bends and spectacular views back over the Cape Flats, False Bay and Table Mountain. The viewpoint at the top is worth a stop. To the east, the N2 continues over the Houw Hoek Pass, a smaller pass through the mountains toward Bot River and the Overberg. The R321 north to Villiersdorp and the Franschhoek Pass offers a quieter route with curves and views. Wind can be fierce on the passes, especially in summer when the southeaster blows, and fog sometimes rolls over the mountains.

The rides from here go in two directions. The Route 62 and Swartberg ride heads east into the Little Karoo, with its dry landscapes, ostrich farms and the gravel climb of the Swartberg Pass. The West Coast Flower Road heads north to the plains of Namaqualand, where in a good year the spring flowers carpet the land in orange, yellow and purple. Both are long rides, so start early and plan for fuel stops.

Grabouw has fuel, shops and fast food, and the farm stalls along the N2 sell fresh fruit, juice, pies and coffee. Elgin's wine estates offer tastings and lunches with views over the orchards. In spring, when the blossom is out, the valley is at its loveliest, and a slow ride through the orchards with the mountains around you is a pleasure in itself.
